This chapter develops the route from a flight specification to inlet boundary conditions. The atmosphere supplies an optional relation between altitude, pressure and temperature. Gas properties turn Mach number into velocity. A stagnation calculation accounts for ram heating. An inlet model supplies losses or a downstream state. Finally, a chosen capture area converts incoming mass flux into mass flow. Each operation requires its own assumptions.

The reader should be able to reconstruct a resolved flight state, explain which quantities are independently specified, and identify when two superficially similar input routes describe different physical conditions. Chapter 2 supplies the detailed stagnation derivation; Chapter 3 supplies corrected-flow conventions. The calibrated variable-property inlet receives its full treatment in Chapter 27.

4.1 Stations before components

Use station 0 for the undisturbed incoming stream and station 2 for a representative inlet exit or compressor entry. At station 0, distinguish static pressure p0p_0 from total pressure pt0p_{t0}. The subscript 0 identifies a location; it does not itself mean stagnation. Likewise, T0T_0 is the local static temperature and Tt0T_{t0} is the temperature associated with bringing that stream to rest adiabatically without shaft work.

For a calorically perfect ideal gas,

ρ0=p0RT0,a0=γRT0,V0=M0a0. \rho_0=\frac{p_0}{RT_0},\qquad a_0=\sqrt{\gamma RT_0},\qquad V_0=M_0a_0.

These relations require composition through RR, and the heat-capacity model through γ\gamma. Mach number alone does not specify speed. Two streams at the same Mach number and different temperatures have different velocities even when their composition is identical.

An adiabatic inlet without shaft work preserves total enthalpy while dissipative mechanisms increase entropy. Its static pressure may increase as velocity decreases, while total pressure decreases. These statements are compatible: static pressure measures one part of the local state, while total pressure also reflects the stream’s recoverable mechanical potential.

A cycle inlet can be represented by total-pressure recovery without resolving its internal geometry. A flowpath inlet instead needs a downstream static state, velocity and area relationship. The amount of information returned by these two models differs. A recovery factor alone cannot locate shocks, predict boundary-layer separation or determine an exit Mach number.

4.2 Standard atmosphere as a closure

An altitude is a geometric coordinate. It becomes a thermodynamic state only after an atmospheric model has been selected. A standard atmosphere provides a reproducible reference profile; it does not measure the weather encountered by a vehicle.

ThrustOne’s standard-atmosphere helper uses a constant-molecular-weight approximation over geometric altitudes from 0 to 86 km. Its sea-level values are

TSL=288.15K,pSL=101325Pa,R=287.05287Jkg−1K−1. T_{\mathrm{SL}}=288.15\ \mathrm{K},\quad p_{\mathrm{SL}}=101325\ \mathrm{Pa},\quad R=287.05287\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}.

The profile uses geopotential altitude HH internally. With geometric altitude zz and reference Earth radius RE=6356766mR_E=6356766\ \mathrm{m},

H=REzRE+z,z=REHRE−H. H=\frac{R_Ez}{R_E+z},\qquad z=\frac{R_EH}{R_E-H}.

This transformation allows a constant reference gravitational acceleration g0=9.80665ms−2g_0=9.80665\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}} in the hydrostatic equations. Under the corresponding inverse-square gravity approximation,

dHdz=RE2(RE+z)2,g(z)dz=g0dH. \frac{dH}{dz}=\frac{R_E^2}{(R_E+z)^2},\qquad g(z)\,dz=g_0\,dH.

Geometric and geopotential altitude are close near sea level, but their difference grows with height. Layer boundaries below are geopotential values; entering a listed boundary as geometric altitude does not place the calculation exactly on that boundary.

Geopotential layer base, km Base temperature, K Lapse rate, K/km
0 288.15 −6.5
11 216.65 0
20 216.65 +1.0
32 228.65 +2.8
47 270.65 0
51 270.65 −2.8
71 214.65 −2.0

The lapse rate is dT/dHdT/dH, with its sign included. The final layer is used only up to the supported upper boundary. This is a piecewise atmospheric reference, not a promise that constant gas properties or an engine model remain physically adequate throughout the full altitude range.

Hydrostatic pressure in a layer

A stationary atmosphere obeys

dpdH=−ρg0=−pg0RT. \frac{dp}{dH}=-\rho g_0=-\frac{pg_0}{RT}.

Within a layer beginning at HbH_b, write

T=Tb+L(H−Hb). T=T_b+L(H-H_b).

For nonzero lapse rate LL, integration gives

ln⁡ppb=−g0RLln⁡TTb,p=pb(TTb)−g0/(RL). \ln\frac{p}{p_b}=-\frac{g_0}{RL}\ln\frac{T}{T_b},\qquad p=p_b\left(\frac{T}{T_b}\right)^{-g_0/(RL)}.

For an isothermal layer, integrate with T=TbT=T_b:

p=pbexp⁡[−g0(H−Hb)RTb]. p=p_b\exp\left[-\frac{g_0(H-H_b)}{RT_b}\right].

The exponential relation is also the limit of the lapse relation as LL approaches zero. Substituting a zero lapse rate directly into the power-law expression creates a division by zero; the separate expression is part of the model’s definition.

Pressure at a new layer base is inherited from the preceding layer. It is not reset to sea-level pressure. This propagation preserves pressure continuity; the specified base temperatures preserve temperature continuity. The slope of temperature can change abruptly even though temperature itself remains continuous. Consequently, derivatives of downstream quantities may change at layer boundaries without indicating a solver defect.

4.3 Dynamic pressure is not stagnation-pressure rise

Dynamic pressure is defined by

q=12ρ0V02. q=\frac{1}{2}\rho_0V_0^2.

For the constant-property ideal gas above,

q=γ2p0M02. q=\frac{\gamma}{2}p_0M_0^2.

Temperature cancels because density varies inversely with temperature while squared speed at fixed Mach varies directly with temperature. This cancellation is conditional on the selected gas model. With temperature-dependent heat capacities, γ\gamma itself changes with temperature.

The corresponding inversions are

p0=2qγM02,M0=2qγp0. p_0=\frac{2q}{\gamma M_0^2},\qquad M_0=\sqrt{\frac{2q}{\gamma p_0}}.

The first inversion requires nonzero Mach number. At M0=0M_0=0, every finite positive static pressure gives q=0q=0; the pair M0=0,q=0M_0=0,q=0 cannot determine pressure. Positive qq paired with zero Mach is inconsistent. The second inversion is well defined at zero dynamic pressure when static pressure is already known.

Total pressure follows the compressible stagnation relation,

pt0p0=(1+γ−12M02)γ/(γ−1). \frac{p_{t0}}{p_0}= \left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_0^2\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

Expanding this relation for small Mach number gives pt0−p0=q+O(M04)p_{t0}-p_0=q+O(M_0^4). Thus dynamic pressure approximates the stagnation-pressure rise at low Mach number. It is not their exact difference at general Mach number. Using pt0=p0+qp_{t0}=p_0+q at supersonic speed discards the compressible pressure relation even if every other part of the cycle uses it correctly.

Dynamic pressure is useful as a loading coordinate. It does not independently establish a vehicle’s structural limit, thermal limit or engine operability boundary. Those limits require additional models or supplied constraints.

4.4 What each flight input route determines

The generic turbojet flight adapter resolves the following routes before the applicable cycle calculation. This adapter is not a universal input resolver for every engine family; component and dual-spool modes have separate handling.

Route Supplied quantities Resolution
Mach and ambient state M0,T0,p0M_0,T_0,p_0 Retain the supplied ambient state
Altitude and Mach Geometric z,M0z,M_0 Obtain T0,p0T_0,p_0 from the standard atmosphere
Mach and dynamic pressure M0,qM_0,q Compute pressure, invert the standard atmosphere, then obtain standard temperature
Altitude and dynamic pressure Geometric z,qz,q Obtain standard temperature and pressure, then compute Mach

The generic dynamic-pressure routes use γ=1.4\gamma=1.4 to resolve the flight condition. This choice is independent of an editable cold-gas ratio used later in a cycle. Changing a cycle property does not automatically redefine the flight adapter’s dynamic-pressure convention. For a comparison involving a different gas-property model, reconstruct the physical ambient state and velocity consistently rather than assuming that matching labels guarantees identical conditions.

The Mach-and-dynamic-pressure route imposes more than the algebraic pressure relation. It also imposes the standard-atmosphere temperature associated with that pressure. A manually entered ambient temperature is therefore not an independent degree of freedom on this route.

Pressure decreases monotonically through the supported standard atmosphere. The App uses that monotonicity to invert pressure to geometric altitude within its supported interval. A pressure outside that interval cannot be assigned a supported standard altitude. Such rejection does not mean the pressure is thermodynamically impossible; it means the chosen atmospheric closure does not represent it.

The altitude-and-dynamic-pressure route permits zero dynamic pressure and resolves zero Mach. The Mach-and-dynamic-pressure route requires both quantities to be positive because pressure inversion would otherwise be underdetermined or inconsistent. Different boundary behavior follows from the different unknowns.

4.5 Ram heating and inlet recovery

Define the ram temperature ratio

τr=1+γ−12M02. \tau_r=1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_0^2.

Then

Tt0=T0τr,pt0=p0τrγ/(γ−1). T_{t0}=T_0\tau_r,\qquad p_{t0}=p_0\tau_r^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

These are freestream total conditions before an inlet loss is applied. For an adiabatic, no-work constant-property inlet,

Tt2=Tt0,pt2=πdpt0. T_{t2}=T_{t0},\qquad p_{t2}=\pi_d p_{t0}.

Here πd\pi_d is total-pressure recovery. Multiplying static pressure by recovery instead produces the wrong station quantity. Reducing total temperature by the same factor would incorrectly remove energy from an adiabatic inlet.

The current constant-property turbojet cycle forms its nonideal inlet ratio from the supplied recovery factor and an empirical Mach-dependent ram-recovery factor:

πd=πd,suppliedηr(M0), \pi_d=\pi_{d,\mathrm{supplied}}\eta_r(M_0),

ηr(M)={1,M≤1,1−0.075(M−1)1.35,1<M<5,800/(M4+935),M≥5. \begin{gathered} \eta_r(M)= \begin{cases} 1,&M\leq1,\\ 1-0.075(M-1)^{1.35},&1<M<5,\\ 800/(M^4+935),&M\geq5. \end{cases} \end{gathered}

The ideal cycle setting uses an inlet ratio of one. The empirical correlation summarizes a loss allowance for a cycle calculation. It does not compute a particular shock arrangement, spill flow or inlet unstart. Nor should its piecewise join be interpreted as a newly predicted physical discontinuity.

For a fixed-composition ideal gas at unchanged total temperature, the entropy change is

Δs=−Rln⁡πd. \Delta s=-R\ln\pi_d.

Recovery below one therefore corresponds to positive entropy production. This provides a physical interpretation of the loss: the total enthalpy remains available in the energy balance, but less pressure potential remains for subsequent components. It also explains why a compressor pressure ratio must multiply pt2p_{t2}, not the loss-free pt0p_{t0}.

4.6 Capture area and incoming mass flow

For a uniform freestream normal to a capture plane,

ṁa=ρ0V0Ac. \dot m_a=\rho_0V_0A_c.

The area AcA_c belongs to the upstream streamtube entering the engine. It need not equal a geometric inlet lip area under conditions with spillage, external compression or a nonuniform incoming flow. Assigning an area to a calculation is not equivalent to predicting the streamtube that a physical installation captures.

For a steady inlet with no bleed or added mass,

ρ0V0Ac=ρ2V2A2. \rho_0V_0A_c=\rho_2V_2A_2.

Defining contraction ratio as CR=Ac/A2CR=A_c/A_2 gives

CR=ρ2V2ρ0V0,A2=AcCR. CR=\frac{\rho_2V_2}{\rho_0V_0},\qquad A_2=\frac{A_c}{CR}.

This is a continuity statement. It does not independently determine the exit state. Energy, entropy or a loss closure, and an appropriate branch selection are still required.

If an inlet slows the flow, density usually rises through compression; whether the area decreases depends on their combined effect on mass flux. Interpreting a velocity decrease alone as evidence for a larger exit area ignores density. The same warning applies when comparing cold ambient air with heated downstream gas.

A specific-thrust result also does not determine absolute thrust until its normalization and mass flow are established. Use the air-flow basis of the selected engine model. In particular, fuel addition changes downstream mass flow, while bypass engines may distinguish core air from total captured air, as developed in Chapter 1.

4.7 Worked flight-to-inlet calculation

Consider an illustrative constant-property stream at geometric altitude 10,000 m and Mach 2. Use standard air, γ=1.4\gamma=1.4, supplied inlet recovery 0.95, and an independently assigned capture area of 0.20m20.20\ \mathrm{m^2}. This example demonstrates bookkeeping; it does not establish the design of a physical inlet.

First convert altitude:

H=6356766(10000)6356766+10000=9984.2934m. H=\frac{6356766(10000)}{6356766+10000}=9984.2934\ \mathrm{m}.

The state lies in the first atmospheric layer. Consequently,

T0=288.15−0.0065H=223.2521K, T_0=288.15-0.0065H=223.2521\ \mathrm{K},

p0=101325(223.2521288.15)9.80665/(0.0065287.05287)≈26499.87Pa. p_0=101325\left(\frac{223.2521}{288.15}\right)^{9.80665/(0.0065\,287.05287)} \approx26499.87\ \mathrm{Pa}.

Using unrounded intermediate values gives the following chain:

Quantity Result Role
Static density 0.413510 kg/m³ Incoming mass per volume
Speed of sound 299.532 m/s Converts Mach to speed
Flight speed 599.063 m/s Momentum and kinetic energy
Dynamic pressure 74.1996 kPa Loading coordinate
Freestream total temperature 401.854 K Inlet total-energy state
Freestream total pressure 207.347 kPa Loss-free stagnation pressure
Combined inlet recovery 0.878750 0.95×0.9250.95\times0.925
Inlet-exit total pressure 182.206 kPa Compressor boundary pressure
Captured air flow 49.5438 kg/s Based on the assigned capture area

At this Mach number, pt0−p0≈180.847kPap_{t0}-p_0\approx180.847\ \mathrm{kPa}, much greater than q≈74.200kPaq\approx74.200\ \mathrm{kPa}. Their difference is a compressibility effect, not an inlet loss. The inlet loss subsequently reduces total pressure by approximately 25.141 kPa.

The same standard-atmosphere condition can be specified by Mach 2 and the computed dynamic pressure: the algebra gives the original static pressure, and atmospheric inversion returns the original altitude and temperature. Altitude 10,000 m with that dynamic pressure likewise recovers Mach 2. Small differences from entering rounded values are expected.

If corrected mass flow is needed at compressor entry, Chapter 3’s correction must use Tt2T_{t2} and pt2p_{t2}. Using loss-free freestream total pressure would reduce the reported corrected flow and conceal the inlet loss. A reference station is part of the definition of a corrected quantity.

4.8 A nonstandard atmosphere is a different case

Now prescribe T0=250KT_0=250\ \mathrm{K}, p0=20kPap_0=20\ \mathrm{kPa}, and Mach 2 directly, with the same constant gas properties and capture area. The dynamic pressure is

q=1.42(20000)(22)=56000Pa. q=\frac{1.4}{2}(20000)(2^2)=56000\ \mathrm{Pa}.

The speed is approximately 633.935 m/s and the captured mass flow is 35.3348 kg/s. This state is fully specified without assigning a standard altitude.

Entering only Mach 2 and 56 kPa dynamic pressure into the generic atmospheric route recovers 20 kPa static pressure, but it obtains temperature from the standard profile. It therefore does not preserve the independently supplied 250 K state. Equal Mach and dynamic pressure are insufficient to guarantee equal velocity or mass flow when atmospheric temperature is not the same.

At fixed p0p_0, M0M_0, composition and constant γ\gamma,

V0∝T0,ρ0∝T0−1,ṁa∝T0−1/2 V_0\propto\sqrt{T_0},\qquad \rho_0\propto T_0^{-1},\qquad \dot m_a\propto T_0^{-1/2}

for fixed capture area. Warming the stream raises speed but lowers captured flow; dynamic pressure remains unchanged. A study at fixed dynamic pressure therefore does not hold every physically important inlet quantity fixed. State explicitly whether altitude, static pressure, temperature, Mach number or capture area is constrained when interpreting a trend.

4.9 The separate calibrated inlet convention

The calibrated inlet uses frozen variable-property air with nitrogen and oxygen mole fractions 0.79 and 0.21. Its current implementation requires the NASA9 property representation. It computes sound speed and enthalpy from that gas model, rather than treating the generic flight adapter’s constant γ=1.4\gamma=1.4 as a universal convention.

Its altitude routes are bounded to geometric altitudes from 0 to 70 km. In the Mach-and-dynamic-pressure route, it searches altitude using dynamic pressure evaluated with its own gas properties. In the altitude-and-dynamic-pressure route, it derives Mach from the dynamic pressure of a unit-Mach state at that altitude. Both procedures preserve the calibrated model’s property convention.

The inlet solution requires supersonic freestream flow. Its reference condition sets an entropy-loss relation, and that relation is then used with total-enthalpy conservation and continuity to obtain downstream states. A constant loss coefficient calibrated from one reference condition is a modeling assumption, not a measured inlet map spanning every flight condition.

The full calibrated scramjet flowpath additionally requires a supersonic inlet exit. A mathematically available subsonic exit cannot silently replace that required branch. The separate inlet model and the complete engine model therefore have different admissibility conditions.

In that flowpath, the captured air flow is computed from freestream density, Mach, local frozen sound speed and the supplied capture area. Inlet exit area follows from contraction ratio. This arrangement connects absolute geometry to mass flow, but it still does not predict external spillage or aircraft installation effects.

Do not multiply the calibrated inlet’s pressure recovery by the generic turbojet ram correlation merely because both are called inlet recovery. Each belongs to a separate loss closure. Combining them without redefining the model counts losses twice and changes the meaning of the calibration.

4.10 Reading a resolved result

A useful flight-state report identifies the input route, the resolved static state, the property convention, and the inlet closure. An altitude label alone omits the atmospheric assumption. A Mach label alone omits the speed of sound. A pressure label without its static or total qualification omits the energy-state definition.

Before comparing two runs, reconstruct those definitions. The most informative discrepancies are often structural: a standard-temperature substitution, a recovery applied to the wrong pressure, a capture area changed between cases, or a different sound-speed convention. These can alter a comparison even when both numerical solutions have converged accurately.

The chapter’s equations provide a short route from independent inputs to interpretable inlet conditions. They also identify what remains outside the result: weather prediction, installation drag, spillage, internal shock layout and general inlet operability. Later engine chapters build on the resolved state and add only the component closures supported by their particular models.

5. Frozen mixtures and property polynomials

A fixed composition does not imply a fixed heat capacity. A stream can retain the same species proportions while its molecular energy storage changes strongly with temperature. Frozen thermodynamics describes that situation: the composition is prescribed, while enthalpy, heat capacities, entropy, density and sound speed are evaluated at the requested state.

The distinction matters in propulsion because temperature changes can be large. A single heat-capacity ratio may offer a useful simplified cycle, but a more detailed temperature calculation requires integrated property relations. Replacing a constant gamma with a local value in every familiar power law does not perform those integrations.

This chapter develops the property model used by the frozen-gas calculation and shared by several flowpath models. It explains composition normalization, polynomial evaluation, reference energies, entropy of mixing and temperature inversion. Chemical equilibrium changes the composition and is treated in Chapter 6. Finite-rate chemistry changes composition over a specified time or distance and is treated in Chapters 7–8 and 29.

5.1 Specifying composition without specifying batch size

Let nin_i be an amount of species ii, WiW_i its molecular weight in kg/kmol, and n=∑inin=\sum_i n_i. The mole fraction is

xi=nin,∑ixi=1. x_i=\frac{n_i}{n},\qquad \sum_i x_i=1.

All amounts must use a common basis. Their absolute scale is irrelevant to an intensive property calculation: amounts 79 and 21 describe the same mixture as 0.79 and 0.21. The App accepts nonnegative relative molar amounts, merges repeated entries for the same recognized species, and normalizes their sum. At least one amount must be positive. Negative amounts and unknown species do not define an admissible mixture.

The mixture molecular weight follows from total mass divided by total molar amount:

W¯=∑iniWi∑ini=∑ixiWi. \overline W=\frac{\sum_i n_iW_i}{\sum_i n_i}=\sum_i x_iW_i.

The mass fraction is therefore

Yi=niWi∑jnjWj=xiWiW¯. Y_i=\frac{n_iW_i}{\sum_jn_jW_j}=\frac{x_iW_i}{\overline W}.

Conversely, supplied mass fractions imply

xi=Yi/Wi∑jYj/Wj,W¯=(∑iYiWi)−1. x_i=\frac{Y_i/W_i}{\sum_jY_j/W_j},\qquad \overline W=\left(\sum_i\frac{Y_i}{W_i}\right)^{-1}.

These transformations explain why mass percentages cannot be entered unchanged in a molar-composition field. The error becomes especially large when light hydrogen is mixed with heavier species. Normalization only makes the entries sum to one; it cannot determine that the wrong physical basis was supplied.

A species with exactly zero amount makes no thermodynamic contribution. In the current property calculation, recognized zero-amount entries are omitted after normalization, including from the active temperature-range intersection. An unknown species name is still rejected even if its entered amount is zero. This separates a valid absent component from an unrecognized component definition.

5.2 Molar and mass-specific quantities

Use an overbar for a molar quantity, such as h¯i\overline h_i in J/kmol. Unbarred hh denotes J/kg. The universal gas constant in the App is

Ru=8314.46261815324Jkmol−1K−1. R_u=8314.46261815324\ \mathrm{J\,kmol^{-1}K^{-1}}.

The mixture mass-specific gas constant is

R=RuW¯. R=\frac{R_u}{\overline W}.

For an ideal mixture with frozen composition,

c¯p=∑ixic¯p,i,h¯=∑ixih¯i, \overline c_p=\sum_i x_i\overline c_{p,i},\qquad \overline h=\sum_i x_i\overline h_i,

cp=c¯pW¯=∑iYicp,i,h=h¯W¯=∑iYihi. c_p=\frac{\overline c_p}{\overline W}=\sum_iY_ic_{p,i},\qquad h=\frac{\overline h}{\overline W}=\sum_iY_ih_i.

Either molar or mass-weighted expressions are valid when the weights and property units match. A mole-weighted sum of species values already expressed in J/kg generally gives the wrong mixture value.

The ideal-gas relation is p=ρRTp=\rho RT. Since h=u+RTh=u+RT and composition is fixed,

cv=cp−R,γ=cpcv,ρ=pRT,af=γRT. c_v=c_p-R,\qquad \gamma=\frac{c_p}{c_v},\qquad \rho=\frac{p}{RT},\qquad a_f=\sqrt{\gamma RT}.

The subscript on afa_f identifies frozen sound speed. The thermal response used in this derivative holds species proportions fixed. An equilibrium acoustic response can include composition changes and need not equal the frozen response. Likewise, the heat capacity of an equilibrium path is not obtained merely by evaluating frozen heat capacities at its current composition: the changing species amounts also contribute to the energy derivative.

Within this ideal frozen model, pressure changes density and entropy but does not change enthalpy or heat capacity at a fixed temperature. Real-gas pressure dependence, liquid phases and condensation are outside the property calculation.

5.3 NASA9: one heat-capacity fit and two integration constants

A property record consists of a temperature interval, a reference pressure and polynomial coefficients. The NASA9 representation can be written with coefficients a1,…,a9a_1,\ldots,a_9:

c¯p∘(T)Ru=a1T−2+a2T−1+a3+a4T+a5T2+a6T3+a7T4. \frac{\overline c_p^{\circ}(T)}{R_u}= a_1T^{-2}+a_2T^{-1}+a_3+a_4T+a_5T^2+a_6T^3+a_7T^4.

The superscript circle denotes the species standard-state function. Temperature is in kelvin; the coefficient units are those required by this expression. Changing the input temperature unit without changing the coefficients destroys the fit.

Enthalpy follows from dh¯/dT=c¯pd\overline h/dT=\overline c_p. Integrating each term gives

h¯∘(T)Ru=−a1T+a2ln⁡T+a3T+a4T22+a5T33+a6T44+a7T55+a8. \frac{\overline h^{\circ}(T)}{R_u}= -\frac{a_1}{T}+a_2\ln T+a_3T+\frac{a_4T^2}{2} +\frac{a_5T^3}{3}+\frac{a_6T^4}{4}+\frac{a_7T^5}{5}+a_8.

Equivalently,

h¯∘(T)RuT=−a1T2+a2ln⁡TT+a3+a4T2+a5T23+a6T34+a7T45+a8T. \frac{\overline h^{\circ}(T)}{R_uT}= -\frac{a_1}{T^2}+\frac{a_2\ln T}{T}+a_3+\frac{a_4T}{2} +\frac{a_5T^2}{3}+\frac{a_6T^3}{4}+\frac{a_7T^4}{5}+\frac{a_8}{T}.

At fixed reference pressure, ds¯∘/dT=c¯p∘/Td\overline s^{\circ}/dT=\overline c_p^{\circ}/T. Integrating once more yields

s¯∘(T)Ru=−a12T2−a2T+a3ln⁡T+a4T+a5T22+a6T33+a7T44+a9. \frac{\overline s^{\circ}(T)}{R_u}= -\frac{a_1}{2T^2}-\frac{a_2}{T}+a_3\ln T+a_4T +\frac{a_5T^2}{2}+\frac{a_6T^3}{3}+\frac{a_7T^4}{4}+a_9.

The logarithms use the temperature convention of the fitted coefficients. The integration constants carry the selected enthalpy and entropy references. They are not optional numerical decorations. Deleting a8a_8 preserves the derivative dh¯/dTd\overline h/dT while changing chemical energy differences; deleting a9a_9 preserves the entropy derivative while changing chemical potentials.

The representation contains nine coefficients because seven terms describe heat capacity and two constants establish the integrated reference states. It does not mean that heat capacity is a ninth-degree polynomial. The inverse powers and logarithms are essential parts of the representation.

Each interval has its own complete coefficient set. The current NASA9 records use a lower interval from 200 to 1000 K and an upper interval from 1000 to 6000 K; the upper set is selected at exactly 1000 K. Coefficient changes approximate the same species functions across a broad range. Small fit inconsistencies at a join should not be interpreted as a phase transition, nor should a polynomial be extended past its recorded upper limit simply because it still returns a number.

5.4 NASA7 and database consistency

The hydrogen–oxygen mechanism uses NASA7 records. With coefficients b1,…,b7b_1,\ldots,b_7, its heat capacity is

c¯p∘Ru=b1+b2T+b3T2+b4T3+b5T4. \frac{\overline c_p^{\circ}}{R_u}=b_1+b_2T+b_3T^2+b_4T^3+b_5T^4.

The integrated functions are

h¯∘RuT=b1+b2T2+b3T23+b4T34+b5T45+b6T, \frac{\overline h^{\circ}}{R_uT}=b_1+\frac{b_2T}{2}+\frac{b_3T^2}{3} +\frac{b_4T^3}{4}+\frac{b_5T^4}{5}+\frac{b_6}{T},

s¯∘Ru=b1ln⁡T+b2T+b3T22+b4T33+b5T44+b7. \frac{\overline s^{\circ}}{R_u}=b_1\ln T+b_2T+\frac{b_3T^2}{2} +\frac{b_4T^3}{3}+\frac{b_5T^4}{4}+b_7.

The App evaluates these through the same algebraic representation by placing two zero coefficients before the seven NASA7 coefficients. This is an exact embedding of the NASA7 functional form, not a refit and not a conversion to a different physical dataset.

Property set Included species Recorded pressure reference Temperature qualifications
General NASA9 set Ar, CH4, CO, CO2, H, H2, H2O, N, N2, NO, O, O2, OH 100,000 Pa 200–6000 K for the included records
Hydrogen–oxygen NASA7 set Ar, H, H2, H2O, H2O2, HO2, N2, O, O2, OH 101,325 Pa Reactive species: 200–3500 K; Ar and N2: 300–5000 K

A database choice changes more than the number of coefficients. It changes the available species, fitted functions, reference conventions and valid intervals. The standalone frozen-property mode uses the general NASA9 set. The NASA7 set is associated with the supported hydrogen–oxygen mechanism where selected; it is not an arbitrary replacement for every model’s property data. In particular, calibrated inlet/engine calculations require their NASA9 convention.

No single common range covers every imaginable mixture. For an actual set of active species, the usable interval is

Tmin=maxiTmin⁡,i,Tmax=miniTmax⁡,i. T_{\min}=\max_iT_{\min,i},\qquad T_{\max}=\min_iT_{\max,i}.

For example, an active NASA7 mixture of H2, O2 and N2 is restricted to 300–3500 K. Pure H2 in that database has a 200 K lower boundary; adding positive N2 narrows it to 300 K. A later reacting calculation may need species that were absent initially, so its admissible domain must account for its own species requirements. An initial-mixture property range alone does not guarantee that an entire reactive trajectory is supported.

5.5 Ideal mixing entropy and the pressure term

For ideal gases, each species contributes entropy at its partial pressure pi=xipp_i=x_ip:

s¯(T,p,𝒙)=∑ixi[s¯i∘(T)−Ruln(xippi∘)]. \overline s(T,p,\boldsymbol{x})= \sum_i x_i\left[\overline s_i^{\circ}(T) -R_u\ln\left(\frac{x_ip}{p_i^{\circ}}\right)\right].

The reference pressure pi∘p_i^{\circ} must match the species record. When every record shares one reference pressure p∘p^{\circ}, this separates into

s¯=∑ixis¯i∘(T)−Ru∑ixiln⁡xi−Ruln⁡(p/p∘). \overline s=\sum_i x_i\overline s_i^{\circ}(T) -R_u\sum_i x_i\ln x_i-R_u\ln(p/p^{\circ}).

The middle term is the ideal entropy of mixing. It is nonnegative because every nonzero mole fraction is at most one. The last term represents the pressure effect: isothermal compression reduces entropy. The mass-specific value is s=s¯/W¯s=\overline s/\overline W.

For fixed composition between two states,

s2−s1=∫T1T2cp(T)TdT−Rln⁡p2p1. s_2-s_1=\int_{T_1}^{T_2}\frac{c_p(T)}{T}\,dT -R\ln\frac{p_2}{p_1}.

The mixing term cancels because composition is unchanged. It must remain when comparing different compositions, such as in a mixing or equilibrium calculation. Removing it because it cancels along one frozen path would corrupt those other problems.

A zero mole fraction contributes the limiting value xln⁡x→0x\ln x\to0. The implementation omits zero components and splits the logarithm into ln⁡xi+ln⁡(p/pi∘)\ln x_i+\ln(p/p_i^{\circ}) for active species. This avoids forming a tiny partial-pressure product that could underflow before taking a logarithm. It does not remove the physical mixing term or turn a trace species into a finite concentration floor.

Changing the reference pressure also requires changing the standard-state entropy convention if the physical entropy is to stay unchanged. Retaining the old entropy coefficients while substituting a new pressure reference shifts the result. This is why the difference between 1 bar and 1 atmosphere belongs in the property definition, even when its numerical effect seems modest.

5.6 Formation enthalpy and sensible heating

A species enthalpy can be expressed schematically as

h¯i(T)=Δfh¯i∘(Tr)+∫TrTc¯p,i(ϑ)dϑ, \overline h_i(T)=\Delta_f\overline h_i^{\circ}(T_r) +\int_{T_r}^{T}\overline c_{p,i}(\vartheta)\,d\vartheta,

with the reference temperature and elemental conventions consistent with the dataset. The polynomial integration constant carries that reference information. Species with negative formation enthalpy can have negative enthalpy over part of the supported range. Negative enthalpy is not negative temperature and does not itself make the state invalid.

For a frozen stream of unchanged composition, the reference contribution cancels from h2−h1h_2-h_1. This is why a constant-cp approximation can sometimes reproduce a temperature rise even when it uses a different zero of enthalpy. In a reacting stream, however, species amounts change. The difference between product and reactant formation terms is then part of the energy balance.

If the energy equation already uses formation-inclusive species enthalpies, adding a fuel heating value as a second chemical-energy source counts reaction energy twice. A heating-value cycle and a formation-enthalpy chemistry calculation are different accounting formulations. Each can be meaningful, but their terms cannot be combined casually.

Similarly, a supplied total enthalpy

ht=h(T,𝒙)+V22 h_t=h(T,\boldsymbol{x})+\frac{V^2}{2}

uses the same enthalpy reference as the property model. A numerical value previously formed as cpT+V2/2c_pT+V^2/2 is not automatically transferable. The reference offset affects an absolute target even when it has no effect on a frozen temperature difference. This point is particularly important for the state-reconstruction modes developed in Chapter 26.

5.7 Inverting an enthalpy or entropy target

The direct property problem supplies temperature and pressure. The enthalpy inversion instead supplies composition, pressure and a mass-specific enthalpy target, and seeks temperature from

f(T)=h(T,𝒙)−htarget=0. f(T)=h(T,\boldsymbol{x})-h_{\mathrm{target}}=0.

For an admissible frozen ideal gas, dh/dT=cp>0dh/dT=c_p>0. Enthalpy is therefore increasing within the supported fit intervals. The App brackets the calculation by the common temperature range, evaluates its endpoint enthalpies, and rejects a target outside them. It then uses bounded bisection to locate the temperature. Its finite iteration count is a numerical procedure, not a statement that the fitted thermodynamic data have that many digits of physical accuracy.

Pressure remains a required positive input for the reported state, even though ideal-gas enthalpy at fixed composition does not depend on it. A pressure change should affect the returned density and entropy, not the temperature recovered from a fixed enthalpy target.

The shared property layer also supports entropy inversion at a supplied pressure. The derivative (∂s/∂T)p=cp/T(\partial s/\partial T)_p=c_p/T is positive over an admissible positive-temperature range, so the same bracketing reasoning applies. Unlike enthalpy inversion, changing the specified pressure generally changes the temperature required to recover the same entropy.

A target outside the bracket does not authorize extrapolation. It may indicate an incorrect unit, an incompatible enthalpy reference, or a real physical state outside the available data. These cases have different engineering meanings, even if all produce a refusal to return an extrapolated temperature.

5.8 Worked composition and entropy example

Consider 79 relative molar units of N2 and 21 of O2 in the general database. Their molecular weights are 28.0134 and 31.9988 kg/kmol. Normalization gives xN2=0.79x_{N2}=0.79 and xO2=0.21x_{O2}=0.21, followed by

W¯=0.79(28.0134)+0.21(31.9988)=28.850334kg/kmol. \overline W=0.79(28.0134)+0.21(31.9988)=28.850334\ \mathrm{kg/kmol}.

The mass fractions and gas constant are

YN2=0.76708249,YO2=0.23291751,R=288.19294Jkg−1K−1. \begin{gathered} Y_{N2}=0.76708249,\\ Y_{O2}=0.23291751,\\ R=288.19294\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}. \end{gathered}

Thus 21% oxygen by moles corresponds to approximately 23.29% by mass. The gas constant differs from the standard-atmosphere value in Chapter 4 because this explicit binary mixture has a different molecular-weight definition. The difference should be retained when moving between these models.

The ideal mixing contribution is

smix=−R[0.79ln⁡0.79+0.21ln⁡0.21]=148.1187Jkg−1K−1. s_{\mathrm{mix}}=-R[0.79\ln0.79+0.21\ln0.21] =148.1187\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}.

This is the mixing contribution, not the complete entropy of the gas. The species standard-state entropies and the pressure term are still required for the complete value.

If pressure is doubled at unchanged temperature and composition,

Δs=−Rln⁡2=−199.7601Jkg−1K−1. \Delta s=-R\ln2=-199.7601\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}}.

Density doubles, while enthalpy, heat capacities and frozen sound speed remain unchanged. This contrasting case separates the ideal pressure effect from temperature and composition effects without requiring a second polynomial evaluation.

5.9 Worked property and inverse example

Argon provides a transparent example in the lower NASA9 interval. Its recorded coefficients reduce to c¯p/Ru=2.5\overline c_p/R_u=2.5, and the enthalpy integration constant gives

R=208.1321372Jkg−1K−1,cp=520.3303431Jkg−1K−1, R=208.1321372\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}},\quad c_p=520.3303431\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}},

h=cp(T−298.15K),γ=5/3. h=c_p(T-298.15\ \mathrm{K}),\qquad \gamma=5/3.

At 600 K and 150 kPa the direct calculation yields

Quantity Illustrative value
Enthalpy 157.061714 kJ/kg
Constant-volume heat capacity 312.198206 J/(kg K)
Density 1.201160 kg/m³
Frozen sound speed 456.215012 m/s

For the inverse calculation, supply h=157061.714J/kgh=157061.714\ \mathrm{J/kg}, the same pure composition and a positive pressure. The analytical lower-interval inverse is

T=298.15+h520.3303431≈600K. T=298.15+\frac{h}{520.3303431}\approx600\ \mathrm{K}.

The App uses its general bracketed property inversion rather than an argon-specific shortcut. The simple analytical result makes the unit and reference convention visible: entering 157.061714 as J/kg would describe a state close to the enthalpy reference temperature, not 600 K.

Heating this gas from 600 to 900 K requires an enthalpy rise of approximately 156.099103 kJ/kg. Isentropically doubling its pressure from the 600 K state instead gives

cpln⁡(T2/600)=Rln⁡2,T2=60020.4=791.704746K. c_p\ln(T_2/600)=R\ln2,\qquad T_2=600\,2^{0.4}=791.704746\ \mathrm{K}.

Both calculations remain within the lower interval, where the constant-cp reduction is exact for the recorded fit. That reduction must not be generalized to every species or temperature interval. A variable-cp mixture requires the integrated functions developed above.

5.10 From a property result to a flow model

The standalone Frozen Composition · Variable-Specific-Heat Properties mode evaluates the prescribed composition directly or recovers temperature from its enthalpy target. Its returned molecular weight, gas constant, heat capacities, gamma, enthalpy, entropy, density and sound speed describe one thermodynamic state. It does not predict whether the mixture would react, how fast it would react, or which composition would be in equilibrium.

A frozen nozzle adds mass continuity, total-enthalpy conservation and an entropy or loss condition. A frozen component adds a particular efficiency or pressure closure. A reacting flowpath instead updates species amounts while maintaining its energy and momentum conventions. The property model supplies constitutive values to those equations; it does not supply the missing component closure.

When reading a result, retain the composition basis, database, reference pressure, enthalpy convention and supported temperature interval alongside the displayed temperature and pressure. Those definitions allow the number to be reused correctly. The later thermochemistry and flowpath chapters rely on this same distinction between a local property evaluation and the physical process that connects two states.

6. Gas-phase equilibrium

A chemical-equilibrium calculation determines a composition compatible with a specified thermodynamic constraint and a conserved elemental inventory. It does not merely balance one reaction equation. It compares all admissible compositions within the selected species set and finds the state with no remaining thermodynamic tendency to change along an allowed reaction direction.

ThrustOne provides two related problems. The temperature–pressure mode fixes temperature and pressure, then determines composition. The constant-pressure energy mode fixes pressure and the incoming enthalpy plus supplied heat, then determines both temperature and composition. Their common chemical model is an ideal gas with a bounded set of 13 species. A converged result is equilibrium within that set; it does not establish that the set contains every important real species or phase.

Chapter 5 developed the formation-inclusive enthalpy and ideal mixing entropy used here. This chapter adds elemental constraints, chemical potentials and the energy closure. Reaction rates and residence times enter later chapters, not this equilibrium calculation.

6.1 The inventory that reactions cannot change

Let nin_i be the amount of species ii, and let AkiA_{ki} count atoms of element kk in one molecule of that species. The elemental inventory is

bk=∑iAkini,𝑨𝒏=𝒃. b_k=\sum_iA_{ki}n_i,\qquad \boldsymbol A\boldsymbol n=\boldsymbol b.

For example, using columns H2, O2, H2O, H, O and OH gives

𝑨=[202101021011], \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol A= \begin{bmatrix} 2&0&2&1&0&1\\ 0&2&1&0&1&1 \end{bmatrix}, \end{gathered}

where the rows are hydrogen and oxygen. An initial amount of 1.2 H2 and 0.7 O2 contains 2.4 hydrogen atom units and 1.4 oxygen atom units. Any admissible equilibrium composition must retain both quantities, regardless of how much water, atomic gas or hydroxyl it contains.

Molecular amount need not be conserved. Dissociating one molecule into two changes total molecular count without changing the elemental inventory or total mass. Consequently, equilibrium mole fractions must be formed from the final total amount N=∑iniN=\sum_i n_i, not from the initial total.

The App derives inventory from the declared initial species. It then admits database species whose constituent elements all have positive inventories. Supplying hydrogen and oxygen does not authorize production of a nitrogen species; nitrogen is absent from that problem. Conversely, a species need not be present initially to appear among the products when its elements are available.

At fixed temperature and pressure, two initial mixtures with the same elemental inventory define the same equilibrium problem. Their chemical preparation history is not an additional constraint. In the energy-closure mode, their incoming enthalpies may differ, so identical inventories alone do not guarantee identical final states.

6.2 What is minimized at fixed temperature and pressure

For a homogeneous ideal gas mixture, the total Gibbs energy is

G=∑iniμi, G=\sum_i n_i\mu_i,

where the chemical potential μi\mu_i is the partial molar Gibbs energy. With a common standard pressure p∘p^{\circ},

μi(T,p,𝒙)=g¯i∘(T)+RuTln⁡(xipp∘),g¯i∘=h¯i∘−Ts¯i∘. \mu_i(T,p,\boldsymbol x)=\overline g_i^{\circ}(T) +R_uT\ln\left(x_i\frac{p}{p^{\circ}}\right), \qquad \overline g_i^{\circ}=\overline h_i^{\circ}-T\overline s_i^{\circ}.

The logarithmic term includes both mixing and pressure. It follows directly from the ideal entropy expression in Chapter 5. Omitting mixing entropy removes the ln⁡xi\ln x_i contribution and changes the composition selected by the calculation.

At fixed TT, pp and elemental inventory, equilibrium minimizes GG over nonnegative species amounts. The imposed temperature implies that heat can be exchanged as needed to maintain that temperature. A TP equilibrium result therefore does not, by itself, predict the temperature of an adiabatic combustor.

For the ideal mixture, the composition-dependent Hessian has quadratic form

δ𝒏T∇2Gδ𝒏=RuT[∑i(δni)2ni−(∑iδni)2N]≥0. \delta\boldsymbol n^T\nabla^2G\,\delta\boldsymbol n =R_uT\left[\sum_i\frac{(\delta n_i)^2}{n_i} -\frac{(\sum_i\delta n_i)^2}{N}\right]\geq0.

The inequality follows from the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. It expresses the convex character of the ideal-mixture problem within its positive domain. The scale direction must still be constrained by inventory; a freely scalable amount is not an independent physical equilibrium branch. This thermodynamic structure is useful, but it does not make finite-precision iteration infallible or make a restricted species set complete.

6.3 Reaction directions and dimensionless equilibrium constants

A reaction direction 𝝂\boldsymbol\nu changes composition through an extent ξ\xi:

𝒏=𝒏(0)+𝝂ξ. \boldsymbol n=\boldsymbol n^{(0)}+\boldsymbol\nu\xi.

Take products as positive and reactants as negative. Element conservation requires 𝑨𝝂=0\boldsymbol A\boldsymbol\nu=0. For an interior equilibrium, differentiation at fixed temperature and pressure gives

dGdξ=∑iνiμi=0. \frac{dG}{d\xi}=\sum_i\nu_i\mu_i=0.

Dividing by RuTR_uT and inserting the chemical potentials yields

∑iνig¯i∘RuT+ln⁡∏i(xipp∘)νi=0. \sum_i\nu_i\frac{\overline g_i^{\circ}}{R_uT} +\ln\prod_i\left(x_i\frac{p}{p^{\circ}}\right)^{\nu_i}=0.

Define the dimensionless reaction quotient and equilibrium constant by

Qp=∏i(xipp∘)νi,Kp(T)=exp⁡[−∑iνig¯i∘(T)RuT]. Q_p=\prod_i\left(x_i\frac{p}{p^{\circ}}\right)^{\nu_i},\qquad K_p(T)=\exp\left[-\sum_i\nu_i\frac{\overline g_i^{\circ}(T)}{R_uT}\right].

Then equilibrium requires Qp=KpQ_p=K_p. A pressure ratio is essential inside this definition. Substituting a numerical pressure in pascals into a formula whose constant assumes atmospheres changes the result whenever Δν=∑iνi≠0\Delta\nu=\sum_i\nu_i\ne0.

For a fixed reaction definition, KpK_p depends on temperature through the standard-state functions. Pressure still affects composition through QpQ_p, even though it does not change Kp(T)K_p(T). At fixed temperature, increasing pressure generally opposes dissociation reactions that increase molecular count. This is a consequence of the pressure exponent, rather than an extra empirical rule imposed on the solver.

The App retains reaction directions to evaluate chemical stationarity after solving for element potentials. Those directions are thermodynamic constraints, not a kinetic mechanism. Redundant directions can check the same equilibrium from different stoichiometric combinations without describing additional reaction rates.

6.4 Positivity, bounds and trace species

For a single reaction, nonnegative species amounts bound its extent:

ξ≥maxνi>0(−ni(0)νi),ξ≤minνi<0(−ni(0)νi). \xi\geq\max_{\nu_i>0}\left(-\frac{n_i^{(0)}}{\nu_i}\right),\qquad \xi\leq\min_{\nu_i<0}\left(-\frac{n_i^{(0)}}{\nu_i}\right).

These inequalities prevent consuming more reactant than is available. In a multireaction system, the feasible set is the intersection of all elemental and nonnegativity constraints; independently pushing each reaction to completion does not generally locate the coupled equilibrium.

Trace species matter because chemical potentials depend on logarithms. A small mole fraction can contribute a large negative ln⁡xi\ln x_i, even while contributing negligibly to bulk molecular weight. Rounding such a value to zero before evaluating chemical affinity can therefore destroy an otherwise balanced equilibrium calculation.

This does not mean every imaginable species must have a positive amount. Species requiring absent elements are excluded first. For the active ideal-gas species set, the numerical method represents positive trace amounts and rejects a solution if necessary amounts fall below its representable range. A printed value that rounds to zero is also different from a mathematically exact zero; reports should preserve sufficient notation to distinguish them.

The general reaction-coordinate routine in the code uses bounded reaction extents and logarithmic endpoint interpolation. The current 13-species gas mode instead uses a coupled element-potential solver. These are different numerical routes to the same ideal equilibrium conditions; the existence of the general routine should not be mistaken for the algorithm driving every gas-equilibrium result.

6.5 Element potentials reduce the coupled problem

Introduce one Lagrange multiplier λk\lambda_k for each active element and minimize

ℒ=G−∑kλk(∑iAkini−bk). \mathcal L=G-\sum_k\lambda_k\left(\sum_iA_{ki}n_i-b_k\right).

Stationarity with respect to an active species amount gives

μi=∑kAkiλk. \mu_i=\sum_kA_{ki}\lambda_k.

Writing ℓk=λk/(RuT)\ell_k=\lambda_k/(R_uT) and gi∘=g¯i∘/(RuT)g_i^{\circ}=\overline g_i^{\circ}/(R_uT), the species mole fractions satisfy

ln⁡xi=∑kAkiℓk−gi∘−ln⁡(p/p∘). \ln x_i=\sum_kA_{ki}\ell_k-g_i^{\circ}-\ln(p/p^{\circ}).

The unknowns are the element potentials plus total molecular amount. They are determined by

N∑iAkixi=bkfor each element,∑ixi=1. N\sum_iA_{ki}x_i=b_k\quad\text{for each element},\qquad \sum_i x_i=1.

This formulation handles species amounts spanning many orders of magnitude without repeatedly subtracting almost exhausted reactant inventories. The implementation normalizes the initial total amount for conditioning, uses logarithmic elemental balances and normalization, and restores the amount scale in the result. It evaluates sums of exponentials with a shifted logarithmic sum to limit overflow and underflow.

Newton-like corrections solve the coupled residual equations. Damping and shorter trial steps are used when an unrestricted step does not reduce the residual. These are numerical safeguards, not combustion efficiencies. The solver has a finite iteration budget and refuses a nonconverged composition rather than returning its last iterate as equilibrium.

Multiplying all initial amounts by a common positive factor leaves the equilibrium mole fractions unchanged, while scaling all final amounts and elemental inventories by the same factor. This scale invariance is a useful interpretation of relative molar inputs. It does not imply that pressure, temperature or the elemental ratios can be rescaled without changing composition.

6.6 What the residuals actually say

Three separate conditions are needed to interpret a computed composition:

Condition Meaning What it does not establish
Element conservation The final atoms match the initial inventory Chemical equilibrium
Mole-fraction normalization and positivity The mixture is a valid composition Correct thermodynamic data
Chemical stationarity Allowed reaction directions have negligible Gibbs derivative Completeness of the species or phase model

The displayed equilibrium residual is the largest absolute dimensionless chemical-potential sum over the active checking directions,

req=maxr|∑iνirμiRuT|. r_{\mathrm{eq}}=\max_r\left|\sum_i\nu_{ir}\frac{\mu_i}{R_uT}\right|.

For one direction this is |ln⁡(Qp/Kp)||\ln(Q_p/K_p)|. Its scale depends on the chosen stoichiometric coefficients: doubling every coefficient doubles this residual even though the equilibrium composition is unchanged. A small residual is therefore a numerical consistency statement for the defined model, not a universal percentage error in every species amount.

The present gas mode requires this affinity residual below 10−810^{-8} and separately checks each positive elemental inventory to a relative tolerance of 10−810^{-8}. Its internal logarithmic closure uses a tighter residual threshold. These tolerances describe acceptance of the numerical equations; they do not imply eight-digit accuracy for real combustion products or property measurements.

An iteration count measures solver work. It is not a reaction time. More iterations do not imply slower chemistry, and a rapidly converged equilibrium does not imply that a flowing combustor has enough residence time to attain it.

6.7 Worked dissociation example with an explicit model boundary

To expose the pressure and extent algebra, consider a hypothetical two-species gas with the single reaction

A2⇌2A. A_2\rightleftharpoons2A.

Assume one initial molar unit of A2A_2, no inert gas, and an illustrative dimensionless Kp=0.16K_p=0.16 at a fixed temperature. This is an analytical teaching model, not a fitted hydrogen or oxygen equilibrium and not a replacement for the App’s 13-species result.

Let α\alpha be the fraction dissociated. Then

nA2=1−α,nA=2α,N=1+α, n_{A_2}=1-\alpha,\quad n_A=2\alpha,\quad N=1+\alpha,

xA2=1−α1+α,xA=2α1+α. x_{A_2}=\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha},\qquad x_A=\frac{2\alpha}{1+\alpha}.

The elemental inventory is 2nA2+nA=22n_{A_2}+n_A=2, independently of α\alpha. The reaction quotient is

Qp=xA2xA2pp∘=4α21−α2pp∘. Q_p=\frac{x_A^2}{x_{A_2}}\frac{p}{p^{\circ}} =\frac{4\alpha^2}{1-\alpha^2}\frac{p}{p^{\circ}}.

Solving Qp=KpQ_p=K_p gives the physical nonnegative root

α=Kp4p/p∘+Kp. \alpha=\sqrt{\frac{K_p}{4p/p^{\circ}+K_p}}.

At p=p∘p=p^{\circ}, α=0.1961161\alpha=0.1961161, while xA=0.3279216x_A=0.3279216. The dissociation fraction and atomic mole fraction are different because dissociation changes total molecular count. Substituting the result back into the quotient gives 0.16, and the atom balance remains exactly two units analytically.

Pressure ratio Dissociation fraction α\alpha Atomic mole fraction xAx_A
0.25 0.3713907 0.5416264
1 0.1961161 0.3279216
4 0.0995037 0.1809975

The pressure trend follows with no temperature change: lower pressure favors the side with more molecules. Adding an inert gas at fixed total pressure would change the partial pressures and this algebra. Holding volume instead of pressure would define a different problem. Neither alteration can be represented by reusing the table unchanged.

6.8 From specified temperature to an energy closure

An adiabatic combustion temperature is unknown. For a constant-pressure process with no shaft work and negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, the mass-specific energy balance is

heq(T,p,𝒃)=hin+q, h_{\mathrm{eq}}(T,p,\boldsymbol b)=h_{\mathrm{in}}+q,

where qq is supplied heat per unit incoming mixture mass. Positive qq adds energy. All species enthalpies use the formation-inclusive convention from Chapter 5.

The App’s HP mode obtains hinh_{\mathrm{in}} from the declared gaseous mixture at one common inlet temperature. At each trial product temperature, it solves TP equilibrium afresh and evaluates the enthalpy of that equilibrium composition. The outer root function is

f(T)=heq(T,p,𝒃)−hin−q. f(T)=h_{\mathrm{eq}}(T,p,\boldsymbol b)-h_{\mathrm{in}}-q.

Thus an HP calculation contains two coupled levels: chemical closure at a trial temperature, and energy closure across temperatures. Evaluating the original frozen composition at every trial temperature would solve a different, nonreacting heating problem.

The declared lower and upper temperatures must bracket the enthalpy target. Both endpoint chemical calculations must succeed. A failed intermediate equilibrium is reported as an energy-root evaluation failure; it is not skipped to construct an apparently smooth enthalpy curve through missing states. The current outer calculation uses bounded bisection and requires an enthalpy residual within the larger of 0.01 J/kg and 10−9|htarget|10^{-9}|h_{\mathrm{target}}|.

With q=0q=0, the calculation is adiabatic gas-phase equilibrium. No extra heating value is added: reaction energy is already encoded in the species reference enthalpies. Liquid injection, vaporization enthalpy and separate inlet-stream temperatures are not implicit features of this standalone closure.

6.9 An energy-closure example that can be reconstructed exactly

Pure argon isolates the HP temperature closure without introducing a chemical-data comparison. Supply pure Ar at 450 K and 200 kPa, with q=130000J/kgq=130000\ \mathrm{J/kg}, and choose a product-temperature bracket of 500–800 K. In the included species set, an inventory containing only argon permits only argon, so its equilibrium mole fraction remains one.

Within this temperature interval, the lower NASA9 argon record gives

cp=520.3303431Jkg−1K−1,h=cp(T−298.15K). c_p=520.3303431\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}K^{-1}},\qquad h=c_p(T-298.15\ \mathrm{K}).

The incoming enthalpy and target are

hin=79012.1626J/kg,htarget=209012.1626J/kg. h_{\mathrm{in}}=79012.1626\ \mathrm{J/kg},\qquad h_{\mathrm{target}}=209012.1626\ \mathrm{J/kg}.

The bracket endpoint enthalpies are approximately 105028.6798 and 261127.7827 J/kg, so they enclose the target. The analytical root is

T=450+130000520.3303431=699.841282K. T=450+\frac{130000}{520.3303431}=699.841282\ \mathrm{K}.

This example demonstrates the same incoming-energy and temperature-bracket definitions used by the HP mode. It does not establish the accuracy of a reactive flame-temperature prediction. In a reacting mixture, dissociation and recombination change the equilibrium enthalpy curve, so replacing the curve with this constant-cp formula would be inappropriate.

The contrast with TP mode is immediate. Specifying pure argon at 699.841282 K and 200 kPa in TP mode reproduces the final composition and properties, but TP mode does not determine that 130 kJ/kg was required to reach it from 450 K. That conclusion uses the inlet state and energy balance.

6.10 Thermal response along equilibrium

The equilibrium mixture’s reported heat capacity is evaluated with its composition frozen at the returned state. If YieqY_i^{\mathrm{eq}} varies with temperature, the total derivative of equilibrium enthalpy at fixed pressure is

dheqdT=∑iYieqcp,i+∑ihidYieqdT. \frac{dh_{\mathrm{eq}}}{dT}= \sum_iY_i^{\mathrm{eq}}c_{p,i} +\sum_i h_i\frac{dY_i^{\mathrm{eq}}}{dT}.

The first term is the frozen mixture heat capacity. The second term represents the energy effect of changing composition. It can be important in dissociation regions and cannot be reconstructed from the displayed frozen gamma alone.

Consequently, an equilibrium result can supply composition and local frozen properties to a downstream frozen nozzle, but a nozzle that remains in equilibrium must repeatedly update composition and enforce its own energy and entropy constraints. Chapter 17 distinguishes those paths. Neither is a finite-rate chemistry prediction merely because the composition differs from the inlet mixture.

6.11 Scope of the two App modes

The TP and HP gas-equilibrium modes use the general NASA9 set: Ar, CH4, CO, CO2, H, H2, H2O, N, N2, NO, O, O2 and OH. They contain no ions, condensed carbon, liquid water or general hydrocarbon species library. Temperature support is bounded by the records and the selected energy-root interval; numerical existence inside a polynomial range does not establish physical adequacy of the omitted-species assumptions.

A carbon-rich mixture can therefore produce a mathematically consistent gas-only result even where condensed carbon would matter in a broader model. A very hot state can likewise require ionization outside the current species set. These are model limitations, not residual failures. The reported conservation and affinity checks cannot detect physics that was never admitted to the calculation.

For a usable interpretation, retain the selected mode, pressure, inventory, species set, and either specified temperature or inlet enthalpy plus supplied heat. Read the equilibrium residual together with the energy residual when applicable. A converged state then has a precise meaning: it solves the declared ideal-gas chemical constraints, and, in HP mode, the declared energy balance. Whether a real engine approaches that state additionally depends on mixing, reaction rates, heat transfer and residence time.

7. Elementary and pressure-dependent rates

Equilibrium identifies a limiting composition; kinetics supplies the speed and direction of local chemical change. A finite-rate model starts from a reaction list, temperature and species concentrations. It returns production and consumption rates that a reactor or flow solver integrates over time or distance. The rate calculation alone does not determine temperature, residence time or the motion of the gas.

This chapter develops the mass-action and pressure-dependent expressions used by ThrustOne. The same rate evaluator supports the constant-temperature reactor and finite-rate flowpaths. Chapter 8 explains the reactor constraint, while Chapter 29 explains spatial transport through a reacting flowpath. Keeping those constraints separate from the reaction law makes a rate coefficient transferable only where its units, species definitions and thermodynamic references remain consistent.

7.1 Reaction progress and species production

Write reaction rr as

∑iνir′Xi⇌∑iνir″Xi,νir=νir″−νir′. \sum_i\nu'_{ir}X_i\rightleftharpoons\sum_i\nu''_{ir}X_i, \qquad \nu_{ir}=\nu''_{ir}-\nu'_{ir}.

Reactant and product coefficients are positive on their respective sides; the net coefficient is positive for net production. Let qrq_r be the net volumetric rate of reaction progress in kmol/(m³ s). The production rate of species ii is

ω̇i=∑rνirqr. \dot\omega_i=\sum_r\nu_{ir}q_r.

The mass source is Wiω̇iW_i\dot\omega_i, in kg/(m³ s). Reaction progress is therefore not the same quantity as the rate of disappearance of an arbitrary reactant: the latter includes that reactant’s stoichiometric coefficient and a sign.

For the illustrative reaction H2+O→H+OH\mathrm{H_2+O\rightarrow H+OH}, one progress unit consumes one unit each of H2 and O and creates one each of H and OH. Hydrogen and oxygen atoms balance separately. Multiplying the net source vector by an element-count row gives zero, so a sum of balanced reactions preserves every element regardless of their instantaneous rates.

The App checks the declared reaction coefficients for element conservation before compiling the rates. It merges repeated terms of the same species on each side and rejects identical net sides. It requires recognized species and positive finite side coefficients. This protects the algebraic inventory; it does not establish that an entered reaction is an experimentally justified elementary step.

7.2 Concentration and reaction order

The concentration convention is

Ci=niV[kmol/m3],Ctot=∑iCi=pRuT. C_i=\frac{n_i}{V}\quad[\mathrm{kmol/m^3}],\qquad C_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_i C_i=\frac{p}{R_uT}.

For an elementary mass-action reaction, the forward progress rate is

qf=kf(T)∏iCiνi′. q_f=k_f(T)\prod_i C_i^{\nu'_i}.

The current implementation uses the entered reactant-side coefficients as reaction orders. It does not provide a separate arbitrary reaction-order field. A globally balanced combustion equation is not automatically an elementary rate law: choosing its stoichiometric coefficients as exponents is a modeling decision that requires kinetic support.

If the total forward order is m=∑iνi′m=\sum_i\nu'_i, the coefficient units are

[kf]=(m3/kmol)m−1s−1. [k_f]=(\mathrm{m^3/kmol})^{m-1}\mathrm{s^{-1}}.

A first-order coefficient has units s−1s^{-1}; a second-order coefficient has units m³/(kmol s). The numerical coefficient changes when the concentration unit changes. For example, numerical concentrations in mol/cm³ are 10−310^{-3} times the corresponding numerical values in kmol/m³. Converting an mm-order coefficient from a mol/cm³ convention to the App’s convention multiplies its numerical value by 10−3(m−1)10^{-3(m-1)}. This follows by converting both the rate and every concentration factor, not by changing a unit label.

For a species with positive order, zero concentration makes that directional rate zero. The reverse rate may still be nonzero if products are present. A negative concentration is not an admissible extension of a fractional power; it is rejected before rate evaluation.

7.3 Modified Arrhenius temperature dependence

The supported temperature law is

kf=ATβexp⁡(−EaRuT). k_f=A T^\beta\exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R_uT}\right).

Temperature is in kelvin, RuR_u is in J/(kmol K), and EaE_a must be in J/kmol. An activation energy stated in J/mol must be multiplied by 1000 before it is paired with this value of RuR_u. The exponent must be dimensionless.

The pre-exponential factor has the coefficient units divided by Kβ^{\beta}. Thus AA does not always have the same dimensions as a conventional first- or second-order rate coefficient. The App’s unit description includes this temperature-power factor.

Taking a logarithm gives

ln⁡kf=ln⁡A+βln⁡T−EaRuT, \ln k_f=\ln A+\beta\ln T-\frac{E_a}{R_uT},

and hence

dln⁡kfdln⁡T=β+EaRuT. \frac{d\ln k_f}{d\ln T}=\beta+\frac{E_a}{R_uT}.

This derivative explains why relatively small temperature changes can strongly affect rates. A fitted negative activation energy is also possible in this representation; it is not automatically an input error. The App requires finite Arrhenius parameters and a nonnegative pre-exponential factor. Whether a particular fit is appropriate over a proposed temperature interval is a separate question.

For two temperatures, a useful comparison is

kf(T2)kf(T1)=(T2T1)βexp⁡[EaRu(1T1−1T2)]. \frac{k_f(T_2)}{k_f(T_1)}= \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^\beta \exp\left[\frac{E_a}{R_u}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right)\right].

The factor AA cancels. This compares coefficients only: if concentrations change with temperature, the full rate changes by additional concentration factors. At fixed pressure, for example, total concentration decreases as temperature rises.

7.4 Reverse rates from thermodynamics

For a reversible mass-action step,

q=qf−qb=kf∏iCiνi′−kb∏iCiνi″. q=q_f-q_b=k_f\prod_iC_i^{\nu'_i}-k_b\prod_iC_i^{\nu''_i}.

At equilibrium the directional rates are equal. Therefore

kfkb=Kc,qquadKc=∏i(Cieq)νi. \frac{k_f}{k_b}=K_c,qquad K_c=\prod_i(C_i^{\mathrm{eq}})^{\nu_i}.

Here KcK_c is the dimensional concentration quotient in the selected concentration units. Chapter 6’s KpK_p is dimensionless. Since pi=CiRuTp_i=C_iR_uT, their relation is

Kc=Kp(p∘RuT)Δν,Δν=∑iνi. K_c=K_p\left(\frac{p^{\circ}}{R_uT}\right)^{\Delta\nu}, \qquad \Delta\nu=\sum_i\nu_i.

The concentration factor has units kmol/m³. It supplies the dimensions needed when the forward and reverse orders differ. Setting kb=kf/Kpk_b=k_f/K_p without this conversion is correct only for the special case Δν=0\Delta\nu=0 under these definitions.

The App obtains Gibbs functions from the selected thermodynamic database and forms

ln⁡Kc=−∑iνig¯i∘RuT+Δνln⁡(p∘RuT). \ln K_c=-\sum_i\nu_i\frac{\overline g_i^{\circ}}{R_uT} +\Delta\nu\ln\left(\frac{p^{\circ}}{R_uT}\right).

It evaluates the species Gibbs functions at a common 100,000 Pa state. The NASA7 records’ own reference pressure is handled inside the property calculation, so this operation includes the required entropy adjustment; it does not simply relabel their coefficient reference pressure. The reverse coefficient then uses the same effective forward coefficient divided by this thermodynamic KcK_c.

This construction enforces thermodynamic consistency for the included reversible steps. It does not prove the accuracy of their forward rates. Multiplying both directional coefficients by the same factor changes relaxation time while preserving their ratio and equilibrium composition.

Near equilibrium, two large directional rates may nearly cancel. The implementation evaluates logarithmic rates and uses an exponential-difference expression based on expm1 to reduce cancellation error. An overflowing rate is rejected rather than interpreted as instantaneous completion. Numerical reformulation expands the range of reliable evaluation; it does not supply a missing stiff integration method.

7.5 Third-body collisions

Some reactions require a collision partner to remove or supply energy. A schematic recombination is

A+B+M⇌AB+M. A+B+M\rightleftharpoons AB+M.

The collider appears unchanged in the net species balance, but its concentration affects the rate. Define

[M]eff=∑iϵiCi, [M]_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_i\epsilon_iC_i,

where ϵi\epsilon_i is the efficiency of species ii as a collider relative to the convention of the rate fit. The forward progress rate for a simple third-body step is

qf=k3(T)[M]eff∏iCiνi′. q_f=k_3(T)[M]_{\mathrm{eff}}\prod_iC_i^{\nu'_i}.

The collider adds one concentration power to the overall rate. Consequently, [k3]=(m3/kmol)m/s[k_3]=(\mathrm{m^3/kmol})^m/\mathrm{s}, before the Arrhenius temperature-power adjustment.

The App uses efficiency one for species not listed in an enabled third-body efficiency map. An explicit zero efficiency removes that species’ collider contribution; it does not remove the species from the mixture. An empty but present efficiency map therefore enables an all-unity collider term, whereas an absent map without falloff leaves an ordinary mass-action coefficient.

Do not add a fictitious database species named M. Collider effects are represented by the efficiency sum. Including a real species on both sides of a reaction introduces its concentration through the side exponents; additionally enabling a third-body term can then count an extra factor unless that is deliberately part of the supplied model.

7.6 Reduced pressure and Lindemann falloff

A falloff reaction transitions between low- and high-pressure rate laws. Let k0(T)k_0(T) be its low-pressure coefficient and k∞(T)k_\infty(T) its high-pressure coefficient. Define the dimensionless reduced pressure

Pr=k0[M]effk∞. P_r=\frac{k_0[M]_{\mathrm{eff}}}{k_\infty}.

The basic Lindemann effective coefficient is

keff=k∞Pr1+Pr. k_{\mathrm{eff}}=k_\infty\frac{P_r}{1+P_r}.

At Pr≪1P_r\ll1, keff≈k0[M]effk_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx k_0[M]_{\mathrm{eff}}. At Pr≫1P_r\gg1, it approaches k∞k_\infty. The low-pressure coefficient therefore has one additional inverse-concentration unit compared with the high-pressure coefficient. Both have independently supplied Arrhenius parameters.

The main reaction parameters represent k∞k_\infty when falloff is enabled; the nested low-pressure parameters represent k0k_0. After forming keffk_{\mathrm{eff}}, the code multiplies by the explicit reactant concentration powers. It does not multiply by the collider sum a second time. The collider is already present through PrP_r.

Reduced pressure is not the physical pressure in pascals. Its value also depends on temperature, mixture efficiencies and the two rate fits. Two gases at the same pressure can occupy different positions on the falloff curve.

7.7 Troe broadening

Troe broadening modifies the transition shape through a factor FF:

keff=k∞Pr1+PrF. k_{\mathrm{eff}}=k_\infty\frac{P_r}{1+P_r}F.

The supported center expression is

Fcent=(1−a)exp⁡(−T/T3)+aexp⁡(−T/T1)+exp⁡(−T2/T), F_{\mathrm{cent}}=(1-a)\exp(-T/T_3)+a\exp(-T/T_1) +\exp(-T_2/T),

where the final term is omitted when T2T_2 is not supplied. The parameter aa lies between zero and one; the characteristic temperatures are positive. This aa is a fit parameter, unrelated to sound speed.

Using base-10 logarithms, define

c=−0.4−0.67log⁡10Fcent,n=0.75−1.27log⁡10Fcent,u=log⁡10Pr+c. \begin{gathered} c=-0.4-0.67\log_{10}F_{\mathrm{cent}},\\ n=0.75-1.27\log_{10}F_{\mathrm{cent}},\\ u=\log_{10}P_r+c. \end{gathered}

The broadening formula is

log⁡10F=log⁡10Fcent1+[u/(n−0.14u)]2. \log_{10}F=\frac{\log_{10}F_{\mathrm{cent}}} {1+[u/(n-0.14u)]^2}.

The implementation evaluates an equivalent scaled form to avoid an unnecessary overflow when the ratio in the denominator becomes large. Its parameters and temperature convention must come from the same rate model as the low- and high-pressure coefficients. Supplying arbitrary valid positive temperatures merely creates a computable curve; it does not calibrate a physical reaction.

The Lindemann factor alone has simple asymptotes. With Troe enabled, the actual coefficient also includes its broadening expression over the fitted domain. Statements about a fitted curve should retain that qualifier rather than assuming that every parameter set behaves like an idealized sketch at unlimited pressure.

7.8 Worked elementary-rate calculation

Consider the balanced step H2 + O → H + OH with illustrative forward parameters

A=2.0×107m3kmol−1s−1K−1/2,β=0.5,Ea=6.0×107J/kmol. \begin{gathered} A=2.0\times10^7\ \mathrm{m^3\,kmol^{-1}s^{-1}K^{-1/2}},\\ \beta=0.5,\\ E_a=6.0\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kmol}. \end{gathered}

These values are chosen for arithmetic demonstration, not as a recommended hydrogen mechanism. At 1000 K,

kf=2.0×1071000exp⁡[−60000000/(8314.462618×1000)]=4.64529×105m3/(kmols). \begin{gathered} k_f=2.0\times10^7\sqrt{1000} \exp[-60000000/(8314.462618\times1000)]\\ =4.64529\times10^5\ \mathrm{m^3/(kmol\,s)}. \end{gathered}

With CH2=0.002C_{H2}=0.002 and CO=0.001kmol/m3C_O=0.001\ \mathrm{kmol/m^3},

qf=kfCH2CO=0.929058kmol/(m3s). q_f=k_fC_{H2}C_O=0.929058\ \mathrm{kmol/(m^3s)}.

For an irreversible step, each reactant source is −0.929058-0.929058 and each product source is +0.929058+0.929058 in the same units. The hydrogen atom source is 2(−qf)+qf+qf=02(-q_f)+q_f+q_f=0, and the oxygen atom source is −qf+qf=0-q_f+q_f=0. Mass conservation follows when the molecular weights use consistent atomic masses.

Raising temperature to 1200 K while holding concentrations fixed multiplies the coefficient and forward rate by approximately 3.646925. Holding pressure and mole fractions fixed instead would also reduce both reactant concentrations by a factor 1000/1200, so the rate ratio would include that factor squared. A temperature-sensitivity statement must identify which quantities are held fixed.

If reversibility is enabled, the net source additionally requires product concentrations and the thermodynamic reverse coefficient. The forward number alone no longer equals the net progress rate.

7.9 Worked collider and falloff comparison

At a selected temperature, suppose a mixture has three collider contributions: 0.003 kmol/m³ with efficiency one, 0.001 kmol/m³ with efficiency two, and 0.002 kmol/m³ with efficiency zero. Then

[M]eff=0.003+2(0.001)+0(0.002)=0.005kmol/m3. [M]_{\mathrm{eff}}=0.003+2(0.001)+0(0.002)=0.005\ \mathrm{kmol/m^3}.

Its total concentration is 0.006 kmol/m³, so replacing the effective collider concentration by total concentration would change the modeled rate.

For an illustrative unimolecular falloff step, take evaluated coefficients k∞=106s−1k_\infty=10^6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} and k0=2×108m3/(kmols)k_0=2\times10^8\ \mathrm{m^3/(kmol\,s)}. The resulting reduced pressure is one, and the Lindemann coefficient is 5×105s−15\times10^5\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}. For reactant concentration 0.0002 kmol/m³, the forward progress rate is 100 kmol/(m³ s). This deliberately rapid example says nothing about whether an explicit time integrator can cover a requested duration economically.

For a Troe comparison at 1000 K, use illustrative a=0.5a=0.5, T3=1000T_3=1000 K, T1=10000T_1=10000 K, and omit T2T_2. Then Fcent=0.63635843F_{\mathrm{cent}}=0.63635843, the supported broadening expression gives F=0.65468982F=0.65468982 at Pr=1P_r=1, and

keff=327344.909s−1. k_{\mathrm{eff}}=327344.909\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.

The forward rate becomes approximately 65.4690 kmol/(m³ s). The change arises from the explicitly selected broadening model. It should not be described as a new collision efficiency or applied again through another multiplier.

7.10 Model inputs, numerical limits and physical meaning

ThrustOne supports 1–50 declared reactions with elementary side-power mass action, reversible rates derived from the chosen thermodynamic data, optional third-body efficiencies, and Lindemann or Troe falloff. A zero main pre-exponential factor disables that reaction. When a collider-dependent coefficient has zero effective collider concentration, it contributes no progress rate. Unsupported or nonfinite rates are refused.

The included hydrogen–oxygen option contains 10 thermodynamic species and 29 reaction entries. It is a bounded mechanism option, not a general hydrocarbon mechanism loader or a complete reacting-flow simulation package. Its thermodynamic data use the NASA7 representation described in Chapter 5. The general demonstration H2 → 2 H with a unit first-order coefficient is an algorithm example and must not be interpreted as calibrated dissociation kinetics.

Rates computed here are local chemical source terms. They omit molecular diffusion, turbulent mixing, heat transfer and transport coefficients. A reaction may be thermodynamically favorable yet remain slow; it may be locally fast yet limited by mixing in a real combustor. Choosing a rate law, computing its source terms and resolving a complete engine are therefore distinct steps. The next chapter supplies one specific time-evolution constraint and explains how to read a completed or interrupted chemical history.

8. Reactor constraints and chemical timescales

A reaction mechanism does not determine a unique temperature or pressure history. Those histories depend on the physical constraints imposed on the reacting mixture. A rigid insulated vessel, a rigid temperature-controlled vessel and a constant-pressure combustor can use the same chemical rates and still produce different trajectories.

ThrustOne’s finite-rate reactor is homogeneous, closed to mass, constant in volume and externally maintained at a specified temperature. It integrates species concentrations and reconstructs pressure from their changing total. It does not integrate an adiabatic temperature rise. This chapter derives that model, explains its numerical stopping behavior, and explains the reported thermostat diagnostic. The energy balance must follow the stated rigid-vessel constraint; a constant-pressure heat load is a different quantity.

8.1 Choose the control boundary first

Take a rigid vessel of volume VV, containing a spatially uniform ideal gas. No mass enters or leaves. Ignore bulk kinetic energy, potential energy, surface reactions and mechanical stirring work. Species can interconvert through the supplied reaction list, while an external thermal boundary maintains a constant temperature TT.

With concentration Ci=ni/VC_i=n_i/V, the species equations are

dCidt=ω̇i(T,𝑪)=∑rνirqr(T,𝑪). \frac{dC_i}{dt}=\dot\omega_i(T,\boldsymbol C) =\sum_r\nu_{ir}q_r(T,\boldsymbol C).

There is no dilution term because volume is fixed, and no inlet or outlet term because the vessel is closed. Chapter 7 supplies the local reaction-rate expressions. An open stirred reactor would require additional mass-exchange terms and a residence-time definition; it is not obtained merely by assigning a longer integration duration here.

A prescribed temperature removes the temperature differential equation from the solved system. The external heat exchange needed to enforce that prescription becomes a diagnostic. For an adiabatic vessel, temperature would instead be an unknown coupled to composition through internal-energy conservation. Those are different mathematical systems.

8.2 Initial pressure sets the concentration scale

Let the entered relative molar amounts be aia_i, with normalized initial fractions xi0=ai/∑jajx_{i0}=a_i/\sum_j a_j. The initial concentrations are

Ci0=xi0p0RuT. C_{i0}=x_{i0}\frac{p_0}{R_uT}.

Thus the relative amounts set composition, while initial pressure and temperature set absolute concentration. Multiplying every relative amount by ten does not increase the physical concentration. Increasing initial pressure at fixed temperature and composition does.

This distinction matters because reaction rates can depend on concentration to different powers. A second-order rate scales quadratically with a uniform concentration increase at an unchanged temperature, while a first-order rate scales linearly. Falloff and collider efficiencies add further dependencies described in Chapter 7.

The reactor does not need a numerical vessel volume to compute concentrations or pressure. Doubling the vessel volume at the same initial state doubles total mass and total heat-transfer rate, but leaves the concentration trajectory and heat-transfer rate per unit volume unchanged. Absolute equipment loads require a separately known volume.

8.3 Pressure can change at constant temperature

At every time,

p(t)=RuT∑iCi(t). p(t)=R_uT\sum_iC_i(t).

Differentiating at constant temperature gives

dpdt=RuT∑iω̇i=RuT∑rΔνrqr. \frac{dp}{dt}=R_uT\sum_i\dot\omega_i =R_uT\sum_r\Delta\nu_r q_r.

Reactions that increase molecular count can raise pressure even though temperature is fixed. Reactions that reduce molecular count can lower it. In a mechanism with several reactions, the net effect is the weighted sum of their progress rates.

Total mass density is different:

ρ=∑iWiCi,dρdt=∑iWiω̇i=0 \rho=\sum_iW_iC_i,\qquad \frac{d\rho}{dt}=\sum_iW_i\dot\omega_i=0
