for balanced reactions and consistent molecular weights. Pressure change therefore does not imply a mass leak. At constant temperature and density, changing mean molecular weight changes the mixture gas constant and hence pressure.

The displayed mole fraction is

xi(t)=Ci(t)∑jCj(t). x_i(t)=\frac{C_i(t)}{\sum_jC_j(t)}.

Its variation reflects both the species concentration and the changing denominator. A mole fraction falling by half does not necessarily mean that half the original amount of that species remains. Use concentration or the analytical inventory relation when reasoning about conversion.

8.4 The thermostat energy balance

For a closed rigid vessel with no other work, the first law is

dUdt=Q̇. \frac{dU}{dt}=\dot Q.

Let positive Q̇\dot Q mean heat added to the gas. Since

UV=∑iCiu¯i(T), \frac{U}{V}=\sum_iC_i\overline u_i(T),

its derivative is

Q̇V=∑iu¯iω̇i+(∑iCic¯v,i)dTdt. \frac{\dot Q}{V}= \sum_i\overline u_i\dot\omega_i +\left(\sum_iC_i\overline c_{v,i}\right)\frac{dT}{dt}.

For the isothermal constraint, dT/dt=0dT/dt=0, so the required volumetric heat-transfer rate is

q̇V=∑iu¯iω̇i. \dot q_V=\sum_i\overline u_i\dot\omega_i.

Formation-inclusive internal energies are required. An exothermic reaction at fixed temperature generally requires heat removal, giving a negative q̇V\dot q_V under this convention. Endothermic dissociation can require positive heat input. No additional fuel heating-value term should be added to the species formation-energy accounting.

For an ideal gas, u¯i=h¯i−RuT\overline u_i=\overline h_i-R_uT. Consequently,

q̇V=∑ih¯iω̇i−RuT∑iω̇i=∑ih¯iω̇i−dpdt. \dot q_V=\sum_i\overline h_i\dot\omega_i -R_uT\sum_i\dot\omega_i =\sum_i\overline h_i\dot\omega_i-\frac{dp}{dt}.

Pressure per time and power per volume have the same dimensions: Pa/s equals W/m³. The correction is nonzero when the net molecular production rate is nonzero.

Interpreting the App thermostat diagnostic

The result named thermostat_heat_rate reports the rigid-vessel heat-transfer rate per unit volume at the final returned state. Define the enthalpy-source sum

Sh=∑ih¯iω̇i. S_h=\sum_i\overline h_i\dot\omega_i.

The reported value is Sh−RuT∑iω̇iS_h-R_uT\sum_i\dot\omega_i, in W/m³. Positive values denote heat supplied to the mixture; negative values denote heat removal. It is an instantaneous final-state rate, not the time-integrated energy supplied during the calculation.

An enthalpy-source sum alone would omit the pressure-production term. That difference matters whenever the reaction changes total molecular amount, even though the vessel volume and temperature are fixed. The diagnostic does not feed back into the concentration integration: the external thermostat imposes temperature independently. Neither a small integration error nor a conserved mass would justify substituting a constant-pressure energy balance for the rigid-vessel balance.

8.5 What an adiabatic calculation would require

Setting heat exchange to zero in the first law gives

dTdt=−∑iu¯iω̇i∑iCic¯v,i. \frac{dT}{dt}=-\frac{\sum_i\overline u_i\dot\omega_i} {\sum_iC_i\overline c_{v,i}}.

Temperature then changes the rates, and the changing rates alter composition and temperature again. This coupling can produce rapid thermal acceleration. It is not present in the externally isothermal reactor.

A constant-temperature species history can reveal kinetic conversion and pressure evolution under thermal control. It cannot show an adiabatic ignition-temperature rise, determine an adiabatic flame temperature or establish heat-release-driven thermal runaway. The HP equilibrium calculation in Chapter 6 solves a limiting energy-constrained state, while an adiabatic finite-rate history would require the coupled differential equation above. Neither is silently activated by selecting a chemical mechanism in the current reactor.

8.6 Chemical timescales and stiffness

For an irreversible first-order loss dC/dt=−kCdC/dt=-kC, the characteristic decay time is τ=1/k\tau=1/k. After one such time, the concentration is e−1e^{-1} of its initial value. For a coupled mechanism, there is usually no single chemical timescale valid for all species and all parts of the trajectory.

A local estimate Ci/|ω̇i|C_i/|\dot\omega_i| can be useful away from zeros, but it becomes misleading near equilibrium: a small net source may result from cancellation between very large directional rates. The linearized source Jacobian then provides fast relaxation scales that are invisible in the small net source alone.

Stiffness arises when fast stable modes constrain an explicit time step much more strongly than the slower evolution of interest would suggest. Tightening a user tolerance does not remove stiffness. Extending the requested duration can increase the number of required steps by orders of magnitude even when the later plotted composition appears nearly flat.

A flow comparison often uses a Damköhler-type ratio Da=τflow/τchemDa=\tau_{\mathrm{flow}}/\tau_{\mathrm{chem}}. Large values suggest chemistry has time to relax relative to the chosen flow scale; small values suggest limited conversion. This is background interpretation, not a universal criterion computed by the homogeneous reactor. A duration is not a combustor residence time until a separate flow and mixing model justifies that correspondence.

8.7 The explicit Heun step

For d𝑪/dt=𝒇(𝑪)d\boldsymbol C/dt=\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol C) at prescribed temperature, the App forms an Euler prediction and a corrected Heun state:

𝒌1=𝒇(𝑪n),𝑪E=𝑪n+Δt𝒌1, \boldsymbol k_1=\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol C_n),\qquad \boldsymbol C_E=\boldsymbol C_n+\Delta t\boldsymbol k_1,

𝒌2=𝒇(𝑪E),𝑪H=𝑪n+Δt2(𝒌1+𝒌2). \boldsymbol k_2=\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol C_E),\qquad \boldsymbol C_H=\boldsymbol C_n+\frac{\Delta t}{2}(\boldsymbol k_1+\boldsymbol k_2).

The predictor–corrector difference supplies a local step-size indicator. The implementation scales each species difference by the largest of its old concentration, corrected concentration and an initial-total-concentration floor:

e=maxi|CH,i−CE,i|max⁡(|Cn,i|,|CH,i|,10−10Ctot,0). e=\max_i\frac{|C_{H,i}-C_{E,i}|} {\max(|C_{n,i}|,|C_{H,i}|,10^{-10}C_{\mathrm{tot},0})}.

The floor prevents vanishing trace species from requiring a meaningless relative error against zero. It does not replace their concentrations with the floor or discard their rates.

If the indicator exceeds the selected tolerance, the attempted step is reduced and retried. Nonfinite or negative predicted or corrected concentrations also cause step reduction. The code does not accept a negative concentration and then clip it to zero; clipping would alter elemental inventories and could conceal a step-size failure.

Accepted steps advance time and update the history. The next step changes within bounded growth or reduction factors. The method remains explicit; adaptivity does not turn it into an implicit stiff solver. A finite local error indicator also does not certify an equally small global error over an arbitrarily long history.

8.8 A reconstructable chemical history

Use the deliberately illustrative irreversible reaction

H2→2H,k=2s−1, \mathrm{H_2\rightarrow2H},\qquad k=2\ \mathrm{s^{-1}},

with pure initial H2 at 1200 K and 80 kPa. This is an algorithm demonstration with a chosen constant rate, not a calibrated hydrogen dissociation mechanism. It differs from the default demonstration coefficient so that the example’s timescale is explicit.

The initial concentration is

C0=800008314.462618(1200)=0.0080181570kmol/m3. C_0=\frac{80000}{8314.462618(1200)}=0.0080181570\ \mathrm{kmol/m^3}.

The exact species solution is

CH2=C0e−kt,CH=2C0(1−e−kt). C_{H2}=C_0e^{-kt},\qquad C_H=2C_0(1-e^{-kt}).

Hence

Ctot=C0(2−e−kt),p=p0(2−e−kt),xH2=e−kt2−e−kt. C_{\mathrm{tot}}=C_0(2-e^{-kt}),\qquad p=p_0(2-e^{-kt}),\qquad x_{H2}=\frac{e^{-kt}}{2-e^{-kt}}.

Time, s H2 concentration, kmol/m³ H mole fraction Pressure, kPa
0 0.00801816 0 80.0000
0.10 0.00656471 0.3069059 94.5015
0.25 0.00486326 0.5647334 111.4775
0.50 0.00294972 0.7746003 130.5696

At 0.50 s, the fraction of original H2 remaining is e−1=0.3678794e^{-1}=0.3678794, while its mole fraction is only 0.2253997. The distinction arises entirely from the increase in molecular count. The hydrogen atom concentration remains 2CH2+CH=2C02C_{H2}+C_H=2C_0, and mass density is unchanged.

The pressure approaches twice its initial value as the imposed one-way reaction exhausts H2. This asymptote is a consequence of the artificial irreversible model. A real reversible mechanism at the same temperature would generally approach a different composition and would require a thermodynamically consistent reverse rate.

For this example, the difference between an enthalpy-source sum and the rigid-vessel thermostat rate is

Sh−q̇V=RuTkCH2=p0ke−kt. S_h-\dot q_V=R_uTkC_{H2}=p_0ke^{-kt}.

It equals approximately 97044.9 W/m³ at 0.25 s. The difference can be computed without knowing the absolute species enthalpies, because it depends only on molecular production and temperature. The App subtracts this pressure-production term. The example demonstrates why the selected energy constraint changes a heat-load calculation even when the species history is identical.

8.9 One step explains the error indicator

For the same first-order loss, normalize the initial reactant concentration to one. A trial step of 0.10 s has kΔt=0.2k\Delta t=0.2. Euler predicts

CE/Cn=1−0.2=0.8, C_E/C_n=1-0.2=0.8,

while Heun gives

CH/Cn=1−0.2+0.222=0.82. C_H/C_n=1-0.2+\frac{0.2^2}{2}=0.82.

The exact exponential factor is 0.81873075. The predictor–corrector difference is 0.02, whereas the Heun error against the exact solution is approximately 0.00126925. The indicator is therefore not numerically identical to the corrected state’s true error.

Halving the step gives Euler 0.9 and Heun 0.905. Their difference falls to 0.005, one quarter of the previous difference, consistent with its leading quadratic dependence on step size. This motivates a square-root step adjustment based on the tolerance ratio. The actual multicomponent calculation takes the largest scaled difference across species and also applies positivity requirements.

These analytical values explain the integration method; they are not a claim that the App uses a fixed 0.10 s step or that every mechanism has this smooth error behavior. In a stiff region, positivity or stability may force much smaller steps.

8.10 Completion, conservation and displayed histories

The requested duration is the target end time. Completion means that accepted integration reaches that time. The App also limits accepted steps and total attempted steps; a sequence of rejected steps can exhaust the attempt budget without advancing the state appreciably. A time step too small to change the floating-point time is another stopping condition.

A returned incomplete history contains the accepted prefix and its actual final time. It must not be read as a prediction at the requested end time. Conversely, completed = 1 means that the integration interval was covered; it does not mean chemical equilibrium was reached. An irreversible example can complete its interval while continuing to react, and a reversible system can be near equilibrium long before the requested duration ends.

The reactor checks final mass density against its initial value and reports a relative mass residual. Balanced sources also imply elemental conservation analytically, but the displayed mass residual alone is not a separate numerical report for every element. A small conservation residual does not establish accurate reaction timing: both an inaccurate and an accurate integrator can preserve a linear invariant.

The plotted history is sampled from accepted states to keep the result manageable, with the final accepted state retained. Plot samples are therefore not a complete record of every numerical step. A straight segment joining samples does not resolve an unrecorded rapid event, and the absence of a narrow feature in the reduced plot is not proof that no such feature occurred.

8.11 Included mechanism and model boundaries

The hydrogen–oxygen option supplies the bounded 10-species, 29-reaction mechanism described in Chapter 7. The current reactor evaluates thermodynamic properties for every species in the selected database at its prescribed temperature. Thus its effective property domain can be narrower than the range of only the initially populated species: the NASA7 mechanism’s common interval is 300–3500 K, while the general NASA9 set spans 200–6000 K. These are data limits, not a claim of mechanism accuracy across the entire interval.

The reactor excludes spatial gradients, diffusion, turbulent mixing, liquid vaporization, wall chemistry and adiabatic thermal feedback. It also does not supply a general stiff integration method. The supported rates and supplied concentrations define a homogeneous kinetic task, and its result must be interpreted within that task.

A useful record retains temperature, initial pressure and composition, mechanism and thermodynamic database, duration, actual returned time, completion status and conservation diagnostic. Interpret the thermostat metric as the final-state rigid-vessel heat-transfer rate derived in Section 8.4. Preserve its sign and volumetric units; multiply by the vessel volume only when an actual total heat-transfer rate is required.

9. Turbojet design-point derivation

A turbojet converts part of the energy added by fuel into compressor work and leaves the remainder available for exhaust acceleration. The turbine is not assigned an independent useful power output in this model: its work is determined by the compressor load and shaft efficiency. The nozzle then converts the remaining total-state potential into jet velocity at a specified exit pressure.

The design-point problem supplies flight conditions, compressor pressure ratio, turbine-entry total temperature, gas properties and component loss parameters. It returns a station chain, fuel–air ratio, exhaust state and thrust normalized by incoming air flow. Optional air mass flow supplies the dimensional scale. It does not select a compressor map operating point or solve a fixed nozzle’s back-pressure response.

This chapter covers the unaugmented constant-property design-point mode. Chapter 10 adds afterburning and distinguishes variable-property cycles. Chapters 11–12 address components and reference-constrained off-design problems.

9.1 Stations and specified quantities

Use stations 2, 3, 4 and 5 for inlet exit, compressor exit, burner exit/turbine entry and turbine exit. Station 9 identifies the nozzle exit. The station table in this App reports total temperature and pressure, including at labels 0 and 9. Static freestream inputs and static nozzle results are separate quantities; a row labeled 9 must not be read as static exit temperature merely because it names the exit plane.

The cold side uses constant cp,cc_{p,c} and γc\gamma_c; the hot side uses constant cp,hc_{p,h} and γh\gamma_h. Their gas constants are derived consistently:

Rc=cp,cγc−1γc,Rh=cp,hγh−1γh. R_c=c_{p,c}\frac{\gamma_c-1}{\gamma_c},\qquad R_h=c_{p,h}\frac{\gamma_h-1}{\gamma_h}.

These are supplied effective gas properties. The cycle does not calculate a species composition or a smooth temperature-dependent heat capacity. Its heating-value energy convention must remain separate from Chapter 5’s formation-inclusive chemistry.

The exit-pressure input is

re=p0p9. r_e=\frac{p_0}{p_9}.

This orientation matters. Values below one mean exit pressure exceeds ambient pressure; values above one mean exit pressure is below ambient. Full expansion corresponds to one. It is not the nozzle total-to-static pressure ratio.

9.2 Inlet total state

From the resolved static freestream state,

a0=γcRcT0,V0=M0a0, a_0=\sqrt{\gamma_cR_cT_0},\qquad V_0=M_0a_0,

τr=1+γc−12M02,πr=τrγc/(γc−1). \tau_r=1+\frac{\gamma_c-1}{2}M_0^2,\qquad \pi_r=\tau_r^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}.

The inlet exit has

Tt2=T0τr,pt2=p0πrπd. T_{t2}=T_0\tau_r,\qquad p_{t2}=p_0\pi_r\pi_d.

Chapter 4 explains how the nonideal cycle combines the supplied inlet recovery with its empirical Mach-dependent recovery factor. The inlet preserves total temperature in this adiabatic no-work approximation, while losing total pressure. Applying recovery to both quantities would incorrectly remove energy.

The inlet calculation does not determine captured mass flow from a lip geometry. Air flow remains an optional supplied dimensional scale in this cycle. Its specific quantities can be computed without a mass-flow value.

9.3 Compressor work and polytropic efficiency

Let πc=pt3/pt2\pi_c=p_{t3}/p_{t2}. For an infinitesimal isentropic compression of a constant-property gas,

dTtsTt=γc−1γcdptpt. \frac{dT_{ts}}{T_t}=\frac{\gamma_c-1}{\gamma_c}\frac{dp_t}{p_t}.

Compressor polytropic efficiency ece_c compares that ideal infinitesimal temperature rise with the actual rise. Integration gives

τc=Tt3Tt2=πc(γc−1)/(γcec). \tau_c=\frac{T_{t3}}{T_{t2}} =\pi_c^{(\gamma_c-1)/(\gamma_ce_c)}.

Therefore

Tt3=Tt2τc,pt3=pt2πc,wc=cp,c(Tt3−Tt2). T_{t3}=T_{t2}\tau_c,\quad p_{t3}=p_{t2}\pi_c,\quad w_c=c_{p,c}(T_{t3}-T_{t2}).

The work wcw_c is per kilogram of incoming air. Lower polytropic efficiency produces a greater temperature rise and more required work for the same pressure ratio.

The corresponding finite pressure-ratio isentropic efficiency is

ηc=πc(γc−1)/γc−1τc−1. \eta_c=\frac{\pi_c^{(\gamma_c-1)/\gamma_c}-1}{\tau_c-1}.

The App’s supplied compressor efficiency in this cycle is polytropic, while the derived ηc\eta_c is an output. They must not be interchanged. At pressure ratio one, compressor work vanishes and the finite-ratio expression becomes a zero-over-zero form; the solver omits that derived efficiency instead of reporting an arbitrary numerical value.

9.4 Burner fuel balance

Let f=ṁf/ṁaf=\dot m_f/\dot m_a, and neglect fuel inlet sensible enthalpy in the heating-value model. With burner efficiency ηb\eta_b and heating value QRQ_R, the nonideal burner energy balance per unit air mass is

cp,cTt3+fηbQR=(1+f)cp,hTt4. c_{p,c}T_{t3}+f\eta_bQ_R=(1+f)c_{p,h}T_{t4}.

The factor 1+f1+f accounts for the fuel mass joining the hot stream. Solving explicitly,

f=cp,hTt4−cp,cTt3ηbQR−cp,hTt4. f=\frac{c_{p,h}T_{t4}-c_{p,c}T_{t3}} {\eta_bQ_R-c_{p,h}T_{t4}}.

A positive numerator requires added energy relative to the compressor outlet. A positive denominator requires that the useful fuel energy exceed the prescribed outgoing enthalpy carried by each additional unit of fuel mass. The solver checks both conditions. An arbitrary turbine-entry temperature is not achievable merely because the field accepts a positive number.

The pressure closure is independently supplied:

pt4=πbpt3. p_{t4}=\pi_b p_{t3}.

Burner pressure loss does not determine burner efficiency or vice versa. One modifies the available expansion pressure; the other modifies fuel required for the specified temperature under the chosen energy model. Neither predicts flame stability, emissions, combustor length or mixing completeness.

Because the hot and cold heat capacities are independently fixed, comparing temperatures alone is not enough to assess the energy-rise requirement. The model compares cp,hTt4c_{p,h}T_{t4} with cp,cTt3c_{p,c}T_{t3}. These effective enthalpy expressions are not a species-resolved chemistry calculation.

9.5 Turbine work closes the shaft

The turbine supplies compressor power through mechanical efficiency ηm\eta_m:

ηm(1+f)cp,h(Tt4−Tt5)=cp,c(Tt3−Tt2). \eta_m(1+f)c_{p,h}(T_{t4}-T_{t5}) =c_{p,c}(T_{t3}-T_{t2}).

Hence

Tt5=Tt4−cp,c(Tt3−Tt2)ηm(1+f)cp,h,τt=Tt5/Tt4. T_{t5}=T_{t4}-\frac{c_{p,c}(T_{t3}-T_{t2})} {\eta_m(1+f)c_{p,h}},\qquad \tau_t=T_{t5}/T_{t4}.

The required temperature drop follows from shaft load, rather than from an independently entered turbine pressure ratio. If the load would require a nonpositive turbine-exit total temperature, the cycle is rejected.

Turbine polytropic efficiency ete_t relates the actual infinitesimal temperature decrease to an isentropic decrease. Integrating gives

τt=πtet(γh−1)/γh,πt=τtγh/[et(γh−1)]. \tau_t=\pi_t^{e_t(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h},\qquad \pi_t=\tau_t^{\gamma_h/[e_t(\gamma_h-1)]}.

The pressure leaving the turbine is pt5=πtpt4p_{t5}=\pi_t p_{t4}. For the same required work and temperature drop, lower turbine efficiency demands a larger pressure drop, leaving less expansion potential for the nozzle.

The derived finite-ratio turbine isentropic efficiency is

ηt=1−τt1−τt1/et. \eta_t=\frac{1-\tau_t}{1-\tau_t^{1/e_t}}.

It is distinct from the input ete_t. Mechanical efficiency is also distinct: it accounts for the fraction of turbine work delivered to the compressor, rather than the thermodynamic pressure cost of producing that work.

9.6 Nozzle expansion at a supplied exit pressure

For the unaugmented cycle,

Tt9=Tt5,pt9=πnpt5. T_{t9}=T_{t5},\qquad p_{t9}=\pi_n p_{t5}.

The supplied πn\pi_n represents total-pressure loss. The remaining expansion is evaluated from total to specified static pressure. Define

NPR=pt9p9=reπrπdπcπbπtπn. NPR=\frac{p_{t9}}{p_9} =r_e\pi_r\pi_d\pi_c\pi_b\pi_t\pi_n.

A positive jet solution requires NPR>1NPR>1. Then

T9=Tt9NPR−(γh−1)/γh, T_9=T_{t9}NPR^{-(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h},

M9=2γh−1[NPR(γh−1)/γh−1],V9=2cp,h(Tt9−T9). M_9=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma_h-1} \left[NPR^{(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h}-1\right]},\qquad V_9=\sqrt{2c_{p,h}(T_{t9}-T_9)}.

The current cycle permits the exit Mach implied by the supplied pressure; it does not cap it at one as a fixed convergent nozzle model would. A supersonic result therefore implies a suitable expansion path within this idealized nozzle closure, not a prediction that a particular convergent nozzle can achieve it.

No exit area is independently imposed to match ambient pressure. The cycle can report an overexpanded or underexpanded pressure contribution, but it does not resolve internal shocks, flow separation or side loads. Those omissions matter when choosing a physically plausible exit-pressure input.

9.7 Thrust and fuel consumption

The uninstalled thrust balance is

F=ṁa[(1+f)V9−V0]+(p9−p0)A9. F=\dot m_a[(1+f)V_9-V_0]+(p_9-p_0)A_9.

Using continuity at the exit,

A9ṁa=1+fρ9V9=(1+f)RhT9p9V9, \frac{A_9}{\dot m_a}=\frac{1+f}{\rho_9V_9} =\frac{(1+f)R_hT_9}{p_9V_9},

so specific thrust becomes

Fs=Fṁa=(1+f)V9−V0+(1+f)RhT9V9(1−re). F_s=\frac{F}{\dot m_a}=(1+f)V_9-V_0 +\frac{(1+f)R_hT_9}{V_9}(1-r_e).

This form eliminates an independently supplied exit area from the thrust expression. The pressure term is positive for re<1r_e<1 and negative for re>1r_e>1. At full expansion it vanishes.

Thrust-specific fuel consumption is

TSFC=ṁfF=fFs, TSFC=\frac{\dot m_f}{F}=\frac{f}{F_s},

in kg/(N s). A numerical value in mg/(N s) is one million times the SI value. If air flow is supplied, F=ṁaFsF=\dot m_aF_s; scaling flow alone leaves the normalized station solution and TSFC unchanged. The App requires positive net specific thrust for this mode rather than reporting a positive fuel-consumption number for a nonpropulsive result.

At full expansion, the kinetic-energy increase per unit air flow is

Δek=(1+f)V92−V022. \Delta e_k=\frac{(1+f)V_9^2-V_0^2}{2}.

The nonideal cycle can report ηth=Δek/(fQR)\eta_{th}=\Delta e_k/(fQ_R) and ηp=V0Fs/Δek\eta_p=V_0F_s/\Delta e_k. Outside full expansion, the current App omits this decomposition because it does not include a corresponding pressure-work term in the kinetic-energy denominator. It retains overall efficiency V0Fs/(fQR)V_0F_s/(fQ_R). Chapter 1 explains the interpretation, including zero propulsive power at zero flight speed despite positive static thrust.

9.8 What the ideal setting changes

The ideal setting is a particular air-standard approximation. It uses cold-side heat capacity and gamma throughout, unit component recoveries and efficiencies, complete expansion, and neglects added fuel mass in turbine work and exhaust momentum. Fuel consumption is still estimated from the heating value:

f=cp(Tt4−Tt3)QR,Tt5=Tt4−(Tt3−Tt2). f=\frac{c_p(T_{t4}-T_{t3})}{Q_R},\qquad T_{t5}=T_{t4}-(T_{t3}-T_{t2}).

Thus enabling ideal mode is not exactly equivalent to setting every loss parameter to one in the nonideal fuel-mass model. The approximation in 1+f1+f and the hot-gas property convention also change. The App requires p0/p9=1p_0/p_9=1 for this ideal cycle.

Using τλ=Tt4/T0\tau_\lambda=T_{t4}/T_0, the ideal full-expansion relations reduce to

T9T0=τλτrτc,V922cpT0=τλ−τr(τc−1)−τλτrτc. \frac{T_9}{T_0}=\frac{\tau_\lambda}{\tau_r\tau_c},\qquad \frac{V_9^2}{2c_pT_0} =\tau_\lambda-\tau_r(\tau_c-1)-\frac{\tau_\lambda}{\tau_r\tau_c}.

At fixed flight state and turbine-entry temperature, differentiating the last expression with respect to τc\tau_c gives a stationary point at

τc=τλτr. \tau_c=\frac{\sqrt{\tau_\lambda}}{\tau_r}.

This idealized velocity optimum is meaningful only if it lies in the admissible compressor and heating domain. It is not a universal engine optimum: it neglects losses, fuel mass, component maps and other design objectives. The nonideal model must retain its full station coupling when evaluating a compressor-ratio trend.

9.9 Worked nonideal design point

Choose an original illustrative state with M0=0.8M_0=0.8, T0=250T_0=250 K and p0=40p_0=40 kPa. Supply πc=8\pi_c=8, Tt4=1500T_{t4}=1500 K, cp,c=1005c_{p,c}=1005, cp,h=1150c_{p,h}=1150 J/(kg K), γc=1.4\gamma_c=1.4, γh=1.33\gamma_h=1.33, and QR=43Q_R=43 MJ/kg. Use inlet recovery 0.97, burner pressure ratio 0.95, nozzle pressure ratio 0.98, polytropic efficiencies 0.90 and 0.92, burner efficiency 0.98 and mechanical efficiency 0.99. Select full expansion and an air flow of 20 kg/s.

At subsonic flight the empirical ram factor is one, so πd=0.97\pi_d=0.97. The ram temperature ratio is 1.128, and the compressor temperature ratio is 1.93506356. Sequential evaluation gives:

Total-state station Temperature, K Pressure, kPa
Inlet exit 2 282.000 59.1444
Compressor exit 3 545.688 473.155
Burner exit 4 1500.000 449.497
Turbine exit 5 1273.817 219.665
Nozzle total state 9 1273.817 215.272

The burner balance gives f=0.0291125482f=0.0291125482. The turbine work balance gives τt=0.84921118\tau_t=0.84921118, followed by πt=0.48869123\pi_t=0.48869123. These values show that much of the compressor’s pressure rise is consumed by the turbine while it supplies shaft work.

The nozzle total-to-static pressure ratio is 5.38180297. Its static exit temperature is 838.974845 K, exit Mach is 1.77234908, and velocity is 1000.06822 m/s. The corresponding freestream velocity is 253.61388 m/s. Because full expansion removes the pressure term,

Fs=(1.0291125482)(1000.06822)−253.61388=775.56887Ns/kg. \begin{gathered} F_s=(1.0291125482)(1000.06822)-253.61388\\ =775.56887\ \mathrm{N\,s/kg}. \end{gathered}

The dimensional thrust is approximately 15.5114 kN and TSFC is 3.7537025×10−53.7537025\times10^{-5} kg/(N s), or 37.5370 mg/(N s). These are direct arithmetic results from the stated simplified equations, not measured engine performance or a component-map design.

The station table’s 1273.817 K at row 9 and the static exit value 838.975 K describe different states and must both be retained correctly. A report that replaced one with the other would obscure the nozzle energy conversion.

9.10 Interpreting trends and refusals

Increasing compressor pressure ratio raises compressor work and temperature. At a fixed turbine-entry temperature it tends to reduce required burner heat, but it also increases the turbine work demand and changes nozzle pressure potential. Specific thrust need not increase monotonically with pressure ratio. The ideal stationary point above illustrates why an apparent tradeoff exists even before losses are included.

Reducing burner or nozzle pressure recovery can reduce exhaust velocity without changing the earlier shaft temperature balance in this prescribed design-point closure. Reducing mechanical efficiency instead increases required turbine temperature drop. These distinct responses help identify which assumption drives a result.

The solver rejects nonfinite states, invalid efficiencies, incompatible burner energy, nonpositive available turbine temperature, insufficient nozzle pressure ratio and nonpositive net specific thrust. A refusal should be interpreted through the first failed balance rather than treated automatically as a missing implementation. Conversely, a numerically accepted result remains a bounded cycle estimate: it does not establish compressor operability, turbine cooling feasibility, nozzle separation behavior, installation drag or a manufacturable engine geometry.

10. Afterburning and variable-property cycles

Afterburning adds fuel downstream of the turbine. It can increase the energy available to the nozzle without requiring that the additional heat pass through the turbine blades. It also consumes fuel, adds exhaust mass and introduces total-pressure loss. Its net effect depends on all three changes, not on afterburner temperature alone.

A second distinction concerns thermodynamics. A constant-property heating-value model prescribes a temperature and estimates fuel required to reach it. The variable-property model in ThrustOne prescribes gaseous fuel amounts and uses formation-inclusive equilibrium chemistry to obtain chamber temperature. These are different closures. A change between them is more than replacing one heat capacity with a temperature-dependent value.

This chapter develops both formulations and their current implementation boundaries. The unaugmented station chain is in Chapter 9; shared property and equilibrium relations are in Chapters 5–6. Turbofan mixing details are deferred to Chapters 13–14.

10.1 Two fuel streams, one normalization

Take one kilogram of incoming core air as the accounting basis. Let ff denote main fuel mass per unit core air, and fABf_{AB} additional afterburner fuel on that same basis. The mass crossing the turbine is 1+f1+f. The mass leaving an active afterburner is 1+f+fAB1+f+f_{AB}.

Station 6 denotes afterburner entry and station 7 its exit. In this simplified turbojet chain, station 6 receives the turbine-exit state without an additional interconnecting loss, so Tt6=Tt5T_{t6}=T_{t5} and pt6=pt5p_{t6}=p_{t5}. The afterburner pressure ratio is

πAB=pt7/pt6. \pi_{AB}=p_{t7}/p_{t6}.

Additional fuel is not normalized by the already enlarged turbine flow. If a fuel ratio f̂AB\widehat f_{AB} is instead defined per kilogram of afterburner inlet gas, conversion requires fAB=(1+f)f̂ABf_{AB}=(1+f)\widehat f_{AB}. Confusing the two bases changes both energy and momentum accounting.

In the prescribed design-point model, the compressor state, main fuel ratio and turbine work closure are established before afterburning. Added downstream fuel does not contribute to the mass flow extracting turbine work. This is a model assumption about an independently closed upstream chain; a real fixed-geometry engine can experience upstream changes through back-pressure and matching interactions that this calculation does not solve.

10.2 Constant-property afterburner energy balance

Let cp,ABc_{p,AB} be the effective exhaust heat capacity, ηAB\eta_{AB} the afterburner combustion efficiency and QRQ_R the heating value. Neglect supplied fuel sensible enthalpy as in Chapter 9. The balance is

(1+f)cp,hTt6+fABηABQR=(1+f+fAB)cp,ABTt7. (1+f)c_{p,h}T_{t6}+f_{AB}\eta_{AB}Q_R =(1+f+f_{AB})c_{p,AB}T_{t7}.

Collecting terms in the added fuel gives

fAB=(1+f)cp,ABTt7−cp,hTt6ηABQR−cp,ABTt7. f_{AB}=(1+f) \frac{c_{p,AB}T_{t7}-c_{p,h}T_{t6}} {\eta_{AB}Q_R-c_{p,AB}T_{t7}}.

The numerator is the increase in effective specific enthalpy, multiplied by the incoming mass. The denominator accounts for the enthalpy carried out by the fuel mass itself. A positive prescribed temperature alone does not guarantee a valid denominator.

The current constant-property branch requires the afterburner outlet temperature and its effective enthalpy to be no lower than at entry. It rejects a nonpositive fuel-energy denominator. If different hot and afterburner heat capacities are supplied, the piecewise cpTc_pT convention can introduce an enthalpy-reference jump; the App warns about that limitation. It does not determine a composition that explains the change in heat capacity.

In the ideal air-standard approximation, heat capacities are the same throughout, efficiencies and recoveries are one, and fuel mass is neglected in the flow balances. The corresponding estimate is

fAB=cp(Tt7−Tt6)/QR. f_{AB}=c_p(T_{t7}-T_{t6})/Q_R.

This approximation should not be confused with the nonideal fuel-mass expression evaluated at unit efficiencies.

10.3 The nozzle must receive the afterburner energy

With nozzle recovery πn\pi_n, the downstream total state should be

Tt9=Tt7,pt9=pt5πABπn. T_{t9}=T_{t7},\qquad p_{t9}=p_{t5}\pi_{AB}\pi_n.

For a constant-property expansion to the selected static exit pressure,

T9=Tt7(p9pt9)(γAB−1)/γAB, T_9=T_{t7}\left(\frac{p_9}{p_{t9}}\right)^{(\gamma_{AB}-1)/\gamma_{AB}},

V9=2cp,AB(Tt7−T9). V_9=\sqrt{2c_{p,AB}(T_{t7}-T_9)}.

The corresponding thrust per unit core air is

Fs=(1+f+fAB)V9−V0+(1+f+fAB)RABT9V9(1−p0/p9). F_s=(1+f+f_{AB})V_9-V_0 +\frac{(1+f+f_{AB})R_{AB}T_9}{V_9}(1-p_0/p_9).

Both fuel streams contribute to consumption:

TSFC=(f+fAB)/Fs. TSFC=(f+f_{AB})/F_s.

Pressure loss reduces expansion potential, while heating raises available enthalpy and added fuel increases exhaust mass. A rise in nozzle velocity is not alone a measure of fuel economy. The fully expanded efficiency qualifications of Chapter 9 remain applicable.

Keeping one consistent nozzle state

The constant-property calculation uses the afterburner outlet total temperature to recover nozzle static temperature and exhaust velocity. The same total state appears in the station chain. Afterburner pressure loss changes the expansion pressure ratio, and added fuel changes the exhaust mass factor. All three effects belong to one nozzle closure.

Using the unaugmented turbine-exit temperature with the augmented nozzle pressure and mass would create an inconsistent state. In particular, the reported exit Mach and static temperature would fail to reconstruct the station total temperature. A plausible-looking thrust value or successful calculation status would not reveal the omitted thermal energy by itself.

The dry and zero-temperature-rise limits can hide such an error. An active-afterburner example with a substantial temperature rise is therefore necessary when interpreting the energy added downstream of the turbine.

10.4 Worked afterburner balance

Extend Chapter 9’s original nonideal example. Its main fuel ratio is 0.0291125482, turbine-exit total temperature is 1273.816775 K, and dry nozzle total pressure is 215.272119 kPa. Retain the hot-gas heat capacity 1150 J/(kg K) and gamma 1.33 for the afterburner. Specify Tt7=1800T_{t7}=1800 K, ηAB=0.96\eta_{AB}=0.96, πAB=0.94\pi_{AB}=0.94, the same 43 MJ/kg heating value and full expansion to 40 kPa.

The energy balance gives

fAB=0.0158818420,f+fAB=0.0449943902. f_{AB}=0.0158818420,\qquad f+f_{AB}=0.0449943902.

The new nozzle total-to-static pressure ratio is 5.05889479. Using the afterburner temperature consistently yields

T9=1203.876692K,V9=1170.932795m/s, T_9=1203.876692\ \mathrm{K},\qquad V_9=1170.932795\ \mathrm{m/s},

Fs=970.004322Ns/kg. F_s=970.004322\ \mathrm{N\,s/kg}.

These values are direct arithmetic consequences of the stated simplified balances. Substituting the dry turbine-exit temperature would instead give approximately 851.954625 K, 985.029413 m/s and 775.736331 N s/kg for the same pressure and mass factors. That deliberately inconsistent comparison isolates the effect of omitting the afterburner heat from the nozzle-energy evaluation.

The App uses the augmented total temperature in this closure. The comparison explains why total-to-static consistency is essential: pressure recovery, fuel mass and thermal energy must all refer to the same operating condition. It is not a separate permissible approximation for an active afterburner.

10.5 Variable properties change the independent inputs

The variable-property turbojet uses dry air with mole fractions 0.79 N2 and 0.21 O2, and a selected gaseous fuel H2, CH4 or CO. Main fuel–air ratio and fuel temperature are inputs. Turbine-entry temperature becomes an equilibrium energy-closure result rather than a prescribed target.

Definition Constant-property cycle Variable-property cycle
Main combustion input Target turbine-entry temperature Gaseous fuel ratio and feed temperature
Chemical energy Heating value and burner efficiency Species formation-inclusive enthalpy
Compression/turbine efficiency Polytropic input Explicit isentropic input
Composition Not solved Equilibrium in chambers, frozen downstream
Exit condition Supplied ambient/exit pressure ratio Full expansion to ambient pressure

The variable-property input values are not direct replacements for the identically named constants in the other branch. In particular, using the same numerical efficiency does not preserve component work when one definition is polytropic and the other isentropic.

The inlet obtains total enthalpy from ht0=h0+V02/2h_{t0}=h_0+V_0^2/2, inverts it for total temperature, and obtains total pressure from entropy. It applies the supplied inlet recovery directly. It does not automatically add the constant-property turbojet’s empirical Mach recovery correlation.

10.6 Compressor and main equilibrium chamber

For a supplied compressor pressure ratio, first find the isentropic outlet from

s(Tt3s,pt3,𝒙a)=s(Tt2,pt2,𝒙a). s(T_{t3s},p_{t3},\boldsymbol x_a)=s(T_{t2},p_{t2},\boldsymbol x_a).

Then the actual work and enthalpy are

wc=ht3s−ht2ηc,ht3=ht2+wc. w_c=\frac{h_{t3s}-h_{t2}}{\eta_c},\qquad h_{t3}=h_{t2}+w_c.

Temperature is recovered from h(T)h(T); a local gamma power law is not substituted for this integral property calculation.

On the unit-core-air basis, the incoming air amounts are xa,i/W¯ax_{a,i}/\overline W_a kmol and the fuel amount is f/Wff/W_f kmol. The adiabatic main chamber target is

h4,target=ha(Tt3)+fhf(Tf)1+f. h_{4,\mathrm{target}}=\frac{h_a(T_{t3})+fh_f(T_f)}{1+f}.

At pt4=πbpt3p_{t4}=\pi_b p_{t3}, the solver finds an equilibrium composition and temperature whose mass-specific enthalpy matches that target. Air and fuel need not have the same feed temperature. Internally, the shared equilibrium helper’s common-temperature reference is adjusted to reproduce the two actual feed enthalpies. That adjustment is bookkeeping, not external heating of the chamber.

There is no additional LHV term or unspecified combustion efficiency. The model assumes equilibrium of the admitted gas species and excludes vaporization and finite reaction time. A fuel-rich input does not guarantee a temperature rise proportional to added fuel; equilibrium composition and the available oxidizer determine the resulting state within the restricted species set.

10.7 Frozen turbine and pressure recovery

After main-chamber equilibrium, composition is frozen through the turbine. For a turbojet with compressor load wcw_c,

ht5=ht4−wc(1+f)ηm. h_{t5}=h_{t4}-\frac{w_c}{(1+f)\eta_m}.

The inversion of this enthalpy gives actual Tt5T_{t5}. Turbine isentropic efficiency defines the ideal enthalpy decrease associated with the same pressure change:

ht5s=ht4−ht4−ht5ηt. h_{t5s}=h_{t4}-\frac{h_{t4}-h_{t5}}{\eta_t}.

Recover Tt5sT_{t5s}, then determine pressure from equal entropy between the inlet and ideal outlet. The actual exit at that pressure has the larger entropy associated with its smaller enthalpy drop. The two temperatures are calculation states used to apply an efficiency definition, not two simultaneously existing exhaust streams.

For the single-spool turbofan extension, shaft load additionally includes fan work on core and bypass air. That normalization is developed in Chapter 13. The turbojet case has zero bypass and no fan pressure rise.

10.8 Variable-property afterburning

The optional afterburner adds a specified fABf_{AB} per kilogram of core air, using the same selected fuel species with its own feed temperature. The main-chamber products are carried as actual kmol per unit core air, not merely as a vector of fractions. This retains their mass 1+f1+f before new fuel is added.

At pt7=πABpt5p_{t7}=\pi_{AB}p_{t5}, the new equilibrium target is

h7,target=(1+f)h5+fABhf,AB1+f+fAB. h_{7,\mathrm{target}}= \frac{(1+f)h_5+f_{AB}h_{f,AB}}{1+f+f_{AB}}.

The chamber solve determines Tt7T_{t7} and new composition. Neither the main shaft work nor the main fuel ratio is recomputed from the added downstream mass. Temperature-root bounds are explicit, and every trial equilibrium must converge.

When the optional afterburner has zero added fuel, the implemented branch retains the incoming temperature and composition while applying its pressure loss. It does not re-equilibrate the turbine’s frozen products in this special case. Thus enabling a zero-fuel afterburner is a pressure-loss element, not necessarily a perfect no-change switch. The deliberately different zero-fuel closure should be retained when interpreting comparisons.

For positive added fuel, this model does not impose a universal temperature-rise promise. Dissociation, feed enthalpy and the chemical inventory affect the energy root. The label afterburner describes the flowpath location and supplied fuel; it does not replace the energy calculation with a prescribed temperature rise.

10.9 Variable-property exhaust and diagnostics

The resulting composition is frozen again through the nozzle. Apply nozzle pressure recovery at unchanged total enthalpy, then solve

s(T9,p0,𝒙7)=s(Tt7,pt9,𝒙7), s(T_9,p_0,\boldsymbol x_7)=s(T_{t7},p_{t9},\boldsymbol x_7),

V9=2[h(Tt7,𝒙7)−h(T9,𝒙7)]. V_9=\sqrt{2[h(T_{t7},\boldsymbol x_7)-h(T_9,\boldsymbol x_7)]}.

For the turbojet, Fs=(1+f+fAB)V9−V0F_s=(1+f+f_{AB})V_9-V_0 and TSFC=(f+fAB)/FsTSFC=(f+f_{AB})/F_s. Full expansion eliminates pressure thrust in this branch. It does not establish compatibility with a fixed exit area or solve a separated nozzle.

The variable-property cycle’s station 9 is explicitly labeled as a static exit state, unlike the total-state row 9 in the constant-property cycle. Preserving these labels is essential when comparing station tables. The result also distinguishes main, afterburner and total fuel ratios; the main fuel_air_ratio field is not their sum.

The implementation returns main-burner, shaft and afterburner energy residuals, plus an afterburner mass residual and chamber equilibrium residuals. Energy balances on this unit-core-air basis have units J/kg of core air, not automatically watts. Multiplying by actual core flow gives a power residual. A small residual establishes closure of these equations, not independent accuracy of a real afterburner model.

No thermal or propulsive efficiency is currently reported by this variable-property cycle, even though its streams are fully expanded. The implementation has not selected a separate fuel chemical-power normalization for those efficiencies. A reader should not import a heating-value denominator silently to manufacture a field the model does not define.

10.10 Comparing models without changing the question

A useful comparison must align fuel basis, feed state, component efficiency definition, pressure losses and nozzle closure. Holding turbine-entry temperature fixed in the constant-property cycle while holding fuel ratio fixed in the variable-property cycle generally describes different experiments. One result cannot be used as a direct correction factor for the other without first matching the independent constraints.

For an energy-accounting illustration, suppose a unit-core-air main chamber receives air enthalpy 400 kJ/kg and gaseous fuel enthalpy 100 kJ/kg at f=0.02f=0.02. Its target is (400+0.02×100)/1.02=394.117647(400+0.02\times100)/1.02=394.117647 kJ/kg of products. If turbine exit enthalpy is 250 kJ/kg and the afterburner adds 0.01 kg of fuel at 100 kJ/kg, its target is (1.02×250+0.01×100)/1.03=248.543689(1.02\times250+0.01\times100)/1.03=248.543689 kJ/kg. The smaller mass-specific target does not by itself imply a colder product: composition and formation enthalpies determine the temperature corresponding to that target. These supplied enthalpies demonstrate normalization only, not an asserted physical flame state.

The present variable-property engine excludes cooling flows, condensed phases, liquid fuel preparation, finite-rate chemistry and unrestricted map matching. Mixed turbofan exhaust adds further compatibility equations described in Chapter 14. The constant-property afterburner instead retains prescribed heat capacities and an explicit heating-value balance. Keeping these boundaries visible allows each model to be interpreted at its stated level of physical detail.

11. Turbojet components and maps

An independent component calculation isolates one thermodynamic transformation. It is useful for examining a pressure loss, efficiency definition or nozzle expansion without requiring a complete engine to close. The same independence limits its meaning: a turbine result does not automatically satisfy a compressor load, and a compressor map query does not automatically match an engine operating point.

ThrustOne’s turbojet component mode contains inlet, compressor, burner, turbine and nozzle calculations. Four also support frozen variable-property thermodynamics; the reacting burner uses its separate equilibrium closure instead. This chapter explains the independent unknowns and the optional compressor map. The full-cycle balances are developed in Chapter 9, and corrected-coordinate definitions in Chapter 3.

11.1 One component, one closure

The total inlet state is normally supplied directly. The component’s defining ratio, temperature or efficiency then determines its outlet. For an inlet, the starting state is instead the static freestream and Mach number. A nozzle additionally needs the static pressure to which it expands.

Component Main prescribed change Principal result
Inlet Flight state and recovery Recovered total state
Compressor Total-pressure ratio and efficiency Temperature rise and specific work
Burner Outlet total temperature and fuel-energy assumptions Fuel ratio and pressure loss
Turbine Total-temperature ratio and efficiency Work and required pressure decrease
Nozzle Recovery and exit static pressure Exit temperature, velocity and Mach

Work in these independent calculations is specific energy, J/kg of the gas crossing the component. Converting it to shaft power requires a mass flow and, where applicable, a mechanical-efficiency convention. A burner adds mass; a compressor does not. Those facts must be handled explicitly when combining component results into an engine.

The common state fields tt_in, pt_in, tt_out and pt_out are total quantities. Nozzle static fields are returned separately. A zero total-temperature change across an adiabatic nozzle is consistent with a large static-temperature decrease and velocity increase.

11.2 Inlet recovery is not a compressor pressure ratio

The constant-property inlet first forms freestream total temperature and pressure from static conditions using the relations of Chapter 2. It then multiplies total pressure by the supplied recovery and empirical Mach recovery described in Chapter 4. It does not perform shaft work or increase total temperature beyond the incoming stagnation value.

A compressor pressure ratio greater than one describes pressure rise supported by work input. Inlet recovery at most one describes loss from a recoverable total state. Both may accompany a static pressure rise, but their energetic meanings differ.

The frozen variable-property inlet obtains the stagnation state from enthalpy and entropy functions. It applies the directly supplied recovery, without adding the constant-property empirical Mach factor. Entering identical recovery numbers in the two component variants does not necessarily give identical total-pressure loss at supersonic flight.

11.3 Compressor efficiency conversions

For constant heat capacities, define a=(γ−1)/γa=(\gamma-1)/\gamma. A compressor with pressure ratio πc\pi_c and polytropic efficiency ece_c has

τc=πca/ec,ηc=πca−1πca/ec−1. \tau_c=\pi_c^{a/e_c},\qquad \eta_c=\frac{\pi_c^a-1}{\pi_c^{a/e_c}-1}.

The isentropic efficiency compares the finite ideal and actual temperature rises. Conversely, with a known isentropic efficiency,

τc=1+πca−1ηc,wc=cpTt,in(τc−1). \tau_c=1+\frac{\pi_c^a-1}{\eta_c},\qquad w_c=c_pT_{t,in}(\tau_c-1).

These expressions are two consistent routes to the same state only when the efficiency conversion is performed at the same pressure ratio. Using an isentropic efficiency converted at one ratio and applying it at another is a distinct empirical model. That distinction becomes important in the map branch below.

At pressure ratio one without a map, the implementation returns unchanged total state and zero work. It omits an undefined finite-rise efficiency. Values slightly above one produce small work, and the code uses exponential-difference functions to avoid subtracting nearly equal powers unnecessarily.

In the variable-property component, efficiency is explicitly isentropic. Find the entropy-matched outlet at the specified pressure, divide its enthalpy rise by efficiency, and invert the resulting actual enthalpy for temperature. A single locally evaluated gamma cannot replace this procedure over a finite temperature change.

11.4 Burner and turbine subproblems

The constant-property burner uses

f=cp,hTt,out−cp,cTt,inηbQR−cp,hTt,out,pt,out=πbpt,in. f=\frac{c_{p,h}T_{t,out}-c_{p,c}T_{t,in}} {\eta_bQ_R-c_{p,h}T_{t,out}},\qquad p_{t,out}=\pi_b p_{t,in}.

The component requires an outlet temperature above inlet temperature, a positive denominator and a nonnegative resulting fuel ratio. Its heat_release is fηbQRf\eta_bQ_R per unit incoming air mass. It is not a heat-transfer rate in watts without a flow scale, nor is it a finite-rate chemical source.

A frozen variable-property burner is deliberately not supplied: frozen composition cannot describe combustion. The gas-phase energy closure in Chapter 6 is the appropriate supported reacting problem. Merely changing heat capacity in the burner subproblem does not silently activate that chemistry.

The independent turbine takes an actual temperature ratio τt\tau_t and polytropic efficiency ete_t. It returns

πt=τtγ/[et(γ−1)],wt=cpTt,in(1−τt), \pi_t=\tau_t^{\gamma/[e_t(\gamma-1)]},\qquad w_t=c_pT_{t,in}(1-\tau_t),

ηt=1−τt1−τt1/et. \eta_t=\frac{1-\tau_t}{1-\tau_t^{1/e_t}}.

Unlike the full engine, this subproblem does not obtain τt\tau_t from compressor work. The supplied ratio fixes work, and efficiency determines its pressure cost. At τt=1\tau_t=1, the total state is unchanged and zero work is returned.

For frozen variable properties, the actual enthalpy decrease follows from the supplied temperature ratio. Dividing it by isentropic efficiency gives the ideal decrease associated with the required pressure ratio. Entropy then determines that pressure. This is the inverse component problem developed in Chapter 10, without an engine shaft-load constraint.

11.5 Nozzle criticality and the missing geometry constraint

The independent constant-property nozzle uses

pt,out=πnpt,in,p9=p0/re, p_{t,out}=\pi_np_{t,in},\qquad p_9=p_0/r_e,

where re=p0/p9r_e=p_0/p_9 is the supplied static-pressure ratio. From NPR=pt,out/p9>1NPR=p_{t,out}/p_9>1, it computes static temperature, Mach and velocity. The critical total-to-static pressure ratio is

NPR*=(γ+12)γ/(γ−1). NPR_* = \left(\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

The output is_choked indicates whether the specified ratio reaches this critical threshold. It does not impose a fixed convergent exit at Mach one. The solver continues to return the Mach number implied by the supplied static pressure, including supersonic values, and does not size throat or exit area in this component result.

A user must therefore distinguish a criticality indicator from a geometric boundary condition. A convergent nozzle with a fixed throat/exit would require a different closure after choking. An internal shock or separation pattern also requires information absent from this component problem.

The frozen nozzle component solves entropy at the requested static pressure and obtains velocity from enthalpy drop. Its boundary permits equal exit static and available total pressure, yielding zero speed. The constant-property variant rejects NPR≤1NPR\leq1. This difference in zero-flow boundary handling is part of current behavior, not evidence that one branch predicts a flowing jet at equal pressures.

11.6 What the compressor map contains

The optional map stores a rectangular grid. Rows correspond to normalized corrected speed and columns to an auxiliary coordinate β\beta. At each point it contains normalized corrected flow, a pressure-ratio multiplier and an efficiency multiplier. All are dimensionless; they are not raw rpm, kg/s or an independently complete compressor specification.

Chapter 3 explains how physical corrected flow and speed require explicit reference conventions. The map record itself does not supply dimensional reference flow or temperature and pressure metadata. A map value of one therefore means a normalization point, not one kilogram per second.

The β\beta coordinate parametrizes a line through the tabulated surface. Its numerical value does not directly mean flow, pressure ratio or surge margin. The user supplies speed and beta to select a point; the tables provide the associated three outputs.

The implementation accepts only compressor maps, with at least two points on each strictly increasing finite axis and matching positive tables. It checks dimensions and finite values, not whether the data came from a physical compressor test. A synthetic demonstration map is available, but its smooth appearance is not experimental validation.

11.7 How a map point enters the component balance

Let the baseline pressure ratio be πc,b\pi_{c,b}, baseline polytropic efficiency ec,be_{c,b}, and sampled map multipliers rπr_\pi and rηr_\eta. The current component first converts the baseline efficiency at the baseline pressure ratio:

ηc,b=πc,ba−1πc,ba/ec,b−1. \eta_{c,b}=\frac{\pi_{c,b}^{a}-1}{\pi_{c,b}^{a/e_{c,b}}-1}.

It then forms

πc=πc,brπ,ηc=ηc,brη, \pi_c=\pi_{c,b}r_\pi,\qquad \eta_c=\eta_{c,b}r_\eta,

and calculates

τc=1+πca−1ηc. \tau_c=1+\frac{\pi_c^a-1}{\eta_c}.

This scales the baseline isentropic efficiency, not the baseline polytropic efficiency. Recomputing an unscaled polytropic law at the new pressure ratio would describe a different model. The returned baseline e_c value must not be read as proof that the final mapped state follows that same polytropic efficiency.

The mapped pressure ratio must exceed one and the resulting efficiency must lie in (0,1](0,1]. Map multipliers can exceed one, but the final physical efficiency cannot. The map’s corrected-flow ratio is reported for interpretation; it is not automatically converted to actual mass flow or used to close an engine shaft balance.

Frozen variable-property compression rejects an attached compressor map. Its explicit isentropic component closure and the current constant-property map scaling remain separate supported paths.

11.8 Shape-preserving interpolation

For adjacent axis points xi,xi+1x_i,x_{i+1}, define hi=xi+1−xih_i=x_{i+1}-x_i, t=(x−xi)/hit=(x-x_i)/h_i, and secant slopes di=(yi+1−yi)/hid_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i. A cubic Hermite interval is

y(x)=(2t3−3t2+1)yi+(t3−2t2+t)himi+(−2t3+3t2)yi+1+(t3−t2)himi+1. \begin{gathered} y(x)=(2t^3-3t^2+1)y_i+(t^3-2t^2+t)h_im_i\\ +(-2t^3+3t^2)y_{i+1}+(t^3-t^2)h_im_{i+1}. \end{gathered}

The endpoint derivatives mim_i determine whether a smooth cubic introduces artificial overshoot. The App sets an interior derivative to zero when adjacent secants change sign or include a zero slope. When they share a sign, it uses a weighted harmonic mean:

mi=w1+w2w1/di−1+w2/di,w1=2hi+hi−1,w2=hi+2hi−1. m_i=\frac{w_1+w_2}{w_1/d_{i-1}+w_2/d_i},\quad w_1=2h_i+h_{i-1},\quad w_2=h_i+2h_{i-1}.

Endpoint slopes use a one-sided estimate limited according to neighboring secants. With only two points, both derivatives equal the secant and the interpolant reduces to a straight line.

The map samples each speed row along beta first, then interpolates those sampled values across speed. This is a specified two-pass operation. It is not a global fitted compressor surface, and the order should not be silently exchanged when reconstructing results. Shape preservation reduces artificial wiggles relative to an unrestricted cubic; it does not supply missing data or prove aerodynamic behavior between widely separated samples.

Every query must lie within both axis bounds. The App rejects exterior points instead of clamping or extrapolating. Clamping would return a boundary value for a different requested operating point, while extrapolation would introduce behavior unsupported by the stored data.

11.9 Inverse lookup and surge interpretation

The supported inverse operation supplies normalized speed and a target map pressure multiplier, then seeks beta. It is not an inverse for dimensional corrected flow. Every stored pressure row must be strictly monotone in the same direction before this operation is admitted. A row with a plateau, a turning point or opposite direction causes rejection, with direct beta selection required instead.

The inverse brackets beta on its stored interval, checks the target against the forward endpoint values and bisects using the same two-pass forward interpolator. A returned point must meet the relative pressure-multiplier residual. This is a deliberately restricted inverse; it does not discover and select among arbitrary multiple compressor branches.

An optional surge-pressure curve provides the indicator

Sπ=rπ,surgerπ,operating−1. S_\pi=\frac{r_{\pi,\mathrm{surge}}}{r_{\pi,\mathrm{operating}}}-1.

The design pressure scale cancels in this ratio. This quantity compares pressure ratios at the selected speed. It contains no additional corrected-flow factor and is not a universal compressor surge-margin definition. A positive value does not independently establish dynamic stability, and a negative value is not an integrated surge simulation. The code reports this indicator when the curve exists; it does not use it as a complete engine operability constraint.

11.10 Worked mapped compressor

Use an illustrative baseline pressure ratio 6, polytropic efficiency 0.88, gamma 1.4, heat capacity 1005 J/(kg K), inlet total temperature 320 K and inlet total pressure 100 kPa. Suppose a supplied map point gives pressure multiplier 0.95, efficiency multiplier 0.98 and normalized corrected-flow value 0.90. Let the associated surge-pressure multiplier be 1.12.

Baseline conversion gives ηc,b=0.8471282884\eta_{c,b}=0.8471282884. The mapped state therefore uses

πc=5.7,ηc=0.8301857226. \pi_c=5.7,\qquad \eta_c=0.8301857226.

Its actual total temperature is

Tt,out=320[1+5.70.4/1.4−10.8301857226]=568.324713K. T_{t,out}=320\left[1+\frac{5.7^{0.4/1.4}-1}{0.8301857226}\right] =568.324713\ \mathrm{K}.

The outlet pressure is 570 kPa, and work is

wc=1005(568.324713−320)=249566.336J/kg. w_c=1005(568.324713-320)=249566.336\ \mathrm{J/kg}.

The pressure-only surge indicator is 1.12/0.95−1=0.178947371.12/0.95-1=0.17894737, or about 17.89%. The flow value 0.90 remains a dimensionless map result. It does not make the compressor power 0.90 times its specific work without a dimensional flow scale.

These sampled map values are illustrative inputs, not a claim about a tested machine or the built-in synthetic map. The example isolates the baseline-efficiency conversion and shows why scaling polytropic efficiency directly would produce a different temperature.

11.11 A small interpolation and inverse example

Consider two speed rows at 0.8 and 1.0, with beta endpoints 0 and 1. Let their pressure multipliers be respectively [0.9,0.7][0.9,0.7] and [1.1,0.9][1.1,0.9]. Because both axes have only two points, the interpolation is linear in each pass.

At beta 0.25, the row values are 0.85 and 1.05. At speed 0.9, the second pass gives 0.95. Reversing the same calculation at speed 0.9 with target multiplier 0.95 returns beta 0.25. Both rows decrease strictly, satisfying the inverse admission rule.

A query at speed 1.1 is outside the data and is rejected. Adding an interior point that makes either pressure row turn upward would still allow a direct forward query within the grid, but would disallow the restricted inverse. This distinction separates interpolation of supplied data from an unambiguous inverse operating-point selection.

11.12 From components to an engine

Independent component results can support a hand-assembled station chain when mass bases, gas properties, efficiency definitions and static/total states are compatible. They do not themselves guarantee that one component supplies exactly the work another consumes, that nozzle area passes the resulting flow, or that a compressor map point matches shaft speed and turbine capacity.

The next chapter adds particular reference-based off-design closures. Those constraints must be read explicitly rather than inferred from the presence of a map file. A clear component calculation is valuable because it reveals each assumption separately; combining its outputs without the missing conservation and matching equations would conceal that advantage.

12. Turbojet off-design closure

A design-point calculation specifies a compressor pressure ratio. An off-design calculation asks how that ratio and the flow change when an already defined engine operates at a different flight condition or throttle setting. Answering the second question requires additional assumptions about the engine. A reference point alone is not enough unless a rule connects that point to the new condition.

The current turbojet off-design modes use reference-normalized relations associated with fixed turbine areas and choked flow. They hold turbine ratios fixed and derive compressor behavior from a normalized thermal loading. They do not match arbitrary compressor and turbine maps or integrate shaft dynamics. This chapter separates those prescribed relations from general off-design physics and derives the associated exit-area diagnostic.

12.1 Reference state versus operating state

Use subscript R for the reference condition. The single-spool reference stores ambient state, inlet ratios, compressor temperature and pressure ratios, compressor isentropic efficiency, turbine ratios, nozzle pressure ratio and air flow. The operating inputs supply current ambient conditions, Mach number, turbine-entry temperature and ambient-to-exit static-pressure ratio.

The reference is an engine definition retained across operating cases. Replacing it with each new operating state would erase the comparison being made. Conversely, changing ambient pressure in the current case does not change the saved reference pressure.

The current compressor pressure ratio is a result of the reference relation. A positive value in the generic design-input field does not independently prescribe that result in this mode. Likewise, an optional current air-flow entry is not the mass-flow closure: air flow is obtained from the reference scaling. Inputs retained for shared data structures should not be mistaken for independent degrees of freedom in every solver.

A consistent reference satisfies its own temperature/pressure/efficiency relations. For example,

πcR=[1+ηcR(τcR−1)]γc/(γc−1). \pi_{cR}=[1+\eta_{cR}(\tau_{cR}-1)]^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}.

Entering independently rounded or incompatible reference quantities can prevent exact recovery of the intended reference operating point. The App can construct a reference from a nonideal design calculation and a supplied air-flow scale. That helper checks compressor work and a critical nozzle-pressure threshold; it does not independently simulate every assumed choked station.

12.2 Why choking enables reference scaling

For a constant-property gas at a choked section,

ṁ=A*ptTtγR(2γ+1)(γ+1)/[2(γ−1)]. \dot m=A_*\frac{p_t}{\sqrt{T_t}} \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{R}} \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{(\gamma+1)/[2(\gamma-1)]}.

At fixed area and gas properties, the combination ṁTt/pt\dot m\sqrt{T_t}/p_t is constant. Referencing removes the unknown dimensional area and retains a ratio between operating states.

The single-spool model assumes choking at turbine entry and nozzle throat, conventionally stations 4 and 8, with fixed turbine temperature and pressure ratios. This allows a closed compressor operating relation and a mass-flow scaling. It is a restricted family of operating states, not proof that choking persists under every supplied throttle or back pressure.

The physical turbine-entry mass flow is (1+f)ṁa(1+f)\dot m_a. An exact comparison with fixed area and composition would retain the changing fuel-mass factor along with burner loss and gas-property factors. The implemented air-flow relation adopts the reference approximation in which those additional factors are treated as constant. Its use of the newly computed fuel ratio in thrust does not make the flow-scaling approximation exact.

12.3 Thermal loading determines compressor rise

Define the thermal-loading parameter

θ=Tt4Tt2,θR=Tt4RTt2R,Tt2=T0τr. \theta=\frac{T_{t4}}{T_{t2}},\qquad \theta_R=\frac{T_{t4R}}{T_{t2R}},\qquad T_{t2}=T_0\tau_r.

The single-spool operating relation is

τc−1=(τcR−1)θθR. \tau_c-1=(\tau_{cR}-1)\frac{\theta}{\theta_R}.

It follows that the compressor temperature rise scales with turbine-entry temperature under the fixed-ratio reference approximation. At higher inlet total temperature with unchanged turbine-entry temperature, the available normalized loading is reduced.

The reference isentropic efficiency then gives

πc=[1+ηcR(τc−1)]γc/(γc−1). \pi_c=[1+\eta_{cR}(\tau_c-1)]^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}.

There is no map beta search here. The resulting compressor line is specified by the reference relation itself. Chapter 11’s independent map capability does not imply that this off-design solver performs map matching.

Once Tt3=Tt2τcT_{t3}=T_{t2}\tau_c is known, main fuel follows the nonideal heating-value balance of Chapter 9. The turbine instead retains

Tt5=Tt4τtR,pt5=pt4πtR. T_{t5}=T_{t4}\tau_{tR},\qquad p_{t5}=p_{t4}\pi_{tR}.

It does not recompute turbine ratios from a fresh exact shaft-work equation using every changed fuel fraction or gas property. Changes outside the assumptions of the reference family should therefore not be interpreted as generally matched engine states.

12.4 Air flow, corrected flow and speed

The implemented air-flow scaling is

ṁaṁaR=p0πrπdπcp0RπrRπdRπcRTt4RTt4. \frac{\dot m_a}{\dot m_{aR}}= \frac{p_0\pi_r\pi_d\pi_c}{p_{0R}\pi_{rR}\pi_{dR}\pi_{cR}} \sqrt{\frac{T_{t4R}}{T_{t4}}}.

At otherwise identical dimensionless conditions, decreasing ambient pressure decreases dimensional mass flow and thrust while leaving specific thrust unchanged. This is one reason that a specific-performance plot cannot replace an absolute-thrust plot.

The reported corrected-flow ratio is

ṁcṁcR=πcπcRθRθ. \frac{\dot m_{c}}{\dot m_{cR}}= \frac{\pi_c}{\pi_{cR}}\sqrt{\frac{\theta_R}{\theta}}.

It is a reference-normalized result, not a dimensional corrected flow in kg/s. The mechanical speed ratio is

NNR=Tt2Tt2Rπc(γc−1)/γc−1πcR(γc−1)/γc−1. \frac{N}{N_R}= \sqrt{\frac{T_{t2}}{T_{t2R}} \frac{\pi_c^{(\gamma_c-1)/\gamma_c}-1} {\pi_{cR}^{(\gamma_c-1)/\gamma_c}-1}}.

The square root is essential: the quantity inside it scales a work-like term with speed squared. This mechanical speed ratio is not the corrected-speed map coordinate discussed in Chapter 3. To form a corrected-speed ratio at the same inlet reference convention, an additional temperature correction is required.

The aliases speed_ratio, n_nr and N_NR refer to the same mechanical ratio. Multiple output names do not represent separate speed definitions.

12.5 Nozzle and admissibility

Available nozzle pressure ratio is

NPR=(p0/p9)πrπdπcπbπtRπn. NPR=(p_0/p_9)\pi_r\pi_d\pi_c\pi_b\pi_{tR}\pi_n.

The exit velocity and pressure thrust are calculated from the specified exit static pressure using Chapter 9’s relations. The model does not solve a fixed exit-area back-pressure problem; its exit area is intended to vary consistently with the requested expansion while throat area remains fixed.

The current single-spool solver checks NPR>1NPR>1 for a jet, but does not require the current NPR to exceed the critical choking ratio. Thus an accepted low-NPR result does not establish the choking assumption on which its reference model relies. Check that assumption when interpreting operating points. The dual-spool branch, described below, explicitly rejects an unchoked nozzle condition.

Other refusals include invalid reference values, insufficient burner energy, nonpositive computed compressor rise, nonpositive thrust and nonfinite results. Such numerical guards cannot prove that the fixed-ratio turbine approximation remains valid under all changed inputs. In particular, independently varying gas properties or loss factors can invalidate cancellations used to obtain the reference scaling.

12.6 Exit-area reconstruction

For an isentropic constant-property nozzle with fixed throat area, the mass-flow parameter gives, up to factors constant between operating and reference states,

A9A*∝NPR(γ+1)/(2γ)NPR(γ−1)/γ−1. \frac{A_9}{A_*}\propto \frac{NPR^{(\gamma+1)/(2\gamma)}} {\sqrt{NPR^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}-1}}.

Therefore the consistent exit-area ratio is

A9A9R=(NPRNPRR)(γ+1)/(2γ)NPRR(γ−1)/γ−1NPR(γ−1)/γ−1. \frac{A_9}{A_{9R}}= \left(\frac{NPR}{NPR_R}\right)^{(\gamma+1)/(2\gamma)} \sqrt{\frac{NPR_R^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}-1} {NPR^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}-1}}.

The area_ratio_9 diagnostic uses the pressure-ratio orientation shown above. Both factors equal one at the reference state. That normalization alone is not enough to establish the formula away from the reference: reversing the first pressure ratio would still reproduce the reference area while producing incorrect off-reference geometry.

The area diagnostic is calculated after thrust and flow and does not feed them back into the solver. It reconstructs the exit area implied by the fixed-throat, isentropic nozzle relation; it does not introduce a geometric matching calculation or validate a real nozzle under separation, shocks or unchoked operation.

12.7 Worked normalized throttle change

Consider an illustrative reference inlet total temperature of 282 K, turbine-entry temperature 1500 K, compressor temperature ratio 1.8 and reference isentropic compressor efficiency 0.85, with gamma 1.4. Choose a consistent reference pressure ratio from the compressor relation:

πcR=[1+0.85(1.8−1)]3.5=6.14585750. \pi_{cR}=[1+0.85(1.8-1)]^{3.5}=6.14585750.

Reduce turbine-entry temperature to 1350 K at unchanged inlet total temperature and unchanged inlet pressure and recovery factors. The loading ratio is 0.9, giving

τc=1+0.8(0.9)=1.72,Tt3=282(1.72)=485.04K, \tau_c=1+0.8(0.9)=1.72,\qquad T_{t3}=282(1.72)=485.04\ \mathrm{K},

πc=[1+0.85(0.72)]3.5=5.31835877. \pi_c=[1+0.85(0.72)]^{3.5}=5.31835877.

The predicted air-flow ratio is

ṁaṁaR=5.318358776.1458575010.9=0.91216602. \frac{\dot m_a}{\dot m_{aR}}= \frac{5.31835877}{6.14585750}\frac{1}{\sqrt{0.9}} =0.91216602.

The mechanical speed ratio is 0.9=0.94868330\sqrt{0.9}=0.94868330. Flow and speed do not fall in the same proportion. The flow relation combines reduced compressor pressure with the square-root turbine-temperature factor; the speed relation follows the compressor work scaling.

These numbers demonstrate the reference equations only. A complete operating point additionally needs turbine ratios, burner assumptions and a nozzle condition that remains inside the choking and thrust domain. No dimensional thrust or physical engine performance is inferred from this partial reference specification.

12.8 Two spools require two reference rises

The dual-spool mode separates low- and high-pressure compressor temperature ratios, τcL\tau_{cL} and τcH\tau_{cH}. Define

Θ=Tt4/T0Tt4R/T0R. \Theta=\frac{T_{t4}/T_0}{T_{t4R}/T_{0R}}.

The implemented relations are

τcL=1+ΘτrRτr(τcLR−1), \tau_{cL}=1+\Theta\frac{\tau_{rR}}{\tau_r}(\tau_{cLR}-1),

τcH=1+ΘτrRτcLRτrτcL(τcHR−1). \tau_{cH}=1+\Theta \frac{\tau_{rR}\tau_{cLR}}{\tau_r\tau_{cL}}(\tau_{cHR}-1).

The second compressor receives the first compressor’s outlet. Its normalization must therefore include τcL\tau_{cL}; treating both compressors as though they had the same inlet temperature would alter high-spool work.

Separate supplied isentropic efficiencies convert each temperature ratio into pressure ratio. Air flow scales with the product πcLπcH\pi_{cL}\pi_{cH}, the actual inlet pressure factors and the turbine-temperature square root. The reference denominator uses its stored recovery. A consistent interpretation requires that stored reference factor represent the intended reference inlet convention, especially when preparing a nonzero-Mach reference.

High- and low-turbine temperature and pressure ratios are explicit fixed inputs. Their product determines the turbine-exit state. The code does not solve new independent turbine maps or integrate two shaft accelerations. The physical rationale involves spool work and choked capacities, but the implementation uses the resulting reference relations rather than an unrestricted coupled matching solve.

12.9 Dual-spool speed and afterburner behavior

The low-spool mechanical speed ratio is formed from the low-compressor pressure-work ratio and its inlet total temperature. The high-spool ratio uses the high-compressor inlet temperature, which includes the low-compressor temperature rise:

NHNHR=T0τrτcLT0RτrRτcLRπcH(γc−1)/γc−1πcHR(γc−1)/γc−1. \frac{N_H}{N_{HR}}= \sqrt{\frac{T_0\tau_r\tau_{cL}}{T_{0R}\tau_{rR}\tau_{cLR}} \frac{\pi_{cH}^{(\gamma_c-1)/\gamma_c}-1} {\pi_{cHR}^{(\gamma_c-1)/\gamma_c}-1}}.

This extra temperature factor is required even though both shafts belong to the same engine. Neither speed ratio alone determines corrected-flow matching on a component map.

Optional afterburning uses the main-fuel-plus-air mass entering the chamber and adds its own fuel mass and pressure loss. The dual-spool implementation uses afterburner temperature in its nozzle static-temperature expression. The constant-property design-point path likewise uses its augmented nozzle total temperature. Similar feature names still do not imply identical matching assumptions or numerical paths.

The dual-spool warning explicitly assumes choking at stations 4, 4.5 and 8 and variable nozzle area to isolate downstream afterburning from turbine matching. It checks the current nozzle’s critical pressure ratio. It does not solve internal turbine throat states to demonstrate all of those assumptions independently.

For unchanged upstream inputs, enabling afterburning leaves reference-derived compressor ratios, core flow and shaft speed ratios unchanged, while changing nozzle pressure, temperature, exhaust mass and thrust. That is the intended variable-area reference model; it is not a prediction of what happens when fuel is added to an arbitrary fixed nozzle.

12.10 Reading a reference-family result

Both off-design modes produce a restricted steady operating relation. They omit compressor-map matching, surge dynamics, spool transients, cooling-flow schedules and general unchoked operation. The single-spool implementation additionally requires care because a simple positive-NPR guard does not enforce its choking assumption, so users must retain the stated choked-flow domain when interpreting its reconstructed exit area.

A useful report retains reference identity, current flight state and throttle, fixed turbine ratios, pressure-loss assumptions and nozzle setting. Interpret mechanical speed, corrected flow and dimensional flow separately. Do not substitute one for another because all three are expressed as ratios near one.

Preserving those distinctions makes reference normalization useful for controlled comparisons. It also identifies where a broader engine model would need new equations or data instead of silently extending the present approximation outside its declared domain.

13. Separate-flow turbofans

A separate-flow turbofan divides incoming air between a heated core and a bypass stream. The turbine supplies work to the compression system, including the work used to accelerate bypass air through the fan. The two streams leave through separate nozzles, and their momentum and pressure contributions combine in the net thrust.

The additional stream introduces two common accounting errors: applying fuel ratio to total air when it is defined on core air, and multiplying a total-air specific thrust by core flow. It also creates a thermodynamic tradeoff. Increasing bypass flow can spread momentum addition over more air, but the fan work must still come from the core turbine.

This chapter covers the constant-property single-spool separate design mode and the separate-exhaust branch of the variable-property single-spool mode. Their compressor pressure ratios have different inlet references. A physically consistent comparison must resolve that difference before numerical inputs are reused.

13.1 Core, bypass and fuel mass

Define bypass ratio and main fuel ratio by

α=ṁbṁc,f=ṁfṁc, \alpha=\frac{\dot m_b}{\dot m_c},\qquad f=\frac{\dot m_f}{\dot m_c},

where ṁc\dot m_c is core air flow and ṁb\dot m_b bypass air flow. Total incoming air is

ṁa=(1+α)ṁc. \dot m_a=(1+\alpha)\dot m_c.

Without afterburning, the core nozzle carries (1+f)ṁc(1+f)\dot m_c, and the bypass nozzle carries αṁc\alpha\dot m_c. Fuel does not belong in the definition of bypass ratio.

Normalize first to one kilogram of core air. The incoming air inventory is then 1+α1+\alpha, fuel is ff, core exhaust is 1+f1+f, and bypass exhaust is α\alpha. This basis makes shaft work and burner energy particularly clear. Divide by 1+α1+\alpha only when forming a quantity explicitly defined per unit total inlet air.

Separate exhaust means the streams need not have equal exit temperatures, velocities or static pressures. They share the ambient reference pressure used for net pressure thrust, but their two nozzle expansions are independently specified in the constant-property design model.

13.2 Constant-property compression convention

The constant-property mode defines core compressor pressure ratio as pt3/pt2p_{t3}/p_{t2}, from inlet exit directly to core burner entry. The fan ratio defines pt13/pt2p_{t13}/p_{t2} for the bypass path. It does not multiply the fan ratio into the supplied core ratio a second time.

Using the inlet total state from Chapter 4,

Tt3=Tt2τc,Tt13=Tt2τf, T_{t3}=T_{t2}\tau_c,\qquad T_{t13}=T_{t2}\tau_f,

τc=πc(γc−1)/(γcec),τf=πf(γc−1)/(γcef). \tau_c=\pi_c^{(\gamma_c-1)/(\gamma_ce_c)},\qquad \tau_f=\pi_f^{(\gamma_c-1)/(\gamma_ce_f)}.

The input efficiencies here are polytropic. Derived isentropic efficiencies follow the finite-rise conversion in Chapter 11. Fan and core compressor are represented as effective compression paths; the model does not require a particular physical split between fan root and additional core stages.

The total compression work per kilogram of core air is

wload=cp,c(Tt3−Tt2)+αcp,c(Tt13−Tt2). w_{\mathrm{load}}=c_{p,c}(T_{t3}-T_{t2}) +\alpha c_{p,c}(T_{t13}-T_{t2}).

The first term already includes the full core compression from station 2. Adding another fan-work term for core air would count part of that path twice under this convention.

13.3 Burner and single-shaft turbine balance

Only core air enters the main burner. The nonideal fuel balance is

cp,cTt3+fηbQR=(1+f)cp,hTt4, c_{p,c}T_{t3}+f\eta_bQ_R=(1+f)c_{p,h}T_{t4},

which gives
