f=cp,hTt4−cp,cTt3ηbQR−cp,hTt4. f=\frac{c_{p,h}T_{t4}-c_{p,c}T_{t3}} {\eta_bQ_R-c_{p,h}T_{t4}}.

At prescribed core pressure ratio and turbine-entry temperature, this expression contains no bypass ratio. Changing bypass ratio alone therefore does not change main fuel ratio in this specific design closure. It does change how much turbine work must be extracted after combustion.

The shaft balance is

ηm(1+f)cp,h(Tt4−Tt5)=wload. \eta_m(1+f)c_{p,h}(T_{t4}-T_{t5})=w_{\mathrm{load}}.

In temperature-ratio notation, with τλ=cp,hTt4/(cp,cT0)\tau_\lambda=c_{p,h}T_{t4}/(c_{p,c}T_0),

τt=1−τr[(τc−1)+α(τf−1)]ηm(1+f)τλ. \tau_t=1- \frac{\tau_r[(\tau_c-1)+\alpha(\tau_f-1)]} {\eta_m(1+f)\tau_\lambda}.

Turbine polytropic efficiency then determines πt\pi_t from τt\tau_t. More bypass work lowers turbine-exit total temperature and pressure at unchanged main-burner conditions. Eventually the chosen fan demand can leave insufficient energy or pressure for a usable core nozzle.

The solver rejects nonpositive turbine temperature ratio and nonpositive total thrust. These guards identify incompatible prescribed operating points; they do not optimize fan pressure ratio or bypass ratio automatically.

13.4 Two nozzle calculations

The constant-property core nozzle receives

Tt9=Tt4τt,pt9=pt2πcπbπtπn,c. T_{t9}=T_{t4}\tau_t,\qquad p_{t9}=p_{t2}\pi_c\pi_b\pi_t\pi_{n,c}.

The bypass nozzle receives

Tt19=Tt2τf,pt19=pt2πfπn,b. T_{t19}=T_{t2}\tau_f,\qquad p_{t19}=p_{t2}\pi_f\pi_{n,b}.

Each has its own prescribed ambient-to-exit static-pressure ratio. Its exit Mach, temperature and velocity follow the total-to-static equations in Chapter 9, with hot-gas properties for the core and cold-air properties for bypass flow.

These are pressure-specified expansions, not fixed-area convergent-nozzle solutions. A Mach number above one does not establish that a particular nozzle geometry supports it. Separation, internal shocks and installed nacelle forces remain outside the calculation.

The current constant-property solver evaluates both nozzle pressure conditions even when bypass ratio is zero. Thus an otherwise valid core calculation can still be rejected by an invalid unused bypass-nozzle setting. The zero-bypass limit of the governing thrust and work equations exists, but the present input guards do not fully remove that inactive calculation. Retain a valid bypass setting when using this limit; do not infer an aerodynamic failure of the core from that rejection.

13.5 Combining thrust on a consistent basis

For the two nozzles,

F=ṁc[(1+f)V9−V0]+(p9−p0)A9+αṁc(V19−V0)+(p19−p0)A19. F=\dot m_c[(1+f)V_9-V_0]+(p_9-p_0)A_9 +\alpha\dot m_c(V_{19}-V_0)+(p_{19}-p_0)A_{19}.

Eliminating areas with each stream’s continuity equation gives a core contribution per unit core air,

Fs,c=(1+f)V9−V0+(1+f)RhT9V9(1−p0/p9), F_{s,c}=(1+f)V_9-V_0+ \frac{(1+f)R_hT_9}{V_9}(1-p_0/p_9),

and a bypass contribution per unit bypass air,

Fs,b=V19−V0+RcT19V19(1−p0/p19). F_{s,b}=V_{19}-V_0+ \frac{R_cT_{19}}{V_{19}}(1-p_0/p_{19}).

The total result on the core-air basis is F/ṁc=Fs,c+αFs,bF/\dot m_c=F_{s,c}+\alpha F_{s,b}. The App’s principal specific thrust uses total air:

Fs=Fs,c+αFs,b1+α. F_s=\frac{F_{s,c}+\alpha F_{s,b}}{1+\alpha}.

Fuel consumption follows

TSFC=fFs,c+αFs,b=f(1+α)Fs. TSFC=\frac{f}{F_{s,c}+\alpha F_{s,b}} =\frac{f}{(1+\alpha)F_s}.

The constant-property mode’s optional dimensional flow input is core air flow. Therefore net thrust is ṁc[Fs,c+αFs,b]\dot m_c[F_{s,c}+\alpha F_{s,b}]. Its reported total mass flow is incoming air flow, not total exhaust including fuel. These definitions should accompany exported values.

13.6 Why bypass flow can improve momentum efficiency

For a single fully expanded stream without added mass, thrust is ṁ(Ve−V0)\dot m(V_e-V_0), while kinetic-energy increase is ṁ(Ve2−V02)/2\dot m(V_e^2-V_0^2)/2. At a fixed thrust, accelerating more mass through a smaller velocity increment can reduce the required kinetic-energy increase. This is the basic motivation for bypass propulsion.

The argument does not mean that arbitrarily large bypass ratio always improves an engine. The fan requires work, inlet and nozzle losses consume pressure potential, and a real installation has size, drag and mass consequences. Only the first two effects are represented in this simplified cycle. The final design tradeoff cannot be inferred from a total-air specific-thrust value alone.

For two fully expanded streams, kinetic power per unit core air is

Δek=(1+f)V92+αV192−(1+α)V022. \Delta e_k=\frac{(1+f)V_9^2+\alpha V_{19}^2-(1+\alpha)V_0^2}{2}.

The constant-property model uses it for thermal and propulsive efficiencies. If either active stream is not fully expanded, the App omits that kinetic decomposition and retains overall thrust-power efficiency. A zero-mass bypass stream is excluded from the full-expansion efficiency condition, even though its nozzle calculation is still evaluated as noted above.

13.7 Worked separate-flow cycle

Choose an illustrative nonideal case: M0=0.8M_0=0.8, T0=250T_0=250 K, bypass ratio 3, fan ratio 1.5, core ratio 10 and turbine-entry temperature 1500 K. Use cp,c=1005c_{p,c}=1005, cp,h=1150c_{p,h}=1150 J/(kg K), gamma 1.4/1.33, heating value 43 MJ/kg, inlet recovery 0.97, burner pressure ratio 0.95 and both nozzle recoveries 0.98. Compressor and fan polytropic efficiencies are 0.90, turbine polytropic efficiency is 0.92, burner efficiency 0.98 and mechanical efficiency 0.99. Both streams expand to ambient pressure.

The inlet total temperature is 282 K. Direct evaluation gives:

Quantity Value
Core compressor outlet total temperature 585.746127 K
Bypass fan outlet total temperature 320.738501 K
Main fuel/core-air ratio 0.028116421
Turbine outlet total temperature 1139.421071 K
Core nozzle pressure ratio 4.12771119
Bypass nozzle pressure ratio 2.17355642
Core exit velocity 881.574083 m/s
Bypass exit velocity 358.124321 m/s

Freestream speed is 253.613880 m/s. The core contributes 652.746911 N s/kg of core air, and bypass contributes 104.510442 N s/kg of bypass air. Therefore

F/ṁc=652.746911+3(104.510442)=966.278236Ns/kg. F/\dot m_c=652.746911+3(104.510442)=966.278236\ \mathrm{N\,s/kg}.

Total-air specific thrust is 241.569559 N s/kg. With core air flow 10 kg/s, total air flow is 40 kg/s, thrust is 9.662782 kN, and fuel flow is approximately 0.281164 kg/s. TSFC is 29.097645 mg/(N s).

Multiplying the principal specific thrust by 10 kg/s would understate thrust by a factor of four. Either multiply it by total air flow or multiply thrust per core flow by core air flow. These are equivalent routes when the definitions are retained.

The example is direct arithmetic for the stated model, not a measured engine. Its absolute ambient pressure can be supplied independently when a dimensional station pressure is needed; the fully expanded specific results above depend on pressure ratios and temperature rather than an absolute pressure scale in this prescribed-flow calculation.

13.8 Variable-property fan and core architecture

The variable-property single-spool mode first compresses all air through the fan. Core air then passes through an additional compressor. Here the compressor pressure ratio is relative to the fan exit:

pt13=pt2πf,pt3=pt13πc,additional. p_{t13}=p_{t2}\pi_f,\qquad p_{t3}=p_{t13}\pi_{c,additional}.

Its work per unit core air is

wload=(1+α)wf+wc,additional. w_{\mathrm{load}}=(1+\alpha)w_f+w_{c,additional}.

This differs in notation from the constant-property closure because the core fan work is now explicit. In the constant-property convention it was already included in the core’s station-2-to-3 work. Neither formula should be transplanted without also changing the compressor reference station.

To align pressure paths, a comparison can set the constant-property core ratio to πfπc,additional\pi_f\pi_{c,additional}. This does not alone align work: the property functions and efficiency definitions also differ. The variable-property fan and compressor use explicit isentropic efficiencies and enthalpy/entropy inversions.

The gaseous main fuel ratio is specified per core air, and equilibrium determines burner temperature from the separate fuel and air feed enthalpies. The turbine extracts the combined shaft load from (1+f)(1+f) core gas. Its composition is frozen after the equilibrium chamber. Chapter 10 supplies the detailed thermodynamic steps.

13.9 Variable-property normalization and optional afterburning

The variable-property mode takes total inlet air flow as its dimensional input and obtains core flow as ṁa/(1+α)\dot m_a/(1+\alpha). This is the opposite input convention from the constant-property mode’s optional core-flow field, though the physical definitions are consistent.

For a separate core afterburner with additional ratio fABf_{AB}, the thrust per core air is

F/ṁc=(1+f+fAB)V9+αV19−(1+α)V0. F/\dot m_c=(1+f+f_{AB})V_9+\alpha V_{19}-(1+\alpha)V_0.

Both nozzles are fully expanded in this branch. Fuel flow is (f+fAB)ṁc(f+f_{AB})\dot m_c, and TSFC is total fuel ratio divided by thrust per core air. Afterburning affects the core exhaust and adds pressure loss after the turbine; it does not heat the bypass stream or alter the already closed fan work.

When bypass ratio is zero, the variable-property implementation skips the bypass nozzle evaluation. Its fan stage can still have a supplied pressure ratio and act on core air in the turbofan configuration. Therefore zero bypass alone is not identical to the turbojet configuration unless the compression paths are also aligned.

No thermal or propulsive efficiency is currently returned by this variable-property cycle. Its energy and shaft residuals describe closure, and its species fractions describe the final frozen nozzle mixture. The absence of a selected chemical-power denominator should not be filled by importing a heating value from another model without an explicit definition.

13.10 Limits of a separate-stream comparison

Separate flow avoids a mixer compatibility problem: there is no requirement that the two internal nozzle-entry streams share one static pressure plane. Each follows its own expansion to its selected exit condition. Mixing them upstream of a common nozzle requires new area, momentum and static-pressure conditions, not an average of the two velocities.

Both design modes are single-spool steady models. They do not solve a multispool operating schedule, component-map matching, cooling extraction, installed drag or fixed-geometry nozzle response. The constant-property ideal option additionally uses unit losses and cold properties throughout while neglecting fuel mass in turbine/exhaust balances; it requires both exit pressure ratios to be one.

A useful comparison reports bypass ratio, the compressor reference stations, fuel and thrust mass bases, both nozzle conditions and the physical flow scale. Those definitions reveal whether an improvement comes from a different core cycle, more bypass mass, a changed fan load or simply a changed normalization. Chapter 14 adds the conservation conditions needed when the two streams are deliberately combined.

14. Mixing and mixed-flow cycles

A common nozzle requires a common stream. Combining separate exhaust thrusts is not equivalent to mixing those streams upstream: a mixer must reconcile mass, species, energy, momentum and static pressure. Its outlet total pressure is a consequence of these constraints, rather than a mass-weighted average of inlet total pressures.

ThrustOne provides constant-property and frozen NASA9 mixing models. Both assume two subsonic incoming streams at equal static pressure and a constant total cross-sectional area. Both reconstruct a subsonic conservation outlet before applying an optional downstream total-pressure loss. This separation of planes is essential to interpreting the result.

14.1 The three distinct planes

The inlet plane contains adjacent core and bypass areas, AcA_c and AbA_b, with a shared static pressure pip_i. Their temperatures, velocities, total pressures and compositions can differ. The conservation outlet has one uniform state at total area A=Ac+AbA=A_c+A_b. A third, conceptual delivery state applies the user-specified additional total-pressure recovery.

The conservation outlet and the delivery state must not be combined into one implied static state. The additional recovery does not feed back into the inlet matching or the momentum balance. Its downstream static Mach is not separately reconstructed by this mixer.

A field named ideal_mixer_exit_mach refers to the conservation outlet before the additional pressure loss. The word ideal here does not mean that unlike-stream mixing is reversible or isentropic. Irreversibility can already arise in the conservation-based mixing process.

14.2 Matching the incoming static pressures

The input supplies both total states and the core Mach number. For constant properties,

Tc=Ttc1+(γc−1)Mc2/2,pi=ptc(Tc/Ttc)γc/(γc−1). T_c=\frac{T_{tc}}{1+(\gamma_c-1)M_c^2/2},\qquad p_i=p_{tc}(T_c/T_{tc})^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}.

The bypass Mach follows from its total pressure and that required common static pressure:

Mb=2γb−1[(ptb/pi)(γb−1)/γb−1]. M_b=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma_b-1} \left[(p_{tb}/p_i)^{(\gamma_b-1)/\gamma_b}-1\right]}.

A positive-flow bypass must have sufficient total pressure and a resulting Mach strictly below one. If its total pressure is below the required static pressure, an isentropic incoming state cannot be formed. If the required Mach is supersonic, it lies outside this two-subsonic-inlet model. Reducing downstream mixer recovery cannot repair either incompatibility, because it acts at a different plane.

After velocities and densities are known, continuity supplies areas:

Ac=ṁcρcVc,Ab=ṁbρbVb. A_c=\frac{\dot m_c}{\rho_cV_c},\qquad A_b=\frac{\dot m_b}{\rho_bV_b}.

Thus the input Mach and total states determine the required inlet geometry for the supplied flows. The model does not accept an arbitrary second inlet area and independently guarantee pressure matching.

For frozen NASA9 properties, the core static temperature is found from h(Tc)+Mc2af(Tc)2/2=htch(T_c)+M_c^2a_f(T_c)^2/2=h_{tc}, and entropy gives static pressure. The bypass static temperature is found at that pressure with its own total entropy; its velocity follows from enthalpy drop. These integrations replace constant-gamma powers while retaining the same physical matching condition.

14.3 Conserved mixture quantities

Total mass flow is ṁ=ṁc+ṁb\dot m=\dot m_c+\dot m_b. With adiabatic walls and no shaft work,

htm=ṁchtc+ṁbhtbṁ. h_{tm}=\frac{\dot m_ch_{tc}+\dot m_bh_{tb}}{\dot m}.

For a constant-area mixer without an imposed external axial force, the incoming axial momentum-plus-pressure flux is

J=piA+ṁcVc+ṁbVb. J=p_iA+\dot m_cV_c+\dot m_bV_b.

The uniform outlet must satisfy

ṁ=ρmVmA,hm+Vm2/2=htm,pmA+ṁVm=J. \dot m=\rho_mV_mA,\qquad h_m+V_m^2/2=h_{tm},\qquad p_mA+\dot mV_m=J.

The quantity JJ is not net engine thrust. It contains internal pressure forces and incoming momentum at the selected mixer boundary. Engine thrust requires a control volume extending to the external incoming and outgoing streams.

For constant effective properties, use mass-weighted cpc_p and RR, then form γ=cp/(cp−R)\gamma=c_p/(c_p-R). Averaging the two gammas directly does not generally reproduce this thermodynamic relation. Mixed total temperature is Ttm=htm/cpT_{tm}=h_{tm}/c_p under the shared cpTc_pT convention; it is a simple mass average only if the two heat capacities are equal.

For frozen species mixtures, sum actual species molar flows,

ṅi=ṁcxicW¯c+ṁbxibW¯b. \dot n_i=\frac{\dot m_cx_{ic}}{\overline W_c} +\frac{\dot m_bx_{ib}}{\overline W_b}.

Normalize their sum to obtain outlet mole fractions. Averaging mole fractions by mass flow would be wrong when molecular weights differ. No equilibrium chemistry is solved inside the frozen mixer, even if the combined mixture could react physically.

14.4 Deriving the constant-property velocity roots

Let B=J/ṁB=J/\dot m. The momentum equation gives pmA/ṁ=B−Vmp_mA/\dot m=B-V_m, while continuity and the ideal-gas law give pmA/ṁ=RTm/Vmp_mA/\dot m=RT_m/V_m. Using Tm=Ttm−Vm2/(2cp)T_m=T_{tm}-V_m^2/(2c_p),

(1−R2cp)Vm2−BVm+RTtm=0. \left(1-\frac{R}{2c_p}\right)V_m^2-BV_m+RT_{tm}=0.

Define a=1−R/(2cp)a=1-R/(2c_p). The discriminant is D=B2−4aRTtmD=B^2-4aRT_{tm}. A negative discriminant means there is no real outlet satisfying the declared momentum, energy and area conditions. It is not fixed by silently replacing the root with Mach one.

The lower-velocity root is evaluated in the cancellation-resistant form

Vm=2RTtmB+D. V_m=\frac{2RT_{tm}}{B+\sqrt D}.

The solver then recovers static temperature, pressure and Mach and checks the subsonic branch and conservation residuals. The constant-property implementation permits a tiny numerical tolerance around Mach one; the variable-property mixer explicitly requires an exit below one. Neither model supplies a supersonic mixer branch or a shock-train transition.

The NASA9 calculation instead calls the frozen flux-state reconstruction with mass, area, total enthalpy and momentum flux, explicitly selecting its subsonic branch. Chapter 26 develops that more general inversion.

14.5 Total-pressure recovery after conservation

At the reconstructed outlet, total temperature comes from the conserved total enthalpy. Total pressure is obtained by isentropically stagnating that outlet state. For constant properties,

ptm=pm(Ttm/Tm)γ/(γ−1). p_{tm}=p_m(T_{tm}/T_m)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

For NASA9 properties, the same operation uses entropy differences. Only after this calculation does the additional loss apply:

pt,delivered=πm,extraptm. p_{t,delivered}=\pi_{m,extra}p_{tm}.

The conserved Mach and momentum residual still describe the preceding outlet. Treating the delivered pressure as though it belonged to the same static state would mix two definitions. No extra temperature drop accompanies this adiabatic total-pressure loss.

14.6 Original mixer example

Choose two illustrative constant-property streams with cp=1000c_p=1000 J/(kg K), R=250R=250 J/(kg K), hence γ=4/3\gamma=4/3. Let core and bypass flow be 2 and 3 kg/s, total temperatures 800 and 400 K, and both inlet Mach numbers 0.4 at common static pressure 100 kPa. Their matching total pressures are equal because gamma and Mach are equal; their velocities are not.

The core static temperature is 779.220779 K and velocity 203.858877 m/s. Bypass static temperature is 389.610390 K and velocity 144.149994 m/s. Continuity gives areas 0.01911177 and 0.02027109 m². Consequently,

A=0.03938286m2,htm=560000J/kg,J=4778.453994N. A=0.03938286\ \mathrm{m^2},\quad h_{tm}=560000\ \mathrm{J/kg},\quad J=4778.453994\ \mathrm{N}.

The subsonic conservation root gives Vm=174.309256V_m=174.309256 m/s, Tm=544.808142T_m=544.808142 K, pm=99.203244p_m=99.203244 kPa and Mm=0.40903388M_m=0.40903388. Its total temperature is 560 K and total pressure is 110.739772 kPa. Applying an additional recovery of 0.96 gives delivered total pressure 106.310181 kPa.

These are direct analytical arithmetic results for an original teaching case. They demonstrate why outlet static pressure need not equal the matched inlet pressure, and why an averaged total temperature alone is insufficient to recover outlet velocity or pressure. They are not a measured mixer-performance dataset.

14.7 Embedding the mixer in a dual-spool cycle

The constant-property mixed turbofan places the fan before the core–bypass split. The fan therefore acts on all incoming air. Its high-pressure compressor acts only on core air, downstream of the fan. Let the core-air flow be the accounting unit and let α\alpha denote bypass air divided by core air. The main fuel ratio ff is also based on core air.

For cold-gas exponent ec=(γc−1)/γce_c=(\gamma_c-1)/\gamma_c, the fan and high-pressure compressor give

Tt13=Tt2πfec/ηpf,Tt3=Tt13πcHec/ηpc. T_{t13}=T_{t2}\pi_f^{e_c/\eta_{pf}},\qquad T_{t3}=T_{t13}\pi_{cH}^{e_c/\eta_{pc}}.

Here πcH\pi_{cH} is an additional pressure ratio after the fan. Thus pt4=pt2πfπcHπbp_{t4}=p_{t2}\pi_f\pi_{cH}\pi_b, rather than an expression in which the fan pressure rise disappears from the core path. The burner balance is

f=cphTt4−cpcTt3ηbQ−cphTt4. f=\frac{c_{ph}T_{t4}-c_{pc}T_{t3}} {\eta_bQ-c_{ph}T_{t4}}.

The high-pressure turbine drives the high-pressure compressor; the low-pressure turbine drives the fan. With separate mechanical efficiencies,

Tt45=Tt4−cpc(Tt3−Tt13)ηmH(1+f)cph, T_{t45}=T_{t4}-\frac{c_{pc}(T_{t3}-T_{t13})} {\eta_{mH}(1+f)c_{ph}},

Tt5=Tt45−(1+α)cpc(Tt13−Tt2)ηmL(1+f)cph. T_{t5}=T_{t45}-\frac{(1+\alpha)c_{pc}(T_{t13}-T_{t2})} {\eta_{mL}(1+f)c_{ph}}.

The factor 1+α1+\alpha in the second equation is essential: core air also passes through the fan. Conversely, only the hot core stream passes through these turbines. Assigning bypass mass to turbine power would overstate the available shaft work.

For hot-gas exponent eh=(γh−1)/γhe_h=(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h, the model uses turbine polytropic efficiency to infer the two pressure ratios:

πtH=(Tt45/Tt4)1/(ehηpt),πtL=(Tt5/Tt45)1/(ehηpt). \pi_{tH}=(T_{t45}/T_{t4})^{1/(e_h\eta_{pt})},\qquad \pi_{tL}=(T_{t5}/T_{t45})^{1/(e_h\eta_{pt})}.

The mixer receives core mass 1+f1+f at Tt5,pt4πtHπtLT_{t5},p_{t4}\pi_{tH}\pi_{tL}, and bypass mass α\alpha at Tt13,pt2πfT_{t13},p_{t2}\pi_f. Positive turbine temperatures alone do not guarantee an admissible engine. These two streams must also satisfy the static-pressure and subsonic conditions of Sections 14.2–14.4. A thermodynamically possible compressor–turbine calculation can therefore end with an incompatible mixer.

This calculation closes shaft power at a prescribed design point. It does not match two rotating component maps, determine shaft speeds, or solve a fixed installed mixer geometry. The mixer areas are consequences of the chosen states, flows and core Mach. A sequence of design-point calculations may imply a different area at every point.

14.8 Post-mixer afterburning and fuel bases

The incoming mass at the afterburner is

μ=1+f+α \mu=1+f+\alpha

per unit core air. Let fabf_{ab} be added afterburner fuel per unit core air, htmh_{tm} the mixed total enthalpy, and ht7=cp,abTt7h_{t7}=c_{p,ab}T_{t7} the target hot-gas total enthalpy in the effective constant-property convention. The energy balance is

μhtm+ηabfabQ=(μ+fab)ht7, \mu h_{tm}+\eta_{ab}f_{ab}Q=(\mu+f_{ab})h_{t7},

hence

fab=μcp,abTt7−cpmTtmηabQ−cp,abTt7. f_{ab}=\mu\frac{c_{p,ab}T_{t7}-c_{pm}T_{tm}} {\eta_{ab}Q-c_{p,ab}T_{t7}}.

Leaving out μ\mu changes the fuel reference to incoming mixed gas. That can be a useful ratio, but it cannot then be added directly to main-chamber ff. The App reports both fuel additions on the core-air basis.

The denominator must be positive, the required enthalpy increase nonnegative, and the target temperature cannot be below the incoming mixed temperature in this mode. Because the effective heat capacity may change across the afterburner, temperature ordering and enthalpy ordering are separate checks. This is an effective sensible-enthalpy model; it does not calculate an equilibrium species inventory.

As an original bookkeeping example, continue the 5 kg/s mixer case with incoming total enthalpy 560 kJ/kg. Specify an afterburner gas with cp=1200c_p=1200 J/(kg K), target total temperature 1000 K, Q=43Q=43 MJ/kg and efficiency 0.98. Direct substitution gives added fuel 0.0781632 kg/s. Relative to the 5 kg/s incoming mixture, the ratio is 0.0156326. If the 2 kg/s hot core stream contains main fuel, neither of these numbers is automatically the added fuel per kilogram of core air: the original core-air flow must first be recovered. This example deliberately preserves the distinction between a stand-alone mixer and an engine’s accounting basis.

Total pressure delivered to the nozzle is the conservation-derived mixed total pressure multiplied successively by the extra mixer recovery, afterburner pressure ratio when enabled, and nozzle pressure ratio. The nozzle uses the post-afterburner total temperature when afterburning is active. Applying its pressure loss upstream in the mixer matching calculation would define a different model.

14.9 Common-nozzle thrust

Write re=p0/p9r_e=p_0/p_9, R9=cp9(γ9−1)/γ9R_9=c_{p9}(\gamma_9-1)/\gamma_9, and pt9p_{t9} for total pressure after all specified downstream losses. The nozzle pressure ratio is pt9/p9=pt9re/p0p_{t9}/p_9=p_{t9}r_e/p_0. In the constant-property mode,

T9=Tt7(p9/pt9)(γ9−1)/γ9,V9=2cp9(Tt7−T9). T_9=T_{t7}(p_9/p_{t9})^{(\gamma_9-1)/\gamma_9},\qquad V_9=\sqrt{2c_{p9}(T_{t7}-T_9)}.

Let μe=1+f+α+fab\mu_e=1+f+\alpha+f_{ab}. Eliminating exit area through continuity gives thrust per unit core-air flow:

Fṁa,c=μeV9−(1+α)V0+μeR9T9V9(1−re). \frac{F}{\dot m_{a,c}}= \mu_eV_9-(1+\alpha)V_0 +\frac{\mu_eR_9T_9}{V_9}(1-r_e).

The pressure term has the sign expected physically: an exit pressure above ambient gives positive pressure thrust. Specific thrust displayed on the total-air basis is this result divided by 1+α1+\alpha. With a user-specified total-air flow, multiply total-air specific thrust by that flow to obtain force. Fuel consumption is

TSFC=f+fabF/ṁa,c. \mathrm{TSFC}=\frac{f+f_{ab}}{F/\dot m_{a,c}}.

Nozzle exit pressure is prescribed here; it is not the result of a supplied convergent–divergent nozzle geometry. A computed supersonic exit does not establish that a physical installed nozzle starts or remains attached. Thermal and propulsive efficiencies based on the kinetic-energy decomposition are provided only for full expansion. Overall efficiency uses thrust power divided by fuel chemical power, as discussed in Chapter 1.

14.10 The variable-property mixed branch

The NASA9 mixed-exhaust option belongs to the variable-property single-spool turbofan model. It is not the constant-property dual-spool calculation with a different value of gamma. The fan acts on all air, the core compressor follows the fan, and the shaft load combines both contributions. Component efficiencies use the variable-property mode’s isentropic convention. Main combustion determines equilibrium products from the prescribed fuel feed; subsequent turbine expansion retains that composition.

The frozen mixer combines the turbine-exit products with bypass air by species molar flow. It conserves their actual NASA9 total enthalpies, then reconstructs a subsonic outlet. No reaction is silently inserted at this mixing step. The resulting total pressure, after the additional recovery, is the pressure available to downstream combustion or expansion.

If post-mixer combustion is enabled, fuel is added on the core-air basis. Using formation-inclusive enthalpies, its target specific enthalpy is

ht7=μhtm+fabhfμ+fab. h_{t7}=\frac{\mu h_{tm}+f_{ab}h_f}{\mu+f_{ab}}.

The equilibrium calculation solves for the temperature and composition consistent with this enthalpy, the combined elemental inventory and the specified afterburner pressure. Do not add a lower heating value to this expression: the chemical reference energies already carry the reaction energy. The available fuel selections and bounded equilibrium species set remain those of the variable-property mode; mixing does not enlarge that chemistry model.

At zero post-mixer fuel, the implementation preserves the incoming frozen mixture and temperature while applying the specified pressure loss. It does not run an extra equilibrium relaxation merely because the afterburner option is present. With mixed exhaust selected, a separate pre-mixer core afterburner input is rejected; the supported location is downstream of mixing.

Finally, the variable-property nozzle expands the resulting frozen composition to ambient pressure. Its exit state is static, whereas the mixer delivery and afterburner states are total states. Its common-exhaust momentum balance is the fully expanded form of Section 14.9. The mode’s total-air input and core-air fuel basis must still be kept distinct.

14.11 Interpreting refusal and comparing designs

A simple incompatible case follows directly from the mixer example. Keep the core conditions that establish an inlet static pressure of 100 kPa, but set bypass total pressure to 95 kPa with positive bypass flow. An adiabatically accelerated bypass stream cannot have static pressure above its total pressure. The computed bypass Mach would therefore not be real. Raising an arbitrary downstream mixer recovery cannot repair this upstream incompatibility.

Setting bypass total pressure exactly to 100 kPa gives zero bypass speed at that matching pressure. Positive mass flow would then require unbounded area. This limiting case is also inadmissible, even though the pressure inequality alone no longer asks for an imaginary Mach. At the other extreme, a sufficiently high bypass total-to-static ratio implies a sonic or supersonic bypass inlet, outside the declared subsonic mixer branch.

These refusals identify a conflict among chosen cycle states, flow split and mixer assumptions. They do not establish that every physical mixer at those engine conditions is impossible. Changing core Mach changes the shared inlet static pressure; changing component pressure ratios changes the entering total states; a different geometry or flow regime would require a different model.

For comparisons, hold the accounting basis and external flight condition fixed. Compare fuel flow and net thrust on the same total-air flow, inspect whether the inferred mixer area changes, and retain the same nozzle-expansion assumption. Equal total-air specific thrust from two runs says nothing by itself about equal engine size or equal shaft speed.

Conservation residuals describe the algebraic closure, not the accuracy of turbulent mixing or an experimental loss correlation. The stand-alone mixers use their supplied dimensional mass flows. The constant-property cycle calls its mixer on a unit-core-air flow basis, so its raw mixer residuals belong to that normalized calculation. The variable-property cycle scales the embedded extensive mixer quantities to the actual core flow. Small residuals from these two outputs should not be compared without accounting for this distinction.

The chapter’s useful physical boundary is therefore explicit: the App can connect specified subsonic streams through a one-dimensional conservation mixer and use the delivered total state in a bounded engine cycle. It does not predict mixing length, temperature pattern, wall heat transfer, acoustics, or installed mixer drag.

15. Turbofan components and off-design

A component calculation asks what happens across one specified device. An off-design calculation asks which component states can coexist when the engine’s reference constraints are retained. The second problem cannot be solved by choosing every component outlet independently: shaft power and flow capacity couple the choices.

ThrustOne exposes both problems. The turbofan component mode provides fan, booster, bypass-nozzle and two-stream mixer subproblems. Its separate-flow off-design mode uses a reference-normalized dual-spool approximation with convergent exhaust nozzles. It does not use the optional component maps to solve an operating line. Keeping these two capabilities distinct is necessary when interpreting the word matching.

15.1 Boundaries of the component problems

The fan and booster selections both call the shared compressor thermodynamics. Their different names specify their intended engine location, not different aerodynamic blade models. A fan normally processes all incoming air in the cycles considered here; a core booster processes core air. The independent component calculation does not infer either mass allocation or shaft coupling.

For a constant-property compressor with pressure ratio π\pi, polytropic efficiency ηp\eta_p, inlet total temperature TtiT_{ti}, and e=(γ−1)/γe=(\gamma-1)/\gamma,

Tto=Ttiπe/ηp,w=cp(Tto−Tti). T_{to}=T_{ti}\pi^{e/\eta_p},\qquad w=c_p(T_{to}-T_{ti}).

Specific work ww is measured in J/kg of gas crossing that component. If a fan requires 60 kJ/kg and processes 40 kg/s, its fluid power is 2.4 MW. If a booster requires the same specific work but processes only 10 kg/s, its fluid power is 0.6 MW. A shared temperature rise does not imply a shared shaft load.

The frozen variable-property option instead uses an isentropic outlet enthalpy and the specified isentropic efficiency, then inverts enthalpy for the actual outlet temperature. Chapter 11 supplies that derivation and the optional constant-property compressor-map scaling. The same map domain, normalized-coordinate and no-extrapolation restrictions apply when that shared compressor calculation is reached through the fan or booster selection. A frozen-property calculation does not silently reuse that constant-property map option.

The bypass-nozzle component also delegates to the common nozzle solver. It uses the specified total state, pressure recovery and requested exit pressure. This independent calculation is not restricted to the convergent-nozzle law used by the off-design engine below. A supersonic result from a prescribed-pressure component nozzle must not be inserted into a convergent-exit interpretation.

For the mixer selection, the constant-property inputs or the supplied variable-property mixer input determine which conservation solver runs. Both match inlet static pressures and select a subsonic outlet as developed in Chapter 14. The mixer requires two complete stream descriptions; a fan pressure ratio alone cannot determine them.

15.2 The reference engine and its flowpath

The off-design model assumes equal fan and low-pressure-compressor outlet states. Thus the core proceeds through a low-pressure compression rise equal to the fan rise, followed by an additional high-pressure compressor. The bypass stream leaves after the fan. The high-pressure turbine powers the high-pressure compressor, and the low-pressure turbine powers the fan and the equivalent low-pressure core compression.

                         bypass air ───────────────→ convergent exit 19
                        /
air → inlet → fan / LP compression
                        \
                         core → HP compressor → burner → HP turbine
                                                             ↓
                                                   LP turbine → exit 9

HP shaft: HP turbine ↔ HP compressor
LP shaft: LP turbine ↔ fan and equivalent LP core compression

Reference data include the flight state, turbine inlet temperature, component pressure and temperature ratios, bypass ratio, two nozzle exit Mach numbers and total-air mass flow. Current inputs supply the new flight state and turbine inlet temperature, together with retained gas properties, efficiencies and pressure losses. High-pressure turbine temperature and pressure ratios are fixed inputs. They are not discovered from a turbine map.

The two high-pressure turbine stations are assumed choked to support the normalized closure. This is a modeling assumption: the program does not reconstruct internal turbine throat areas and confirm choking from local measured geometry. The two exhaust nozzles, in contrast, may become unchoked and are explicitly switched between subsonic and sonic exit states.

Use a subscript RR for reference values, τ=Tto/Tti\tau=T_{to}/T_{ti} for component total-temperature ratios, and π=pto/pti\pi=p_{to}/p_{ti} for total-pressure ratios. Define

τr=1+γc−12M02,τλ=cphTt4cpcT0,H=τλ/τrτλR/τrR. \tau_r=1+\frac{\gamma_c-1}{2}M_0^2,\qquad \tau_\lambda=\frac{c_{ph}T_{t4}}{c_{pc}T_0},\qquad H=\frac{\tau_\lambda/\tau_r}{\tau_{\lambda R}/\tau_{rR}}.

The dimensionless HH compares turbine inlet thermal level to incoming total-air thermal level. It is not simply the ratio of the two turbine inlet temperatures when the flight state changes.

15.3 Convergent-nozzle closure

Let q=pt/p0q=p_t/p_0 denote the total-to-ambient pressure ratio after nozzle losses. Forward flow requires q>1q>1. For a convergent nozzle, the exit is its minimum-area plane, giving the critical ratio

q*=(γ+12)γ/(γ−1). q_* = \left(\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

The actual total-to-exit pressure ratio is qe=min⁡(q,q*)q_e=\min(q,q_*), so

Me=2γ−1(qe(γ−1)/γ−1),p0pe=qeq. M_e=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma-1}(q_e^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}-1)}, \qquad \frac{p_0}{p_e}=\frac{q_e}{q}.

Below choking, pe=p0p_e=p_0 and Me<1M_e<1. Above choking, Me=1M_e=1, while exit pressure remains above ambient. The model retains the resulting pressure thrust. It does not continue an isentropic expansion to a supersonic exit inside a convergent nozzle.

For an original example, take γ=1.4\gamma=1.4, cp=1000c_p=1000 J/(kg K), and Tt=360T_t=360 K. At q=1.5q=1.5, direct arithmetic gives Me=0.783659M_e=0.783659, Te=320.6201T_e=320.6201 K and Ve=280.6419V_e=280.6419 m/s, with no pressure thrust. At q=3q=3, the critical ratio is 1.892929, giving Me=1M_e=1, Te=300T_e=300 K and Ve=346.4102V_e=346.4102 m/s. Now p0/pe=0.630976p_0/p_e=0.630976. Further increasing total pressure at fixed total temperature increases mass capacity and pressure thrust, rather than raising this exit Mach above one.

15.4 How fixed flow areas create coupling

For a fixed gas, mass flow can be written

ṁ=AptTtγRΦ(M),Φ(M)=M(1+γ−12M2)−γ+12(γ−1). \dot m=\frac{A p_t}{\sqrt{T_t}}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{R}}\, \Phi(M),\qquad \Phi(M)=M\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{-\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

Constants cancel when comparing the same gas and station with its reference. This is why the implementation’s mass-flow function omits γ/R\sqrt{\gamma/R}. Comparing different gases would require restoring it.

The bypass/core flow ratio becomes

α=αRπcH,RπcHHτfRτfΦc(M19)Φc(M19R). \alpha=\alpha_R\frac{\pi_{cH,R}}{\pi_{cH}} \sqrt{H\frac{\tau_{fR}}{\tau_f}} \frac{\Phi_c(M_{19})}{\Phi_c(M_{19R})}.

This relation combines bypass-nozzle capacity with the assumed choked core capacity. It makes bypass ratio an output. Holding it independently fixed would overconstrain this model. The fan nozzle can unchoke, changing Φc(M19)\Phi_c(M_{19}) even before any change in the component pressure ratios is considered.

The low-pressure turbine pressure ratio obeys

πtL=πtL,RτtLτtL,RΦh(M9R)Φh(M9), \pi_{tL}=\pi_{tL,R}\sqrt{\frac{\tau_{tL}}{\tau_{tL,R}}} \frac{\Phi_h(M_{9R})}{\Phi_h(M_9)},

with the isentropic-efficiency relation

τtL=1−ηtL(1−πtL(γh−1)/γh). \tau_{tL}=1-\eta_{tL}\left(1-\pi_{tL}^{(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h}\right).

If the core exit remains choked in both states, its mass-flow-function ratio is one. This removes one source of variation but does not make every engine variable constant. Unchoking restores direct feedback from exhaust conditions into the turbine relation.

The retained normalized equations neglect changes in some fuel-mass factors used in deriving reference flow and power ratios. Fuel is recovered later for thrust and consumption. Thus fuel mass appearing in final exhaust momentum does not make the preceding matching equations exact fuel-inclusive component matching.

15.5 Shaft relations and the unknowns

The high-pressure spool relation is

τcH=1+HτfRτf(τcH,R−1),πcH=[1+ηcH(τcH−1)]γc/(γc−1). \tau_{cH}=1+H\frac{\tau_{fR}}{\tau_f}(\tau_{cH,R}-1), \qquad \pi_{cH}=[1+\eta_{cH}(\tau_{cH}-1)]^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}.

The factor τfR/τf\tau_{fR}/\tau_f accounts for the high-pressure compressor’s changing inlet temperature. Omitting it incorrectly treats that compressor as though it still ingested the inlet state ahead of the fan.

The low-pressure spool gives

τf=1+1−τtL1−τtL,RH1+αR1+α(τfR−1),πf=[1+ηf(τf−1)]γc/(γc−1). \begin{gathered} \tau_f=1+\frac{1-\tau_{tL}}{1-\tau_{tL,R}} H\frac{1+\alpha_R}{1+\alpha}(\tau_{fR}-1),\\ \pi_f=[1+\eta_f(\tau_f-1)]^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}. \end{gathered}

An increasing bypass ratio spreads available low-spool work over more air, reducing the rise available per kilogram. These relations use component isentropic efficiencies, unlike the polytropic inputs of several design-point modes.

Nine quantities are mutually dependent: the fan, high-pressure compressor and low-pressure turbine pressure and temperature ratios, bypass ratio, and the two exit Mach numbers. The program starts from reference fan temperature ratio and low-pressure turbine pressure ratio, evaluates the dependent state, and repeatedly updates the fan and low-turbine relations.

Its convergence measure is the largest successive change in those nine quantities, each divided by the larger of the new magnitude and one. A value below 10−910^{-9} ends iteration, with a limit of 1000 updates. This is a fixed-point change criterion. It is not a dimensional shaft-power residual, nor proof of uniqueness or experimental agreement. Invalid intermediate states can terminate the calculation before the iteration limit.

15.6 A transparent reference-closure example

A useful original check of the equations is a deliberately consistent algebraic reference. Set both gas gammas to 1.4, all component efficiencies to one, τfR=1.2\tau_{fR}=1.2, τcH,R=2\tau_{cH,R}=2, τtL,R=5/6\tau_{tL,R}=5/6, and αR=3\alpha_R=3. Define pressure ratios from these temperatures: πfR=1.892929\pi_{fR}=1.892929, πcH,R=11.313708\pi_{cH,R}=11.313708, and πtL,R=0.528282\pi_{tL,R}=0.528282. Choose fixed high-turbine pressure ratio 0.83.5=0.4579470.8^{3.5}=0.457947, no pressure losses, static flight and both reference exit Mach numbers equal to one.

At the unchanged flight and turbine-temperature state, H=1H=1. The high-compressor equation gives

τcH=1+(1.2/1.2)(2−1)=2. \tau_{cH}=1+(1.2/1.2)(2-1)=2.

The bypass mass-flow-function ratio is one and the pressure-ratio factor is one, so α=3\alpha=3. The low-spool equation then gives

τf=1+1−5/61−5/61+31+3(1.2−1)=1.2. \tau_f=1+\frac{1-5/6}{1-5/6}\frac{1+3}{1+3}(1.2-1)=1.2.

Both nozzle branches remain sonic: the bypass is exactly at the critical pressure ratio, while the product of core pressure ratios exceeds it. The low-turbine update also returns its reference value. Every normalized update therefore reproduces the declared point.

This is a constructed demonstration of reference consistency, not a measured engine or a numerical fixture generated by the App. It isolates an important user responsibility: reference pressure ratios, temperature ratios and efficiencies must describe the same state. Changing only πfR\pi_{fR} while leaving its temperature ratio and efficiency inconsistent removes this fixed point. Passing the input range checks alone does not guarantee coherent reference data.

15.7 Recovering dimensional performance

After matching, the fuel ratio follows the main-burner balance:

f=τλ−τrτfτcHηbQ/(cpcT0)−τλ. f=\frac{\tau_\lambda-\tau_r\tau_f\tau_{cH}} {\eta_bQ/(c_{pc}T_0)-\tau_\lambda}.

A positive denominator and positive heating are required. Total air flow is recovered as

ṁaṁaR=1+α1+αRp0πrπdπfπcHp0RπrRπdRπfRπcH,RTt4,RTt4. \frac{\dot m_a}{\dot m_{aR}}= \frac{1+\alpha}{1+\alpha_R} \frac{p_0\pi_r\pi_d\pi_f\pi_{cH}} {p_{0R}\pi_{rR}\pi_{dR}\pi_{fR}\pi_{cH,R}} \sqrt{\frac{T_{t4,R}}{T_{t4}}}.

Current inlet recovery includes the specified Mach-dependent empirical factor. The stored reference recovery is used directly in the denominator, so it must represent the intended complete reference recovery. A raw maximum inlet recovery is not interchangeable with a recovered reference value at supersonic flight.

The core exit temperature is obtained from Tt4τtHτtLT_{t4}\tau_{tH}\tau_{tL} and its convergent-nozzle pressure ratio. The bypass total temperature is T0τrτfT_0\tau_r\tau_f. Apply the nozzle equations to obtain both static temperatures and velocities, then the separate-stream momentum balance of Chapter 13, including each pressure term.

Specific thrust is based on total incoming air; fuel ratio is based on core air. Consequently,

F=ṁaFs,TSFC=f(1+α)Fs. F=\dot m_a F_s,\qquad \mathrm{TSFC}=\frac{f}{(1+\alpha)F_s}.

The speed outputs are estimated mechanical ratios from temperature-scaled compressor work. For example,

NfNfR=T0τrT0RτrRπfec−1πfRec−1. \frac{N_f}{N_{fR}}= \sqrt{\frac{T_0\tau_r}{T_{0R}\tau_{rR}} \frac{\pi_f^{e_c}-1}{\pi_{fR}^{e_c}-1}}.

The high-spool expression additionally includes τf/τfR\tau_f/\tau_{fR} and uses high-compressor pressure ratios. These are not corrected map speeds, and they do not establish blade stress or a permissible operating-speed limit.

15.8 Refusal and interpretation

A nozzle total pressure at or below ambient admits no positive forward-flow solution under this closure. A low-turbine pressure ratio outside zero to one contradicts expansion; a fan temperature ratio at or below one contradicts the required compressing branch. Nonpositive fuel, insufficient heating value, nonpositive net thrust and nonconverged iteration also cause refusal.

The reference bypass ratio must be positive and reference exit Mach numbers lie above zero and at most one. This off-design mode does not offer a zero-bypass turbojet limit through a zero reference bypass input. That boundary differs from some design-point modes and is intentional in interpreting the accepted input domain.

A successful result establishes a fixed point within the specified approximation. It does not supply component surge prediction, a mixed-flow operating line, cooling and bleed schedules, shaft transients or installed inlet interaction. The App omits kinetic-decomposition thermal and propulsive efficiencies when either active nozzle has pressure thrust; overall efficiency still follows thrust power divided by fuel power.

Use this model to understand how a declared reference engine redistributes flow and work as flight or thermal level changes. Use the independent component mode to inspect a particular transformation. Neither should be described as a general replacement for a complete engine performance deck.

16. Rocket chamber and nozzle performance

A rocket carries the material that becomes its exhaust. There is no captured-air momentum subtraction in the thrust-chamber calculation. The chamber supplies a high-pressure, high-enthalpy reservoir; the nozzle converts part of that enthalpy into directed kinetic energy. Ambient pressure changes the external pressure force and can change the physical flow regime, even though the simplest attached-flow calculation retains the same internal isentropic solution.

This chapter develops the explicit constant-property model shared by ThrustOne’s thrust-chamber performance and stand-alone nozzle performance modes. The gas temperature, molecular weight and ratio of specific heats are supplied inputs. They are not inferred from a propellant name or mixture ratio. Equilibrium and frozen variable-property chemistry are separate calculations developed in Chapter 17.

16.1 Reservoir state, throat and exit

The chamber pressure pcp_c and temperature TcT_c in this model act as nozzle-inlet total conditions. A sufficiently large, slowly moving chamber makes static and total conditions nearly equal, but the distinction is physical rather than merely a naming convention. A finite-velocity chamber plane requires the separate conversion of Chapter 18.

       reservoir / chamber           sonic throat          supersonic exit
       total state pc, Tc                 At                    Ae
   ┌─────────────────────┐              /  \                 /     |
   │ prescribed gas      │─────────────/    \───────────────/      | → Ve
   │ composition model   │                         expansion       | pe
   └─────────────────────┘                                      ambient pa

                       ε = Ae / At          F = ṁ Ve + (pe − pa) Ae

The assumed flow is steady, one-dimensional, adiabatic and isentropic, with constant γ>1\gamma>1 and gas constant RR. In the explicit-property model, frozen means the effective gas properties remain fixed; it does not mean a species-resolved NASA calculation has been performed. There is no wall-friction, boundary-layer displacement, shock or separated-flow reconstruction in this equation chain.

Molecular weight W¯\overline W is entered in kg/kmol. The App uses

R=RuW¯,Ru=8314.462618J/(kmolK),cp=γRγ−1. R=\frac{R_u}{\overline W},\qquad R_u=8314.462618\ \mathrm{J/(kmol\,K)},\qquad c_p=\frac{\gamma R}{\gamma-1}.

Using a mol-based gas constant with a kmol-based molecular weight introduces a factor of one thousand in RR. All subsequent temperature-to-velocity and choked-flow results would then be wrong.

16.2 Deriving the critical mass flow

Continuity gives ṁ=ρVA\dot m=\rho VA. Substitute ρ=p/(RT)\rho=p/(RT), V=MγRTV=M\sqrt{\gamma RT}, and the static-to-total relations from Chapter 2:

ṁA=pcRTcγM(1+γ−12M2)−γ+12(γ−1). \frac{\dot m}{A}= \frac{p_c}{\sqrt{RT_c}}\sqrt\gamma\, M\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)^{-\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

The mass flux has its maximum at M=1M=1. At the choked throat,

ṁi=pcAtRTcΓ(γ),Γ(γ)=γ(2γ+1)γ+12(γ−1). \dot m_i=\frac{p_cA_t}{\sqrt{RT_c}}\,\Gamma(\gamma), \qquad \Gamma(\gamma)=\sqrt\gamma \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

The subscript ii marks the ideal reference. Pressure times area has units of force; division by a velocity has units of mass flow. This dimensional check also explains the usefulness of characteristic velocity:

ci*=pcAtṁi=RTcΓ(γ). c_i^*=\frac{p_cA_t}{\dot m_i} =\frac{\sqrt{RT_c}}{\Gamma(\gamma)}.

Characteristic velocity has units of m/s but is not the gas velocity at the throat or at the exit. It expresses the relation between chamber pressure, throat area and mass flow. Its star belongs to the conventional name; it should not be read as a claim that it equals sonic speed.

At fixed R,Tc,γR,T_c,\gamma, ideal mass flow is proportional to pcAtp_cA_t. Temperature raises the specific energy available for expansion but reduces density and choked mass flux at fixed chamber pressure. These two effects must be distinguished when interpreting a hotter chamber.

16.3 Geometry selects the expansion branch

Define expansion ratio ϵ=Ae/At\epsilon=A_e/A_t. Equating the exit and sonic mass-flow expressions produces

ϵ=1Me[2γ+1(1+γ−12Me2)]γ+12(γ−1). \epsilon=\frac{1}{M_e} \left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1} \left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_e^2\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

For ϵ>1\epsilon>1, this relation has subsonic and supersonic roots. The rocket performance modes select the supersonic root. An area ratio of one gives the sonic state. A subsonic root is mathematically meaningful elsewhere, such as a chamber contraction calculation, but it is not an alternative exhaust branch silently selected by these modes.

Once MeM_e is known,

Te=Tc1+(γ−1)Me2/2,pepc=(1+γ−12Me2)−γ/(γ−1). T_e=\frac{T_c}{1+(\gamma-1)M_e^2/2},\qquad \frac{p_e}{p_c}=\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_e^2\right)^{-\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

The velocity can be reconstructed either from Mach or from energy:

Ve,i=MeγRTe=2γγ−1RTc[1−(pepc)(γ−1)/γ]. V_{e,i}=M_e\sqrt{\gamma RT_e} =\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma-1}RT_c \left[1-\left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\right]}.

The second form follows from Ve2/2=cp(Tc−Te)V_e^2/2=c_p(T_c-T_e). It shows that an arbitrarily large expansion ratio cannot produce an arbitrarily large velocity. Within the constant-property model, velocity approaches 2cpTc\sqrt{2c_pT_c} as exit pressure approaches zero, while the required area diverges. The zero-temperature mathematical limit is not an attainable material or chemistry model.

The App inverts area ratio by a bracketed search restricted to the requested branch. Near ϵ=1\epsilon=1, the two roots merge and area changes only weakly with Mach, as discussed in Chapter 2. It treats an area ratio within 10−1210^{-12} above one as sonic. Iteration failure is reported rather than replacing a failed root by an arbitrary large Mach.

16.4 Equivalent nozzle input choices

Area ratio is not the only way to specify the same ideal expansion. ThrustOne also accepts exit Mach, exit static pressure, chamber-to-exit pressure ratio, or an altitude at which the nozzle is ideally expanded. Each is converted into the supersonic area ratio before performance is calculated.

A specified exit pressure gives

Me2=2γ−1[(pcpe)(γ−1)/γ−1]. M_e^2=\frac{2}{\gamma-1} \left[\left(\frac{p_c}{p_e}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}-1\right].

A real positive Mach is not sufficient: this expansion-nozzle interface requires Me≥1M_e\ge1. Thus an exit pressure below chamber pressure can still be rejected if the implied Mach is subsonic. Equivalently, the accepted chamber-to-exit ratio must reach the sonic critical ratio.

The optimum-altitude input sets exit pressure equal to the standard-atmosphere pressure at that design altitude. The separate environment input sets the ambient pressure used for the current thrust calculation. Designing for one altitude and evaluating at another is therefore a meaningful and supported distinction. Choosing an optimum altitude does not continuously resize the nozzle whenever the environment changes.

Vacuum is an environment choice, pa=0p_a=0. It is not a finite-area nozzle choice with pe=0p_e=0. A finite expansion ratio leaves positive exit pressure and consequently retains a positive vacuum pressure-thrust term.

16.5 Thrust coefficient separates geometry from scale

The ideal thrust balance is

Fi=ṁiVe,i+(pe−pa)Ae. F_i=\dot m_iV_{e,i}+(p_e-p_a)A_e.

Divide by pcAtp_cA_t, substitute ṁi=pcAt/ci*\dot m_i=p_cA_t/c_i^*, and define

CF,i=CF,m+CF,p,CF,m=Ve,ici*,CF,p=(pepc−papc)ϵ. C_{F,i}=C_{F,m}+C_{F,p},\qquad C_{F,m}=\frac{V_{e,i}}{c_i^*},\qquad C_{F,p}=\left(\frac{p_e}{p_c}-\frac{p_a}{p_c}\right)\epsilon.

Both contributions are dimensionless. The momentum coefficient depends on the gas exponent and expansion. The pressure coefficient also depends on the external pressure relative to chamber pressure. No captured-air term belongs in this chamber model; whole-vehicle drag remains a separate problem.

If pe>pap_e>p_a, the nozzle is underexpanded and pressure thrust is positive. If pe=pap_e=p_a, pressure thrust vanishes, but momentum thrust remains. If pe<pap_e<p_a, the negative pressure term reduces total thrust. A negative pressure contribution does not by itself make total thrust negative.

For a fixed attached nozzle state,

CF,vac=CF,m+pepcϵ,CF,vac−CF,i=papcϵ. C_{F,vac}=C_{F,m}+\frac{p_e}{p_c}\epsilon, \qquad C_{F,vac}-C_{F,i}=\frac{p_a}{p_c}\epsilon.

This is a comparison of the same geometry in different environments. It is not a comparison between two nozzles separately optimized for each environment.

16.6 Why ideal expansion is optimal

Consider varying exit area along a family of ideal, attached expansions while holding reservoir state and choked throat flow fixed. Differentiate the thrust expression:

dFi=ṁidVe+Aedpe+(pe−pa)dAe. dF_i=\dot m_i\,dV_e+A_e\,dp_e+(p_e-p_a)\,dA_e.

The inviscid momentum relation along the expansion is dp=−ρVdVdp=-\rho V\,dV. Continuity gives ṁi=ρVA\dot m_i=\rho VA, so the first two terms cancel:

dFi=(pe−pa)dAe. dF_i=(p_e-p_a)\,dA_e.

Adding exit area improves ideal thrust while the exit pressure exceeds ambient. Once it falls below ambient, further area reduces thrust in this family. The stationary point occurs at pe=pap_e=p_a.

This result does not include nozzle mass, length, cooling, flight trajectory or separation. It is an ideal local thrust optimum under specified constraints. In vacuum the derivative remains positive for finite positive exit pressure, so there is no finite-area optimum from this criterion alone. A practical vacuum nozzle needs additional constraints that this performance model does not optimize.

16.7 Effective exhaust velocity and specific impulse

Define effective exhaust velocity ceff=F/ṁc_{eff}=F/\dot m. It includes pressure thrust and therefore generally differs from local exit velocity. Specific impulse is

Isp=Fṁg0=ceffg0,ceff=c*CF, I_{sp}=\frac{F}{\dot m g_0}=\frac{c_{eff}}{g_0},\qquad c_{eff}=c^*C_F,

where g0=9.80665g_0=9.80665 m/s² is the fixed standard-gravity conversion, not the local gravitational acceleration at the operating altitude. Specific impulse is reported in seconds. A change in local gravity does not change the same engine’s reported IspI_{sp} under this definition.

These relations divide performance into two useful questions: how much mass crosses a given pressure–throat scale, and how effectively that scale produces thrust. They are definitions and bookkeeping relations, not proof that combustion and nozzle losses are physically independent.

16.8 The App’s two performance factors

The explicit-property solver accepts a characteristic-velocity factor ηc*\eta_{c^*} and a thrust-coefficient factor ηCF\eta_{C_F}, each in (0,1](0,1]. It applies them as

c*=ηc*ci*,CF=ηCF(CF,m+CF,p), c^*=\eta_{c^*}c_i^*,\qquad C_F=\eta_{C_F}(C_{F,m}+C_{F,p}),

ṁ=pcAtηc*ci*,F=ηCFCF,ipcAt,Isp=ηc*ηCFci*CF,ig0. \dot m=\frac{p_cA_t}{\eta_{c^*}c_i^*},\qquad F=\eta_{C_F}C_{F,i}p_cA_t,\qquad I_{sp}=\eta_{c^*}\eta_{C_F}\frac{c_i^*C_{F,i}}{g_0}.

At fixed chamber pressure and throat area, reducing ηc*\eta_{c^*} increases the inferred mass flow. This follows from the definition; it should not be described as an increase in combustion quality. At fixed input mass flow, the same change instead reduces the resolved throat area. Always state which scale is held fixed before discussing an efficiency trend.

The thrust-coefficient factor multiplies the sum of momentum and pressure terms, including the vacuum result. The separately reported cf_momentum and cf_pressure remain the ideal reference components. They must be multiplied by the factor before their sum is compared to the reported final cf.

Crucially, these empirical performance factors do not reconstruct a new exit static state. The reported exit Mach, temperature, pressure and velocity remain the ideal thermodynamic reference, and exit_velocity equals exit_velocity_ideal. Combining that reference velocity with the corrected mass flow in the raw momentum equation will generally not recover the corrected thrust. Use F=CFpcAtF=C_Fp_cA_t and F/ṁ=c*CFF/\dot m=c^*C_F for the corrected performance. A physically resolved lossy nozzle would need additional state equations beyond these two factors.

16.9 Original numerical example

Choose an illustrative gas with γ=1.25\gamma=1.25, R=400R=400 J/(kg K), and Tc=3200T_c=3200 K. Its corresponding molecular weight is 20.786156545 kg/kmol. Set pc=5p_c=5 MPa, At=0.002A_t=0.002 m², ambient pressure 100 kPa and exit Mach 3. These are teaching inputs, not a named propellant or measured motor.

First, the static-to-total temperature factor is 1+0.25(32)/2=2.1251+0.25(3^2)/2=2.125. It gives Te=1505.882353T_e=1505.882353 K and pe=115391.902p_e=115391.902 Pa. The area–Mach relation gives ϵ=5.831866839\epsilon=5.831866839, so Ae=0.011663734A_e=0.011663734 m². The ideal exit velocity is 2603.165494 m/s.

Next, Γ=0.658064792\Gamma=0.658064792, and ci*=1719.239297c_i^*=1719.239297 m/s. The pressure–throat scale is pcAt=10000p_cA_t=10000 N. Therefore ideal mass flow is 5.816525959 kg/s. The momentum coefficient is 1.514137967, and the positive pressure coefficient is 0.017952705. Their sum is 1.532090672, giving thrust 15320.906717 N and specific impulse 268.596360 s.

The exit pressure slightly exceeds ambient; the pressure term adds approximately 179.53 N to the momentum thrust. In vacuum the coefficient becomes 1.648728009. The change in force is paAep_aA_e, approximately 1166.37 N, with the same ideal internal nozzle state.

Now retain the same pressure, temperature and geometry, but set ηc*=0.95\eta_{c^*}=0.95 and ηCF=0.97\eta_{C_F}=0.97. The reported mass flow becomes 6.122658904 kg/s, thrust 14861.279516 N, and specific impulse 247.511545 s. The exit reference velocity remains 2603.165494 m/s. These numbers illustrate the exact performance-factor convention; they are direct analytical arithmetic, not App-generated evidence of experimental agreement.

16.10 Scale choices and the two mode names

The same dimensionless nozzle can be assigned a throat area or throat diameter. For a circular throat, At=πdt2/4A_t=\pi d_t^2/4. Alternatively, the user can specify mass flow, sea-level thrust or vacuum thrust. The first requires At=ṁc*/pcA_t=\dot m c^*/p_c. A thrust target requires At=Ftarget/(CFpc)A_t=F_{target}/(C_Fp_c), with the coefficient evaluated in the target environment.

The sea-level-thrust scale uses 101325 Pa for sizing even when the separately selected current environment differs. Vacuum-thrust scale uses zero ambient pressure. After resolving area, the calculation evaluates the current environment. Therefore a nozzle sized to produce a chosen sea-level thrust need not display that same force when the current environment is vacuum.

Scale-free mode reports specific performance without absolute thrust, mass flow or areas. Its internal unit-area evaluation is a normalization device, not a declaration that the user has designed a one-square-metre throat.

The current thrust-chamber and stand-alone nozzle mode names share this explicit-property performance chain. The nozzle selection does not infer a chamber’s chemical state, and the thrust-chamber selection does not add an injector, feed system or cooling calculation. Scale choices are resolved before either result is returned.

16.11 Back pressure and the boundary of the result

The model warns when exit pressure falls below ambient. It also adds a possible-separation warning when pe<pa/2.5p_e<p_a/2.5. This is a fixed screening threshold, not a geometry-resolved separation calculation or a universal operating boundary. No separation location, side load or corrected post-separation thrust is returned.

The solver continues the attached supersonic calculation while its coefficient stays positive. If back pressure makes that coefficient nonpositive, it rejects the state. A positive coefficient alone does not establish that the nozzle can physically sustain the assumed supersonic attached branch. In particular, the explicit model does not solve startup, an internal normal shock or an unchoked alternative when back pressure is high.

Report overexpanded results as conditional ideal predictions and retain their warnings. Do not use the presence of a numeric result to erase the flow-regime assumptions. Chapters17–20 add thermochemistry, chamber geometry, contours and parameter studies while preserving this distinction between a computed reference and a complete physical engine.

17. Equilibrium and frozen rocket expansion

A hot chamber mixture can contain dissociated species as well as stable combustion products. As pressure and temperature change through a nozzle, the preferred chemical composition changes. Whether the gas can approach that composition depends on reaction times compared with the available flow time. An equilibrium calculation assumes continuous chemical adjustment; a frozen calculation suppresses adjustment. Neither assumption supplies a finite-rate chemical history.

ThrustOne provides three thermochemical rocket paths: composition frozen from the chamber, equilibrium maintained through the nozzle, and equilibrium followed by freezing at a user-specified area. They use formation-inclusive NASA9 gas properties and the bounded gas-phase equilibrium model introduced in Chapters 5–6. This chapter follows their energy, entropy and mass-flow closures and explains why their throat definitions must differ.

17.1 Two independent chamber decisions

First decide how chamber temperature is obtained. In a specified-temperature calculation, chamber pressure and temperature are inputs. The calculation determines compatible properties or equilibrium composition at that state; it does not prove that a supplied feed can produce that temperature.

Alternatively, the chamber temperature can be obtained from a constant-pressure enthalpy balance. With negligible chamber velocity,

hc=hin+q, h_c=h_{in}+q,

where hinh_{in} is the gaseous inlet mixture’s specific enthalpy and qq is heat added per unit inlet mass. The solver searches the supplied temperature bracket for equilibrium products with the target enthalpy. Setting q=0q=0 means adiabatic conversion of the prescribed gaseous feed. Chemical energy is already included in species formation enthalpies; adding a separate heating value would count it twice.

The second decision concerns chamber composition. The frozen rocket mode permits either equilibrium at the chamber temperature and pressure or a directly specified frozen mixture. Solving chamber temperature from the equilibrium enthalpy balance requires chamber equilibrium to be enabled. The equilibrium and specified-freeze-area nozzle modes also require an equilibrium chamber.

These decisions should not be collapsed into the phrase combustion calculation. Specifying a hot mixture, equilibrating a specified hot mixture, and solving an adiabatic reaction temperature are different problems. The current gaseous enthalpy closure excludes liquid vaporization, injector pressure losses, two-phase feed properties and condensed combustion products.

17.2 What is preserved along each path

For steady adiabatic flow with no shaft work,

h+V22=hc. h+\frac{V^2}{2}=h_c.

For the ideal reversible expansion,

s=sc. s=s_c.

These are specific enthalpy in J/kg and specific entropy in J/(kg K), referenced consistently to the chamber state. All paths preserve elemental inventory. A frozen path additionally preserves every species amount relative to the total composition. An equilibrium path preserves elements while allowing the species distribution and total mole count to change.

chamber equilibrium ──┬── freeze composition ── frozen throat ── frozen exit
                      │
                      ├── equilibrium throat ── equilibrium exit
                      │
                      └── equilibrium throat ── specified freeze area
                                                     └── frozen exit

The frozen and equilibrium paths can have different throat mass fluxes even for the same chamber pressure, temperature, elemental inventory and physical throat area. Thus comparing exit velocity alone does not compare thrust at a fixed throat scale. Both mass flow and pressure thrust must be retained.

17.3 Frozen throat from energy and sound speed

For fixed composition 𝒙c\mathbf x_c, define frozen sound speed

af2(T)=γf(T)RcT,γf(T)=cp(T)cp(T)−Rc. a_f^2(T)=\gamma_f(T)R_cT,\qquad \gamma_f(T)=\frac{c_p(T)}{c_p(T)-R_c}.

Although species fractions and RcR_c remain fixed, heat capacity and gamma can vary with temperature. At the frozen sonic throat, V*=af(T*)V_*=a_f(T_*). Substitution into energy gives the scalar equation

h(T*,𝒙c)+af2(T*,𝒙c)2=hc. h(T_*,\mathbf x_c)+\frac{a_f^2(T_*,\mathbf x_c)}{2}=h_c.

The App brackets this temperature between the common lower data limit and chamber temperature. It then finds the throat pressure from entropy conservation. With a reference pressure prp_r,

s(T,p,𝒙c)=s(T,pr,𝒙c)−Rcln⁡(p/pr), s(T,p,\mathbf x_c)=s(T,p_r,\mathbf x_c)-R_c\ln(p/p_r),

so

p*=prexp⁡[s(T*,pr,𝒙c)−scRc]. p_*=p_r\exp\left[\frac{s(T_*,p_r,\mathbf x_c)-s_c}{R_c}\right].

This expression includes the mixture’s entropy convention consistently. It does not replace the variable-property expansion by a power law using a locally evaluated gamma. Mass flow follows from ṁ=ρ*afAt\dot m=\rho_*a_fA_t. The frozen chamber-to-nozzle mode requires ambient pressure below this critical static pressure before proceeding with its choked expansion assumption.

17.4 Frozen expansion from an already moving inlet

The shared frozen-nozzle solver also has a stand-alone scramjet-family entry. Its temperature and pressure are static inlet quantities, and its inlet Mach is at least one. Consequently its conserved total enthalpy is

ht=hi+Mi2af,i22, h_t=h_i+\frac{M_i^2a_{f,i}^2}{2},

not simply hih_i. Its mass flow is ρiMiaf,iAi\rho_iM_ia_{f,i}A_i. A rocket calls this same solver using the sonic throat just calculated; a stand-alone nozzle can start farther downstream at a supersonic state.

At any trial temperature, entropy determines pressure and energy determines velocity:

p(T)=prexp⁡[(s(T,pr)−si)/R],V(T)=2[ht−h(T)]. p(T)=p_r\exp[(s(T,p_r)-s_i)/R],\qquad V(T)=\sqrt{2[h_t-h(T)]}.

Continuity then supplies the implied area,

A(T)=ṁρ(T)V(T). A(T)=\frac{\dot m}{\rho(T)V(T)}.

For each requested downstream area, the solver inverts this relation on the supersonic branch, decreasing temperature as area increases. It rejects a state that leaves this branch or requires a temperature below the property-data range. No extrapolation is used to manufacture a large-area exit.

The displayed profile uses linearly increasing area along the specified length. Length assigns an axial coordinate; it does not add friction, reaction residence time or a wall-pressure solution. Two lengths with the same inlet and exit areas have the same ideal endpoint thermodynamics in this model.

17.5 Constructing an equilibrium isentrope

For equilibrium expansion, composition is a function of both temperature and pressure, subject to the fixed elemental inventory. At each trial temperature TT, the App solves

𝒙=𝒙eq(T,p;𝒃),s(T,p,𝒙)=sc. \mathbf x=\mathbf x_{eq}(T,p;\mathbf b),\qquad s(T,p,\mathbf x)=s_c.

The pressure root cannot be found by treating composition as constant in an entropy pressure correction. Each pressure trial requires its own equilibrium composition and thermodynamic properties. The implementation brackets pressure progressively below chamber pressure and searches in logarithmic pressure, preserving positive pressure.

Once the entropy root is found,

V(T)=2[hc−h(T,p(T),𝒙(T))],j(T)=ρ(T)V(T). V(T)=\sqrt{2[h_c-h(T,p(T),\mathbf x(T))]},\qquad j(T)=\rho(T)V(T).

Here jj is mass flux in kg/(m² s). The chamber endpoint has zero velocity and zero flux. Moving down the isentrope initially increases velocity fast enough to increase flux; farther into expansion, decreasing density eventually dominates. The interior maximum determines the critical flux.

The chemistry calculation remains the included ideal-gas species model. No equilibrium with unlisted ions, liquids or solids is implied. An equilibrium residual belongs to that declared system; it does not establish that omitted species are physically negligible under every possible input.

17.6 Why frozen Mach is not the equilibrium choking test

For a reversible equilibrium path with fixed elemental composition, the thermodynamic relation is dh=dp/ρdh=dp/\rho. Differentiating energy gives VdV=−dp/ρV\,dV=-dp/\rho. Introduce the equilibrium sound speed through

aeq2=(∂p∂ρ)s,𝒃,eq. a_{eq}^2=\left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial\rho}\right)_{s,\mathbf b,eq}.

Then the derivative of mass flux along that path is

djdρ=V+ρdVdρ=V−aeq2V. \frac{dj}{d\rho}=V+\rho\frac{dV}{d\rho} =V-\frac{a_{eq}^2}{V}.

At an interior stationary flux, V=aeqV=a_{eq}. This is the chemical-equilibrium choking condition. By contrast, γfRT\sqrt{\gamma_fRT} holds local species fixed during the perturbation. It generally represents a different derivative because chemical rearrangement contributes to the equilibrium response.

The App therefore maximizes ρV\rho V on its computed equilibrium isentrope instead of imposing V/af=1V/a_f=1. It reports throat_frozen_mach and exit_frozen_mach using local frozen sound speed. A throat value different from one is not by itself a failed choking calculation. It must not be relabeled equilibrium Mach.

The search first samples the allowed temperature interval, requires a single sampled interior peak, and refines its bracket. An endpoint maximum or multiple sampled critical candidates is rejected. This guards the intended branch but does not prove that an arbitrarily complicated isentrope is globally unimodal. The current solver is explicitly restricted to this single-maximum regime.

17.7 Area selects the downstream equilibrium state

Once critical flux j*j_* is known, ṁ=j*At\dot m=j_*A_t. For exit expansion ratio ϵ\epsilon, the target is

je=j*ϵ. j_e=\frac{j_*}{\epsilon}.

The same flux below its maximum can occur on two sides of the throat. The nozzle selects the lower-temperature downstream branch, searching between its minimum allowed temperature and the throat. At ϵ=1\epsilon=1, it returns the throat directly. It checks the area/mass-flow residual after inversion.

The user-specified minimum nozzle temperature bounds the equilibrium path search. If the critical peak is outside the interval, or the desired exit flux requires a still colder state, the result is refused. Increasing area without extending physically supported thermodynamic data cannot be resolved by changing an iteration count.

Ambient pressure must lie below critical static pressure, but this condition alone is not a complete test for attached supersonic flow throughout a long nozzle. The thermochemical modes do not reconstruct shocks or post-separation states. Their final thrust expression remains conditional on the ideal expansion path.

17.8 A specified freezing area

In the partially frozen model, equilibrium is followed to ϵf=Af/At\epsilon_f=A_f/A_t, where 1<ϵf≤ϵe1<\epsilon_f\le\epsilon_e. The transition transfers the equilibrium temperature, pressure, velocity, mass flow and full composition to the frozen solver. No heat or impulse is introduced at that interface. Total enthalpy and entropy remain continuous, and the downstream species fractions are held at their transition values.

The frozen continuation requires Vf/af,f>1V_f/a_{f,f}>1. Being downstream of the equilibrium critical flux does not automatically satisfy this separate frozen-branch condition. A selected point too close to the equilibrium throat may therefore be refused, with a request for a farther downstream freeze area.

When freeze area equals exit area, there is no downstream frozen segment. The endpoint is the equilibrium exit, provided the frozen-Mach eligibility condition passes. Freezing exactly at the throat is not accepted by this interface; the input must be strictly greater than one. The chamber-frozen model is a separate path with its own throat and mass flow, not a shortcut obtained by assigning zero downstream equilibrium length.

The freeze location is prescribed. No reaction mechanism, Damköhler-number criterion, residence-time estimate or chemical relaxation equation predicts it here. Varying it is a sensitivity study of an assumption, not a simulation of where a real gas ceases to equilibrate.

17.9 Original inert-limit example

An inert monatomic ideal gas makes the relation between these paths transparent. Take γ=5/3\gamma=5/3, R=8314.462618/39.948=208.132137R=8314.462618/39.948=208.132137 J/(kg K), cp=2.5Rc_p=2.5R, chamber temperature 2400 K, chamber pressure 1 MPa and throat area 0.001 m². These define an analytical constant-property teaching limit; the numbers are not represented as a run of the full NASA9 equilibrium solver.

Because no species conversion is available in this constructed gas, equilibrium and frozen thermodynamic derivatives coincide. The throat temperature is 1800 K, throat pressure 487139.290 Pa and critical mass flux 1027.476053 kg/(m² s). Thus mass flow is 1.027476053 kg/s and characteristic velocity 973.258692 m/s.

Choose exit Mach 2. The area–Mach relation gives ϵ=1.53125\epsilon=1.53125; the exit temperature is 1028.571429 K, pressure 120242.511 Pa and velocity 1194.651329 m/s. The equilibrium flux-maximum construction and frozen sonic construction reduce to the same result because both use the same constant-composition isentrope. An arbitrary freeze point between throat and exit cannot change this gas’s composition or endpoint state.

This example explains what should disappear in the inert limit: the distinction between frozen and equilibrium sound speeds, the chemical shift in critical flux, and sensitivity to the chosen freeze location. It does not demonstrate how much recombination occurs in a reacting hydrogen–oxygen mixture. That requires an actual equilibrium calculation with its declared species and temperature bounds.

17.10 Interpreting reactive comparisons

Dissociation stores part of the mixture energy in chemical form. As equilibrium shifts toward more strongly bound species, energy may become available for thermal and kinetic changes. Frozen expansion cannot redistribute that stored energy through changing composition. This explains why equilibrium and frozen performance can differ without an external heat source.

Do not turn that explanation into a universal ranking of every reported quantity. Exit temperature, pressure, mass flow, velocity and thrust are coupled. Comparisons must retain the same chamber closure, elemental inventory, throat area, exit area and environment. In particular, comparing a specified-temperature chamber in one path with an adiabatic enthalpy-closed chamber in another changes two assumptions simultaneously.

Nor do equilibrium and chamber-frozen results constitute rigorous upper and lower bounds on every real engine. Finite-rate chemistry, viscous losses, heat transfer, two-phase effects and separated flow add physical mechanisms absent from both ideal calculations. The partially frozen path is an intermediate chemical assumption, not a correction for those other losses.

17.11 Reading the outputs

For all thermochemical rocket paths, thrust is evaluated from

F=ṁVe+(pe−pa)Ae,c*=pcAtṁ,CF=FpcAt,Isp=Fṁg0. \begin{gathered} F=\dot mV_e+(p_e-p_a)A_e,\\ c^*=\frac{p_cA_t}{\dot m},\\ C_F=\frac{F}{p_cA_t},\\ I_{sp}=\frac{F}{\dot m g_0}. \end{gathered}

The explicit-property empirical factors of Chapter 16 are not automatically applied to these paths. Their results follow the computed gas states and ideal momentum balance. Unlike the explicit-property solver’s positive-coefficient check, these routines check final finiteness without imposing a general positive-thrust acceptance rule. A finite output is therefore not an assertion of useful propulsion at that back pressure.

The stand-alone frozen nozzle reports gross_thrust. It lacks a complete upstream engine control volume and cannot subtract captured-air momentum on its own. The rocket wrapper can identify this same exhaust force as chamber thrust, while a full airbreathing engine must add the appropriate inlet accounting.

Energy residuals measure consistency of total enthalpy; entropy residuals measure the isentropic closure; area residuals measure flow compatibility. They answer different questions. A displayed zero equilibrium residual when chamber equilibrium is disabled indicates that no equilibrium solve was performed, not that the prescribed composition was proved to be an equilibrium mixture.

Profiles show composition changes on the equilibrium segment and fixed fractions after freezing. Their axial coordinate is generated from the prescribed linear area variation, not from a solved nozzle wall contour. A completed value confirms that the chosen mathematical path reached its requested endpoint. It does not establish chemical-rate accuracy, attached flow or measured hardware performance.

18. Chamber and convergent geometry

A chamber-volume calculation and a chamber-flow calculation answer different questions. The first assigns space upstream of the throat. The second relates a moving gas at a finite-area plane to a total state and a choked throat. Neither, by itself, predicts how an injector vaporizes propellant or how completely combustion occurs.

ThrustOne separates these tasks into three modes: equivalent chamber sizing, cylindrical chamber plus convergent-section sizing, and finite contraction from an explicitly static chamber plane. This chapter develops their equations and the boundaries between them. The separation prevents a geometrical length from being mistaken for a combustion-performance prediction, or a static pressure from being silently reused as a total pressure.

18.1 Characteristic length is a volume measure

Let AtA_t be throat area and VcV_c the chamber volume measured from the injector face to the throat plane. Characteristic length is
