L*=VcAt. L^*=\frac{V_c}{A_t}.

It has units of length, but it is not generally the physical injector-to-throat distance. Different chamber radii and convergent shapes can have the same volume and hence the same L*L^*. The input is a prescribed volume criterion; the App does not derive its required value from propellant chemistry.

Define contraction ratio

χ=AcAt>1, \chi=\frac{A_c}{A_t}>1,

where AcA_c is the cylindrical chamber cross-section. For circular sections,

rt=At/π,rc=rtχ. r_t=\sqrt{A_t/\pi},\qquad r_c=r_t\sqrt\chi.

An equivalent cylinder occupying the entire prescribed volume would have length

Leq=VcAc=L*χ. L_{eq}=\frac{V_c}{A_c}=\frac{L^*}{\chi}.

This is precisely the equivalent-sizing interpretation. It does not reserve part of the volume for a convergent section. Adding a convergent volume to that equivalent cylinder without shortening the cylinder would exceed the original L*L^* requirement.

18.2 Why volume is not residence time

As a rough background estimate, a uniform gas occupying volume VcV_c would have an inventory ρcVc\rho_cV_c and inventory-to-flow time tinv=ρcVc/ṁt_{inv}=\rho_cV_c/\dot m. Substituting Vc=L*AtV_c=L^*A_t, ρc=pc/(RTc)\rho_c=p_c/(RT_c) and ṁ=pcAt/c*\dot m=p_cA_t/c^* gives

tinv≈L*c*RTc. t_{inv}\approx\frac{L^*c^*}{RT_c}.

The units are seconds. This derivation explains why a volume normalized by throat area can be useful when comparing similar chambers. It also exposes the assumptions: approximately uniform density, a compatible pressure convention and a steady mass flow.

Actual spray penetration, vaporization, mixing, recirculation and reaction times need not equal this inventory time. Spatially varying density and a finite convergent volume further weaken the uniform approximation. The current sizing modes do not calculate these processes or certify a minimum combustion residence time. A supplied L*L^* must therefore carry its own engineering rationale outside the calculation.

18.3 Allocating a conical convergent section

The explicit geometry mode uses a circular cylinder followed by a straight conical frustum terminating at the throat. Let θc\theta_c be the convergent half-angle measured from the axis. The required convergent length is

Lconv=rc−rttan⁡θc,0<θc<π2. L_{conv}=\frac{r_c-r_t}{\tan\theta_c},\qquad 0<\theta_c<\frac{\pi}{2}.

The full included angle is 2θc2\theta_c. Confusing the included angle with the half-angle changes both length and allocated volume.

To derive the volume rather than memorize a frustum formula, measure xx from the start of convergence and write

r(x)=rc−rc−rtLconvx. r(x)=r_c-\frac{r_c-r_t}{L_{conv}}x.

Integrating the circular cross-section gives

Vconv=∫0Lconvπr(x)2dx=πLconv3(rc2+rcrt+rt2). V_{conv}=\int_0^{L_{conv}}\pi r(x)^2\,dx =\frac{\pi L_{conv}}{3}(r_c^2+r_cr_t+r_t^2).

The cylinder receives the remaining volume:

Vcyl=L*At−Vconv,Lcyl=VcylAc,Ltotal=Lcyl+Lconv. V_{cyl}=L^*A_t-V_{conv},\qquad L_{cyl}=\frac{V_{cyl}}{A_c},\qquad L_{total}=L_{cyl}+L_{conv}.

The cylindrical volume fraction is Vcyl/(L*At)V_{cyl}/(L^*A_t). It is a geometric fraction, not the fraction of heat release occurring in the cylinder.

injector face       start of convergence                 throat plane
     |                       |                                |
     |<------ Lcyl --------->|<----------- Lconv ------------>|
     ┌───────────────────────┐
     │       radius rc       └───────────────╲
axis ├────────────────────────────────────────╲───────────────→
     │                    cylindrical volume    throat radius rt

             Vcyl + Vconv = L* At

The sketch identifies volume boundaries, not a manufactured wall contour. The current profile joins cylinder and frustum directly without a fillet or throat rounding. Those omissions matter for mechanical and thermal design but do not change the declared elementary volume allocation.

18.4 The minimum admissible characteristic length

The convergent section alone must fit inside the prescribed volume. Therefore

L*≥VconvAt. L^*\ge\frac{V_{conv}}{A_t}.

Substitute rc=rtχr_c=r_t\sqrt\chi and At=πrt2A_t=\pi r_t^2:

Lmin*=rt(χ−1)(χ+χ+1)3tan⁡θc=rt(χ3/2−1)3tan⁡θc. L^*_{min}=\frac{r_t(\sqrt\chi-1)(\chi+\sqrt\chi+1)}{3\tan\theta_c} =\frac{r_t(\chi^{3/2}-1)}{3\tan\theta_c}.

This compact relation shows three effects. A larger throat at the same contraction and angle requires a larger absolute L*L^* just to contain the convergent volume. Increasing contraction ratio raises that minimum. A shallower half-angle also raises it because the convergent section becomes longer.

At equality, the cylinder has zero length and the whole volume is the frustum. The implementation accepts that geometric limit. Below it, a negative cylinder length would be required, so the input is rejected. It does not clip the length to zero and silently change the requested volume.

This also explains why scaling a chamber is not always simple. If every linear dimension is multiplied by kk, volume scales as k3k^3, throat area as k2k^2, and L*L^* as kk. Holding L*L^* fixed while increasing throat diameter does not preserve geometric similarity.

18.5 Original volume-allocation example

Choose throat radius 25 mm, contraction ratio 4, characteristic length 0.6 m and convergent half-angle 45°. These are illustrative geometric inputs, not a recommended chamber design. The throat area is 0.0019634954 m²; chamber radius is 50 mm and chamber area0.0078539816 m².

The convergent length is 25 mm. Its volume is 0.0001145372 m³, or0.114537 L. The total required volume is 0.0011780972 m³, or1.178097 L. Thus the cylinder receives 1.063560 L and has length 0.1354167 m. Injector-to-throat length is 0.1604167 m.

The equivalent-cylinder result for the same volume would instead be Leq=0.6/4=0.15L_{eq}=0.6/4=0.15 m. It is neither the actual cylindrical segment length nor the complete cylinder-plus-convergent length. The tapered section contains less volume per unit axial length than the full chamber cylinder, which is why allocating it increases total physical length beyond the equivalent value.

For this throat and angle, Lmin*=0.0583333L^*_{min}=0.0583333 m. Requesting L*=0.05L^*=0.05 m would provide only 0.098175 L, less than the convergent section’s0.114537 L. Refusal is the correct geometric outcome. Reducing a numerical tolerance would not solve that incompatibility; the requested geometry or volume must change.

18.6 A finite-area chamber plane has velocity

Now consider the separate flow problem. Inputs are throat area, contraction ratio, constant γ\gamma, specific gas constant RR, and chamber-plane static pressure pcp_c and temperature TcT_c. Assume an isentropic subsonic contraction to a choked throat. The chamber Mach is the subsonic solution of

χ=1Mc[2γ+1(1+γ−12Mc2)]γ+12(γ−1). \chi=\frac{1}{M_c} \left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1} \left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_c^2\right)\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

The selected root lies strictly between zero and one. A supersonic root would describe a different branch and is not an alternative chamber solution in this mode. The implementation solves the logarithm of the area relation, which avoids directly raising large factors during the search. Contraction ratio must be greater than one; the exactly sonic chamber plane is outside this interface.

Once McM_c is obtained,

Vc=McγRTc,Ttc=Tc(1+γ−12Mc2), V_c=M_c\sqrt{\gamma RT_c},\quad T_{tc}=T_c\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_c^2\right),

ptc=pc(1+γ−12Mc2)γ/(γ−1). p_{tc}=p_c\left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M_c^2\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

The total pressure is higher than the supplied static pressure because the static plane contains kinetic energy. This is an isentropic state conversion. It must not be confused with a combustion-induced total-pressure loss or with a correction between two different heat-addition chamber models.

At large contraction ratio, McM_c approaches zero and static and total states approach each other. At a contraction ratio close to one, kinetic energy is substantial and treating static pressure as reservoir pressure produces a meaningful flow error.

18.7 Mass continuity links the two planes

The chamber-plane flow is

ṁc=pcRTcVcAc. \dot m_c=\frac{p_c}{RT_c}V_cA_c.

Using the recovered total state, the choked-throat expression is

ṁ*=AtptcγRTtc(2γ+1)γ+12(γ−1). \dot m_*= A_tp_{tc}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{RT_{tc}}} \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

These must agree because the area–Mach equation was derived from that same isentropic continuity relation. The reported mass residual is ṁc−ṁ*\dot m_c-\dot m_*, in kg/s; its internal acceptance uses the residual relative to throat flow. The separate area residual is dimensionless. Neither residual measures combustion completeness or real nozzle discharge behavior.

The current mode does not insert its total state into other rocket calculations automatically. Its inputs belong to an independent static-plane problem. Transferring its results to a performance calculation requires deliberately using the recovered total pressure and temperature, with compatible gas properties and scale. Reusing its original static inputs as total conditions would erase the very distinction the mode computes.

18.8 Original static-to-total example

Use the same throat radius 25 mm for scale, but specify a separate flow case with γ=1.4\gamma=1.4, R=300R=300 J/(kg K), static temperature 2000 K and static pressure 3 MPa. Choose a contraction ratio 2.96352; this was constructed from Mc=0.2M_c=0.2 using the area relation, so the subsonic inverse is transparent.

The temperature factor is 1.008, giving total temperature 2016 K. The total pressure is 3.084843363 MPa and the chamber velocity 183.303028 m/s. Continuity gives mass flow 5.333071369 kg/s. The throat calculation using the recovered total state gives the same analytical flow.

If static pressure and temperature were mistakenly inserted directly as the throat reservoir state, the inferred mass flow would be smaller by the factor

ṁ*ṁwrong=ptcpcTcTtc=1.008γ/(γ−1)−1/2=1.0083. \frac{\dot m_*}{\dot m_{wrong}}= \frac{p_{tc}}{p_c}\sqrt{\frac{T_c}{T_{tc}}} =1.008^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)-1/2}=1.008^3.

The ratio is about 1.02419. Even this modest chamber Mach therefore produces a roughly 2.4% change relative to that mistaken flow estimate. This original example tests the meaning of the input planes; it is not a measured finite-contraction combustion correction.

18.9 What the App combines, and what it keeps separate

Equivalent sizing and cylinder-plus-convergent sizing obtain their absolute throat scale from the resolved explicit-property rocket definition. Scale-free input is rejected for these dimensions. Because the current routing first resolves the base performance point, an invalid base rocket input can prevent geometry output even when the elementary geometry formulas themselves would be meaningful. The geometric mode does not repair that upstream input.

Equivalent sizing retains the base performance results and adds equivalent dimensions. The explicit convergent allocation returns its volume and length metrics with a simple radius profile. Neither applies a finite-contraction total-pressure correction to the base thrust calculation. The static-plane finite-contraction mode uses its own independent inputs and does not require that base performance route.

For the explicit geometry, radians enter the mathematical kernel; the UI half-angle in degrees is converted before evaluation. Volumes are m³ and lengths m. Reporting a value in litres or millimetres requires the corresponding unit conversion, not a new geometric model.

The finite-contraction mode warns that finite-velocity heat-addition losses can matter at small contraction ratios, but does not calculate them. The volume modes exclude evaporation, combustion completion and injector design. Wall thickness, cooling passages, throat erosion, manufacturing fillets and structural life are also outside the result. The correct deliverable is a clearly defined ideal state or volume allocation, with enough information to use it consistently in the next calculation.

19. Nozzle reference contours

An expansion ratio fixes the inlet-to-exit area relationship of an ideal nozzle. It does not fix the wall shape between those planes. A long cone and a shorter bell can share the same throat and exit areas while having different wall angles, lengths and real flow losses. The one-dimensional performance calculation cannot distinguish those effects unless an additional model supplies them.

ThrustOne’s contour mode constructs reference geometry: a straight cone or a circular throat turn followed by a quadratic parabolic arc. The bell’s endpoint angles are explicit inputs. No method-of-characteristics solution, empirical angle chart or thrust optimization selects them. This chapter develops the construction so that the resulting curve can be interpreted as geometry rather than as an implied aerodynamic optimum.

19.1 Coordinates and scale

Use axial coordinate xx, radius rr, and the throat plane as x=0x=0. For circular throat area AtA_t and expansion ratio ϵ\epsilon,

rt=At/π,re=rtϵ. r_t=\sqrt{A_t/\pi},\qquad r_e=r_t\sqrt\epsilon.

A radius profile determines area through A(x)=πr(x)2A(x)=\pi r(x)^2. The plotted curve is the gas-side reference radius, not wall thickness or an outer structural envelope. The model includes no cooling-channel allowance or manufacturing tolerance.

Absolute scale is required for the App’s exported contour coordinates. The scale-free performance option therefore cannot supply this profile. Scaling every radius and axial coordinate by a common factor preserves shape and expansion ratio, while all areas scale by the square of that factor.

19.2 The straight conical section

For a cone with half-angle θ\theta measured from the axis,

Lcone=re−rttan⁡θ,r(x)=rt+xtan⁡θ,0≤x≤Lcone. L_{cone}=\frac{r_e-r_t}{\tan\theta},\qquad r(x)=r_t+x\tan\theta,\quad 0\le x\le L_{cone}.

This is the divergent section only. It begins at the throat radius but does not include a smooth throat arc or the upstream convergent chamber. In the App, points are spaced uniformly in axial coordinate. The resulting area is quadratic in xx, even though radius is linear.

At fixed end radii, a smaller angle increases length. A very large angle shortens the cone but does not establish that a physically attached, efficient exhaust follows it. The numerical domain is an angle strictly between zero and90°, with finite positive throat area. It is a geometric domain rather than a recommended design-angle range.

The conical implementation permits expansion ratio one through the underlying performance definition. In that limiting case its length is zero and its points coincide at the throat radius. This is a degenerate profile, not a finite divergent nozzle. The bell interface instead requires expansion ratio strictly greater than one.

19.3 Meaning of the conical divergence factor

The contour output includes

λcone=1+cos⁡θ2. \lambda_{cone}=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}.

A simple background interpretation comes from averaging axial projection over an idealized spherical outflow cap. If momentum per solid angle and speed are uniform, the mean axial projection is

∫0θcos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdϕ∫0θsin⁡ϕdϕ=sin⁡2θ2(1−cos⁡θ)=1+cos⁡θ2. \frac{\int_0^\theta\cos\phi\sin\phi\,d\phi} {\int_0^\theta\sin\phi\,d\phi} =\frac{\sin^2\theta}{2(1-\cos\theta)} =\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}.

This derivation explains the geometric projection factor and its assumptions. It does not establish a resolved velocity distribution on a real conical nozzle’s exit plane. At15° the factor is 0.9829629; it tends to one as angle tends to zero, while cone length diverges for nonzero radius change.

The App reports this factor separately and does not multiply it into the already prescribed thrust-coefficient efficiency. Applying it again without knowing what that supplied efficiency represents could double-count a loss. A reference contour calculation is not an instruction to replace every nozzle loss by this single projection factor.

19.4 Bell length and the throat-turn circle

The bell uses a length fraction fL>0f_L>0 relative to a 15° reference cone:

L=fLre−rttan⁡15∘. L=f_L\frac{r_e-r_t}{\tan 15^\circ}.

The input is a multiplier:0.8 means80% of that reference length. The implementation does not impose an upper bound of one. A value greater than one is geometrically possible if the remaining constraints permit it; the word fraction does not itself force a shorter contour.

Let the throat-turn radius be ra=kartr_a=k_ar_t, with positive supplied ratio kak_a. Starting at (0,rt)(0,r_t), parameterize the circular arc by its tangent angle ϕ\phi:

x(ϕ)=rasin⁡ϕ,r(ϕ)=rt+ra(1−cos⁡ϕ),0≤ϕ≤θn. x(\phi)=r_a\sin\phi,\qquad r(\phi)=r_t+r_a(1-\cos\phi),\qquad 0\le\phi\le\theta_n.

Differentiating gives dr/dx=tan⁡ϕdr/dx=\tan\phi. The throat tangent is axial, and the join point NN has prescribed tangent angle θn\theta_n:

xn=rasin⁡θn,rn=rt+ra(1−cos⁡θn). x_n=r_a\sin\theta_n,\qquad r_n=r_t+r_a(1-\cos\theta_n).

The circular segment is downstream of the throat. It does not construct an upstream rounding or join to the convergent geometry of Chapter18.

19.5 The tangent intersection fixes the parabola

Let the exit be E=(L,re)E=(L,r_e), with tangent slope me=tan⁡θem_e=\tan\theta_e. The join tangent has slope mn=tan⁡θnm_n=\tan\theta_n. Their intersection Q=(xq,rq)Q=(x_q,r_q) satisfies

rq=rn+mn(xq−xn)=re+me(xq−L). r_q=r_n+m_n(x_q-x_n)=r_e+m_e(x_q-L).

Solving these two line equations gives

xq=re−rn+mnxn−meLmn−me,rq=rn+mn(xq−xn). x_q=\frac{r_e-r_n+m_nx_n-m_eL}{m_n-m_e},\qquad r_q=r_n+m_n(x_q-x_n).

With N,Q,EN,Q,E as control points, the quadratic curve is

𝑩(t)=(1−t)2𝑵+2(1−t)t𝑸+t2𝑬,0≤t≤1. \mathbf B(t)=(1-t)^2\mathbf N+2(1-t)t\mathbf Q+t^2\mathbf E, \qquad0\le t\le1.

Its derivative is 2[(1−t)(𝑸−𝑵)+t(𝑬−𝑸)]2[(1-t)(\mathbf Q-\mathbf N)+t(\mathbf E-\mathbf Q)]. Therefore its initial tangent lies along NQNQ, and its exit tangent along QEQE. These tangents have exactly the two prescribed slopes. The curve generally does not pass through QQ; QQ controls direction and shape.

A nondegenerate quadratic curve of this form is a parabolic arc in its own orientation. It need not be representable as a simple quadratic radius function r=ax2+bx+cr=ax^2+bx+c in the nozzle’s chosen axes. The parametric representation avoids imposing that extra restriction.

The arc and parabola share position and tangent at NN. They are not required to share curvature. A tangent-continuous join is not automatically a curvature-continuous or aerodynamically optimized join.

19.6 Monotonicity and admissible endpoint angles

The model requires

0≤θe<θn<90∘,xn<xq<L,rn<rq≤re. 0\le\theta_e<\theta_n<90^\circ,\qquad x_n<x_q<L,\qquad r_n<r_q\le r_e.

The ordered control-point coordinates keep the quadratic segment moving downstream and outward. Its derivatives are convex combinations of positive axial increments and nonnegative radial increments, so it cannot double back between sampled points under these constraints. At zero exit angle, rq=rer_q=r_e, permitting a horizontal exit tangent.

An equivalent way to understand the length restriction is to compare the endpoint secant slope

s=re−rnL−xn s=\frac{r_e-r_n}{L-x_n}

with the endpoint tangent slopes. A useful monotonic construction requires me<s<mnm_e<s<m_n. For a positive exit angle this becomes

xn+re−rnmn<L<xn+re−rnme. x_n+\frac{r_e-r_n}{m_n}<L< x_n+\frac{r_e-r_n}{m_e}.

Too short a bell asks for a mean outward slope larger than its initial tangent. Too long a bell asks for a mean slope smaller than its exit tangent. Either makes the chosen tangent intersection incompatible with the required control-point order. When me=0m_e=0, there is no finite upper bound from this secant test, although the other positivity constraints still apply.

Changing the throat-turn radius changes NN, and therefore changes these length bounds. It cannot be varied independently while assuming that the previously acceptable parabola remains valid.

19.7 Original bell construction

Choose throat radius 20 mm, expansion ratio 9, throat-turn ratio 0.5, initial angle 35°, exit angle 5° and length multiplier 0.8. The exit radius is 60 mm. The15° reference cone is 149.282032 mm long; the selected bell length is 119.425626 mm.

The circular arc ends at

N=(5.735764,21.808480)mm. N=(5.735764,21.808480)\ \mathrm{mm}.

The tangent intersection is

Q=(51.833490,54.086454)mm, Q=(51.833490,54.086454)\ \mathrm{mm},

and the exit is E=(119.425626,60)E=(119.425626,60) mm. These satisfy both coordinate-order conditions. At t=0.5t=0.5, the parabolic segment passes through (57.207092,47.495347)(57.207092,47.495347) mm. This midpoint is neither the tangent intersection nor necessarily the point halfway along physical arc length.

The secant-derived length bounds are approximately 60.278908 and442.266841 mm. Selecting 40 mm while retaining the same throat arc, end radius and angles violates the lower bound. The correct response is to reject that shape, not to draw an inward-turning or backward-running curve and label it a bell.

These coordinates were obtained directly from the displayed construction for an original example. They describe a reference curve and do not carry a measured thrust efficiency or wall-pressure prediction.

19.8 Sampling and profile interpretation

The bell profile allocates roughly one fifth of its requested points to the circular arc, with at least two arc points. It uses the remaining count for the quadratic segment and avoids duplicating the shared join. Arc points are uniform in angle; quadratic points are uniform in parameter tt. Neither spacing is generally uniform in xx or physical arc length.

Increasing point count makes a plotted polyline smoother and changes the discretization of exported geometry. It does not improve the underlying aerodynamic physics, because no aerodynamic field is solved. Point-count limits are 5–1000 for the bell and2–1000 for the conical profile. Each row reports axial coordinate, radius and local area ratio (r/rt)2(r/r_t)^2.

The end area of the constructed bell is the requested expansion ratio, and its end slopes are fixed analytically. A smooth-looking polyline alone cannot establish curvature quality near the join, manufacturability, absence of internal shocks or acceptable heat flux. These are separate physical or geometric questions beyond the supplied construction.

19.9 Geometry versus optimized nozzle design

A thrust-optimized contour requires an objective, constraints and a flow model connecting wall shape to performance. Depending on the design problem, those constraints might include length, exit area, chamber conditions, pressure distribution or integrated wall force. The present mode does not solve that optimization. Its explicit length and angle inputs already choose the geometry before the points are generated.

The familiar use of a parabola as an approximation to a designed bell does not imply that every parabola with plausible angles is optimal. Likewise, an 80% reference length is a geometric convention, not an 80% efficiency. The underlying performance remains the one-dimensional reference calculated from the same throat, expansion ratio, gas properties and supplied efficiency factors.

Changing the contour angles while keeping those performance inputs fixed therefore does not automatically change the App’s predicted thrust. That behavior follows the current separation of geometry and performance; it should not be read as evidence that real nozzle thrust is independent of wall shape.

Use the profile to inspect endpoint geometry, length allocation and admissibility. Preserve the declared boundary when handing the curve onward: it excludes wall pressure, boundary layers, separation position, side loads, cooling, thickness and a method-of-characteristics flowfield. A reference contour can support later engineering work without pretending that those additional analyses have already been performed.

20. Rocket performance studies

A parameter study is defined as much by what stays fixed as by what changes. Raising chamber pressure at fixed throat area is different from resizing a throat to preserve thrust. Changing mixture ratio at fixed chamber temperature is different from predicting a new adiabatic temperature. Curves without these constraints are easy to misinterpret even when every individual point is calculated correctly.

ThrustOne provides altitude, area-ratio and chamber-pressure studies using the explicit-property rocket model, plus a gaseous mixture-ratio study using a selected thermochemical expansion path. Each is a sequence of bounded point calculations. The program does not turn these scans into a trajectory, feed-system model or unrestricted optimization.

20.1 The baseline is resolved once

For the three explicit-property studies, the initial rocket definition first resolves the environment, nozzle input and absolute scale as described in Chapter16. The resulting throat area and effective gas properties become the baseline. Each scan row copies that resolved input and changes one quantity.

Study Quantity changed per row Important quantities retained
Altitude Ambient pressure from standard atmosphere Chamber state, gas properties, throat and exit geometry
Area ratio Exit-to-throat area ratio Chamber state, throat area, gas properties, ambient pressure
Chamber pressure Chamber total pressure Chamber temperature, gas properties, throat and exit geometry, ambient pressure

A baseline sized for a specified thrust is therefore not resized at every scan point. Similarly, a baseline nozzle defined by an optimum altitude is converted once into area ratio. The altitude study subsequently evaluates that fixed nozzle at changing back pressure.

The top-level metrics retain the resolved baseline performance and add scan counts. The row profiles contain the changing study results. Reading a baseline metric as the last scan point would mix two meanings. Scale-free mode suppresses absolute thrust, mass flow and area fields in the rows, preserving only the specific and dimensionless interpretation.

20.2 Altitude changes external pressure force

Under the fixed attached-flow assumptions of Chapter16, altitude changes ambient pressure pap_a, while exit pressure, velocity and choked mass flow stay fixed. With the supplied thrust-coefficient factor ηCF\eta_{C_F},

F(pa)=ηCF[pcAtCF,vac,i−paAe]. F(p_a)=\eta_{C_F}[p_cA_tC_{F,vac,i}-p_aA_e].

Hence

dFdpa=−ηCFAe. \frac{dF}{dp_a}=-\eta_{C_F}A_e.

The force response is linear in ambient pressure, but not generally linear in altitude because atmosphere pressure is not linear in height. The calculation uses the bounded standard-atmosphere relation; it does not use weather, vehicle speed or aerodynamic drag to modify chamber thrust.

This study therefore isolates back-pressure sensitivity. It does not predict vehicle acceleration, required thrust, propellant depletion or altitude reached. Those require vehicle mass, trajectory and operating schedules absent from this model.

20.3 Area ratio changes the internal expansion

Changing ϵ=Ae/At\epsilon=A_e/A_t at fixed throat area changes both exit area and the supersonic area–Mach solution. Exit temperature, pressure and velocity must be recomputed. Mass flow remains fixed in this explicit-property study because chamber state, throat area and characteristic-velocity factor remain fixed.

For ideal attached expansions, Chapter16 derived

dFi=(pe−pa)dAe. dF_i=(p_e-p_a)\,dA_e.

A positive exit-pressure excess rewards more area; a negative excess penalizes it. At nonzero ambient pressure, the ideal stationary point occurs at matched exit pressure. In vacuum, no finite-area maximum follows from this relation alone. A discrete scan can still show diminishing gains without establishing a practical optimum.

The area-ratio study does not generate a new wall contour at every point, estimate nozzle weight or apply a separation correction. The larger exit might imply a longer or differently shaped nozzle in hardware, but that geometry is not inferred by this curve.

20.4 Chamber-pressure scaling and the meaning of throttle

Let ke=pe/pck_e=p_e/p_c and hold the explicit gas state and expansion ratio fixed. Both kek_e and the ideal momentum coefficient remain constant. Then

F=ηCFAt[pc(CF,m+keϵ)−paϵ],ṁ=pcAtηc*ci*. F=\eta_{C_F}A_t[p_c(C_{F,m}+k_e\epsilon)-p_a\epsilon], \qquad \dot m=\frac{p_cA_t}{\eta_{c^*}c_i^*}.

Mass flow is proportional to chamber pressure. Thrust has a linear pressure dependence with a fixed negative ambient-force intercept. Specific impulse follows

Isp=ηc*ηCFci*g0[CF,m+keϵ−paϵpc]. I_{sp}=\frac{\eta_{c^*}\eta_{C_F}c_i^*}{g_0} \left[C_{F,m}+k_e\epsilon-\frac{p_a\epsilon}{p_c}\right].

At vacuum back pressure it is constant in this explicit-property scan. At positive ambient pressure, increasing chamber pressure reduces the relative pressure penalty. This is an algebraic pressure sweep, not a complete throttling model: chamber temperature, combustion efficiency, mixture ratio, injector pressure drop and pump behavior do not automatically change with pressure.

The finite coefficient becomes nonpositive below a model-specific pressure threshold. A failed row there should not be interpreted as a solved low-throttle operating state. Even above that threshold, a physical nozzle may not sustain the assumed attached supersonic branch.

20.5 Original pressure-study example

Reuse the original gas and geometry of Chapter16: γ=1.25\gamma=1.25, R=400R=400 J/(kg K), chamber temperature 3200 K, throat area 0.002 m², expansion ratio 5.831866839 and unity performance factors. At chamber pressure 5 MPa, the vacuum coefficient is 1.648728009, characteristic velocity1719.239297 m/s and exit pressure 115.391902 kPa.

At ambient pressure 100 kPa, thrust is 15320.906717 N. Reducing back pressure to 50 kPa raises thrust by 50000Ae=583.18668450000A_e=583.186684 N, giving 15904.093401 N. Mass flow stays 5.816525959 kg/s. These are pressure levels for a transparent arithmetic example; they are not assigned invented standard-atmosphere altitudes.

Now instead retain ambient pressure 100 kPa and raise chamber pressure to 10 MPa. Mass flow doubles to 11.633051918 kg/s and exit pressure doubles to 230.783804 kPa. Thrust becomes

F=20000(1.648728009)−1166.373368≈31808.186802N. F=20000(1.648728009)-1166.373368 \approx31808.186802\ \mathrm N.

This exceeds twice the original thrust by 1166.373368 N because the ambient-force penalty is subtracted once, not twice. Calling the result simply twice the thrust would overlook that fixed force term.

The example is direct arithmetic from the earlier analytical state, not a numerical dataset generated by the App. It demonstrates which outputs are proportional and which retain an ambient offset.

20.6 Mixture ratio is a mass ratio

The thermochemical study defines

MR=moxidizermfuel. MR=\frac{m_{oxidizer}}{m_{fuel}}.

The supported scan selects H2, CH4 or CO fuel with O2 oxidizer. On a basis of one kilogram of fuel, the feed amounts are

nf=1W¯f,no=MRW¯o, n_f=\frac{1}{\overline W_f},\qquad n_o=\frac{MR}{\overline W_o},

in kmol when molecular weights are kg/kmol. The total feed mass is 1+MR1+MR kg on this bookkeeping basis. These amounts set the elemental inventory; they are not a mass-flow schedule for the sized nozzle.

For an illustrative molecular-weight approximation of 2 kg/kmol for H2 and 32 kg/kmol for O2, a mass ratio 8 gives0.5 kmol fuel and 0.25 kmol oxidizer: a 2:1 molecular ratio. Entering8 as a mole ratio would describe an entirely different mixture. The App uses its property database molecular weights rather than these deliberately rounded teaching values.

Stoichiometry identifies elemental proportions for a chosen complete reaction. It does not alone identify the maximum specific impulse. Temperature, molecular weight, dissociation, recombination and nozzle expansion all contribute to that objective.

20.7 What changes in each chemical sample

Every mixture sample uses chamber equilibrium and the same selected nozzle model: frozen, equilibrium or specified-area freezing. Geometry and back pressure stay fixed. The selected freeze area, when applicable, remains a prescribed assumption at every sample; a sample can fail if that location does not admit the required supersonic frozen continuation.

With specified chamber temperature, that temperature is held constant while feed composition and equilibrium products change. This examines composition sensitivity at an imposed thermal state. It is not an adiabatic combustion-temperature prediction.

With enthalpy closure, the inlet temperature and added heat per unit mixture mass are retained. Each mixture has a new inlet specific enthalpy and elemental inventory, so the chamber temperature is solved afresh. Holding heat per unit mixture mass fixed does not mean a fixed total heater power: the sized nozzle’s mass flow can change.

Formation-inclusive properties carry chemical energy throughout this calculation. No separate fuel heating value should be added on top of the equilibrium enthalpy balance. The scan remains gaseous and excludes liquid vaporization, condensed phases and finite-rate chemistry. It is not interpolation between tabulated propellant performance rows.

20.8 Sampling, failed rows and maxima

Explicit-property scans use equally spaced coordinates between finite endpoints, with 2–1000 samples. Their implementation permits decreasing or identical endpoints; those choices give reverse ordering or repeated points rather than a new physical branch. The mixture scan specifically requires a positive increasing mass-ratio interval and 2–101 points.

Each attempted point retains its coordinate and a status. Successful rows contain numerical metrics; failed rows do not acquire fabricated zero thrust or interpolated properties. Failure may indicate invalid input, an unsupported flow branch, insufficient thermodynamic range or a solver limitation. It is not automatically evidence of a physical discontinuity.

The mixture scan reports the largest specific impulse among its successful samples. If the largest value occurs at an endpoint, the selected interval does not establish a surrounding maximum. If neighboring samples fail, the missing region remains unknown. Even an interior sampled maximum is not proof of a continuous or global optimum.

If all mixture points fail, scan counts remain available but no best-sample pair is reported. The three explicit-property studies do not themselves return an optimized design. Their role is to expose trends under the declared fixed conditions.

20.9 Warning propagation and result limits

The current explicit-property scan records thrown point failures, but it does not append each successful point’s individual warning list to the aggregate result. Its baseline warnings therefore must not be treated as a complete per-row overexpansion or separation assessment. A sweep can move into lower exit-to-ambient pressure ratios after a benign baseline. Inspect a selected point through the corresponding single-point calculation before interpreting it as an attached-flow prediction.

Likewise, successful mixture rows carry metrics rather than a full collection of each point’s warnings. General scan warnings describe the common chemistry and scope. Neither a status value of one nor a smooth curve establishes freedom from nozzle separation, acceptable materials, combustion stability or practical feed-system operation.

These limits do not prevent useful comparison. They determine what the comparison supports: an ideal pressure trend, an explicit expansion tradeoff, or a bounded chemical sensitivity under fixed geometry. Retain the input state, scan interval, failed rows and chosen objective whenever presenting a conclusion. Chapter34 develops the general interpretation of discrete studies across all engine families.

21. Solid-propellant equilibrium pressure

A burning solid surface supplies gas while the nozzle removes it. In a steady lumped balance, chamber pressure adjusts until these two mass rates agree. Pressure also changes the prescribed surface regression rate, creating feedback between gas generation and discharge. This chapter derives the equilibrium of that simplified model and explains what its sensitivity can and cannot establish.

The App’s equilibrium pressure mode takes an explicit burning area, a reference burn rate and pressure exponent, solid density, characteristic velocity and throat area. It does not identify a propellant formulation or infer a burn law from chemistry. Its output is conditional on the supplied law and the assumption of choked discharge.

21.1 Surface regression and generated mass

Burn rate rbr_b is the speed at which the burning surface recedes normal to itself, measured in m/s. It is not the gas velocity in the port. For burning area AbA_b and solid density ρp\rho_p, a small regression distance dwdw consumes volume AbdwA_b\,dw. With dw/dt=rbdw/dt=r_b, gas generation is

ṁg=ρpAbrb. \dot m_g=\rho_pA_br_b.

This relation assumes that the consumed solid mass enters the represented gas inventory. It does not resolve condensed particles, incomplete conversion or separate solid and gas velocities. The burning area is the active surface area, not necessarily the frontal area, port area or exterior grain area.

For the equilibrium mode, AbA_b is supplied directly and remains fixed during the calculation. Grain dimensions do not determine it. The transient mode instead derives active area from its selected geometry, as developed in Chapter 22. Passing the same input structure to both modes does not make their area definitions interchangeable.

21.2 A reference-pressure burn law

The implemented law is

rb(p)=rref(ppref)n,0<n<1. r_b(p)=r_{ref}\left(\frac{p}{p_{ref}}\right)^n, \qquad0<n<1.

The ratio inside the power is dimensionless, rrefr_{ref} has units of m/s, and prefp_{ref} is the pressure at which that rate is specified. This representation avoids burying pressure units inside a fitted coefficient. The App evaluates it using the logarithm of the pressure ratio.

An equivalent form is rb=apnr_b=ap^n, with a=rref/prefna=r_{ref}/p_{ref}^n. The numerical value and units of aa depend on the pressure unit used. A coefficient fitted using MPa cannot be inserted into a Pa-based expression without conversion. For example, converting pressure from MPa to Pa multiplies the corresponding coefficient by 10−6n10^{-6n}, before any additional conversion of regression-rate units.

Reference pressure is a representation choice if the reference rate is transformed consistently. Replacing prefp_{ref} by kprefkp_{ref} while representing the same physical curve requires replacing rrefr_{ref} by knrrefk^nr_{ref}. Changing reference pressure alone changes the law rather than merely relabeling it.

A power law is normally an approximation over a declared pressure and material-temperature range. The current input has no fitted validity interval or grain-temperature correction. The program therefore cannot certify that a mathematically accepted pressure lies within the range of the supplied empirical data.

21.3 Choked discharge and the pressure balance

With supplied characteristic velocity c*>0c^*>0, the nozzle mass-flow model is

ṁn=pAtc*. \dot m_n=\frac{pA_t}{c^*}.

This uses chamber pressure in the reservoir sense adopted by the lumped model. No finite chamber-velocity correction is inferred. The supplied c*c^* is not recomputed from the input gas temperature and molecular weight in this equilibrium mode.

At equilibrium, gas storage is stationary:

ρpAbrref(peqpref)n=peqAtc*. \rho_pA_br_{ref}\left(\frac{p_{eq}}{p_{ref}}\right)^n =\frac{p_{eq}A_t}{c^*}.

Collecting the pressure terms gives

peq1−n=ρpAbrrefc*Atprefn. p_{eq}^{1-n}=\frac{\rho_pA_br_{ref}c^*}{A_tp_{ref}^n}.

A dimensionless version makes the scaling especially clear. Define

S=ρpAbrrefc*Atpref,peqpref=S1/(1−n). S=\frac{\rho_pA_br_{ref}c^*}{A_tp_{ref}},\qquad \frac{p_{eq}}{p_{ref}}=S^{1/(1-n)}.

The numerator of SS has units of force and so does its denominator. The equilibrium is positive and unique for positive parameters with 0<n<10<n<1. The implementation evaluates the logarithm of the dimensional expression before exponentiation to reduce avoidable overflow in intermediate products. An extreme result can still exceed finite numerical range and is not accepted.

21.4 Choking is an additional requirement

An algebraic intersection is not enough. The discharge law assumes a choked throat. For nonzero ambient pressure, the App requires

peqpa≥(γ+12)γ/(γ−1). \frac{p_{eq}}{p_a}\ge \left(\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

At vacuum ambient pressure, this pressure-ratio check is automatically satisfied. At finite back pressure, an equilibrium below the critical ratio is rejected; the program does not replace the nozzle relation with an unchoked discharge equation and find a different equilibrium.

Gamma affects this admissibility test. In the current equilibrium formula it does not separately alter the mass flow after c*c^* has been supplied. Treating gamma and c*c^* as independently calibrated inputs is therefore part of the model. Giving them mutually inconsistent physical interpretations can produce a numerical result without a coherent gas model.

Choking does not establish the absence of shocks or separation downstream, nor does it qualify a complete nozzle. This mode has no exit area or wall contour from which to calculate those effects.

21.5 Sensitivity to area and burn-law inputs

For fixed exponent and reference pressure, logarithmic differentiation gives

dln⁡peq=11−n(dln⁡ρp+dln⁡Ab+dln⁡rref+dln⁡c*−dln⁡At). d\ln p_{eq}=\frac{1}{1-n} (d\ln\rho_p+d\ln A_b+d\ln r_{ref}+d\ln c^*-d\ln A_t).

The pressure elasticity with respect to burning area is 1/(1−n)1/(1-n), while the elasticity with respect to throat area is its negative. As nn approaches one, a small fractional input change causes a much larger fractional pressure change. This is sensitivity of the supplied algebraic model, not a numerical defect that should be hidden by rounding.

For a finite change in burning area by a factor kk,

peq,newpeq,old=k1/(1−n). \frac{p_{eq,new}}{p_{eq,old}}=k^{1/(1-n)}.

Using the differential approximation for a large change can be inaccurate. For example, at n=0.5n=0.5, a 10% increase in area gives a 21% pressure increase, because 1.12=1.211.1^2=1.21. The first-order estimate would give20%.

Exponent sensitivity depends on the position relative to the reference state:

∂ln⁡(peq/pref)∂n=ln⁡S(1−n)2, \frac{\partial\ln(p_{eq}/p_{ref})}{\partial n} =\frac{\ln S}{(1-n)^2},

when SS is held fixed. Raising the exponent increases equilibrium pressure if S>1S>1, decreases it if S<1S<1, and leaves the reference intersection unchanged if S=1S=1. A universal statement that larger exponent always means larger equilibrium pressure would therefore be incorrect.

21.6 Original normalized example

Choose a purely illustrative aggregate supply parameter S=1.5S=1.5 and exponent n=0.5n=0.5. No real propellant coefficients are assigned. The equilibrium ratio is

P=peqpref=1.52=2.25. P=\frac{p_{eq}}{p_{ref}}=1.5^2=2.25.

Normalize mass flow by ṁref=Atpref/c*\dot m_{ref}=A_tp_{ref}/c^*. The discharge is ṁn/ṁref=P=2.25\dot m_n/\dot m_{ref}=P=2.25. Generation is ṁg/ṁref=SPn=1.52.25=2.25\dot m_g/\dot m_{ref}=S P^n=1.5\sqrt{2.25}=2.25. The two rates agree, and the burn rate is 1.5 times its reference value.

Increasing burning area by 10% changes SS to 1.65 and gives P=2.7225P=2.7225, a 21% increase. Increasing throat area by 10% instead gives S=1.5/1.1S=1.5/1.1 and P=2.25/1.21≈1.85950P=2.25/1.21\approx1.85950. The same percentage change in different areas has opposite effects because one supplies gas and the other removes it.

Now let ambient pressure equal reference pressure and choose γ=1.4\gamma=1.4. The critical ratio is approximately1.89293. The initial 2.25 pressure ratio passes the model’s choking test, but the enlarged-throat result 1.85950 does not. The latter algebraic number must therefore be rejected under the choked-only model. It is not a valid prediction of an unchoked motor state.

21.7 Limited pressure-feedback interpretation

For a fixed gas volume VV, fixed gas temperature and constant RR, a background lumped pressure equation is

dpdt=RTV(ṁg−ṁn). \frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{RT}{V}(\dot m_g-\dot m_n).

At the equilibrium point, differentiating the two mass rates gives

d(ṁg−ṁn)dp|eq=(n−1)Atc*. \left.\frac{d(\dot m_g-\dot m_n)}{dp}\right|_{eq} =(n-1)\frac{A_t}{c^*}.

For 0<n<10<n<1, a small positive pressure perturbation increases discharge faster than generation, producing negative feedback under these assumptions. A linearized perturbation obeys

dδpdt=−RT(1−n)AtVc*δp. \frac{d\delta p}{dt}=-\frac{RT(1-n)A_t}{Vc^*}\delta p.

This calculation explains a local relaxation tendency in a fixed-volume, instantaneous burn-law model. It is not a combustion-stability assessment. Acoustic modes, delayed surface response, erosive burning, temperature feedback, structural motion and changing burning area can alter real behavior. The App does not compute those mechanisms or report a qualified stability margin.

The transient model also permits chamber free volume and burning area to change. Its pressure equation contains a volume-growth contribution, so this fixed-volume linearization must not be used as a complete explanation of its time history.

21.8 Thrust and supplied coefficients

The equilibrium mode reports

F=CFpeqAt, F=C_Fp_{eq}A_t,

using the supplied positive thrust coefficient. It does not recompute CFC_F from ambient pressure, expansion ratio or nozzle geometry. Ambient pressure enters the choking test; it does not independently subtract a pressure force from this supplied-coefficient thrust expression.

A meaningful use of CFC_F therefore requires knowing the conditions it represents. If a coefficient already includes a particular pressure-thrust contribution, adding another one externally can double-count it. Conversely, using one constant coefficient across different back pressures does not constitute an altitude-performance model.

Gas temperature and molecular weight are used in the transient gas-storage relation, but not in this equilibrium algebra beyond the separately supplied c*c^*. Initial pressure, free volume and time-step settings likewise do not alter the equilibrium root. The shared input validation nevertheless requires their values to remain in the common input domain. A field’s presence is not evidence that it contributes to every mode’s equations.

21.9 From an equilibrium point to a history

The result describes one frozen geometry and one supplied burn law. It contains no elapsed burn time or propellant depletion. As a grain regresses, its active surface can change; applying the equilibrium relation repeatedly then gives a sequence of quasi-steady reference pressures. A real lumped transient additionally stores gas and may lag that sequence.

Chapter 22 develops the implemented established-burning history with geometric regression and discharged mass. Keep the roles separate: the equilibrium mode locates the steady mass-balance intersection; the transient mode follows a finite gas inventory under changing geometry. Neither supplies ignition, tail-off, a qualified material dataset or a complete motor design.

22. Established-burning transients

A steady pressure balance suppresses gas storage. A transient chamber can accumulate or lose gas while the burning surface changes, so its pressure need not equal the instantaneous equilibrium value. ThrustOne’s transient solid-rocket mode follows this lumped storage problem from an already pressurized, burning state. It does not calculate ignition or the discharge after propellant burnout.

The model retains the reference burn law and supplied nozzle coefficients of Chapter 21. It adds two idealized regression geometries, a prescribed constant gas temperature and a finite initial free volume. The state variables are regression distance and cumulative discharged mass; chamber gas mass is reconstructed from the exact volume swept by regression.

22.1 Initial inventory and state variables

Let ww be regression distance in metres, with w=0w=0 at the initial surface, and DD cumulative discharged mass in kilograms. With initial chamber pressure pip_i, free volume ViV_i, gas temperature TT and specific gas constant RR, initial gas mass is

mg,i=piViRT. m_{g,i}=\frac{p_iV_i}{RT}.

The App obtains R=8314.462618/W¯R=8314.462618/\overline W, with molecular weight in kg/kmol. Temperature and molecular weight remain fixed throughout this history. There is no gas energy equation predicting cooling or a changing combustion temperature.

If Vb(w)V_b(w) is the consumed solid volume, gas mass and free volume become

mg(w,D)=mg,i+ρpVb(w)−D,Vg(w)=Vi+Vb(w). m_g(w,D)=m_{g,i}+\rho_pV_b(w)-D, \qquad V_g(w)=V_i+V_b(w).

Pressure is reconstructed algebraically:

p(w,D)=[mg,i+ρpVb(w)−D]RTVi+Vb(w). p(w,D)=\frac{[m_{g,i}+\rho_pV_b(w)-D]RT}{V_i+V_b(w)}.

The initial free volume is an independent input. It must represent the intended gas space consistently with the chosen grain geometry; the solver does not derive an initial casing volume and subtract the grain to obtain it.

22.2 End-burning geometry

For an end burner of outer radius ror_o, optional inner radius rir_i, and axial grain length LgL_g, the active face area is

Ab=π(ro2−ri2). A_b=\pi(r_o^2-r_i^2).

The model exposes one annular or circular end face, with the other surfaces effectively inhibited. Regression proceeds axially:

Vb(w)=π(ro2−ri2)w,0≤w≤Lg. V_b(w)=\pi(r_o^2-r_i^2)w, \qquad0\le w\le L_g.

Thus dVb/dw=AbdV_b/dw=A_b, and the area remains constant before burnout. A nonzero inner radius does not activate inner-bore burning in this mode. It simply removes material from the end face and initial propellant volume.

Constant burning area does not force constant chamber pressure. Initial storage, free-volume growth and the pressure-dependent regression law can still produce a transient. Calling the geometry neutral describes its area history, not a guarantee of a perfectly flat thrust curve.

22.3 Internal-bore geometry

For internal-bore burning, only the cylindrical inner surface regresses; end faces and outer surface do not burn. The instantaneous port radius is ri+wr_i+w, and

Ab(w)=2π(ri+w)Lg, A_b(w)=2\pi(r_i+w)L_g,

Vb(w)=π[(ri+w)2−ri2]Lg=π(2riw+w2)Lg. V_b(w)=\pi[(r_i+w)^2-r_i^2]L_g =\pi(2r_iw+w^2)L_g.

Burnout occurs at w=ro−riw=r_o-r_i. A strictly positive initial bore radius is required for this mode. Its area increases with regression, creating a progressive gas-generation tendency. Free volume increases simultaneously, so the pressure response cannot be inferred from area alone.

Both geometries begin with propellant volume π(ro2−ri2)Lg\pi(r_o^2-r_i^2)L_g. Remaining propellant mass is that initial volume minus Vb(w)V_b(w), multiplied by density. These are ideal geometric inventories; no sliver, cracking, deformation or erosion correction is inferred.

22.4 Evolution equations and pressure storage

The integrated equations are

dwdt=rref(p/pref)n,dDdt=pAtc*. \frac{dw}{dt}=r_{ref}(p/p_{ref})^n, \qquad \frac{dD}{dt}=\frac{pA_t}{c^*}.

They are coupled through the reconstructed pressure. To understand their physical content, differentiate pVg=mgRTpV_g=m_gRT at constant R,TR,T. Since V̇g=Abrb\dot V_g=A_br_b and ṁg=ρpAbrb−ṁn\dot m_g=\rho_pA_br_b-\dot m_n,

dpdt=RTVg(ρpAbrb−ṁn)−pVgAbrb. \frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{RT}{V_g}(\rho_pA_br_b-\dot m_n) -\frac{p}{V_g}A_br_b.

The final term is the pressure effect of newly available volume. It is absent from a fixed-volume chamber equation. At an instant when generated and discharged mass rates are equal, pressure still decreases if the gas volume is growing. An instantaneous mass-flow equilibrium is therefore not exactly a constant-pressure condition in this model.

The equations assume immediate conversion of the consumed solid into the represented gas inventory and instantaneous response to the pressure-dependent burn law. They contain no ignition delay, surface thermal memory or acoustic pressure variation.

22.5 Why the implementation integrates discharged mass

Integrating regression determines consumed volume from the exact geometry. Integrating discharged mass then gives the gas inventory by subtraction. This retains the bookkeeping identity

mg,i+mburned−D−mg=0 m_{g,i}+m_{burned}-D-m_g=0

at the reconstructed state, up to arithmetic error. It avoids separately integrating gas generation and remaining solid mass with inconsistent geometric approximations.

This identity is useful but limited. A small mass residual does not prove that a large time step has accurately followed the pressure history. The integration can preserve its inventory equation while approximating the timing of regression poorly. Conservation and temporal accuracy answer different questions.

The App uses classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta updates for w,Dw,D. Intermediate states must have nonnegative regression and discharge, positive gas mass and finite positive pressure. An invalid tentative update is retried with a smaller step, for a bounded number of halvings. This is a validity recovery mechanism, not a local truncation-error estimator or an automatic accuracy guarantee.

22.6 Original inventory example

Consider a dimensionless teaching snapshot. Let initial gas mass be one mass unit, initial free volume one volume unit, and choose units so RT=1RT=1. Suppose regression has consumed 0.2 volume units of solid, whose density is 10 mass units per volume unit, while cumulative discharge is 1.5 mass units.

Burned mass is 2 units. Gas mass is 1+2−1.5=1.51+2-1.5=1.5, free volume is 1.2, and pressure is 1.5/1.2=1.251.5/1.2=1.25 pressure units. The inventory residual is exactly zero in this algebraic example.

If the added free volume were omitted, the same gas inventory would incorrectly give pressure 1.5. If discharge were incorrectly set to3.2, the reconstructed gas mass would be negative; the state must be rejected rather than assigning a small positive pressure. These numbers illustrate bookkeeping only and are not propellant properties or an App-generated time history.

For an internal bore, a regression of w=0.1riw=0.1r_i increases active area by 10%, but the consumed cross-sectional area is πri2(1.12−1)=0.21πri2\pi r_i^2(1.1^2-1)=0.21\pi r_i^2. Replacing that finite swept area by the initial circumference times regression would give 0.20πri2\pi r_i^2, undercounting the consumed volume. The exact quadratic expression used by the model avoids that discrepancy.

22.7 Burnout and validity stops

The simulation starts only if initial pressure meets the choked-nozzle criterion. It advances until the requested duration, burnout, loss of the accepted choked regime, or its step limit. These stopping conditions have different meanings.

When an update crosses the geometric web limit, the App bisects the time increment to locate burnout and sets regression to the limiting value. The final burnout row has zero remaining propellant, burn rate and active burning area. Chamber pressure and nozzle discharge can still be positive at that instant. The calculation then stops; it does not integrate the subsequent gas blowdown.

If a candidate endpoint no longer meets the choking criterion, that candidate is not appended. The preceding accepted history is retained. This stop is not a precisely interpolated unchoking event. The reported final time is the last accepted point, not necessarily the instant at which the critical pressure ratio was crossed.

A limit of 10000 accepted steps also bounds work. A requested nominal duration/time-step ratio above that limit is rejected initially; step reductions can nevertheless reach the accepted-step limit before the requested duration. Such an interrupted history is retained with an explanatory reason. It must not be presented as a complete burn.

22.8 Impulse and sampled peaks

With constant supplied CFC_F and c*c^*,

F=CFpAt=CFc*ṁn. F=C_FpA_t=C_Fc^*\dot m_n.

Integrating gives

I=∫Fdt=CFc*D. I=\int F\,dt=C_Fc^*D.

The App uses cumulative discharged mass to obtain total impulse, rather than independently integrating a displayed thrust polyline. The result includes only the simulated interval. At burnout, unexpelled gas can remain, so it excludes any later tail-off impulse.

Peak pressure and peak thrust are maxima among stored history points. They are not continuously optimized extrema between samples. The reported burn time is the simulated elapsed time; if the requested duration is reached with remaining propellant, it is not the complete material consumption time.

The completed indicator is true when the requested duration is reached or burnout is reached. The separate burnout_reached field distinguishes these cases. Always read them with remaining propellant mass and the stop reason. A completed requested interval can legitimately end before burnout.

22.9 Relating histories to equilibrium predictions

One can use the instantaneous burning area in Chapter 21’s equilibrium relation as a reference curve. A history close to that curve suggests rapid storage adjustment relative to geometric change under the model assumptions. A difference can arise from initial gas inventory, growing free volume or finite response; it is not automatically an integration failure.

The equilibrium mode’s explicit burnArea does not control the transient surface. The selected geometry does. Conversely, changing grain geometry while leaving equilibrium burning area unchanged does not change that separate equilibrium calculation. This input distinction is essential when comparing the two modes.

The prescribed gas temperature, characteristic velocity and thrust coefficient remain independent model inputs. No energy balance enforces mutual thermochemical consistency, and ambient pressure affects regime validity rather than recalculating the supplied thrust coefficient. Neither a smooth pressure history nor a small mass residual resolves that modeling limitation.

The useful result is a bounded established-burning history with explicit inventory, regression and stopping semantics. It excludes ignition, tail-off, erosive burning, star grains, structural response, two-phase flow and motor qualification. Those exclusions should remain attached to any use of the plotted history.

23. Shock waves

A shock compresses a supersonic gas through an irreversible transition. Static pressure and temperature rise while total pressure falls. These statements are compatible: static pressure measures the local mechanical state, whereas total pressure measures the pressure recoverable by an isentropic stagnation from that state. A shock destroys some of that recoverability without removing total enthalpy from an adiabatic, stationary flow.

ThrustOne provides independent normal- and oblique-shock calculations for a calorically perfect gas. Their results are ratios and downstream Mach numbers. They do not locate a shock inside a complete inlet, determine a shock train or predict a detached bow-shock shape.

23.1 Conservation across a normal shock

Place a thin stationary control volume across a plane shock normal to the incoming velocity. Let states1 and 2 denote upstream and downstream. The area is unchanged and there is no heat or shaft work crossing the control volume. Conservation gives

ρ1V1=ρ2V2=j, \rho_1V_1=\rho_2V_2=j,

p1+ρ1V12=p2+ρ2V22, p_1+\rho_1V_1^2=p_2+\rho_2V_2^2,

cpT1+V12/2=cpT2+V22/2. c_pT_1+V_1^2/2=c_pT_2+V_2^2/2.

The pressure term in momentum cannot be omitted. Equating momentum flux alone would incorrectly force equal velocities when mass flux is conserved. The energy equation states that total temperature is unchanged; static temperature is free to rise as velocity falls.

Introduce the density ratio d=ρ2/ρ1d=\rho_2/\rho_1. Continuity gives V2=V1/dV_2=V_1/d. With V12=γRT1M12V_1^2=\gamma RT_1M_1^2, momentum becomes

p2p1=1+γM12(1−1/d). \frac{p_2}{p_1}=1+\gamma M_1^2(1-1/d).

The ideal-gas relation gives T2/T1=(p2/p1)/dT_2/T_1=(p_2/p_1)/d. Substituting these expressions into energy gives the unchanged-state root d=1d=1 and the compressive shock root

d=(γ+1)M122+(γ−1)M12. d=\frac{(\gamma+1)M_1^2}{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2}.

The unchanged-state solution is not a shock. Selecting the compressive branch for M1>1M_1>1 gives

p2p1=1+2γγ+1(M12−1),T2T1=p2/p1d. \frac{p_2}{p_1}=1+\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma+1}(M_1^2-1),\qquad \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\frac{p_2/p_1}{d}.

Finally, use the new velocity and sound speed to obtain

M22=1+(γ−1)M12/2γM12−(γ−1)/2. M_2^2=\frac{1+(\gamma-1)M_1^2/2} {\gamma M_1^2-(\gamma-1)/2}.

The downstream normal-shock state is subsonic. The App requires upstream Mach strictly greater than one and gamma greater than one; the exactly sonic unchanged-state limit is not an accepted normal-shock input.

23.2 Entropy and total-pressure loss

For constant heat capacities,

s2−s1R=γγ−1ln⁡(T2/T1)−ln⁡(p2/p1). \frac{s_2-s_1}{R}=\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}\ln(T_2/T_1)-\ln(p_2/p_1).

Because total temperature is conserved, the same entropy difference can be written using the two stagnation states:

s2−s1=−Rln⁡(pt2/pt1). s_2-s_1=-R\ln(p_{t2}/p_{t1}).

Thus positive entropy production implies total-pressure recovery below one. Combining the static jump relations gives

pt2pt1=[(γ+1)M122+(γ−1)M12]γ/(γ−1)[γ+12γM12−(γ−1)]1/(γ−1). \frac{p_{t2}}{p_{t1}}= \left[\frac{(\gamma+1)M_1^2}{2+(\gamma-1)M_1^2}\right]^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)} \left[\frac{\gamma+1}{2\gamma M_1^2-(\gamma-1)}\right]^{1/(\gamma-1)}.

Total-pressure loss is not a heat-loss fraction. Total enthalpy remains constant across this ideal adiabatic shock. A downstream compressor must nevertheless perform more work to recover a given delivery pressure because the gas has lost stagnation-pressure capability.

In the limit M1→1+M_1\to1^+, pressure, density and temperature ratios approach one and entropy generation approaches zero. For very large upstream Mach at fixed gamma, density ratio approaches (γ+1)/(γ−1)(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1), while pressure and temperature can continue increasing. Real high-temperature gases may then require variable properties and chemistry outside this component model.

23.3 Original normal-shock example

Choose M1=2.5M_1=2.5 and γ=1.4\gamma=1.4. The density ratio is 10/3, pressure ratio 7.125 and temperature ratio 2.1375. Downstream Mach is 0.512989176. Total-pressure recovery is 0.499014812, corresponding to (s2−s1)/R=0.695119500(s_2-s_1)/R=0.695119500.

For illustrative upstream static values of 40 kPa and 240 K, the downstream pressure is 285 kPa and temperature513 K. Both stagnation temperatures are540 K, since 240[1+0.2(2.5)2]=540240[1+0.2(2.5)^2]=540. Static heating therefore does not contradict conservation of total temperature.

The velocity ratio is 0.3, fixed by continuity. Total pressure is approximately halved despite the static pressure rising by more than a factor of seven. These values are direct analytical arithmetic for an original teaching case, not a measured inlet or an App-generated verification dataset.

23.4 Foundation for an oblique shock

An oblique shock retains the same normal compression physics but also has a tangential velocity component. Let β\beta be the shock angle measured from the upstream flow and θ\theta the flow deflection. The upstream normal Mach is Mn1=M1sin⁡βM_{n1}=M_1\sin\beta. In inviscid flow the tangential velocity is unchanged across the shock; the normal component follows the normal-shock jump relations.

The downstream normal Mach is obtained using Mn1M_{n1}, and the full downstream Mach follows from

M2=Mn2sin⁡(β−θ). M_2=\frac{M_{n2}}{\sin(\beta-\theta)}.

Pressure, density, temperature and total-pressure recovery are the normal-shock ratios evaluated at Mn1M_{n1}. They must not be evaluated at the full upstream Mach unless the shock is normal. The angle relation below closes the problem and exposes the two attached branches.

23.5 Deriving the deflection relation

Resolve velocity perpendicular and parallel to the shock. Tangential continuity gives Vt2=Vt1V_{t2}=V_{t1}; normal mass continuity gives Vn2=Vn1/dV_{n2}=V_{n1}/d, where dd is the density jump evaluated at M1sin⁡βM_1\sin\beta. Therefore

tan⁡(β−θ)=Vn2Vt2=tan⁡βd. \tan(\beta-\theta)=\frac{V_{n2}}{V_{t2}}=\frac{\tan\beta}{d}.

Substitute the normal density ratio and use the tangent difference identity. After collecting terms,

tan⁡θ=2cot⁡βM12sin⁡2β−1M12(γ+cos⁡2β)+2. \tan\theta=2\cot\beta\, \frac{M_1^2\sin^2\beta-1}{M_1^2(\gamma+\cos2\beta)+2}.

The admissible compressive shock angle lies between the Mach angle μ=sin⁡−1(1/M1)\mu=\sin^{-1}(1/M_1) and 90°. A smaller angle would give a subsonic normal upstream component and cannot support this compressive shock. The deflection is measured between upstream and downstream flow directions, not between the shock and the wall normal.

23.6 Two roots and the attached limit

For fixed upstream Mach and gamma, deflection is zero at both the Mach angle and 90°. Between them it reaches a maximum. For a positive deflection below that maximum, the smaller shock angle is the weak branch and the larger angle is the strong branch. They are distinct states with different compression and entropy production, not two numerical approximations to one state.

A weak oblique shock often leaves supersonic downstream flow, but weakness does not guarantee downstream Mach above one near the attachment limit. Selecting weak solely because a subsequent component requires supersonic flow is insufficient; inspect the actual downstream result. The surrounding flow and downstream conditions determine which physical configuration can occur. This isolated component does not solve that global selection problem.

The App maximizes the angle relation over the physical interval, then brackets the requested branch on the corresponding side of the maximum. It uses bounded golden-section search for the peak and bisection for the root. A requested deflection above the maximum is refused; a detached-shock substitute is not returned. A small angular tolerance merges the roots at the computed peak.

At exactly zero deflection, weak returns the unchanged Mach-wave limit with all property ratios one. Strong returns the normal-shock state at 90°. This explicit distinction matters even though the specified turning angle is identical. Angles in the mathematical routines are radians; the App’s displayed deflection and shock angles are degrees.

23.7 Original weak–strong comparison

Choose upstream Mach 2 and gamma 1.4. Select a 45° shock angle to construct a convenient weak-branch teaching case. Substitution into the angle relation gives deflection 14.743562836°. Its normal upstream Mach is 2\sqrt2, so the pressure ratio is 13/6, density ratio 12/7 and temperature ratio 91/72. Downstream Mach is 1.456323838 and total-pressure recovery 0.954577001.

Solving the same angle relation on its larger-angle branch gives shock angle 80.055319827°. The strong result has downstream Mach 0.641200943, pressure ratio 4.360819743, density ratio 2.621888917, temperature ratio 1.663235888 and total-pressure recovery 0.734902406.

Both states turn the flow through the same angle and satisfy the same conservation laws. The strong shock produces more static compression and more stagnation-pressure loss. Using the full upstream Mach 2 in a normal-shock formula for the weak case would wrongly predict a pressure ratio 4.5 instead of 2.166666667: the normal component, not the full velocity, drives the compression.

These are direct arithmetic and a scalar angle-root calculation for an original example. They are not generated by calling the App or presented as a measured inlet dataset.

23.8 Interpreting component outputs

The reported pressure, temperature and density ratios are downstream divided by upstream. To recover dimensional states, multiply them by compatible upstream static values. Total-pressure recovery multiplies upstream total pressure. Static and total ratios must not be interchanged.

The normal and oblique modes do not determine capture area, inlet drag, wall heat transfer or downstream combustor compatibility. Several isolated shock calculations can explain a proposed compression sequence, but they do not automatically establish a self-consistent installed inlet. Reflections, boundary-layer interactions and detached structures require additional closure.

Finally, constant gamma is an explicit assumption. A high predicted temperature is a reason to examine its applicability, not evidence that equilibrium chemistry has already been included. The result is an ideal jump across the selected compressive branch, with the irreversible loss that follows from those assumptions.

24. Friction, heating and quasi-one-dimensional flow

Friction and heat addition can both drive compressible flow toward a sonic limit, but they do not conserve the same quantities. Fanno flow preserves total enthalpy while wall drag removes axial momentum. Rayleigh flow preserves momentum flux while external heating changes total enthalpy. The common appearance of choking does not make these models interchangeable.

ThrustOne exposes each idealized component and a more general quasi-one-dimensional segment calculation. The special cases provide useful physical reference paths; the segment calculation also admits area variation and mass injection. Its additional terms must be interpreted with their own units and control-volume conventions.

24.1 Fanno assumptions and wall force

Consider steady flow in a constant-area duct with no heat addition, shaft work or mass injection. For fixed gas composition and constant heat capacities,

ṁ=ρVA=constant,cpT+V2/2=cpTt=constant. \dot m=\rho VA=\text{constant},\qquad c_pT+V^2/2=c_pT_t=\text{constant}.

The differential momentum balance is

dp+ρVdV=−fDDρV22dx. dp+\rho V\,dV=-\frac{f_D}{D}\frac{\rho V^2}{2}\,dx.

Here fDf_D is the Darcy friction factor and DD the duct diameter, or the compatible hydraulic diameter for the intended model. The Darcy convention satisfies fD=4fFf_D=4f_F, where fFf_F is the Fanning factor. Entering a Fanning value into a Darcy field underestimates the specified friction parameter by a factor of four.

The App’s isolated Fanno input is the product fDL/Df_DL/D. It does not infer friction factor from Reynolds number or roughness. A fitted or estimated factor must therefore be supplied consistently with its convention and intended regime.

24.2 Deriving the remaining choking length

Continuity gives dρ/ρ=−dV/Vd\rho/\rho=-dV/V, and the ideal-gas law gives dp/p=dT/T−dV/Vdp/p=dT/T-dV/V. Constant total enthalpy supplies cpdT=−VdVc_p\,dT=-V\,dV. Substitution into momentum yields

(1−M2)dVV=γM22fDdxD. (1-M^2)\frac{dV}{V}=\frac{\gamma M^2}{2}\frac{f_D\,dx}{D}.

Thus wall friction accelerates subsonic flow and decelerates supersonic flow under these assumptions. Both move toward Mach one. Friction does not necessarily reduce local velocity; its momentum loss combines with changes in pressure and density.

Since M=V/γRTM=V/\sqrt{\gamma RT}, the energy relation gives

dMM=[1+γ−12M2]dVV. \frac{dM}{M}=\left[1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right]\frac{dV}{V}.

Eliminating velocity and integrating to the sonic state produces

ℱ(M)=1−M2γM2+γ+12γln⁡[(γ+1)M22+(γ−1)M2]. \mathcal F(M)=\frac{1-M^2}{\gamma M^2} +\frac{\gamma+1}{2\gamma}\ln \left[\frac{(\gamma+1)M^2}{2+(\gamma-1)M^2}\right].

This is the remaining dimensionless friction length to choking. For a segment,

fDLD=ℱ(M1)−ℱ(M2). \frac{f_DL}{D}=\mathcal F(M_1)-\mathcal F(M_2).

The App finds M2M_2 on the same side of Mach one as the inlet. A prescribed friction length larger than the available value is rejected. It does not cross the sonic point by switching branches. At the choking limit it returns Mach one within its numerical tolerance; zero friction leaves the state unchanged.

24.3 Fanno static and total ratios

A star denotes the sonic state on the same Fanno line. Constant total temperature and continuity give

TT*=γ+12+(γ−1)M2,pp*=1Mγ+12+(γ−1)M2, \frac{T}{T^*}=\frac{\gamma+1}{2+(\gamma-1)M^2},\qquad \frac{p}{p^*}=\frac{1}{M}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma+1}{2+(\gamma-1)M^2}},

ρρ*=1M2+(γ−1)M2γ+1. \frac{\rho}{\rho^*}=\frac{1}{M}\sqrt{\frac{2+(\gamma-1)M^2}{\gamma+1}}.

Isentropically stagnating each local state yields

ptpt*=1M[2+(γ−1)M2γ+1]γ+12(γ−1). \frac{p_t}{p_t^*}=\frac{1}{M} \left[\frac{2+(\gamma-1)M^2}{\gamma+1}\right]^{\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}}.

The ratio between states2 and 1 is obtained by dividing their respective starred expressions. The starred quantities are normalization references, not an assertion that the requested segment actually reaches choking. Total pressure decreases downstream with positive friction while total temperature stays constant.

24.4 Original friction-length example

For γ=1.4\gamma=1.4, choose a supersonic segment from Mach 2 to Mach 1.5. Direct evaluation gives ℱ(2)=0.304996503\mathcal F(2)=0.304996503 and ℱ(1.5)=0.136050217\mathcal F(1.5)=0.136050217. The required Darcy friction length is 0.168946285.

For an illustrative supplied fD=0.02f_D=0.02, this corresponds to L/D=8.44731426L/D=8.44731426. The total available distance to choking from the same inlet is L*/D=15.2498251L^*/D=15.2498251. A request for fDL/D=0.4f_DL/D=0.4 exceeds that capacity and must be refused under the fixed inlet conditions.

The Mach numbers and friction factor here are teaching values. The arithmetic demonstrates the component closure; it does not establish an experimentally appropriate friction factor or a real duct’s flow capacity.

24.5 Rayleigh mass and momentum constraints

Rayleigh flow instead has constant area, no wall friction and no mass injection, but permits heat transfer. Mass and momentum conservation imply

ρV=j=constant,p+ρV2=p(1+γM2)=constant. \rho V=j=\text{constant},\qquad p+\rho V^2=p(1+\gamma M^2)=\text{constant}.

Energy changes according to q=cp(Tt2−Tt1)q=c_p(T_{t2}-T_{t1}), with qq in J/kg. The isolated App component specifies the ratio of downstream to upstream total temperature. It does not obtain this heat from a reacting fuel mixture.

Using the sonic state on the same Rayleigh line as reference gives

pp*=1+γ1+γM2,TT*=(1+γ)2M2(1+γM2)2. \frac{p}{p^*}=\frac{1+\gamma}{1+\gamma M^2},\qquad \frac{T}{T^*}=\frac{(1+\gamma)^2M^2}{(1+\gamma M^2)^2}.

Combining static and total temperature relations gives

ℛ(M)=TtTt*=(1+γ)M2[2+(γ−1)M2](1+γM2)2. \mathcal R(M)=\frac{T_t}{T_t^*} =\frac{(1+\gamma)M^2[2+(\gamma-1)M^2]}{(1+\gamma M^2)^2}.

If the specified total-temperature ratio is τq\tau_q, the downstream target is ℛ(M2)=τqℛ(M1)\mathcal R(M_2)=\tau_q\mathcal R(M_1). Its maximum is one at the sonic state. Heating raises the target toward that maximum; the solver rejects a target above it rather than continuing through thermal choking.

24.6 Heating does not imply monotonic static temperature

Positive heat raises total temperature, but static temperature also reflects changing kinetic energy. Differentiating the starred static-temperature expression shows that its maximum occurs at M=1/γM=1/\sqrt\gamma, rather than at Mach one. A subsonic stream approaching choking can therefore have increasing total temperature while static temperature falls over the final part of the path.

The App selects the downstream Rayleigh root on the branch implied by upstream Mach. An exactly sonic inlet is assigned to the subsonic search branch for subsequent cooling. This is a numerical branch convention, not a general physical selection rule at a sonic junction.

On the supersonic branch, ℛ(M)\mathcal R(M) approaches 1−1/γ21-1/\gamma^2 as Mach tends to infinity. Sufficiently strong cooling can request a target below that limiting value, so no finite supersonic state exists on the selected line. The current bounded search then refuses to establish a root; positivity of the requested temperature ratio alone does not ensure a solution.

24.7 Original thermal-choking example

For γ=1.4\gamma=1.4 and upstream Mach 2, ℛ(M1)=0.793388430\mathcal R(M_1)=0.793388430. A downstream Mach 1.5 corresponds to 0.909275657, requiring total-temperature ratio1.146066192. If the inlet total temperature were 1000 K, the target would be 1146.066192 K, with heat per mass 146.066192cp146.066192c_p J/kg when cpc_p is entered in J/(kg K).

The largest supported heating ratio on this line is 1/ℛ(2)=1.2604166671/\mathcal R(2)=1.260416667. A ratio1.3 therefore crosses the thermal limit. That input must not be interpreted as a completed segment with a chosen downstream subsonic branch. These values are direct analytical arithmetic, not App-generated validation data.

24.8 General segment inputs and units

The quasi-one-dimensional solver advances static pressure pp, temperature TT, axial velocity VV, mass flow ṁ\dot m and area AA along xx. The inlet must satisfy ṁ=ρVA\dot m=\rho VA; these five supplied quantities are not independent. A helper can synchronize mass flow from the other state inputs, but the solver itself rejects an inconsistent inlet rather than silently replacing it.

Each segment specifies positive length and exit area. Area varies linearly from the area at that segment’s entrance, so A′=(Aout−Ain)/LA'=(A_{out}-A_{in})/L. The following distributed sources are constant inputs within the segment:

Quantity Meaning Units
Q′Q' External heat supplied per unit axial length W/m
qmq_m Injected mass flow per unit axial length kg/(s m)
htjh_{tj} Total specific enthalpy of injected material J/kg
VjV_j Axial injection velocity m/s
fDf_D Darcy wall-friction factor Dimensionless

Heat per length is a power density along the duct, not heat per unit gas mass. Its integral over length is watts; dividing by an appropriate mass flow produces a specific-energy change. When mass is injected, that mass flow changes along the segment and cannot be treated as a single fixed denominator without accounting for energy carried by the injection.

The solver uses the circular equivalent diameter D=2A/πD=2\sqrt{A/\pi} for wall drag. It does not accept an independent wetted perimeter or arbitrary-section hydraulic diameter. A rectangular or annular duct interpreted through this area-only diameter is therefore an additional approximation.

24.9 Mass, momentum and energy with injection

Mass conservation is

ṁ′=qm. \dot m'=q_m.

For momentum, include injected axial momentum, pressure force on a changing-area wall, and wall drag. The flux form is

(pA+ṁV)′=pA′+qmVj−Fw′,Fw′=fDρV2A2D. (pA+\dot mV)'=pA'+q_mV_j-F'_w, \qquad F'_w=\frac{f_D\rho V^2A}{2D}.

Expanding the derivative and cancelling pA′pA' yields

Ap′+ṁV′=qm(Vj−V)−Fw′≡F′. Ap'+\dot mV'=q_m(V_j-V)-F'_w\equiv F'.

The −qmV-q_mV term is essential: added mass must acquire the stream velocity. A zero axial injection velocity does not mean zero momentum effect. The quantity F′F' is an effective force per length, in N/m, rather than the total force on the engine.

The total-enthalpy flux balance is

(ṁht)′=Q′+qmhtj,ht=h+V2/2. (\dot m h_t)'=Q'+q_mh_{tj},\qquad h_t=h+V^2/2.

Using ṁ′=qm\dot m'=q_m gives

ṁht′=Q′+qm(htj−ht)≡Qeff′. \dot m h_t'=Q'+q_m(h_{tj}-h_t)\equiv Q'_{eff}.

Injection can increase total energy flux while reducing the stream’s specific total enthalpy if the added material has lower htjh_{tj}. This is dilution, not energy destruction. For constant composition, dh=cp(T)dTdh=c_p(T)dT, so

cpT′+VV′=Qeff′/ṁ. c_pT'+VV'=Q'_{eff}/\dot m.

No chemical source is introduced by calling the injection fuel. A different species inventory requires a composition-aware mixing or reacting model, developed in Chapter29.

24.10 The velocity differential equation

Differentiate continuity in logarithmic form with fixed gas constant:

qmṁ=p′p−T′T+V′V+A′A. \frac{q_m}{\dot m}=\frac{p'}p-\frac{T'}T+\frac{V'}V+\frac{A'}A.
