Substitute p′=(F′−ṁV′)/Ap'=(F'-\dot mV')/A and T′=(Qeff′/ṁ−VV′)/cpT'=(Q'_{eff}/\dot m-VV')/c_p. Collecting velocity terms gives

V′=V1−M2[qmṁ−A′A−F′Ap+Qeff′ṁcpT]. V'=\frac{V}{1-M^2} \left[\frac{q_m}{\dot m}-\frac{A'}A- \frac{F'}{Ap}+\frac{Q'_{eff}}{\dot m c_pT}\right].

Every bracketed term has units of inverse length. The factor 1−M21-M^2 reveals the sonic singularity of this formulation. A numerator that happens to approach zero does not authorize the current solver to construct a transonic continuation; that would require a separate critical-point compatibility treatment.

With no sources, the relation reduces to (1−M2)dV/V=−dA/A(1-M^2)dV/V=-dA/A. A convergent passage accelerates subsonic flow; a divergent passage accelerates supersonic flow. With constant area, no injection and no heat, the wall-force term recovers Fanno flow. With constant area, no injection and no drag, the heat term recovers Rayleigh flow. These reductions identify meaningful comparisons without pretending that the three numerical interfaces have identical stopping behavior.

24.11 Original injection bookkeeping example

Take an illustrative inlet mass flow 2 kg/s and total specific enthalpy 400 kJ/kg. A one-metre segment supplies 10 kW/m external heat and 0.2 kg/(s m) injection with total enthalpy 300 kJ/kg. The exit mass flow must be 2.2 kg/s. The inlet energy flux is 800 kW; external heat adds10 kW and injection adds60 kW. Therefore any completed adiabatic-wall calculation with those declared sources must have

ht,out=800+10+602.2=395.454545kJ/kg. h_{t,out}=\frac{800+10+60}{2.2} =395.454545\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}.

Total energy flux increases while specific total enthalpy decreases. Adding10 kJ/kg directly to the inlet enthalpy would be wrong: the supplied heat has different units, and the added mass carries its own energy.

This is a necessary flux balance, not a complete outlet-state solution. Pressure, temperature and velocity still depend on area, momentum injection and the selected flow branch. In particular, changing VjV_j at fixed injection total enthalpy changes injected static enthalpy and the momentum balance. The same total-energy target can therefore accompany different admissible outlet states.

24.12 Property and composition restrictions

The constant-property variant uses supplied gamma and gas constant, with h=cpTh=c_pT. Its injection total enthalpy must be nonnegative. The frozen NASA9 variant instead evaluates cp(T)c_p(T), formation-inclusive enthalpy and frozen sound speed from one fixed mixture; its gas constant remains fixed because composition does not evolve.

Active injection with a separately specified injection composition is rejected in this solver. The frozen calculation cannot silently combine different compositions while keeping one mixture property law. For same-composition frozen injection, the model checks that htj−Vj2/2h_{tj}-V_j^2/2 can be inverted to a supported static temperature. Negative formation-inclusive total enthalpy is not automatically invalid in that convention.

External heat can be negative to represent cooling, and injection velocity is a signed axial quantity. Injected mass rate and friction factor must be nonnegative. These input domains do not make the model a resolved injector calculation: no penetration, mixing length or transverse momentum field is predicted.

24.13 Integration and sonic stopping

The App applies a fixed-step fourth-order Runge–Kutta method within each segment, with at most 10000 total requested steps. It preserves the subsonic or supersonic side selected by the initial Mach. Intermediate and candidate states must remain finite and positive, and |1−M2||1-M^2| must exceed 10−410^{-4}.

If a step approaches that sonic exclusion region, crosses branches, produces an invalid state or exceeds its conservation-residual criteria, the solver returns the previous accepted points with completed=false and a stop reason. It does not append a synthetic Mach-one endpoint or adaptively locate the exact choking coordinate. The last plotted position is therefore a retained valid station, not necessarily the true critical station.

Inlet continuity is checked to a tighter relative tolerance than accepted downstream steps. Frozen-property steps also check integrated energy flux against accumulated heat and injection enthalpy. These checks expose gross inconsistency; they do not replace an accuracy estimate for the spatial discretization. A smaller step can resolve a numerical difficulty but cannot create a physically missing branch beyond choking.

The isolated Fanno component can return its analytic sonic endpoint, whereas this general differential solver stops short of its singularity. The Rayleigh component may return a numerical state close to the thermal limit. Those endpoint differences must be respected when comparing results. Agreement should be assessed at compatible pre-sonic states with the same gas, area and source conventions.

A completed segment supplies a one-dimensional state history under these assumptions. It does not provide engine thrust by itself, infer a shock train, or guarantee that downstream back pressure can support the computed branch. The subsequent full-engine chapters add their own inlet, combustor and nozzle closures around these local balances.

25. Ramjet cycle and complete subsonic flowpath

A ramjet uses incoming flight motion to provide compression before heat addition. It has no shaft-driven compressor or turbine in the ideal cycle considered here. The inlet slows the captured stream, the combustor raises its total enthalpy, and the nozzle accelerates the exhaust. Net thrust is the difference between exhaust force and captured-air momentum, with any nozzle pressure term retained.

ThrustOne offers a design-point cycle and a spatial subsonic-combustion flowpath. The first specifies a combustor outlet total temperature and pressure-loss factors. The second integrates prescribed area, heat, drag and injection sources before attaching a pressure-specified nozzle. They answer different questions and should not be described as interchangeable ways of solving the same fixed hardware.

25.1 Inlet total conditions

For ambient static temperature T0T_0, pressure p0p_0, flight Mach M0M_0 and cold-gas gamma γc\gamma_c,

τr=1+γc−12M02,Tt2=T0τr,pt2=p0τrγc/(γc−1)πd. \tau_r=1+\frac{\gamma_c-1}{2}M_0^2,\qquad T_{t2}=T_0\tau_r,\qquad p_{t2}=p_0\tau_r^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}\pi_d.

The total-pressure recovery πd\pi_d represents inlet loss. In the nonideal design-point mode it combines the supplied recovery with the empirical Mach-dependent factor discussed in Chapter 4. The ideal selection uses unity recovery. Neither option determines a shock position, capture geometry or inlet starting margin.

At zero flight Mach, an ideal inlet provides no ram pressure rise. A conventional ramjet therefore cannot obtain its normal propulsion cycle merely by adding heat to static ambient air in this ideal pressure chain. The current cycle also requires a positive nozzle pressure ratio above one and positive net specific thrust.

25.2 Combustor fuel balance

Let Tt4T_{t4} be the prescribed combustor exit total temperature. On a unit captured-air mass basis, with effective cold and hot heat capacities, the nonideal energy balance is

cpcTt2+ηbfQ=(1+f)cphTt4. c_{pc}T_{t2}+\eta_b fQ=(1+f)c_{ph}T_{t4}.

Solving for fuel-to-air mass ratio gives

f=cphTt4−cpcTt2ηbQ−cphTt4. f=\frac{c_{ph}T_{t4}-c_{pc}T_{t2}} {\eta_bQ-c_{ph}T_{t4}}.

The denominator must remain positive, and the numerator cannot require negative fuel. This is a prescribed effective sensible-enthalpy and heating-value model. It does not infer equilibrium species or gaseous feed enthalpies from chemical data.

The ideal selection uses one cold-gas property set throughout, unity efficiencies and pressure recoveries, and neglects fuel mass in exhaust momentum. Its fuel balance becomes

fi=cp(Tt4−Tt2)Q. f_i=\frac{c_p(T_{t4}-T_{t2})}{Q}.

Fuel energy is retained while its added exhaust mass is neglected. This is a deliberate cycle approximation, not an exact finite-fuel mass balance. The ideal mode also requires complete expansion to ambient pressure.

25.3 Specified-pressure nozzle and thrust

Let re=p0/p9r_e=p_0/p_9. With combustor and nozzle pressure ratios πb\pi_b and πn\pi_n,

pt9p9=reτrγc/(γc−1)πdπbπn. \frac{p_{t9}}{p_9}=r_e\tau_r^{\gamma_c/(\gamma_c-1)}\pi_d\pi_b\pi_n.

The nozzle uses the hot-gas gamma and gas constant Rh=cph(γh−1)/γhR_h=c_{ph}(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h to recover static temperature and velocity:

T9=Tt4(p9/pt9)(γh−1)/γh,V9=2cph(Tt4−T9). T_9=T_{t4}(p_9/p_{t9})^{(\gamma_h-1)/\gamma_h},\qquad V_9=\sqrt{2c_{ph}(T_{t4}-T_9)}.

For the nonideal cycle, net thrust per unit captured-air flow is

Fs=(1+f)V9−V0+(1+f)RhT9V9(1−re). F_s=(1+f)V_9-V_0+ \frac{(1+f)R_hT_9}{V_9}(1-r_e).

The last term follows by eliminating exit area through continuity. Positive excess exit pressure adds thrust; overexpansion subtracts it. The nozzle geometry is not supplied or solved as a fixed-area back-pressure problem. A prescribed exit pressure can imply a supersonic expansion without proving that an installed nozzle sustains that branch.

Specific fuel consumption is f/Fsf/F_s. An optional air mass flow converts specific thrust to net force. Overall efficiency is thrust power divided by fuel chemical power when fuel is positive; kinetic-decomposition thermal and propulsive efficiencies are reported only for full expansion.

25.4 Ideal limiting relation

With one gas, unity recoveries and full expansion, the inlet and nozzle pressure ratios cancel so that M9=M0M_9=M_0. Nevertheless exhaust velocity exceeds flight velocity if heat has raised the nozzle temperature. Specifically,

T9=Tt4/τr,V9V0=Tt4T0τr, T_9=T_{t4}/\tau_r,\qquad \frac{V_9}{V_0}=\sqrt{\frac{T_{t4}}{T_0\tau_r}},

and, neglecting fuel mass,

Fs,i=V0[Tt4T0τr−1]. F_{s,i}=V_0\left[\sqrt{\frac{T_{t4}}{T_0\tau_r}}-1\right].

Equal inlet and exit Mach numbers do not imply equal velocities because their sound speeds differ. Positive heating requires Tt4>T0τrT_{t4}>T_0\tau_r. Increasing flight Mach at fixed maximum combustor temperature eventually reduces the available temperature rise; a larger ram pressure rise is not an unlimited performance benefit.

25.5 Original ideal-cycle example

Choose an illustrative constant gas with γ=1.4\gamma=1.4, cp=1000c_p=1000 J/(kg K), ambient temperature 250 K and flight Mach2. Set combustor total temperature 1800 K and heating value40 MJ/kg. These inputs are an ideal teaching case, not a fuel-property recommendation.

The inlet temperature factor is 1.8 and its total temperature 450 K. The gas constant is 285.714286 J/(kg K), giving ambient sound speed316.227766 m/s and flight velocity632.455532 m/s. Full ideal expansion gives exit temperature 1000 K and exit Mach2, so exhaust speed1264.911064 m/s.

The ideal specific thrust is 632.455532 N per kg/s of captured air. The approximate fuel ratio is 1000(1800−450)/(40×106)=0.033751000(1800-450)/(40\times10^6)=0.03375. These values follow directly from the limiting equations. Restoring fuel mass, different hot-gas properties or pressure losses changes the model and therefore the result; it should not be treated as a rounding correction to this ideal calculation.

25.6 A captured stream and a subsonic combustor inlet

The spatial full-flowpath mode requires a supersonic freestream and a positive capture area. It first computes captured air flow,

ṁa=p0RT0V0Acapture,V0=M0γRT0. \dot m_a=\frac{p_0}{RT_0}V_0A_{capture},\qquad V_0=M_0\sqrt{\gamma RT_0}.

Its inlet total temperature follows ram heating, and total pressure is multiplied by the directly supplied recovery. Unlike the nonideal design-point cycle, this inlet does not add the empirical Mach recovery factor. Identical numerical recovery inputs therefore need not describe identical recovered total pressures in the two modes.

The selected inlet closure specifies exit Mach, static temperature, static pressure, or an area constraint with recovery. A temperature input gives Mi2=2(Tt/Ti−1)/(γ−1)M_i^2=2(T_t/T_i-1)/(\gamma-1); a pressure input gives the corresponding isentropic Mach relation. Given Mach,

Ti=Tt1+(γ−1)Mi2/2,pi=pt(Ti/Tt)γ/(γ−1),Ai=ṁaRTipiVi. T_i=\frac{T_t}{1+(\gamma-1)M_i^2/2},\quad p_i=p_t(T_i/T_t)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)},\quad A_i=\frac{\dot m_aRT_i}{p_iV_i}.

The inlet must decelerate the freestream into a positive subsonic Mach and produce static pressure no lower than ambient. No shock sequence is reconstructed to prove how that specified recovery and state are achieved.

For contraction/recovery closures, the area is capture area divided by contraction ratio. The solver checks its sonic mass-flow capacity, then selects the subsonic root compatible with captured flow and recovered total conditions. In the current implementation, both named closure routes use the same supplied contraction and recovery relation; recovery is not inferred from a separate shock solution.

25.7 Distributed heat and injected mass

The combustor is one or more constant-property segments governed by Chapter 24’s equations. They permit area change, Darcy drag, external heat per length and injected mass carrying specified momentum and total enthalpy. The calculation follows the subsonic branch and refuses to integrate through its sonic singularity.

This is not a resolved combustion-chemistry calculation. A heat input in W/m is an imposed energy source; a mass source in kg/(s m) is an imposed material addition. Neither alone supplies a fuel heating value or establishes combustion efficiency. If the user represents fuel through both mass injection and heat, the chosen conventions must avoid counting its chemical energy twice.

In particular, the design-point fuel ratio from Section 25.2 is not automatically transferred to this spatial model. The full-flowpath output has captured and exit mass flows, but does not report a chemically inferred fuel-to-air ratio or TSFC. An energy residual checks the supplied flux balance, not combustion completeness.

If the combustor stops early, the returned exit fields describe its last accepted point. The downstream nozzle is not calculated and no completed full-engine thrust is supplied. More heat cannot be accommodated merely by allowing a plotted line to jump from a subsonic to a supersonic combustor state.

25.8 A pressure-specified nozzle after the combustor

At a completed combustor exit, the wrapper reconstructs total conditions from its static state:

Ttn=Tb+Vb2/(2cp),ptn=pb[1+(γ−1)Mb2/2]γ/(γ−1). T_{tn}=T_b+V_b^2/(2c_p),\qquad p_{tn}=p_b[1+(\gamma-1)M_b^2/2]^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

The nozzle recovery reduces total pressure while total temperature is retained. The specified ambient-to-exit pressure ratio determines pep_e. The shared nozzle component then obtains exit temperature and velocity from the available enthalpy drop. Finally,

Ae=ṁeRTepeVe. A_e=\frac{\dot m_eRT_e}{p_eV_e}.

Exit area is a result. The full ramjet route ignores separately supplied nozzle segments and uses this pressure closure instead. A nozzle length input positions the final station but does not determine the area solution or internal flow distribution.

Only inlet and exit nozzle states are reported in a separate station profile. Connecting them visually does not turn them into a solved continuous nozzle. A supersonic exit would require a suitable throat and expansion in hardware, but the current wrapper does not construct that throat or solve its back-pressure operating regimes.

25.9 Original nozzle and momentum example

Consider a constructed nozzle interface with total temperature 1000 K, total pressure 200 kPa before a recovery of 0.9, mass flow 2 kg/s, γ=1.4\gamma=1.4, R=300R=300 J/(kg K), and exit pressure 100 kPa equal to ambient. The available nozzle total pressure is 180 kPa and cp=1050c_p=1050 J/(kg K).

The isentropic endpoint is Te=845.405363T_e=845.405363 K, Ve=569.779552V_e=569.779552 m/s and Me=0.956202148M_e=0.956202148. Continuity yields Ae=0.008902447A_e=0.008902447 m². This example deliberately gives a subsonic nozzle exit: a ramjet nozzle result is not forced to be supersonic when the prescribed pressure ratio is below the critical ratio.

Gross thrust is 1139.559104 N. If the upstream bookkeeping gives captured air flow 1.8 kg/s at 500 m/s, captured momentum is 900 N and net thrust is 239.559104 N. The 0.2 kg/s difference between exit and captured flow would need to be supplied consistently by the upstream mass sources. These selected interface values illustrate endpoint and force accounting; they do not claim a fully integrated combustor history.

The nozzle area cannot be prescribed independently while retaining all these endpoint quantities. Choosing a different area would require changing a pressure, velocity, mass-flow or upstream state constraint. That is why this model is described as pressure-specified rather than fixed-geometry ambient matching.

25.10 Full-flowpath force and diagnostics

The completed engine uses

F=ṁeVe−ṁaV0+(pe−p0)Ae,Fs=F/ṁa. F=\dot m_eV_e-\dot m_aV_0+(p_e-p_0)A_e, \qquad F_s=F/\dot m_a.

Captured air flow remains the denominator even when injection increases exit mass. Gross thrust omits the captured-momentum subtraction. The current full-flowpath routine checks finiteness but does not require positive net thrust, unlike the design-point cycle. A finite negative result represents drag under the declared model, not useful propulsion.

The retained flow profile ends at the combustor. Its mass-flow field and final static state remain useful for interpreting the nozzle inlet. The final overall exit fields are then replaced by the nozzle result. The energy residual retained from the upstream calculation belongs to the integrated combustor source balance, not to a separately integrated nozzle flowfield.

Neither capture area nor a specified recovery predicts spillage, installation drag, inlet unstart or shock–boundary-layer interaction. Nozzle pressure specification likewise does not prove that the combustor and an installed nozzle can share a stable operating point. The calculation connects a bounded subsonic source-term flowpath to a thermodynamically consistent endpoint expansion; that is the scope of the completed result.

26. Frozen variable-property flow and state reconstruction

A flow state can be specified through temperature and pressure, density and velocity, or conserved flux quantities. These forms describe the same physical variables only when they share a composition, an enthalpy reference and a branch. ThrustOne’s frozen variable-property flow mode reconstructs an inlet from seven input forms, then advances that fixed composition through the source-term equations of Chapter24.

Frozen composition does not require constant heat capacity. NASA9 enthalpy, heat capacity and sound speed are evaluated at the local temperature. The distinction is essential for the reconstruction from momentum and total enthalpy, where an incorrect reference energy can select an entirely different state or leave no admissible root.

26.1 Seven forms, one physical inlet

The supported forms are temperature–pressure–Mach, temperature–pressure–velocity, temperature–density–Mach, temperature–density–velocity, pressure–density–Mach, pressure–density–velocity, and momentum/energy flux reconstruction. Every form also requires a positive area and a declared mixture.

For the first six, the ideal-gas relation closes the missing thermodynamic variable:

p=ρRT,T=p/(ρR). p=\rho RT,\qquad T=p/(\rho R).

A supplied velocity is used directly. A supplied Mach number instead gives V=Maf(T)V=Ma_f(T), with afa_f obtained from the frozen mixture properties. Finally,

ṁ=pVART. \dot m=\frac{pVA}{RT}.

Mass flow is an output of these forms. It is not another independent condition that can be chosen arbitrarily alongside pressure, temperature, velocity and area. The properties and reconstructed state must stay finite, positive and within their supported temperature range.

These are seven inlet representations, not seven chemical models or seven flow-regime predictions. Composition remains fixed after reconstruction unless a different, explicitly mixing or reacting mode is selected.

26.2 What F and G mean

The final input form supplies

F=pA+ṁV,G=h+V2/2, F=pA+\dot mV,\qquad G=h+V^2/2,

along with mass flow, area and an explicit subsonic or supersonic branch. FF has units of newtons and is the pressure-plus-momentum flux at the selected plane. It is not net engine thrust. GG has units of J/kg and is total specific enthalpy, not energy flow in watts.

The associated energy flux is ṁG\dot mG. Subtracting incoming momentum and including external pressure forces is still necessary before a full control volume yields thrust. A positive FF therefore says nothing by itself about whether a complete engine produces positive propulsion.

NASA enthalpy includes formation reference energies. Consequently GG can legitimately be negative. The velocity contribution is nonnegative, but it need not exceed a negative mixture enthalpy. Rejecting every negative total enthalpy would remove physically representable states from this convention.

26.3 Reduce momentum to a velocity–temperature curve

Let qF=F/ṁq_F=F/\dot m, a quantity with units of m/s. Continuity gives pA/ṁ=RT/VpA/\dot m=RT/V. Substituting into the momentum definition yields

qF=V+RT/V,T(V)=V(qF−V)R. q_F=V+RT/V,\qquad T(V)=\frac{V(q_F-V)}R.

Positive temperature requires 0<V<qF0<V<q_F. The temperature curve reaches its maximum qF2/(4R)q_F^2/(4R) at V=qF/2V=q_F/2. If even that maximum is below the mixture’s minimum supported temperature, there is no admissible reconstruction.

For any admissible temperature, the two momentum-compatible velocities are

V±=qF±qF2−4RT2. V_{\pm}=\frac{q_F\pm\sqrt{q_F^2-4RT}}2.

The low-speed expression is evaluated in the cancellation-resistant form

V−=2RT/qF1+1−4RT/qF2,V+=qF−V−. V_- =\frac{2RT/q_F}{1+\sqrt{1-4RT/q_F^2}},\qquad V_+=q_F-V_-.

These two momentum roots do not alone identify the requested flow state. They construct the allowable velocity intervals associated with the property’s temperature limits. Energy then selects roots within those intervals.

26.4 Energy closure and the sonic partition

Substitute the momentum temperature into total enthalpy:

E(V)=h[T(V)]+V2/2−G=0. E(V)=h[T(V)]+V^2/2-G=0.

The App evaluates mixture properties at each trial temperature, brackets roots and partitions the search around a frozen sonic point where needed. To see why that point is significant, differentiate at fixed composition:

E′(V)=cpqF−2VR+V. E'(V)=c_p\frac{q_F-2V}{R}+V.

On the momentum curve, qF=V+RT/Vq_F=V+RT/V, so

E′(V)=cpTV−cvVR. E'(V)=\frac{c_pT}{V}-\frac{c_vV}{R}.

The stationary condition is V2=(cp/cv)RT=af2V^2=(c_p/c_v)RT=a_f^2. The energy curve therefore turns at the frozen sonic state, separating the subsonic and supersonic branches. This gives a physical basis for the branch partition rather than treating two roots as an arbitrary numerical nuisance.

The current implementation accepts exactly one nonsonic root on the requested branch within the valid temperature domain. It excludes roots within its small sonic-Mach tolerance and rejects no-root or nonunique outcomes. It does not silently choose whichever root happens to be discovered first.

Once velocity is selected, pressure follows from

p=ṁRTAV. p=\frac{\dot mRT}{AV}.

Area controls dimensional pressure for this fixed F/ṁ,GF/\dot m,G reconstruction. It does not change the velocity–temperature root when the composition and other flux inputs stay fixed.

26.5 Original two-root illustration

Use an analytical constant-property gas to make the roots transparent: R=250R=250 J/(kg K), cp=1000c_p=1000 J/(kg K), hence γ=4/3\gamma=4/3, with the deliberate reference h=cpTh=c_pT. Set qF=1000q_F=1000 m/s and G=900000G=900000 J/kg. This is a teaching limit, not an assertion that these energies use the NASA9 formation reference.

Substitution gives

G=4V(1000−V)+V2/2=4000V−3.5V2. G=4V(1000-V)+V^2/2=4000V-3.5V^2.

There are two roots. The low-speed state has velocity308.013016 m/s, temperature852.563991 K and Mach0.577784920. The high-speed state has velocity834.844127 m/s, temperature551.517642 K and Mach1.947091314.

For mass flow2 kg/s and area0.01 m², their pressures are138397.396899 Pa and33031.174530 Pa respectively. Both have F=2000F=2000 N and G=900000G=900000 J/kg. Flux values alone do not say which branch the user intends.

The two states can also be viewed as compatible constant-area adiabatic jump endpoints. Entropy direction would matter if interpreting them as a shock, but this reconstruction does not impose an upstream-to-downstream shock event. Its branch input selects a state, not an irreversible process connecting the roots.

These numbers were calculated directly from the quadratic. A NASA9 calculation must use its actual h(T)h(T), including the reference term. Adding a constant enthalpy offset to both the property law and supplied GG preserves the state; changing only one of them does not.

26.6 Advancing the reconstructed state

The variable-property flow mode passes the inlet and fixed mixture to the same quasi-one-dimensional solver developed in Chapter24. Area, drag, external heat and same-composition mass injection can change the local state. The gas constant remains fixed; local heat capacity, enthalpy and sound speed vary with temperature.

A separately specified injection composition is not accepted with active injection in this frozen flow. Different-composition mixing belongs to the appropriate composition-aware mode. Similarly, an explicit heat source is not a finite-rate chemical mechanism. Renaming a segment combustor does not create species evolution.

At each accepted point, the profile includes static pressure, temperature, velocity, area, mass flow, Mach, heat capacity, gamma and specific enthalpy. The enthalpy field is static hh; add V2/2V^2/2 to obtain GG. Comparing that static field directly with an inlet total-enthalpy input would create a false apparent energy discrepancy.

26.7 Partial histories and energy diagnostics

The general solver retains the initial subsonic or supersonic side and stops before its sonic singularity or an invalid state. The frozen-flow wrapper reports the final accepted point even when completed is false. The exit fields then describe a partial segment, not the requested endpoint.

Its energy diagnostic is the dimensional flux difference

ℰ=ṁe(he+Ve2/2)−ṁi(hi+Vi2/2)−∫0xe(Q′+qmhtj)dx. \mathcal E=\dot m_e(h_e+V_e^2/2)-\dot m_i(h_i+V_i^2/2) -\int_0^{x_e}(Q'+q_mh_{tj})\,dx.

It has units of watts. For a partial history, the source integral includes only the length actually reached, including a partially completed segment. It must not include all the heat specified beyond the retained endpoint.

The wrapper exposes this value as flow_energy_residual; it is not the same normalized quantity as the general solver’s internal relative checks. A small dimensional residual depends on the flow scale and does not certify chemistry, temporal response or an installed flowpath.

26.8 Choosing the appropriate frozen calculation

Use the standalone frozen nozzle of Chapter17 when the problem is an adiabatic, isentropic, sonic-or-supersonic expansion through nondecreasing area. That solver reconstructs states from conserved entropy and total enthalpy. Use the present source-term segment when heating, friction, general area change or permitted mass injection must be represented.

The nozzle can begin at a sonic throat. The general differential flow solver excludes its sonic singularity. A comparison that starts both calculations at exactly Mach one is therefore not a comparison of compatible numerical domains. Compare common nonsonic states and consistent source assumptions instead.

Neither calculation predicts a shock train, composition relaxation, cooling system or automatic transition between branches. Their common strength is explicit thermodynamic and flow accounting within a fixed-composition model, with the reference state and root choice made visible.

27. Calibrated variable-property inlets

An inlet model can conserve energy while requiring an empirical description of irreversibility. ThrustOne’s calibrated inlet uses one explicit reference state to set the relationship between entropy production and static-pressure rise. It then combines that relationship with frozen dry-air properties to reconstruct other compression states.

The word calibrated does not mean the App contains measured data for an unspecified inlet. The reference altitude, flight Mach, exit Mach and contraction ratio are user inputs. Their consistency and relevance determine what the resulting model represents. The calculation does not find shock locations, boundary layers, capture spillage or inlet starting limits.

27.1 The property and freestream model

The mixture is fixed at0.79 N2 and0.21 O2 by mole, using NASA9 properties. It does not react or dissociate as it heats. Its gas constant is constant, but heat capacity, enthalpy and frozen sound speed depend on temperature.

For an atmosphere state T0,p0T_0,p_0,

V0=M0af(T0),ρ0=p0/(RT0),q0=ρ0V02/2, V_0=M_0a_f(T_0),\quad \rho_0=p_0/(RT_0),\quad q_0=\rho_0V_0^2/2,

ht=h(T0)+V02/2,s0=s(T0,p0). h_t=h(T_0)+V_0^2/2,\qquad s_0=s(T_0,p_0).

The supported geometric altitude range is0–70 km. The calculation uses its bundled atmosphere and property data, not measured weather. The actual flight state must be supersonic. Property-temperature limits can constrain high-energy cases even when altitude is within the declared range.

Three freestream input forms are available. Altitude and Mach directly determine the state. At specified altitude and dynamic pressure, Mach follows from M0=q0/qM=1M_0=\sqrt{q_0/q_{M=1}}, because the local thermodynamic state is fixed. At specified Mach and dynamic pressure, altitude is bracketed within the allowed atmosphere range and solved numerically. An unbracketed pressure request is rejected rather than assigned an extrapolated altitude.

27.2 Recovering the reference exit

Apply the same freestream construction to the reference inputs, denoted by subscript R. Given reference exit Mach MeRM_{eR}, find its static temperature from

h(TeR)+MeR2af(TeR)22=htR. h(T_{eR})+\frac{M_{eR}^2a_f(T_{eR})^2}{2}=h_{tR}.

The reference exit Mach must be positive and lower than the reference flight Mach. Temperature is bracketed between freestream temperature and the stagnation temperature obtained by enthalpy inversion. This avoids treating a locally evaluated gamma as a global calorically perfect relation.

Define contraction ratio C=Acapture/AeC=A_{capture}/A_e. Continuity implies

ρeVe=Cρ0V0. \rho_eV_e=C\rho_0V_0.

Thus reference pressure is recovered from

peR=CRρ0RV0RRTeRVeR. p_{eR}=C_R\rho_{0R}V_{0R}\frac{RT_{eR}}{V_{eR}}.

Reference contraction must exceed one and this reconstructed pressure must exceed reference ambient pressure. The entropy change is then evaluated from the two actual property states.

27.3 The calibrated entropy law

The implemented relationship is

Δs=Kln⁡(pe/p0),K=seR−s0Rln⁡(peR/p0R). \Delta s=K\ln(p_e/p_0),\qquad K=\frac{s_{eR}-s_{0R}}{\ln(p_{eR}/p_{0R})}.

The coefficient KK has units of J/(kg K), not a dimensionless efficiency. The model requires a finite positive coefficient, so a reversible reference with zero entropy change is outside this lossy calibration interface. A negative-entropy reference is rejected.

This law is a supplied reference approximation. It is not derived from a universal shock train or wall-friction correlation. One reference fixes one parameter; it does not demonstrate accuracy over all Mach numbers, altitudes or contractions. Changing the reference changes the model even if the current flight inputs stay identical.

The calibration and the current-flow closure are distinct steps. The App reconstructs the coefficient from the saved reference each time, then applies it to the selected current state. It does not overwrite the reference with each newly computed point.

27.4 Deriving the current compression path

At a trial exit temperature, write the ideal-gas entropy pressure correction for the same frozen mixture:

s(T,pe)=s(T,p0)−Rln⁡(pe/p0). s(T,p_e)=s(T,p_0)-R\ln(p_e/p_0).

Set this equal to s0+Kln⁡(pe/p0)s_0+K\ln(p_e/p_0), obtaining

ln⁡(pe/p0)=s(T,p0)−s0R+K. \ln(p_e/p_0)=\frac{s(T,p_0)-s_0}{R+K}.

Energy and continuity then give

Ve=2[ht−h(T)],Me=Ve/af(T),C=ρeVeρ0V0. V_e=\sqrt{2[h_t-h(T)]},\quad M_e=V_e/a_f(T),\quad C=\frac{\rho_eV_e}{\rho_0V_0}.

The accepted state must have temperature above freestream temperature, positive remaining kinetic energy and pressure above freestream pressure. Those conditions describe adiabatic deceleration and compression on the modeled path. They do not determine the physical devices or shocks producing it.

Absolute capture area is absent from this independent calculation: continuity provides an area ratio through mass fluxes. A dimensional mass flow requires an additional capture-area scale outside this mode.

27.5 Total-pressure recovery without a local-gamma power law

Because total enthalpy and composition are unchanged, isentropically stagnating the upstream and downstream states gives the same total temperature. Their entropy difference therefore satisfies

Δs=−Rln⁡(pte/pt0),πd=exp⁡(−Δs/R). \Delta s=-R\ln(p_{te}/p_{t0}),\qquad \pi_d=\exp(-\Delta s/R).

Together with the calibrated law,

πd=(pe/p0)−K/R. \pi_d=(p_e/p_0)^{-K/R}.

This power describes the fitted entropy relation, not a calorically perfect static-to-total formula. Static pressure can increase while total-pressure recovery falls, consistent with irreversible compression.

As an original dimensionless illustration, suppose K/R=0.1K/R=0.1 and the chosen path state has static-pressure ratio10. Then Δs/R=0.1ln⁡10\Delta s/R=0.1\ln10 and recovery is 10−0.1≈0.79432810^{-0.1}\approx0.794328. Conversely, a recovery of0.8 requires pressure ratio 0.8−10≈9.3132260.8^{-10}\approx9.313226 under this particular calibration. These relationships alone do not establish that the corresponding temperature and kinetic energy are admissible for a given flight state; those closures must still be solved.

27.6 Five exit constraints

Exit Mach uses the energy inversion of Section27.2, followed by the calibrated pressure relation. Exit temperature directly selects a point on that path. Specified exit pressure sets its logarithmic pressure rise and obtains temperature by entropy inversion:

s(T,p0)=s0+(R+K)ln⁡(pe/p0). s(T,p_0)=s_0+(R+K)\ln(p_e/p_0).

Specified total-pressure recovery first gives

ln⁡(pe/p0)=−RKln⁡πd, \ln(p_e/p_0)=-\frac{R}{K}\ln\pi_d,

then uses the same temperature inversion. This branch requires recovery strictly between zero and one. The lossless endpoint is not an accepted calibration limit merely because other inlet models permit unity recovery.

The fifth constraint is contraction ratio. It requires inversion of the computed mass-flux ratio C(Me)C(M_e). Multiple exits can satisfy the same contraction because velocity and density change in competing directions along the compression path. The root choice becomes part of the input, not an optional plotting preference.

27.7 Higher- and lower-Mach roots

For contraction inversion, the App samples candidate exit Mach values from0.05 to0.999 times flight Mach, detects sign-change brackets and refines the selected bracket. The higher-Mach choice takes the highest detected bracket; the lower-Mach choice takes the lowest. It reports the number of detected brackets.

Higher and lower are relative labels. They do not necessarily mean supersonic and subsonic. The returned Mach itself establishes that distinction. For directly specified exit temperature, pressure, Mach or recovery, the high/low selection is not used and root_count is set to one; it is not a survey of every possible inverse solution.

A root near a tangency can fail to produce a sign change in the sampled grid. Likewise, a root outside the scanned Mach interval is not discovered. The implementation rejects a contraction without distinguishable brackets rather than inventing a limiting solution. A reported root count therefore describes the search result, not a mathematical proof that no other roots exist in every possible domain.

27.8 Interpreting a result and a refusal

The energy residual describes he+Ve2/2−hth_e+V_e^2/2-h_t, in J/kg. Entropy change and recovered total-pressure ratio describe the calibrated irreversible path. Contraction is a mass-flux ratio. These quantities should not be relabeled thrust, captured mass flow or measured inlet efficiency.

An impossible reference can fail before the current-state calculation begins. A current pressure or recovery can require a temperature outside available property data or leave no positive kinetic energy. A contraction can fail the bracketing condition. Each refusal concerns a specific combination of assumptions and inputs; it does not prove that every physical inlet at that flight condition is impossible.

The fixed dry-air chemistry remains a major boundary at high temperatures. The mode does not automatically substitute equilibrium air, predict dissociation losses or match a reacting combustor. A full-engine calculation using this inlet adds further interface constraints, described in Chapter29. The independent result remains a reference-calibrated compression state with explicit thermodynamic and inverse-root assumptions.

28. Constant-property scramjet flowpaths

A scramjet retains supersonic flow through its modeled heat-addition region. This avoids requiring the entire captured stream to be decelerated to subsonic conditions, but it does not remove the coupling between heat, area, momentum and choking. Adding sufficient heat at fixed area can still drive the flow toward a sonic limit.

ThrustOne’s constant-property scramjet modes assemble the source-term equations of Chapter24 into a combustor, a nozzle, or a complete inlet–combustor–nozzle path. Their gas constant and gamma remain fixed. They do not solve chemical rates, molecular mixing or an automatic change to subsonic combustion.

28.1 Three boundaries for three questions

The combustor-only mode begins from an explicitly reconstructed static flow state and advances the combustor segments. The nozzle-only mode begins from its own reconstructed state and advances the nozzle segments. Neither has a freestream capture calculation from which to determine full-engine net thrust.

The full-engine mode first constructs a compressed supersonic inlet state from flight conditions and a specified total-pressure recovery. It then advances combustor segments followed by nozzle segments as one connected flowpath. The last accepted state of one segment becomes the initial state of the next.

Full engine:  freestream → prescribed inlet → source-term combustor → nozzle
Combustor:                         supplied inlet → combustor exit
Nozzle:                                                  supplied inlet → exit

At least one segment is required in the selected combined list. The code does not infer a missing physical component merely because the mode is named full engine. The actual supplied segment list determines what is integrated.

28.2 Supersonic inlet closure

For positive capture area and ambient state, captured air flow is ṁa=ρ0V0Acapture\dot m_a=\rho_0V_0A_{capture}. Total temperature is obtained by ram heating; total pressure is multiplied by the directly supplied recovery. The inlet is adiabatic, so it retains total enthalpy while losing total pressure.

Exit Mach, temperature or pressure can specify a state as in Chapter25, but here the selected branch must remain supersonic and slower than the freestream. The static exit pressure must not fall below ambient. The implementation does not reconstruct oblique shocks to derive the specified loss.

For an area-contraction constraint, recovered total state and area determine the mass-flow curve. The sonic capacity must accommodate captured flow, and a decelerating supersonic root must exist between Mach one and flight Mach. Otherwise the input is refused. A physically possible subsonic root does not rescue this supersonic-flow mode.

The recovery-named and contraction-named closures share the same current area/recovery equation. This conventional inlet is separate from the NASA9 reference-calibrated model of Chapter27. Their property and loss laws must not be mixed without explicitly changing the model.

28.3 Heat addition and area compensation

In a constant-area segment with no injection or drag, Chapter24 gives

V′=V1−M2Q′ṁcpT. V'=\frac{V}{1-M^2}\frac{Q'}{\dot m c_pT}.

For supersonic flow, positive heat decreases velocity while increasing total enthalpy. Density, pressure and sound speed also change, driving Mach toward one. The added energy is not simply converted into immediate axial acceleration inside the combustor.

Area divergence contributes the term −A′/A-A'/A inside the same bracket. On the supersonic branch, divergence tends to accelerate the flow and can counter part of the heat-addition tendency. This is why area schedule and heat schedule must be considered together. It does not mean that arbitrary expansion can guarantee an acceptable combustor state: pressure, temperature, finite length and downstream conditions still constrain the result.

Darcy drag and mass injection add the forces and energy-dilution terms already derived in Chapter24. Injection with low axial velocity can reduce stream momentum even while its mass and total enthalpy increase the downstream fluxes. The fixed-property model does not infer those source values from a detailed injector or combustion mechanism.

28.4 What the nozzle accepts

Nozzle segments in the full-engine and nozzle-only modes must have zero heat source and zero mass injection. Their area variation and nonnegative Darcy friction remain available. Thus a nozzle can be adiabatic yet lose total pressure through drag. It should only be called isentropic when the relevant dissipative sources are absent.

The model does not impose monotonically increasing area on every constant-property nozzle segment. A decreasing-area supersonic segment decelerates the stream and may approach choking. The branch guard prevents continuation through the sonic region; it does not redesign the area schedule.

Unlike the full ramjet wrapper of Chapter25, this full scramjet integrates supplied nozzle segments. Exit pressure is an output of that integration. Ambient pressure is used in the final force balance but does not adjust the internal solution to match an installed nozzle back pressure. A mismatch is therefore not solved by relocating a shock or changing the inlet state.

28.5 Original energy and force bookkeeping

Take an illustrative completed path with captured air flow1 kg/s and no mass injection. If inlet total temperature is600 K, constant cp=1000c_p=1000 J/(kg K), and the combustor receives200 kW total heat, outlet total enthalpy is800 kJ/kg. An adiabatic nozzle retains this total enthalpy. The actual exit temperature and velocity must still satisfy its momentum and geometry solution.

For a separate illustrative endpoint force calculation, let exit mass flow1.1 kg/s, velocity1200 m/s, exit pressure30 kPa, ambient pressure20 kPa and exit area0.02 m². Gross thrust is

Fg=1.1(1200)+(30000−20000)(0.02)=1520N. F_g=1.1(1200)+(30000-20000)(0.02)=1520\ \mathrm N.

With captured air flow1 kg/s at900 m/s, net thrust is620 N. The additional0.1 kg/s must be represented by the upstream source bookkeeping; it is not automatically counted as a fuel species or assigned a heating value by this calculation.

These are transparent flux and force examples, not a claimed spatial solver run. They separate the energy constraint from the endpoint momentum accounting. A proposed endpoint must still be attainable through a completed flowpath before it can be interpreted as its prediction.

28.6 Incomplete histories are not completed engines

The general solver uses finite-step integration and retains the selected Mach branch. When a step enters its sonic exclusion region, becomes invalid or exceeds its conservation checks, it returns the previous valid history. The last state remains available for diagnosis, and completed is false.

The scramjet wrapper then omits gross and full-engine thrust. A pressure and velocity shown in the exit fields of such a result describe the retained stopping point, not the intended physical exit. Combining those fields manually with the originally requested exit area would produce an inconsistent force estimate.

The stop does not automatically mean the real engine changes to ramjet mode. A shock train, isolator response, combustor unstart or mode transition would require a different coupled flow solution. Increasing the integration resolution can address a discretization problem; it cannot authorize crossing a physically singular branch in this model.

28.7 Completed outputs and their conventions

On a completed path,

Fg=ṁeVe+(pe−pa)Ae,F=Fg−ṁaV0. F_g=\dot m_eV_e+(p_e-p_a)A_e, \qquad F=F_g-\dot m_aV_0.

The full-engine specific thrust uses captured air flow, even if injected mass increases exit flow. Component-only modes report gross exhaust force without a captured-air subtraction. This quantity is not the net axial force on the nozzle wall or a complete component control-volume force balance; its inlet momentum and pressure terms would also be needed for that interpretation.

The output energy residual compares inlet and exit total-enthalpy flux with integrated heat and injected total enthalpy. Its denominator scales with the magnitudes of those terms. A small residual demonstrates consistency with the specified sources, not chemical accuracy or thrust agreement with a real engine.

The wrapper does not derive fuel consumption, combustion efficiency or specific impulse from unnamed mass and heat sources. It also does not require positive net thrust in the completed calculation. A negative value is possible under unfavorable supplied conditions and should not be silently described as successful propulsion.

28.8 Choosing a more detailed path

Use the fixed-property modes when the intended question is how prescribed area, heat, drag and mass sources influence an assumed constant-gas flowpath. Use frozen variable-property flow when temperature-dependent properties matter but composition is held fixed. Use the composition-aware and finite-rate paths of Chapter29 when injected species or reaction evolution are part of the actual question.

Changing the model is more than replacing gamma with a local value. It changes the enthalpy reference, sound speed, species accounting and sometimes the inlet closure. Comparisons must therefore retain common boundary conditions and clearly state which physical assumptions were changed.

The constant-property scramjet remains a bounded one-dimensional model. Capture area does not predict spillage or installed drag, source terms do not predict mixing, and a completed supersonic integration does not prove that downstream back pressure permits stable hardware operation. These distinctions are the conditions under which its plots and force results remain useful.

29. Mixing and finite-rate scramjet flowpaths

A reacting flowpath must carry chemical composition as part of its state. Temperature alone cannot identify its stored energy: two mixtures at the same temperature can have different formation enthalpies, gas constants and heat capacities. Injection introduces a second complication. Even with every chemical rate set to zero, adding a different gas changes the mixture and its thermodynamic properties. This chapter develops a conservation formulation that handles both effects without adding an artificial combustion heat source.

The three relevant models are the standalone finite-rate quasi-one-dimensional flowpath, the calibrated-inlet nonreacting mixed-flow engine, and the calibrated-inlet finite-rate reacting engine. They share the spatial flow solver. The full-engine modes additionally establish captured-air conditions and calculate exhaust force after the complete supplied geometry has been traversed. Their common mathematical structure does not make them a multidimensional mixing or combustion simulation.

29.1 Control boundary and state variables

Consider a stationary duct with axial coordinate x, cross-sectional area A(x), and a positive axial bulk velocity V. Each cross section has one pressure p, one temperature T and one composition. Side injection contributes mass, axial momentum and total enthalpy. Heat transfer is positive into the gas; wall friction opposes its motion.

The sequence of control boundaries is:

captured dry air -> calibrated inlet -> supplied duct segments -> exit
                                           ↑ mass, momentum,
                                           | total enthalpy
                                           ↔ wall heat

The standalone model starts at the first supplied duct station. It does not require the calibrated inlet or assign flight momentum to that inlet state.

Let N_i be the molar flow of species i, measured in kmol/s, and W_i its molecular weight in kg/kmol. Then

ṁ=∑iWiNi,Xi=Ni∑jNj,W¯=∑iXiWi. \dot m=\sum_i W_iN_i,\qquad X_i=\frac{N_i}{\sum_jN_j},\qquad \overline W=\sum_iX_iW_i.

The solver advances the vector of N_i together with momentum flux, energy flux and elapsed residence time:

ℱ=pA+ṁV,ℰ=ṁ(h+V22),τ. \mathcal F=pA+\dot mV,\qquad \mathcal E=\dot m\left(h+\frac{V^2}{2}\right),\qquad \tau.

Here h includes the species reference and formation enthalpies of the chosen property database. Momentum flux has units of force; energy flux has units of power. Neither should be confused with a specific quantity. The total specific enthalpy used in state reconstruction is ℰ/ṁ\mathcal E/\dot m.

This choice of variables makes conservation transparent. Chemistry rearranges species amounts while preserving elemental inventory. It need not be represented as a separately guessed change in temperature. Temperature, pressure and velocity are recovered from the conserved fluxes and the current composition, using the branch construction developed in Chapter 26.

29.2 Species transport and injection

Let ωi\omega_i be the net chemical production rate in kmol/(m³ s). A slice of length dx has volume A dx, so its chemical contribution to species flow is AωidxA\omega_i dx. Let qm=dṁinj/dxq_m=d\dot m_{inj}/dx denote injected mass per unit length, in kg/(s m), with injected mole fractions Xi,injX_{i,inj} and mean molecular weight W¯inj\overline W_{inj}. The balance is

dNidx=Aωi+qmXi,injW¯inj. \frac{dN_i}{dx}=A\omega_i+ q_m\frac{X_{i,inj}}{\overline W_{inj}}.

Both terms have units kmol/(s m). Using a mass fraction in place of the mole fraction in this expression would be incorrect. The equivalent mass-flow source is qmYi,injq_mY_{i,inj}, where Yi,inj=Xi,injWi/W¯injY_{i,inj}=X_{i,inj}W_i/\overline W_{inj}.

Concentrations required by the kinetic laws follow from the transported molar flows:

Ci=NiAV. C_i=\frac{N_i}{AV}.

This relation is also a useful conceptual link between residence time and reaction. A slower flow contains more material in a fixed duct volume at the same molar throughput. Reaction rates depend on concentrations and temperature; they do not depend on axial distance alone. Chapter 7 explains how elementary, reverse and pressure-dependent rates contribute to ωi\omega_i.

For a chemically balanced mechanism,

∑iWiωi=0,dṁdx=qm. \sum_iW_i\omega_i=0, \qquad \frac{d\dot m}{dx}=q_m.

Total molar flow need not be conserved. Dissociation can increase the number of moles without creating mass. Consequently, a change in ∑iNi\sum_iN_i is not itself evidence of a conservation failure.

The App accepts a composition for each injecting segment. If that composition is omitted, it uses the initial flow composition, not the local composition reached after earlier reactions or injections. This default matters in a multisegment calculation. A later segment with unspecified injection composition does not automatically sample the gas currently passing through it.

29.3 Momentum and energy balances

The pressure force exerted by a gradually varying wall produces a pdA/dxp\,dA/dx contribution to the derivative of momentum flux. With Darcy friction factor f_D and the circular-equivalent diameter D=2A/πD=2\sqrt{A/\pi}, the implemented balance is

dℱdx=pdAdx−fDρV2A2D+qmVinj. \frac{d\mathcal F}{dx} =p\frac{dA}{dx} -\frac{f_D\rho V^2A}{2D} +q_mV_{inj}.

The injection velocity here is its prescribed axial component. The equation accounts for its axial momentum contribution; it does not solve the transverse jet, penetration distance or shear layer. The friction convention is the Darcy convention discussed in Chapter 24. Substituting a Fanning coefficient without conversion changes the intended drag.

Write Q’ for external heat supplied per unit length, in W/m, and ht,injh_{t,inj} for injected total specific enthalpy. Then

dℰdx=Q′+qmht,inj. \frac{d\mathcal E}{dx}=Q'+q_mh_{t,inj}.

No extra lower-heating-value term belongs in this equation when formation enthalpy is already included. In an adiabatic reacting segment without injection, ℰ\mathcal E remains constant. Chemical conversion changes the relation between h, T and composition, and the reconstruction finds the resulting thermal and kinetic state. Adding a fuel heating value again would count chemical energy twice.

Injected total enthalpy includes kinetic energy:

ht,inj=hinj+Vinj22. h_{t,inj}=h_{inj}+\frac{V_{inj}^2}{2}.

The App checks that the corresponding static enthalpy can be inverted within the selected property model when injection is positive. Supplying an arbitrary positive number is not enough to establish consistency: enthalpy values depend on the database reference convention. A negative formation-inclusive enthalpy is not automatically unphysical.

Finally,

dτdx=1V. \frac{d\tau}{dx}=\frac1V.

The integrated residence time is therefore ∫dx/V(x)\int dx/V(x). Dividing total length by inlet velocity is only an approximation. Heating, injection, area variation and reactions can all change velocity along the path.

29.4 Closing the local state

After an integration step, the species flows define composition and mass flow. At the local area, the solver recovers a state satisfying

pA+ṁV=ℱ,h(T,𝑿)+V22=ℰṁ,ṁ=ρAV. pA+\dot mV=\mathcal F, \qquad h(T,\mathbf X)+\frac{V^2}{2}=\frac{\mathcal E}{\dot m}, \qquad \dot m=\rho AV.

The ideal-gas mixture relation provides density. Property evaluation supplies h, heat capacity and the frozen sound speed. These equations close the thermodynamic state without an independent temperature evolution equation.

The initial state selects a subsonic or supersonic branch using the frozen Mach number. Subsequent reconstruction retains that branch. The model rejects an initial state too close to Mach one and stops if it cannot continue an admissible state. It does not pass through a sonic singularity by switching branches, insert a shock, or solve an isolator adjustment. In this context a reported Mach number is based on the local frozen sound speed; it is not an equilibrium acoustic derivative for an infinitely fast reacting mixture.

Within each segment, area varies linearly between its entrance and specified exit area. The source coefficients supplied for that segment prescribe the distributed forcing. Making many short segments allows a piecewise description, but it does not add radial resolution. Every cross section still has one uniform mixed state.

29.5 Nonreacting mixing is a variable-composition problem

The calibrated nonreacting engine sets chemical rates to zero while retaining species transport and property reconstruction. If the injected gas differs from the entering air, its mole fractions change downstream. Thus nonreacting does not mean constant composition, constant heat capacity or constant gas constant.

As an original bookkeeping example, suppose 1 kg/s of an inert carrier with molecular weight 28 kg/kmol receives 0.10 kg/s of a second inert species with molecular weight 32 kg/kmol. The species molar flows after injection are

N1=1/28=0.0357143kmol/s,N2=0.10/32=0.003125kmol/s. \begin{gathered} N_1=1/28=0.0357143\;\mathrm{kmol/s},\\ N_2=0.10/32=0.003125\;\mathrm{kmol/s}. \end{gathered}

The second species has mass fraction 0.090909 but mole fraction approximately 0.080460. The mixture molecular weight is approximately 28.3218 kg/kmol. Treating 0.090909 as its mole fraction would change the gas constant and therefore the recovered state.

For a separate energy illustration, take an entering energy flux of 1 MW, injected total enthalpy of 0.5 MJ/kg and no wall heat. The added energy flux is 50 kW. The downstream total specific enthalpy is

ht,out=1.05MW1.10kg/s=0.954545MJ/kg. h_{t,out}=\frac{1.05\;\mathrm{MW}}{1.10\;\mathrm{kg/s}} =0.954545\;\mathrm{MJ/kg}.

Total energy throughput increased, but energy per unit mass decreased. This is not an energy loss. If the injection has axial velocity 100 m/s, its direct axial momentum contribution is 10 N. These balances alone do not determine the outlet temperature: the area, entering momentum flux, property model and selected branch are still required. The numbers illustrate independent conservation arithmetic, not a computed complete engine history.

29.6 Finite-rate evolution and conservation diagnostics

With reactions enabled, the chemical source is recomputed from the reconstructed temperature and concentrations. A faster intrinsic rate does not guarantee complete conversion. The gas may leave the duct before it approaches equilibrium, cool during expansion, or enter conditions where the reverse reaction matters. Equilibrium and finite-rate calculations therefore answer different questions.

For each element k, let a_ki be the number of its atoms in species i. The elemental molar flow is

Bk=∑iakiNi. B_k=\sum_i a_{ki}N_i.

A balanced chemical mechanism satisfies ∑iakiωi=0\sum_i a_{ki}\omega_i=0. Changes in B_k must then equal the integrated injection of that element. ThrustOne reports elemental balance diagnostics for the supported element set together with mass, momentum and energy residuals. These checks detect failures of conservation accounting. Small residuals do not establish that supplied rate coefficients describe a real fuel or that a uniform-flow approximation captures physical mixing.

The spatial integrator uses an Euler predictor and a Heun corrector. Their difference estimates local error. Rejected steps are shortened; accepted steps may grow, subject to the segment’s scheduled maximum step. This method differs from the fixed-step Runge–Kutta treatment used by some constant-property flow modes. Its tolerance controls a scaled numerical error estimate, not a guaranteed relative error in every trace-species concentration.

Chemical timescales can become much shorter than the convective timescale. An explicit method may then require very small steps. Hitting a step or attempt limit is a numerical termination condition, not proof that the physical flow cannot exist. Conversely, repeated reconstruction failure near a sonic boundary may reflect the limits of the selected steady branch. Increasing an iteration allowance cannot supply missing shock physics.

29.7 From calibrated inlet to full engine

The full-engine modes use the calibrated dry-air inlet of Chapter 27. Flight density and velocity determine captured flow:

ṁa=ρ0V0Acapture. \dot m_a=\rho_0V_0A_{capture}.

The inlet-exit area is capture area divided by contraction ratio. The wrapper checks that the reconstructed inlet-exit mass flow agrees with captured air. Its inlet mixture is 0.79 nitrogen and 0.21 oxygen by mole. The selected inlet-exit root must be supersonic; a low-Mach selection is not silently exchanged for a different root.

These full-engine modes require NASA9 properties through inlet and downstream flow. The standalone reacting-flow mode can use its supported NASA7 option, but the full-engine wrapper rejects that substitution because the inlet and downstream enthalpy references must remain consistent.

The supplied combustor and nozzle segment lists are concatenated into one flowpath. Reactions can continue through the nozzle list. Unlike the constant-property scramjet nozzle wrapper, this implementation does not impose zero heat or zero injection merely because a segment appears in the nozzle list. Its specified sources remain active. The list name describes the intended region; it does not override its equations.

On a completed path, the exit mass flow must equal captured air plus all integrated injection. With ambient pressure p_a,

Fg=ṁeVe+(pe−pa)Ae,Fn=Fg−ṁaV0. F_g=\dot m_eV_e+(p_e-p_a)A_e, \qquad F_n=F_g-\dot m_aV_0.

Specific thrust uses captured-air flow. The reported injected-mass specific impulse uses the sum of every injected stream:

Isp,inj=Fng0ṁinj. I_{sp,inj}=\frac{F_n}{g_0\dot m_{inj}}.

If injection includes oxidizer, diluent or air, none of those contributions is reclassified as fuel. For illustration, a net force of 600 N with total injection of 0.20 kg/s gives about 305.915 s. Using only a 0.05 kg/s fuel portion would give about 1,223.659 s, a different normalization rather than a better result. The App reports the former definition. Without injection it does not construct an injected-mass specific impulse.

29.8 Reading a completed or interrupted result

A completed calculation means the integration traversed the supplied segment lengths and passed its conservation checks. It does not mean the exit pressure matches ambient or that thrust is positive. Fixed downstream geometry is not adjusted for back pressure. External drag, spillage, shock trains and automatic operating-mode transition remain outside this calculation.

An interrupted calculation retains its valid prefix. The final retained row is the last admissible computed state, not necessarily the precisely located physical termination point. The full-engine wrapper withholds engine thrust for an incomplete path. A prefix ending at high temperature or pressure must not be presented as the intended nozzle exit.

Profiles may be reduced to roughly five hundred retained samples for output. This is a presentation reduction of the accepted history; it is not the internal step count. A smooth exported curve cannot establish that an unresolved steep chemical transition was accurately integrated.

The most informative comparison is therefore specific: hold inlet, geometry, injection and enthalpy conventions fixed; compare zero-rate mixing with the chosen finite-rate mechanism; then explain changes through species, residence time and energy redistribution. Such a comparison isolates the consequences of the supplied chemistry within this model. It does not establish a validated combustion mechanism or resolve transport processes that the equations do not contain.

30. TBCC with an explicit air split

A turbine-based combined-cycle concept uses different propulsion processes over a broad flight envelope. A turbine branch can supply compression at flight conditions where a ramjet lacks sufficient ram compression. At other conditions a ramjet branch can avoid passing all captured flow through rotating machinery. This architectural motivation does not, by itself, determine how much air enters each branch or whether both branches can operate together.

The ThrustOne explicit-split model answers a deliberately narrower question: given a common freestream, a total air flow and a prescribed fraction sent to each of two independently calculated cycles, what are their combined thrust and fuel flow? It is a separate-exhaust accounting model. It does not solve a common inlet, a mixer, a shared nozzle or a transition controller.

30.1 The two control volumes

Define total captured-air flow as ṁa\dot m_a and the ramjet fraction as λ\lambda. The branch air flows are

ṁa,r=λṁa,ṁa,t=(1−λ)ṁa,0≤λ≤1. \dot m_{a,r}=\lambda\dot m_a, \qquad \dot m_{a,t}=(1-\lambda)\dot m_a, \qquad 0\leq\lambda\leq1.

The subscripts r and t identify ramjet and turbojet. Each branch has its own fuel stream and exhaust:

                       +-> turbojet + fuel t -> exhaust t
common freestream ----|
 total captured air    +-> ramjet   + fuel r -> exhaust r
                       prescribed air allocation

There is no downstream recombination plane in this diagram. Adding thrusts is not the same operation as mixing exhaust states. A physical mixer would require static-pressure compatibility, area, momentum and energy closure as in Chapter 14; none of those quantities can be inferred from the sum of two thrust numbers.

The air-flow split is an input, not an unknown obtained from pressure matching. Once it is specified, each branch can be solved using its own design-point cycle equations. Chapter 9 gives the turbojet station and shaft balances, and Chapter 25 gives the ramjet design-point calculation. This model calls those cycle calculations; it does not substitute the spatial ramjet flowpath or finite-rate scramjet model.

30.2 A common flight condition

For both branches to belong to one operating point, they must receive the same prescribed freestream Mach number, static temperature and static pressure. ThrustOne takes those three inputs from the turbojet portion of the form. It replaces the corresponding ramjet flight inputs with them before solving the active ramjet branch. The shared-flight fields remain relevant even at the all-ramjet endpoint.

A common flight condition is necessary but not sufficient for a physically matched inlet. It says where the vehicle is operating; it does not establish that the two branch entrances can simultaneously accept their assigned flows. The explicit-split formulation contains no equation equating their inlet-exit static pressures or enforcing a common capture-area geometry.

Care is also needed with user-supplied gas properties. Identical Mach number and static temperature imply identical dimensional speed only when the freestream sound-speed convention agrees. For a calorically perfect gas,

V0=M0γRT0,R=cpγ−1γ. V_0=M_0\sqrt{\gamma R T_0},\qquad R=c_p\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}.

The branch property assumptions should therefore represent the same entering air if the result is interpreted as one physical flight state. Sharing the three flight inputs does not automatically reconcile independently chosen caloric approximations.

30.3 Recovering dimensional thrust and fuel flow

Let s_t and s_r be branch net specific thrusts, each normalized by its own entering air flow. Their units are N/(kg/s), equivalently m/s. Let f_t and f_r be the corresponding fuel-to-air mass ratios. Then

Ft=stṁa,t,Fr=srṁa,r, F_t=s_t\dot m_{a,t},\qquad F_r=s_r\dot m_{a,r},

ṁf,t=ftṁa,t,ṁf,r=frṁa,r. \dot m_{f,t}=f_t\dot m_{a,t},\qquad \dot m_{f,r}=f_r\dot m_{a,r}.

The combined outputs are

F=Ft+Fr,ṁf=ṁf,t+ṁf,r. F=F_t+F_r, \qquad \dot m_f=\dot m_{f,t}+\dot m_{f,r}.

Because each branch result is already a net thrust, its entering-air momentum debit is already present. With compatible freestream conventions, those debits sum to ṁaV0\dot m_aV_0. Subtracting the total captured-air momentum a second time would understate the result. Likewise, pressure-thrust contributions already included by a branch cycle must not be independently added again.

Dividing by total air flow gives

s=(1−λ)st+λsr, s=(1-\lambda)s_t+\lambda s_r,

foverall=(1−λ)ft+λfr. f_{overall}=(1-\lambda)f_t+\lambda f_r.

The second expression is a useful derived bookkeeping quantity; the App reports dimensional combined fuel flow rather than requiring this additional metric. Both relations are air-flow-weighted sums. They should not be confused with an unweighted average of the branch values.

30.4 Why TSFC is not averaged by air fraction

Combined thrust-specific fuel consumption is

TSFC=ṁfF=(1−λ)ft+λfr(1−λ)st+λsr. \mathrm{TSFC}=\frac{\dot m_f}{F} =\frac{(1-\lambda)f_t+\lambda f_r} {(1-\lambda)s_t+\lambda s_r}.

Its SI units are kg/(N s). Multiplication by 3,600 converts it to kg/(N h). Air-flow weighting the two branch TSFC values generally gives the wrong answer because their thrust per unit air differs.

When both branch thrusts are positive, an equivalent expression is

TSFC=FtFTSFCt+FrFTSFCr. \mathrm{TSFC} =\frac{F_t}{F}\mathrm{TSFC}_t +\frac{F_r}{F}\mathrm{TSFC}_r.

It is a thrust-weighted average. Under those conditions the combined value lies between the branch values. This bound is a statement about a positive weighted mixture, not a claim that the combined hardware has no installation penalties.

If the two branches use different fuel heating values, minimum TSFC need not mean minimum chemical-energy input per unit thrust. A separate energy accounting would use

Q̇fuel=ṁf,tHt+ṁf,rHr. \dot Q_{fuel}=\dot m_{f,t}H_t+\dot m_{f,r}H_r.

The explicit-split result does not calculate a combined thermal or overall efficiency. One should not invent such an efficiency by averaging branch efficiencies or by assigning one heating value to unlike fuels.

30.5 Original worked accounting example

Consider a hypothetical pair of already solved branch cycles at one compatible freestream condition:

Quantity Turbojet Ramjet
Net specific thrust 500 N/(kg/s) 800 N/(kg/s)
Fuel-to-air ratio 0.020 0.040

These deliberately simple values illustrate the combining equations; they are not a reference engine or an independently confirmed pair of ThrustOne cycle solutions.

Set total air flow to 80 kg/s and ramjet fraction to 0.25. The turbojet receives 60 kg/s and the ramjet receives 20 kg/s. Therefore

Ft=500(60)=30,000N,Fr=800(20)=16,000N. F_t=500(60)=30,000\;\mathrm N, \qquad F_r=800(20)=16,000\;\mathrm N.

The fuel flows are 1.20 and 0.80 kg/s. Combined thrust is 46,000 N, fuel flow is 2.00 kg/s, and total-air specific thrust is 575 N/(kg/s). The TSFC is

246,000=4.347826×10−5kg/(Ns)=0.156522kg/(Nh). \frac{2}{46,000}=4.347826\times10^{-5} \;\mathrm{kg/(N\,s)} =0.156522\;\mathrm{kg/(N\,h)}.

The branch TSFC values are 0.000040 and 0.000050 kg/(N s). Their air-fraction average would be 0.0000425, which differs from the correct result. The ramjet supplies about 34.78% of thrust although it receives only 25% of air, explaining why thrust weighting is different.

For a contrast, keep both branch states fixed and change the ramjet fraction to 0.75. Branch air flows become 20 and 60 kg/s. Combined thrust becomes 58,000 N and fuel flow becomes 2.80 kg/s. Specific thrust rises to 725 N/(kg/s), while TSFC rises to approximately 0.0000482759 kg/(N s). This example improves thrust per unit captured air but worsens fuel mass per unit thrust. Calling one split “better” requires an objective.

Doubling total air flow with the same branch assumptions and fraction doubles thrust and fuel flow. It leaves specific thrust and TSFC unchanged. This proportionality reflects the design-point accounting model. It does not establish that a fixed physical inlet, compressor or nozzle can pass twice as much air.

30.6 What a split sweep can and cannot optimize

If branch specific thrusts and fuel ratios remain fixed while only the allocation changes,

dsdλ=sr−st. \frac{ds}{d\lambda}=s_r-s_t.

Specific thrust is linear in the split. Its maximum is at an endpoint unless the branch values are equal. For positive combined thrust, differentiating the TSFC ratio gives

dTSFCdλ=frst−ftsr[st+λ(sr−st)]2. \frac{d\,\mathrm{TSFC}}{d\lambda} =\frac{f_rs_t-f_ts_r} {\left[s_t+\lambda(s_r-s_t)\right]^2}.

The numerator is independent of the split. TSFC is therefore monotonic, or constant, under these fixed-branch assumptions. An interior optimum cannot arise from simple allocation alone. It would require another dependence or constraint: changing branch efficiencies, admissible flow limits, installation penalties, temperature restrictions, or a prescribed thrust requirement, for example.

This result prevents a common interpretation error. A smooth curve generated by moving a split slider is not a computed transition schedule. The model has not solved how geometry, inlet recovery or operating limits evolve during a transition. It has repeated the explicit accounting at different allocations.

30.7 Endpoints, failures and reporting

At λ=0\lambda=0, only the turbojet branch is solved. At λ=1\lambda=1, only the ramjet branch is solved. ThrustOne deliberately skips a zero-flow branch so that an irrelevant cycle failure does not invalidate the selected endpoint. Metrics for an inactive branch need not exist; absence does not mean a hidden calculation returned zero.

For any positive assigned branch flow, that branch must solve successfully. An invalid active cycle is not replaced by the other branch, and its mass allocation is not automatically changed. Even a very small positive allocation invokes its cycle. Endpoint behavior therefore distinguishes a truly inactive branch from an active branch operating outside its supported conditions.

The wrapper requires finite positive total air flow, a finite split in [0,1], finite positive resultant thrust, and finite nonnegative combined fuel flow. Passing these checks establishes an admissible result for this synthesis. It does not certify inlet matching, stable simultaneous operation or hardware feasibility.

The reported warnings identify the independence of the cycles and the absence of common-inlet/back-pressure matching, mixing, variable geometry, channel gating and automatic mode switching. The wrapper does not aggregate all child-cycle warnings. Consequently, the absence of a particular branch warning from the combined warning list should not be read as an additional acceptance test. The branch assumptions and any known branch limitations remain applicable.

30.8 Relation to a physical combined-cycle engine

A transition analysis would need to connect the assigned flow split to realizable flow areas and compatible pressures. It would also need to establish acceptable rotating-machine conditions while the ramjet path changes its demand, account for inactive-path drag and thermal exposure, and determine a stable evolution through the changeover. Those are coupled physical questions, not missing arithmetic in the weighted sum.

The current mode is useful before those questions are addressed: it makes normalization explicit, separates branch contributions, and shows the trade between thrust and fuel consumption under declared cycle assumptions. Its proper conclusion is a conditional one: these independently calculated branch performances produce this combined accounting result at this prescribed split. It does not establish that an integrated engine will realize that operating point.

31. The ideal ejector–ramjet

An ejector transfers momentum and energy from a primary stream to an entrained secondary stream. The primary material is carried on the vehicle; the secondary material is drawn from the surrounding air. Unlike the explicit allocation of Chapter 30, the entrainment ratio in this model is an output of a coupled mixing calculation. No compressor shaft is needed, but the absence of rotating machinery does not make the transfer reversible.

ThrustOne implements one specific branch: a supersonic primary stream and a subsonic secondary stream enter a constant-area mixing passage at equal static pressure, and the fully mixed passage exit is sonic. An idealized downstream heater and fully expanded nozzle complete the performance calculation. This is a local ejector–ramjet submodel, not a complete rocket-based combined-cycle engine.

31.1 Stations, assumptions and closure

Use p and s for the primary and secondary streams, I for their common-pressure entrance plane, E for the sonic mixed exit, and N for the final nozzle exit. A subscript t denotes a total state. The flow sequence is

primary total state -> supersonic primary at I --+
                                                +-> sonic mixed E -> heat -> N
ambient secondary -> subsonic secondary at I ---+
                       equal static pressure       constant-area mixer

Both streams have the same constant gas properties, including gamma and gas constant R. The mixer is steady, adiabatic and free of wall friction and shock waves. There is no mixing before the specified entrance plane. Downstream heat addition occurs in an ideal zero-Mach limit without an imposed total-pressure loss, and its fuel mass is neglected. The final nozzle expands isentropically to ambient pressure.

The inputs specify the two total states, primary critical area A_p*, total mixer area A, common gamma, ambient conditions, secondary freestream Mach number and final total temperature. The unknown common inlet pressure p_I determines both inlet Mach numbers, their area allocation and the entrainment ratio. Conservation then determines the sonic exit state. One remaining momentum equation selects p_I.

This ordering is essential. The inlet pressure cannot be specified independently along with an arbitrary entrainment ratio and still be expected to satisfy the same sonic-exit problem. A hand calculation may try a pressure, but a trial with a nonzero momentum residual is not a converged operating point.

31.2 The permitted pressure interval

For a calorically perfect gas, define

Θ(M)=1+γ−12M2,ptp=Θ(M)γ/(γ−1). \Theta(M)=1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2, \qquad \frac{p_t}{p}=\Theta(M)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

At a trial p_I,

MpI=2γ−1[(ptppI)(γ−1)/γ−1], M_{pI}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\gamma-1} \left[\left(\frac{p_{tp}}{p_I}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}-1\right]},

with the analogous expression using p_ts for M_sI. Define the sonic static-to-total pressure ratio

r*=(2γ+1)γ/(γ−1). r_* =\left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

The selected branches require

ptsr*<pI<min⁡(pts,ptpr*). p_{ts}r_*<p_I<\min(p_{ts},p_{tp}r_*).

The lower limit excludes sonic or supersonic secondary entry. The upper limits exclude zero secondary velocity and subsonic primary entry. These are strict inequalities. An empty interval means the specified total pressures cannot support the requested pair of branches.

A pressure inside the interval is only a candidate. It must also yield a positive remaining area for the secondary stream and satisfy the downstream requirements. Pressure admissibility alone does not establish an ejector solution.

31.3 Area allocation and entrainment

The primary critical area establishes its mass-flow scale. Its inlet area follows from the supersonic area relation:

ApIAp*=1MpI[2γ+1Θ(MpI)]n,n=γ+12(γ−1). \frac{A_{pI}}{A_p^*}= \frac1{M_{pI}} \left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\Theta(M_{pI})\right]^n, \qquad n=\frac{\gamma+1}{2(\gamma-1)}.

Define area fractions ϕp=ApI/A\phi_p=A_{pI}/A and ϕs=1−ϕp\phi_s=1-\phi_p. Both must be positive. If the primary stream alone occupies the whole passage, a positive secondary mass flow cannot be accommodated on this branch.

The ideal mass-flow expression at a station is

ṁ=AptTtγRMΘ(M)−n. \dot m=A\frac{p_t}{\sqrt{T_t}} \sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{R}}M\Theta(M)^{-n}.

Taking the secondary-to-primary ratio cancels the common gas constant and gives the entrainment ratio

β=ṁsṁp=ptsptpϕsϕpMsIMpITtpTts[Θ(MpI)Θ(MsI)]n. \beta=\frac{\dot m_s}{\dot m_p} =\frac{p_{ts}}{p_{tp}}\frac{\phi_s}{\phi_p} \frac{M_{sI}}{M_{pI}} \sqrt{\frac{T_{tp}}{T_{ts}}} \left[\frac{\Theta(M_{pI})}{\Theta(M_{sI})}\right]^n.

This is a mass-flow ratio. It is not an area ratio, a fuel-to-air ratio or a freely assigned bypass ratio. In particular, a large secondary area does not necessarily imply equally large entrainment: its total pressure, temperature and Mach number also determine the mass flux.

31.4 Energy and mass at the sonic exit

Adiabatic mixing with the same constant heat capacity gives
