ṁpcpTtp+ṁscpTts=(ṁp+ṁs)cpTtE. \dot m_pc_pT_{tp}+\dot m_sc_pT_{ts} =(\dot m_p+\dot m_s)c_pT_{tE}.

Therefore

TtE=Ttp+βTts1+β,TE=2TtEγ+1. T_{tE}=\frac{T_{tp}+\beta T_{ts}}{1+\beta}, \qquad T_E=\frac{2T_{tE}}{\gamma+1}.

The second relation uses the imposed sonic exit. The mixed total temperature lies between the two entering total temperatures; the static exit temperature is lower because some energy remains kinetic.

Primary choked flow is

ṁp=Ap*ptpγRTtp(2γ+1)n. \dot m_p=A_p^*p_{tp}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{RT_{tp}}} \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^n.

At the sonic mixed exit, ṁE=ApEγ/(RTE)\dot m_E=Ap_E\sqrt{\gamma/(RT_E)}. Equating this with (1+β)ṁp(1+\beta)\dot m_p gives

pE=(1+β)Ap*AptpTETtp(2γ+1)n. p_E=(1+\beta)\frac{A_p^*}{A}p_{tp} \sqrt{\frac{T_E}{T_{tp}}} \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^n.

No dimensional R is required to calculate this pressure or the entrainment ratio because it cancels. This is why the submodel can report useful nondimensional performance without requiring a separately supplied gas constant or a dimensional primary mass flow.

31.5 Momentum selects the inlet pressure

For an ideal gas, ρV2=γpM2\rho V^2=\gamma pM^2, so pressure plus axial momentum flux through area A_i is piAi(1+γMi2)p_iA_i(1+\gamma M_i^2). The constant-area mixer momentum equation is

pIA[ϕp(1+γMpI2)+ϕs(1+γMsI2)]=pEA(1+γ). p_IA\left[\phi_p(1+\gamma M_{pI}^2) +\phi_s(1+\gamma M_{sI}^2)\right] =p_EA(1+\gamma).

The area cancels. ThrustOne reports the dimensionless residual

rF=pE(1+γ)pI[ϕp(1+γMpI2)+ϕs(1+γMsI2)]−1. r_F=\frac{p_E(1+\gamma)} {p_I[\phi_p(1+\gamma M_{pI}^2)+\phi_s(1+\gamma M_{sI}^2)]}-1.

A zero residual closes the selected problem. It does not prove reversibility. In particular, an adiabatic mixer can redistribute momentum and generate entropy while conserving total enthalpy. “No prescribed total-pressure-loss factor” should not be interpreted as preservation of either entering total pressure.

The sonic exit total pressure is recovered from its local state:

ptE=pE(γ+12)γ/(γ−1). p_{tE}=p_E\left(\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}.

Its value is an output, not an average of the two entering total pressures.

31.6 Ideal heating and thrust augmentation

The final total temperature T_tN is prescribed. The implementation requires it to be at least T_tE, so this stage represents heating or zero additional heating. It does not solve fuel chemistry or calculate the fuel mass needed to reach that temperature. The ideal heater retains p_tE. The final nozzle Mach number follows from p_tE/p_a and must be supersonic on the supported branch.

For comparison, imagine the primary stream alone expanding to ambient pressure. Denote its resulting speed by V_p0. Let V_0 be the secondary freestream speed and V_N the mixed final exhaust speed. With no final pressure thrust and negligible heater fuel mass,

F=(ṁp+ṁs)VN−ṁsV0. F=(\dot m_p+\dot m_s)V_N-\dot m_sV_0.

There is no captured-air momentum debit for the onboard primary stream. Dividing by the primary-alone thrust ṁpVp0\dot m_pV_{p0} gives

𝒜F=(1+β)VNVp0−βV0Vp0. \mathcal A_F=(1+\beta)\frac{V_N}{V_{p0}} -\beta\frac{V_0}{V_{p0}}.

Velocity ratios follow from V=MγRTt/Θ(M)V=M\sqrt{\gamma RT_t/\Theta(M)}, so R again cancels. An augmentation above one means increased force relative to this particular primary-only reference. It is not a fuel efficiency or specific impulse. Additional downstream heating can contribute energy without a corresponding fuel-mass penalty in this ideal model.

31.7 Original accounting example and a failed trial

To isolate the balances, consider an illustrative candidate with gamma 1.4, entrainment ratio 2, primary total temperature 2,400 K and secondary total temperature 300 K. These numbers are not asserted to form a solved geometry. The mixed total temperature is

TtE=2400+2(300)3=1000K,TE=1000/1.2=833.333K. T_{tE}=\frac{2400+2(300)}3=1000\;\mathrm K, \qquad T_E=1000/1.2=833.333\;\mathrm K.

Per unit primary mass flow, the incoming total-enthalpy factor is cp[2400+2(300)]=3000cpc_p[2400+2(300)]=3000c_p. The outgoing factor is 3cp(1000)=3000cp3c_p(1000)=3000c_p, demonstrating energy closure. Prescribing a final total temperature of 900 K would violate the heating-only condition; 1,200 K would require an external specific heat input of cp(1200−1000)c_p(1200-1000) per unit mixed mass, with fuel mass still unmodeled.

For a separate momentum trial, take p_I=100 kPa, gamma=1.4, primary Mach 2, secondary Mach 0.5 and area fractions 0.2 and 0.8. The entering pressure-plus-momentum flux per unit total area is

100[0.2(1+1.4×4)+0.8(1+1.4×0.25)]=240kPa. 100[0.2(1+1.4\times4)+0.8(1+1.4\times0.25)] =240\;\mathrm{kPa}.

A sonic exit would need p_E=100 kPa for momentum closure. If the independently recovered mass/energy exit pressure were 110 kPa, the residual would be 0.10. The positive temperatures and admissible Mach branches would not rescue that trial. It would still have a ten-percent momentum imbalance and require a different trial pressure.

Finally, illustrative speed ratios V_N/V_p0=0.6 and V_0/V_p0=0.1 with beta=2 give augmentation 1.6. The exhaust speed is lower than the primary-alone speed, but three times the primary mass leaves the nozzle. Increasing entrainment cannot be assessed while holding these speed ratios arbitrarily fixed: the coupled mixing solution normally changes them.

31.8 Numerical and physical boundaries

The solver samples the admissible inlet-pressure interval to seek a residual sign change, then bisects a detected bracket. Invalid candidates break the continuity of the scan. Multiple detected sign-change brackets are rejected rather than silently selecting one; a sampled near-zero residual can be accepted directly. This finite search is not a mathematical proof that every possible root has been enumerated. Failure to detect a bracket means the implemented search did not find a solution on its permitted states.

The secondary freestream Mach input is distinct from the secondary Mach at the mixer entrance. Its total temperature and pressure must agree with the ambient static state through isentropic relations; the narrow input allowance accommodates rounded values, not an independently pressurized secondary supply. Final static pressure must equal ambient. Both the primary-alone reference expansion and final mixed expansion must be supersonic.

The model excludes a choked secondary inlet, an unchoked mixed exit, shocks, wall friction, finite-rate mixing and combustion, and additional fuel mass. It does not predict a mixing length, injector geometry, rocket feed system or mode transition. Its internal trial evaluator can report a nonzero residual for a hand-iteration worksheet; that output must be distinguished from the automatic solver’s converged result.

The App mode rbcc.ideal_ejector is consequently best read as an ideal entrainment and augmentation calculation under explicit branch assumptions. The broader combined-cycle label supplies architectural context. It does not expand the equations into the other operating modes of a vehicle engine.

32. The ideal air-turboramjet

An air-turboramjet uses a supplied hot primary stream to drive a turbine, whose shaft powers a fan in the captured-air stream. The streams then mix and may receive additional heat before expansion. Its defining transfer is mechanical: energy removed from the primary stream raises the total pressure and temperature of the air. This differs from the direct momentum exchange in the ejector of Chapter 31.

The ThrustOne model begins with the primary total pressure and temperature already specified. It does not derive that state from a gas generator, propellant combination, pump or cooling circuit. Its output describes the ideal downstream use of that supplied stream.

32.1 Flow sequence and the zero-Mach mixing limit

Let a denote captured air, p the primary stream, f the fan exit, q the primary turbine exit, m the mixed state and N the final exhaust. The topology is

captured air -> ideal fan -----------+
                    ↑ shaft power    +-> slow mixing -> heating -> nozzle
supplied primary -> ideal turbine --+

Both streams use the same calorically perfect gas properties. Fan and turbine processes are isentropic, shaft transfer is lossless, and the incoming air total state is the isentropic total state of the prescribed freestream. Mixing and downstream heating are idealized as occurring at negligible Mach number. At the mixing plane, static and total pressures therefore coincide in the approximation.

This is not the finite-velocity, momentum-conserving mixer of Chapter 14. It has no solved area, entrance velocity or mixing-length requirement. The zero-Mach assumption removes kinetic mixing and Rayleigh total-pressure penalties. The primary turbine is assigned the fan-exit total pressure at its outlet so the streams meet at a common pressure.

32.2 Fan work and available turbine expansion

Define the fan pressure ratio as πf=ptf/pta>1\pi_f=p_{tf}/p_{ta}>1, and let k=(γ−1)/γk=(\gamma-1)/\gamma. Isentropic compression gives

Ttf=Ttaπfk,wf=cpTta(πfk−1). T_{tf}=T_{ta}\pi_f^k, \qquad w_f=c_pT_{ta}(\pi_f^k-1).

The primary turbine expands from p_tp to ptq=πfptap_{tq}=\pi_fp_{ta}, giving

Ttq=Ttp(πfptaptp)k, T_{tq}=T_{tp}\left(\frac{\pi_fp_{ta}}{p_{tp}}\right)^k,

wt=cpTtp[1−(πfptaptp)k]. w_t=c_pT_{tp}\left[1- \left(\frac{\pi_fp_{ta}}{p_{tp}}\right)^k\right].

The fan-exit pressure must be lower than the supplied primary total pressure. Otherwise the assumed turbine expansion cannot supply positive shaft work. Both pressure availability and a positive fan temperature rise are needed; a nominally hot primary stream alone does not guarantee a solution.

Let β=ṁa/ṁp\beta=\dot m_a/\dot m_p. Equating turbine power to fan power,

ṁpcp(Ttp−Ttq)=ṁacp(Ttf−Tta), \dot m_pc_p(T_{tp}-T_{tq}) =\dot m_ac_p(T_{tf}-T_{ta}),

so

β=TtpTta1−(πfpta/ptp)kπfk−1. \beta=\frac{T_{tp}}{T_{ta}} \frac{1-(\pi_fp_{ta}/p_{tp})^k}{\pi_f^k-1}.

The bypass ratio is therefore an output of shaft balance, not a selected air split. Gas constant and common heat capacity cancel from this expression. Their cancellation relies on the shared-property assumptions; it does not authorize substituting two unrelated gases while keeping this equation unchanged.

32.3 Mixing and conservation of the original energy

The mixed total temperature is

Ttm=βTtf+Ttq1+β. T_{tm}=\frac{\beta T_{tf}+T_{tq}}{1+\beta}.

Using the work balance to eliminate the temperatures changed by the machinery gives a particularly useful equivalent expression:

βTtf+Ttq=βTta+Ttp,Ttm=βTta+Ttp1+β. \beta T_{tf}+T_{tq}=\beta T_{ta}+T_{tp}, \qquad T_{tm}=\frac{\beta T_{ta}+T_{tp}}{1+\beta}.

The fan and turbine redistribute energy between the streams; their internal shaft transfer does not create energy in the combined control volume. The machinery changes pressure and establishes the air throughput even though the combined incoming and mixed total enthalpies agree.

ThrustOne reports two residuals in temperature units:

rW=Ttq−Ttp+β(Ttf−Tta), r_W=T_{tq}-T_{tp}+\beta(T_{tf}-T_{ta}),

rM=βTtf+Ttq−(1+β)Ttm. r_M=\beta T_{tf}+T_{tq}-(1+\beta)T_{tm}.

Multiplying r_W by ṁpcp\dot m_pc_p converts its scale to a power imbalance. A small residual confirms these algebraic balances, not fan efficiency, turbine cooling adequacy or a verified primary-stream source.

32.4 Downstream heating and the reported fuel ratio

The target exhaust total temperature must not be below the mixed total temperature. Equality describes no additional heating. Define the supplied dimensionless fuel-energy parameter

ℋ=ηbHcpT0, \mathcal H=\frac{\eta_bH}{c_pT_0},

where H is fuel heating value and ηb\eta_b is the assumed heat-release efficiency. The implemented simplified relation is

f=TtN−TtmT0ℋ. f=\frac{T_{tN}-T_{tm}}{T_0\mathcal H}.

The App uses this f as added fuel per captured-air mass in exhaust-mass accounting. It is a reduced heat-addition convention, not the exact mass-inclusive energy balance for the whole primary-plus-air mixture.

To see the distinction, neglect fuel sensible enthalpy and retain all mass in a constant-cp balance. With f=ṁf/ṁaf=\dot m_f/\dot m_a, the exact algebra under those additional assumptions would give

fηbH=cp[(1+1/β+f)TtN−(1+1/β)Ttm], f\eta_bH=c_p\left[(1+1/\beta+f)T_{tN} -(1+1/\beta)T_{tm}\right],

or

f=(1+1/β)(TtN−Ttm)T0ℋ−TtN. f=\frac{(1+1/\beta)(T_{tN}-T_{tm})} {T_0\mathcal H-T_{tN}}.

This last equation is background for interpreting the approximation; it is not an alternative option implemented by the current mode. The App’s simpler expression neglects the primary-to-air correction and the extra fuel’s sensible-energy demand in this heating estimate. Those approximations become more consequential when beta is small or final temperature is not small relative to T0ℋT_0\mathcal H. The reported fuel ratio should not be promoted to a complete gas-generator or propellant-system requirement.

32.5 Expansion and two force normalizations

The nozzle total pressure is ptN=πfptap_{tN}=\pi_fp_{ta}, retained through ideal slow mixing and heating. With final static pressure equal to ambient,

MN=2γ−1[(πfptap0)k−1]. M_N=\sqrt{\frac2{\gamma-1} \left[\left(\frac{\pi_fp_{ta}}{p_0}\right)^k-1\right]}.

The current mode admits subsonic and supersonic exhaust solutions. Unlike the ejector model, it does not require a supersonic nozzle exit. The branch is determined by the pressure ratio rather than independently chosen. The exact sonic boundary is classified with the non-subsonic branch in the implementation; it represents Mach one, not a finite supersonic margin.

Neglecting final pressure thrust, the exhaust mass per unit primary mass is 1+β(1+f)1+\beta(1+f). If V_p0 denotes the speed obtained by expanding the supplied primary stream alone to ambient pressure, augmentation is

𝒜F=[1+β(1+f)]VNVp0−βV0Vp0. \mathcal A_F=[1+\beta(1+f)]\frac{V_N}{V_{p0}} -\beta\frac{V_0}{V_{p0}}.

Only captured air incurs the incoming momentum debit. The primary and added fuel are onboard streams. Specific thrust per captured-air flow is

sa=(1+f+1/β)VN−V0. s_a=(1+f+1/\beta)V_N-V_0.

The two outputs use different denominators and cannot be numerically compared as though both were specific thrust. Velocity ratios follow the common-gas total-to-static relations. The dimensional scale is supplied by the ambient sound speed and freestream Mach through V0=a0M0V_0=a_0M_0.

32.6 Original shaft and mixing example

Choose illustrative temperatures T_ta=300 K, T_tp=1,800 K and fan temperature ratio 1.2. Suppose the turbine temperature ratio is 0.8. The fan exit is 360 K and the turbine exit is 1,440 K. The shaft balance gives

β=1800−1440360−300=6. \beta=\frac{1800-1440}{360-300}=6.

For gamma 1.4, consistent pressure ratios can be constructed as πf=1.23.5\pi_f=1.2^{3.5} and ptq/ptp=0.83.5p_{tq}/p_{tp}=0.8^{3.5}; these ensure the temperatures describe isentropic machines. The example is an original subsystem balance, not a complete freestream/nozzle solution.

The mixed total temperature is

Ttm=6(360)+14407=514.286K. T_{tm}=\frac{6(360)+1440}{7}=514.286\;\mathrm K.

Using the original incoming temperatures gives [6(300)+1800]/7[6(300)+1800]/7, exactly the same value. The residuals vanish because the turbine temperature drop of 360 K per primary mass equals the fan temperature rise of 60 K multiplied by six times as much air.

For a separate illustration of the heating convention, let T0ℋ=120,000T_0\mathcal H=120,000 K and prescribe T_tN=1,200 K. The implemented relation gives f=0.00571429. The mass-inclusive background expression above would give approximately 0.00673401. The difference arises from different energy bookkeeping assumptions, not numerical precision. Neither number supplies the propellant consumption needed to create the primary stream.

32.7 Limiting behavior and admissibility

As fan-exit pressure approaches primary total pressure from below, available turbine work vanishes and beta tends toward zero for a fixed fan ratio above one. Specific thrust per captured-air mass then becomes a poorly conditioned normalization because its denominator shrinks. The App requires a finite positive beta and does not continue to a primary-only endpoint as a separate mode.

As fan pressure ratio approaches one from above while positive turbine expansion remains available, required work per unit air approaches zero and the ideal formula can imply very large beta. This is a limitation of the ideal unbounded-throughput model. No fan area, speed or flow map constrains the inferred air mass flow. The exact ratio one is excluded rather than evaluated by division by zero.

The freestream Mach number must be positive. Although the architecture is motivated partly by low-speed operation, a static-takeoff result at exactly zero Mach is not supported by this implementation’s velocity-ratio normalization. The air total state must be consistent with its prescribed ambient static state and Mach, allowing only a narrow rounding tolerance. Final pressure must equal ambient, and returned net specific thrust must be finite and positive.

The model assumes no primary fuel remains to react during mixing, no gas-generator chemistry, no pumps, no cooling, no component maps and no automatic transition. It cannot calculate the cost of maintaining the supplied primary pressure and temperature. Its proper role is to expose how that given primary stream can ideally power compression, combine with air and contribute to a fully expanded exhaust under the stated approximations.

33. Numerical solutions as engineering results

A numerical answer is more than a value that stopped changing. It represents an equation, a physical branch, a set of input assumptions and a termination condition. Two calculations can print the same temperature while answering different questions; two calculations can print slightly different temperatures while representing the same solution within meaningful precision. This chapter explains how to read the numerical evidence accompanying the models developed earlier.

ThrustOne uses several kinds of numerical calculation: scalar root searches, coupled state reconstruction, interpolation and spatial or temporal integration. Their convergence indicators are not interchangeable. A small root residual is different from a small integration error estimate, and neither is a statement that the underlying physical approximation is valid for a particular engine.

33.1 Three different questions

A useful interpretation separates three questions. First, do the inputs define a problem admitted by the model? Second, did the numerical method solve that problem to its stated termination criterion? Third, does the model represent the intended physical situation closely enough to support the conclusion being drawn?

For example, a fully expanded ideal nozzle can have a tightly converged exit Mach number. If the actual task concerns a fixed nozzle under varying back pressure, convergence does not supply the missing shock or separation response. Conversely, failure to finish an explicit reacting-flow integration may reflect chemical stiffness rather than the nonexistence of a physical flow.

The dependencies can be pictured as

specified inputs -> admissible model/branch -> numerical solution -> interpretation
                         |                         |
                  rejected definition       residual or stop reason

A rejection before solving has no numerical answer to interpret. An interrupted integration may have valid intermediate states but no completed exit. A completed result still carries the physical limits of its model.

33.2 Residuals and units

Suppose a scalar unknown x is defined by R(x)=0. The residual R measures failure to satisfy the equation; its units follow the equation. A residual of 0.01 K in an enthalpy inversion rewritten in temperature units is not comparable with 0.01 N in a momentum balance or 0.01 in a normalized pressure ratio.

Scaling makes residuals easier to interpret:

r=RS, r=\frac{R}{S},

where S is a stated reference scale. However, a reference that approaches zero can make a relative residual misleading or undefined. A useful combined acceptance form is

|R|≤ϵabs+ϵrelS. |R|\leq\epsilon_{abs}+\epsilon_{rel}S.

The absolute allowance protects quantities whose correct value vanishes. The relative allowance expresses proportional accuracy away from zero. These are explanatory forms, not a claim that every ThrustOne solver uses one shared formula or tolerance.

Consider an energy balance with incoming and outgoing powers near 2 MW and a difference of 0.1 W. Relative to transported energy, the discrepancy is five parts in one hundred million. If the intended output is a net power of only 0.2 W obtained by subtracting those large flows, the same discrepancy is half the net result. The acceptable accuracy depends on what the user is trying to infer, not just the size of the operands.

The reacting-flow diagnostics in Chapter 29 distinguish mass-relative residual, elemental-relative residual and dimensional energy and momentum residuals. The turbine–fan residuals in Chapter 32 use temperature units. Their labels are part of the meaning of the result.

33.3 A small residual need not mean a small state error

Near a simple root x*, a first-order expansion gives

R(x)≈R′(x*)(x−x*),x−x*≈R(x)R′(x*). R(x)\approx R'(x^*)(x-x^*), \qquad x-x^*\approx\frac{R(x)}{R'(x^*)}.

If the derivative is small, a small residual can coexist with a appreciable state error. This is conditioning: it describes sensitivity inherent in the equation, not merely the quality of the algorithm.

The area–Mach relation provides a physical example. At the sonic minimum, the first derivative of area ratio with respect to Mach vanishes. Its local expansion for a calorically perfect gas is

AA*≈1+2γ+1(M−1)2. \frac{A}{A^*}\approx1+\frac{2}{\gamma+1}(M-1)^2.

Thus a small positive area excess delta corresponds approximately to

M−1≈±γ+12δ. M-1\approx\pm\sqrt{\frac{\gamma+1}{2}\,\delta}.

For gamma=1.4 and delta=0.0001, this gives M approximately 0.98905 or 1.01095. An area ratio only one ten-thousandth above its minimum produces two distinct states roughly one percent from sonic speed. Specifying more digits in the area ratio does not remove the need to choose a branch.

At delta=0 the roots merge. Below zero there is no real area–Mach state. A solver must distinguish these cases rather than interpreting every failure near the minimum as a request for more iterations.

33.4 Brackets and physical branches

For a continuous residual, opposite signs at two admissible endpoints guarantee at least one zero between them. Bisection repeatedly halves the interval while preserving that sign change. After n halvings, an initial width W becomes W/2^n. This is a transparent numerical guarantee about a continuous bracket; it does not prove the root is physically desired or unique.

As an original arithmetic example, use R(x)=x²−2 on [1,2]. The first midpoint 1.5 has positive residual 0.25, so the root remains in [1,1.5]. The next midpoint 1.25 has negative residual −0.4375, leaving [1.25,1.5]. After twenty halvings the bracket width is below one millionth. The argument works because the residual is continuous and each retained interval contains a sign change.

A pole can imitate a sign change without containing a zero: R(x)=1/(x−1) is negative below one and positive above one, but has no root there. An implementation must not bridge an invalid state and call the resulting interval a physical bracket. The ejector search described in Chapter 31 breaks its scan across inadmissible candidates for this reason.

A finite scan can also miss a root that touches zero without changing sign, or two nearby crossings within a single sampled interval. Detected bracket counts describe what the search found. They should not be reported as a universal proof of the number of mathematical solutions.

For oblique shocks, branch selection has a physical meaning: weak and strong attached roots describe different compression states. For frozen flux reconstruction, the retained subsonic or supersonic state is part of the supplied closure. Choosing whichever root converges first would change the problem.

33.5 Coupled equations and conservation checks

Several models calculate one quantity from a balance and then use it in another. Each stage may be locally converged while the assembled result is inconsistent if conventions differ. Typical causes include total versus static temperature, fuel-to-core-air versus fuel-to-total-air normalization, and mixing enthalpies with incompatible reference states.

A conservation check is valuable because it recombines the final quantities into the original balance. For a steady duct with injection,

ṁout−ṁin−∫qmdx=0, \dot m_{out}-\dot m_{in}-\int q_mdx=0,

ℰout−ℰin−∫(Q′+qmht,inj)dx=0. \mathcal E_{out}-\mathcal E_{in} -\int(Q'+q_mh_{t,inj})dx=0.

These checks ask whether the computed solution obeys the imposed bookkeeping. They do not show that an injection profile, heat-transfer coefficient or kinetic mechanism was correctly chosen for an experiment. Conservation is necessary for the model; it is not a replacement for the model’s assumptions.

Likewise, the zero turbine–fan work residual in Chapter 32 follows the equations used to calculate bypass ratio. It is useful for detecting implementation or arithmetic inconsistency, but it is not independent evidence for the realism of ideal machinery.

33.6 Interpolation and inverse maps

A component map defines supported data coordinates. Interpolation estimates between those coordinates according to a chosen shape rule. It does not establish performance outside the measured or supplied domain. Extrapolation introduces an additional model even when software can produce a smooth line.

The map operations discussed in Chapter 11 preserve their declared domain and branch restrictions. An inverse query can have more than one answer when the mapped quantity turns around. A target value alone may therefore be insufficient; a branch or interval is needed to close the inverse problem.

A visually smooth interpolant is not evidence that every derivative represents measured physics. Derivative-sensitive conclusions, such as a predicted optimum close to a sparse endpoint, require particular care. A maximum among supplied samples, a maximum of the interpolant and the actual maximum of a component are three different quantities.

33.7 Integration accuracy and stiffness

A trajectory solves differential equations over time or distance. A local error estimate controls the discrepancy of one step, not the uncertainty of the complete physical prediction. Errors can accumulate or be amplified by sensitive dynamics. Conversely, some stable balances constrain the trajectory even when individual local changes are large.

The reacting-flow method of Chapter 29 compares an Euler predictor with a Heun corrector. The constant-property duct and established-burning transient use other stepping arrangements. Their step counts and tolerances should not be compared as though they were one universal accuracy scale.

Stiffness arises when the equations contain widely separated timescales. For illustration, the decay equation y’=−ky integrated by explicit Euler gives

yn+1=(1−kΔt)yn. y_{n+1}=(1-k\Delta t)y_n.

A positive monotonically decaying solution requires a sufficiently small step; if k delta-t exceeds two, even linear stability is lost. This analytical example explains why a rapidly relaxing chemical component can force short explicit steps while the bulk flow changes slowly. It is not the exact stability bound for the App’s multicomponent Heun system.

Reaching an accepted-step limit therefore has a different meaning from reaching an imposed sonic boundary. The first is a computational stop. The second concerns the supported branch of the steady equations. Both can leave a valid prefix, but neither produces a completed downstream solution.

33.8 Events, prefixes and displayed samples

An event is a condition such as burnout, unchoking or approach to Mach one. Event handling can retain the last admissible state, interpolate to a boundary, or solve for a precise event location. These approaches yield different meanings for the final row.

The established-burning model of Chapter 22 interpolates its burnout boundary but retains a previous valid state for certain other stops. The duct and reacting-flow chapters state their own prefix behavior. A reader should not assume that the last printed coordinate is an exactly located physical endpoint simply because its label says “final.”

A further distinction is output sampling. A solver may accept many internal steps but retain fewer rows for export. Connecting those rows produces a readable chart; it does not disclose every internal step or prove the resolution of a steep transition. Conversely, more plotted points can be interpolation rather than additional solved information.

A useful report preserves the original input, model and branch, completion flag, stop explanation, meaningful residuals and units. It presents interrupted results as partial histories and reserves final-engine performance for a completed path where the selected model requires one.

33.9 Precision and defensible conclusions

Digits should reflect the information available. A calculator may determine a root to many digits while using rounded gas properties, ideal efficiencies or a prescribed empirical coefficient with much larger uncertainty. Printing all numerical digits does not improve those inputs.

The appropriate conclusion connects the result to its question: a root on the specified branch, a conservation-consistent state, a completed history under the supplied sources, or a best sampled point under fixed assumptions. When a result fails, the useful next action is to identify whether the input, physical branch, numerical search or unsupported model assumption caused the failure. Repeatedly tightening tolerances cannot repair a problem whose required physics is absent.

34. Parameter studies and defensible comparisons

A parameter study is a sequence of individually defined problems. Its value comes from the relationship between them: what changes, what remains fixed, what is recalculated, and which results satisfy the chosen constraints. A dense plot without those definitions is difficult to interpret even when every point has been calculated correctly.

The engine-specific chapters supply the equations and limitations. This chapter explains how to use their outputs to compare alternatives without turning a sampled trend into an unsupported design claim.

34.1 Define the question before the axis

Suppose the question is how rocket thrust changes with chamber pressure. At least three studies are possible: hold throat area fixed; resize throat area to preserve mass flow; or resize it to preserve target thrust. All vary chamber pressure, but they answer different questions.

For fixed gas properties and choked flow,

ṁ=pcAtc*. \dot m=\frac{p_cA_t}{c^*}.

Holding A_t and c* fixed makes mass flow proportional to pressure. Holding mass flow fixed instead requires A_t to vary inversely with pressure. The resulting exhaust size, pressure thrust and interpretation are different. A curve labeled only “thrust versus chamber pressure” conceals this distinction.

A useful study definition states the model, varied inputs, held inputs, recomputed states, constraints and objective. For a turbine cycle, pressure ratio may be a design input or an off-design output. The same axis cannot be treated as independent in both problems without changing the closure.

34.2 Fixed inputs are not fixed outputs

Changing an input can alter several dependent quantities. In a chemistry calculation at fixed chamber temperature, changing mixture ratio changes composition and properties. In an enthalpy-closed chamber, changing the mixture may also change chamber temperature. Those two curves cannot be interpreted as though they differ only by numerical method.

Similarly, increasing the target turbine-inlet temperature can change fuel ratio, turbine work balance and nozzle state. Holding the displayed efficiency inputs constant does not hold the cycle outputs constant. A sensitivity statement should identify the dependent path rather than describing every quantity as independently adjustable.

The rocket scans in Chapter 20 preserve their declared baseline scale. An original target-thrust sizing operation is not repeated at every scan point merely because it was used to create the baseline. Once throat area has been resolved and held fixed, the scan is a fixed-scale study. Its changing thrust is part of the answer.

34.3 Design families versus one engine off design

A design-point sweep usually compares a family of cycles that each satisfy the same type of station equations with different prescribed design inputs. It does not automatically represent one piece of hardware moving through an operating envelope.

An off-design calculation retains reference constraints, such as normalized flow or area relationships, and solves dependent quantities. The legacy turbojet sweep consequently rejects compressor pressure ratio as an independent off-design axis: that quantity is determined by the reference model. It also rejects unsupported combinations rather than silently routing every mode through the same constant-property calculation.

A fair comparison makes this distinction visible:

reference inputs + chosen study variable
                 |
          selected model closure
                 |
     recomputed dependent states and outputs
                 |
      admissibility, constraints, objective

Changing the reference point between rows creates another study. It may be useful, but it is no longer the original fixed-reference off-design question.

34.4 Sampling and axis construction

For n uniformly spaced samples between x_min and x_max,

xi=xmin+in−1(xmax−xmin),i=0,…,n−1. x_i=x_{min}+\frac{i}{n-1}(x_{max}-x_{min}), \qquad i=0,\ldots,n-1.

The endpoints are included. A two-axis study forms pairs of samples, so its cost grows as the product of the axis counts. The legacy turbojet sweep accepts two to one thousand points per axis but limits the combined number to one thousand. Those limits govern that executor, not every study mode in the App.

Uniform sampling in x is not uniform sampling in log x. If a parameter spans several orders of magnitude, those distributions emphasize different regions. A plot must identify the actual sample locations; a logarithmic display axis does not retroactively convert a linearly sampled calculation into a logarithmic sample set.

Some existing scan implementations allow descending or repeated endpoint values; others impose increasing bounds. The relevant mode’s input rules control admissibility. Reversing an axis changes row ordering, not the governing physics. Repeated values do not add independent information.

34.5 Successful, failed and unattempted rows

A failed row is information about a specified problem, not a zero performance value. Substituting zero thrust for a failure can create false minima, slopes and averages. Connecting a curve across an invalid interval can imply continuous operability where none has been established.

Cancellation creates a different category: planned rows that were never attempted. A study with one hundred planned points, thirty successful points, five failures and sixty-five unattempted points has not examined its full requested range. A maximum among the thirty successes is only a maximum within that evaluated subset.

The legacy turbojet executor retains each attempted row with either a result or an error, and separately records planned count and cancellation. Other mode-specific study outputs have their own semantics. Chapter 20 records an additional caveat: successful per-point warnings are not propagated by the rocket scan loops. The top-level baseline warning list therefore cannot certify every row against a condition such as overexpansion.

The appropriate interpretation keeps four questions separate: did the row calculate, did it satisfy the model’s admissibility conditions, did it satisfy the user’s additional constraints, and is it suitable for the intended comparison? Numerical success answers only part of this sequence.

34.6 A sampled maximum is not a continuous optimum

Consider the original illustrative objective

J(x)=100−(x−2.3)2,0≤x≤4. J(x)=100-(x-2.3)^2, \qquad 0\leq x\leq4.

At samples x=0,1,2,3,4, the values are 94.71, 98.31, 99.91, 99.51 and 97.11. The best sampled point is x=2. The actual stationary maximum is x=2.3, where J=100. Calling x=2 the optimum would confuse the grid with the underlying function.

Now impose a constraint x≤1.8. The continuous constrained optimum moves to x=1.8, with J=99.75. Among the original admissible samples, the best is x=1, with J=98.31. Refining the unconstrained peak would not answer this constrained problem. The first useful refinement is near the admissible boundary.

For a smooth function with an interior maximum, Taylor expansion gives an estimate of grid loss. If the nearest sample lies a distance d from the true maximum,

J(x*)−J(x*+d)≈−12J″(x*)d2. J(x^*)-J(x^*+d)\approx-\frac12J''(x^*)d^2.

This explains why finer sampling can help near a well-behaved peak. It is not an error bound when curvature is unknown, a branch changes, or failed rows interrupt the neighborhood.

A sampled rocket mixture-ratio maximum should therefore be reported with its sample spacing, evaluated range and success count. If every sample fails, there is no best result. The absence of a best-value field is preferable to a fabricated optimum.

34.7 Changing the objective changes the answer

Maximum thrust, maximum specific impulse and minimum fuel consumption are different objectives. A change that raises thrust can increase fuel use faster than it raises force. Chapter 30 gives an explicit example in which a larger ramjet allocation improves specific thrust but worsens TSFC.

Consider two hypothetical candidates: A produces 10 kN while consuming 0.30 kg/s of fuel; B produces 12 kN while consuming 0.40 kg/s. B has greater thrust, while A has lower TSFC: 0.000030 versus approximately 0.00003333 kg/(N s). If a mission requires at least 11 kN, A is infeasible despite its better consumption ratio. If the thrust requirement is 9 kN, selecting B solely because it is larger does not establish a benefit.

Ratios also conceal scale. A small engine and a large engine can have identical specific thrust while delivering very different total forces. Comparisons must preserve the denominator: core air, total captured air, primary stream, fuel alone or all injected mass. Chapters 3, 13, 29, 31 and 32 explain the mode-specific conventions.

A set of nondominated alternatives can be more informative than one scalar winner. Such a comparison is an interpretation of results, not an additional optimizer implemented by every App study mode. The constraints and priority among objectives remain the user’s engineering decision.

34.8 Sensitivity and meaningful changes

For an output y depending on input x, the derivative dy/dx describes a local change. A dimensionless sensitivity is

Sxy=xydydx, S_x^y=\frac{x}{y}\frac{dy}{dx},

when x and y are nonzero. It approximates the percentage output change caused by a one-percent input change near that state. It becomes unsuitable when y is close to zero, where an absolute sensitivity is clearer.

A central difference,

dydx≈y(x+h)−y(x−h)2h, \frac{dy}{dx}\approx\frac{y(x+h)-y(x-h)}{2h},

requires both neighboring problems to lie on the same admissible branch. Shrinking h indefinitely is not always helpful: subtraction can amplify numerical noise, and the printed precision may hide the change. Crossing a sonic boundary or map limit does not produce an ordinary smooth derivative.

Sensitivity is also conditional on the fixed quantities. For an ideal fixed-throat rocket at fixed exhaust state, changing ambient pressure gives dF/dp_a=−A_e. If exit area is resized at each point, that derivative no longer describes the study. The short phrase “all else equal” should be replaced by the actual held variables whenever ambiguity matters.

34.9 Preserve the comparison, not only the plot

A reusable study record contains the original model and inputs, reference state, units, axes and sample values, completion information, failed-row explanations and selected objective. The result table should remain associated with that definition. A figure alone rarely contains enough information to reconstruct the calculation.

The legacy turbojet executor copies the baseline input before applying each point’s axes and retains the request with its rows. This prevents an earlier sample from becoming the next sample’s unintended baseline. It is an important distinction from a manual workflow that repeatedly edits whatever state the previous solve left on screen.

Interpretation should retain the same discipline. Report “highest specific impulse among the successful samples at fixed throat area and this chamber closure,” rather than “best engine.” Report a partial range when execution was cancelled. Report an excluded region when the model rejected it, without claiming that all physical engines are impossible there.

The strongest comparison is the one whose conclusion remains true after its assumptions are stated. Additional rows are useful when they resolve a peak, boundary or ambiguity that matters to the intended decision. They add little when they merely reproduce a trend already implied by the equations. A purposeful study connects every calculated point to a question that the current model can answer.

Symbols are defined again where an equation first uses them. This index collects recurring meanings; it does not override a chapter’s local definition. In particular, distinguish a mass-specific quantity from a molar quantity before combining thermochemical expressions.

Molar heat capacities and enthalpies carry units per kmol rather than per kilogram. Multiplication or division by W_i performs the conversion. A numerical universal gas constant expressed per mol must not be combined unchanged with kmol-based concentrations and enthalpies.

Formation-inclusive enthalpy carries a chemical reference. It is not generally interchangeable with c_pT measured from an arbitrary zero. Adding a heating value on top of formation-inclusive reaction energy can count the same chemical contribution twice. Chapters 5–8 and 29 explain the relevant conventions.

f_D Darcy friction factor Dimensionless; not a Fanning factor

A.4 Subscripts and symbols that need particular care

The subscript 0 identifies a reference freestream in most cycle equations. The subscript e or N commonly identifies an exit, while t identifies a total state. In A_t, however, t denotes a throat. Read the complete symbol and its context rather than assigning one universal meaning to a letter.

A superscript star often identifies a sonic reference in a calorically perfect flow. For equilibrium expansion, the critical mass-flux condition must be defined along the specified thermochemical path; a reported frozen Mach number need not equal one there. Chapter 17 explains that distinction.

The symbols beta and theta are angles in oblique-shock geometry, usually expressed in degrees at an interface but used consistently in mathematical functions. A beta used as an entrainment ratio is dimensionless without an angular interpretation. Likewise, a temperature ratio tau and a residence time tau are distinguished by definition and units.

Pressure ratios differ among controls. An ambient-to-exit static-pressure ratio is the inverse of an exit-to-ambient ratio. An inlet total-pressure recovery is downstream total pressure divided by its upstream reference. A fan or compressor pressure ratio is greater than one for compression; a turbine exit-to-inlet pressure ratio is less than one for expansion. The word “ratio” alone does not specify the direction.

A.5 Useful unit identities

One newton is one kg m/s². One watt is one joule per second. Thus mass flow times specific enthalpy is power, and mass flow times velocity is force. Pressure times area is also force, which allows pressure and momentum terms to be added in a control-volume balance.

Specific thrust and speed have the same dimensions, but specific thrust is not necessarily exhaust velocity. Pressure thrust, inlet momentum and different mass-flow denominators can all contribute. Similarly, an impulse measured in seconds is a force divided by a weight-flow rate, not a physical burn duration.

To convert TSFC from kg/(N s) to kg/(N h), multiply by 3,600. To express the latter per kilonewton-hour, multiply by a further 1,000. Keep the full unit visible whenever comparing values from different tables.

Temperature differences in kelvin and degrees Celsius have equal numerical size, but absolute temperatures do not. Pressure-ratio and gas-state equations require absolute pressure and absolute temperature. Unit conversion belongs before applying those equations, not after an invalid ratio has been formed.

Appendix B. Performance normalization

A performance ratio is defined by its numerator, denominator and control boundary. This appendix collects the conventions developed in the chapters so that outputs from different models can be compared without silently changing their basis.

B.1 Recover dimensional quantities first

For a reported specific thrust s referred to mass flow mdot_ref,

F=sṁref. F=s\dot m_{ref}.

To change the reference flow from one stream to another, recover F and divide by the new denominator. Do not rescale a fuel ratio in the same way unless its own denominator has been identified.

For example, a turbofan with bypass ratio beta=4 has total air flow five times its core air flow. A force of 25 kN with core flow 10 kg/s corresponds to 2,500 N/(kg/s) per core flow but 500 N/(kg/s) per total air flow. These are descriptions of one force. If fuel flow is 0.5 kg/s, fuel-to-core-air ratio is 0.05, while fuel-to-total-air ratio is 0.01. TSFC is 0.5/25,000=0.000020 kg/(N s), regardless of which air basis is used consistently in the intermediate calculation.

B.2 Reading common outputs

Output or family Numerator Denominator or reference Interpretation
Turbojet net specific thrust Branch net force Entering air flow Includes the branch’s incoming momentum debit
Turbofan overall specific thrust Combined net force Total core plus bypass air Do not confuse with separately reported core-based quantities
Turbofan thrust per core flow Combined net force Core air flow Equals total-air specific thrust multiplied by 1+beta
Explicit-split TBCC specific thrust Sum of independent branch net forces Total assigned air flow Branch net forces already include their own inlet debits
Full flowpath captured-air specific thrust Completed-engine net force Captured-air flow Partial paths do not establish the intended exit performance
Rocket specific impulse Rocket force Propellant mass flow times g_0 Mass denominator includes the propellant flow represented by the mode
Calibrated-engine injected-mass impulse Net force All injected mass flow times g_0 Air or oxidizer injection is not relabeled as fuel
Ejector augmentation Combined net force Primary-alone ambient-expanded force Dimensionless; not a fuel efficiency
ATR augmentation Combined net force Primary-alone ambient-expanded force Includes primary, air and simplified additional-fuel accounting
ATR air-based specific thrust Combined net force Captured secondary air flow Different from its primary-based augmentation
TSFC Fuel mass flow Net force The fuel definition follows the selected cycle

The table is a reading aid, not a statement that every listed quantity exists in every result. A component, thermodynamic property calculation, shock or geometry construction may have no meaningful engine thrust at all.

B.3 Gross, net and pressure force

At an exhaust plane, the common gross expression is

Fg=ṁeVe+(pe−pa)Ae. F_g=\dot m_eV_e+(p_e-p_a)A_e.

A full airbreathing control volume subtracts the momentum of its captured air. A rocket does not acquire the same ambient-air debit merely because it operates in the atmosphere. A standalone duct momentum function pA+ṁVpA+\dot mV uses absolute pressure and describes an internal flux. It is not automatically either gross or net engine thrust.

Pressure thrust must be treated once. When a branch solver has already included it, a combined calculation should not add it again. When the nozzle is explicitly fully expanded, its exit pressure term vanishes under that model. This does not establish that a fixed physical nozzle would remain fully expanded at another ambient condition.

B.4 Fuel and injected mass

Fuel-to-air ratios conventionally divide fuel by a specified air flow. A mixed-flow afterburner may introduce a second fuel ratio with a different intermediate basis. The correct total fuel flow is obtained by following the mass bookkeeping in its chapter, not by adding differently normalized ratios.

In finite-rate mixed-flow engines, total injected mass can include several species and streams. The metric specific_impulse_injected uses all of it. To construct a fuel-only metric externally, one would need a defensible identification of fuel mass; its denominator is not supplied merely by seeing that injection exists.

The ideal ATR heating convention is reduced, as explained in Chapter32. Its additional fuel ratio does not account for the propellant expenditure needed to create the supplied primary stream. Comparing that ratio with a complete propulsion system’s onboard propellant consumption would mix boundaries.

B.5 Useful identities and their conditions

If thrust and mass flow use one consistent propellant basis,

Isp=Fṁpg0,ceff=Fṁp=g0Isp. I_{sp}=\frac{F}{\dot m_pg_0},\qquad c_{eff}=\frac{F}{\dot m_p}=g_0I_{sp}.

For a rocket model defining c*=pcAt/ṁpc^*=p_cA_t/\dot m_p and CF=F/(pcAt)C_F=F/(p_cA_t),

Isp=CFc*g0. I_{sp}=\frac{C_Fc^*}{g_0}.

Correction factors can change the definitions of the effective mass flow or force used in these identities. Chapter16 explains the current performance-factor convention. One should not reconstruct corrected force from an ideal exit velocity and corrected mass without checking how those factors were applied.

TSFC and fuel-only impulse are reciprocally related only if they refer to the same positive force and fuel flow. A rocket propellant impulse, a fuel-only airbreathing impulse and an all-injected-mass impulse do not become interchangeable because each is measured in seconds.

B.6 Comparing two reports

Before comparing magnitudes, recover the dimensional force and all relevant mass flows. Identify whether ambient pressure force and incoming momentum are already included. Then choose a common denominator and retain the model’s physical constraints.

A higher ratio can arise from a smaller denominator rather than a larger useful output. In the ATR limit of vanishing air flow, air-based specific thrust can become large even while the usefulness of that normalization deteriorates. A large primary-normalized augmentation may include extra downstream heating. The denominator is part of the engineering conclusion.

Appendix C. Domain and closure guide

This appendix summarizes the boundaries explained in the main text. It distinguishes an admissible mathematical state, a completed numerical calculation and a physically appropriate application. It is not an additional certification or a universal validity range for real engines.

C.1 State and property choices

Model choice What is held or solved Boundary that matters Chapters
Constant-property gas Fixed heat capacity and gamma Thermal range and chemistry are approximations 2,9,16,24
Frozen mixture Composition fixed while properties vary with temperature “Frozen” does not require constant gamma 5,17,26
Equilibrium at T,p Composition satisfying chemical equilibrium at prescribed temperature and pressure No chemical residence time predicted 6
Equilibrium with enthalpy closure Temperature and composition adjusted to meet energy at pressure Formation enthalpy references must agree 6,17
Specified-area freezing Equilibrium path changes to frozen composition at the supplied area Freeze location is prescribed, not kinetically predicted 17
Finite-rate reactor Species evolve under imposed reactor constraints The included rigid reactor is externally isothermal 7–8
Finite-rate spatial flow Species and fluxes evolve along a supplied geometry Uniform cross-sectional state; no diffusion or shock train 29

A property polynomial is valid only over its supported temperature interval. A mixture inversion must remain within the common usable range of the required species. Failure outside that range is not an invitation to extrapolate without another property model.

C.2 Cycle and geometry closures

Calculation Closure What must not be inferred Chapters
Turbojet/turbofan design point Specified cycle inputs and component balances Fixed hardware operability over an unrestricted envelope 9–15
Reference-based off design Selected reference, area/flow or normalized constraints Complete map matching for all components 12,15
Rocket explicit-gas performance Supplied gas properties, pressure and scale Feed-system or chamber chemistry prediction 16
Chemical rocket expansion Declared chamber and expansion chemistry Liquid vaporization, condensed phases or injector dynamics 17
Chamber and convergent sizing Supplied characteristic length and geometric assumptions Cooling, structure or combustion stability 18
Conical/bell contour Reference geometry with declared endpoints and slopes Optimized characteristics, wall pressure or separation loads 19
Solid equilibrium pressure Supplied burn law plus choked discharge Qualified propellant behavior or ignition 21
Solid transient Established burning and supported grain regression Complete ignition and tail-off histories 22

A geometry result can be dimensionally consistent and still be unsuitable for a physical design. The current contour and chamber modules intentionally supply reference shapes and volumes, not a coupled thermal, structural or reacting-flow design.

C.3 Flow branches and termination

Normal shocks require an upstream supersonic state. Oblique shocks require an attached solution on the chosen weak or strong branch. A weak branch is not a guarantee that the downstream flow remains supersonic. Beyond the attached turning limit, the current attached-shock equations do not become a detached-shock solver.

Fanno and Rayleigh relations approach sonic limits under their respective assumptions. A general source-term duct combines area, friction, heat and injection but still retains a chosen branch. An integration that stops near its sonic boundary does not calculate a transition through it. The final row may be a last valid state rather than a precisely located event.

Frozen flux reconstruction can admit two thermodynamic states for the same supplied flux quantities. The branch selection is an input to the problem. Calibrated inlets have their own high/low root conventions; a high root does not universally mean supersonic. A full calibrated scramjet additionally requires a supersonic inlet exit and rejects an incompatible selection.

Nozzle closure differs by mode. A specified exit pressure determines an expansion state and can imply an exit area. A supplied geometry determines the area and generally leaves an exit pressure that differs from ambient. The full scramjet geometry is not automatically adjusted for ambient back pressure. These modes should not be compared as though they solve the same external condition.

C.4 Combined-cycle boundaries

The explicit TBCC mode adds two independent design-point branch results at a prescribed allocation. A zero-flow branch is skipped. Active branches must solve; the allocation is not adjusted to repair one of them. Common freestream inputs do not establish pressure matching in a shared inlet.

The ideal ejector requires supersonic primary entry, subsonic secondary entry, equal inlet static pressure and a sonic mixed exit. Its final expansion is fully expanded and supersonic. Alternative secondary-choked or exit-unchoked operation is outside that branch.

The ideal ATR starts from a supplied primary total state. It requires positive fan work and sufficient primary expansion to supply it. Its nozzle can be subsonic or supersonic, but exactly zero freestream Mach is excluded by the current formulation. Its heating estimate is explicitly simplified. None of these combined-cycle modes derives a gas generator, pump system, cooling network, installation drag or automatic transition control.

C.5 Interpreting warning and completion states

A warning can identify an approximation or a risky interpretation without invalidating the algebra. A rejection means the current solve did not return an admissible result. A partial history contains accepted states before termination; it is not a completed engine. A completed result satisfies the selected solver’s completion criteria but retains all physical assumptions.

Study outputs require additional care. Failed samples are not zeros, cancelled samples are not evaluated, and successful samples may still require the user’s constraints. Some rocket scan outputs do not propagate each successful row’s warnings. A baseline warning list therefore does not describe every sampled state.

Residual magnitudes must be read with units and scales. A small conservation residual establishes consistency with the imposed balance, not the accuracy of empirical inputs. More iterations cannot supply missing physics. The useful response to a failure is to identify which assumption, branch or numerical condition failed before changing the study.

C.6 Energy and geometry interpretation checks

Chapters 8, 10 and 12 develop three useful interpretation checks: use internal energy for the rigid isothermal reactor heat load, use the augmented total temperature throughout an afterburning nozzle, and retain the pressure-ratio orientation in fixed-throat exit-area reconstruction. The current App follows these closures. Numerical convergence alone does not establish that a selected physical constraint describes a real engine.

This reference guide should be used together with the relevant chapter. It is deliberately explicit about where the current implementation ends, so that a broad family title does not imply a broader solved problem.

Property and chemistry modes support several engine families even when grouped under one family in the interface. Likewise, a component or flow-segment calculation is not a complete engine. Read the chapter’s control boundary and closure before transferring its result into another mode.

For a combined task, follow dependencies: properties before variable-property reconstruction, reconstruction before spatial flow, and completed flow before full-engine force. The separate user guide describes interface navigation; this directory identifies the explanatory content.
